title: Five Companies to Evaluate for Connected AI Workflows: An Engineering Comparison
description:
Connecting an AI agent to several applications creates an integration problem before it creates an automation opportunity.

Consider a hypothetical workflow: a meeting produces a customer commitment, an agent identifies the relevant account, and a proposed task enters a project management system. The difficult questions concern execution. Which source supports the commitment? Whose permissions authorize the update? What happens if the destination system accepts the request but the agent times out?

GeekyAnts, Microsoft, IBM, AWS, and Salesforce offer different approaches to parts of this problem. The following comparison examines their documented capabilities and suggests questions for a technical evaluation. It is a shortlist, rather than a performance ranking based on independent benchmarks.

What Does the AntFabric Article Contribute?

GeekyAnts’ explanation of AntFabric’s connected AI workflows describes an architecture connecting organizational knowledge, business applications, and agents.

Its main components include an agent runtime, a gateway for model access and routing, shared memory linked to original sources, access controls, audit trails, and approval checkpoints. The article recommends beginning with one operational workflow before expanding. It also explicitly describes its workflow examples as possibilities, rather than verified outcomes from a named enterprise deployment.

That distinction matters when assessing an architecture announcement. A proposed capability should become a testable requirement before it influences a purchasing decision.

Which Companies Belong on the Shortlist?

GeekyAnts: Custom Engineering Around AntFabric

GeekyAnts describes both engineering support for AntFabric implementations and a licensing option for teams with internal development capabilities.

A technical evaluation should request connector documentation, deployment boundaries, and a demonstration using the organization’s own workflow. Particular attention should go to how permissions propagate across systems and how source changes affect stored context.

The relevant question is how much implementation work remains after adopting the foundation.

Microsoft: Connector-Based Workflows Through Copilot Studio

Copilot Studio supports Power Platform connectors as agent tools. These connectors wrap APIs and enable communication with Microsoft services and external applications; custom connectors can extend that integration surface.

For teams already evaluating Power Platform, this offers a concrete place to investigate available integrations.

The pilot should distinguish connector availability from workflow completeness. Authentication, supported operations, connection ownership, and error handling all need examination against the actual business process.

IBM: Coordinating Agents, Tools, and Models

IBM describes watsonx Orchestrate as a centralized orchestration layer for agents, tools, workflows, and foundation models. Its documentation discusses multiple execution approaches, including deterministic orchestration when predictability matters.

An evaluation should examine whether each step needs model reasoning. Updating a validated record may be better expressed as a defined operation, while interpreting an ambiguous request may require an agent.

The useful demonstration is one that makes those boundaries visible.

AWS: Modular Infrastructure Through AgentCore

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides modular capabilities including runtime, memory, and a gateway that can expose existing services as MCP-compatible tools. Its observability documentation covers execution traces, metrics, and integrations with CloudWatch.

This merits investigation when an engineering team wants to assemble and operate its agent infrastructure.

The evaluation should identify which components are managed and which responsibilities remain with application developers, including instrumentation, workflow behavior, and operational support.

Salesforce: Agent Actions Within Business Processes

Agentforce actions can invoke capabilities such as Salesforce Flow, prompt templates, and Apex classes. Salesforce also documents invoking agents from flows or Apex for background and event-driven tasks.

This makes Salesforce relevant when the proposed workflow centers on existing Salesforce processes.

A pilot should test the boundary between Salesforce and external systems. Developers should establish where validation happens, which identity executes each action, and how failures return to the originating process.

What Should Every Pilot Demonstrate?

A shared test scenario makes these different approaches easier to assess. The hypothetical customer-commitment workflow could include four acceptance checks:

  • Traceable evidence: Every proposed update references the source that justified it.
  • Permission changes: Removing a user’s access prevents subsequent unauthorized retrieval or action.
  • Repeat execution: Retrying the same event does not create duplicate tasks.
  • Partial failure: An accepted external update followed by a timeout produces a recoverable state.

These are proposed evaluation criteria, not claims that every platform implements them automatically.

Teams should also record completion rate, manual corrections, recovery time, and cost per completed workflow. A successful model response alone does not establish that the business process finished correctly.

Compare the Work That Remains

The five companies occupy different positions across engineering services, application platforms, orchestration, and infrastructure. Their offerings may also be combined.

A useful shortlist therefore starts with one workflow and a clear ownership model. The strongest candidate is the one whose demonstrated behavior fits the process, whose remaining engineering work is understood, and whose failures the operating team can diagnose.

Disclosure: This article was prepared with AI assistance using the linked source article and public vendor documentation. It does not report hands-on benchmark results.

title: How Do You Find the Lua Function That Is Actually Costing You Frame Time?
description:
A Lua entry in the top-20 cost list is the start of the investigation, not the answer. Three stack views plus a reversed call tree point you at the leaf function worth fixing.

Lua rarely shows up in a Unity performance report as one big number. It shows up as a handful of function names inside the logic-code cost ranking, and the expensive part is usually not the function listed there — it is a leaf several levels down its call stack.

The practical workflow is short: open the GOT Online Lua report's Code Efficiency → CPU Time page, choose the stack view that matches the question you are asking (whole-session, single-scene, or single-frame), then reverse the stack so the deepest and most expensive children surface first. This article walks through that sequence, explains the Lua function naming format the report uses, and covers the one test setting that silently breaks the whole analysis.

Summary

  • Lua cost appears in reports as individual functions in the top-20 logic cost list, not as a single aggregate figure.
  • The report offers three stack views: overall cost, specified scene, and any single frame. Each answers a different question; using the wrong one sends you to the wrong function.
  • Lua functions are identified as X@Y:Z — function name, defining file, defining line. When the name cannot be resolved, X becomes unknown.
  • When Lua runs as bytecode, the line number Z is always 0. Test with Lua source if you want line-level attribution.
  • Reverse stack analysis reorders the cost stack so deep sub-functions that actually consume the time appear on top, instead of forcing you to expand dozens of levels by hand.

What Is the Core Problem?

When Lua usage grows in a commercial project, CPU cost spreads across many small functions rather than concentrating in one obviously slow place. In a report, that looks like several Lua functions mixed into the top-20 logic cost list — enough to know Lua is involved, not enough to know where to change code.

The cost hides for two reasons:

  1. The entry function is not the expensive function. A Lua call often passes through wrappers, dispatch tables, and utility layers before reaching the function that does the work. The top-level name accumulates cost; the leaf generates it.
  2. Aggregate and peak are different measurements. A function can dominate total session cost while never appearing in the frame where the game stuttered, and vice versa. Locating one does not locate the other.

Why Does the Cost Hide in the Call Stack?

A stack trace orders calls from the outermost caller to the innermost callee. Read top-down, the first entries are the ones you recognize — event handlers, update loops, framework entry points — and they carry the largest accumulated totals simply because everything below them rolls up into their number.

The actual work sits at the bottom. To see it in the default view, you expand frame after frame, often dozens of levels deep, and the numbers you are comparing are already diluted by sibling branches. That is the structural reason a "Lua is slow" finding stalls: the report is correct, but the ordering hides the answer.

Reversing the stack fixes the ordering. Instead of reading caller → callee, you read callee → caller, so the deepest sub-function with the highest self-cost lands at the top of the view. The bottleneck becomes visible without manual expansion.

How Is a Lua Function Identified in the Report?

Every Lua entry carries a name in a fixed format that maps it back to source:

Part Meaning Notes
X Function name Falls back to unknown when it cannot be resolved
Y File where the function is defined The script location, not the call site
Z Line where the function is defined Always 0 under bytecode execution

X@Y:Z is enough to search your codebase directly: file plus line lands you on the definition, and the function name confirms it. This is why the format matters more than the visual stack — it converts a profiler row into a code location.

The bytecode caveat is the one that trips teams up. If the Lua scripts are shipped as bytecode, Z is 0 for everything, and you lose line-level attribution entirely. The recommendation is to run the test with Lua source wherever possible, so the stack data stays resolvable.

How Can You Tell Whether the Function Is Actually a Problem?

Match the stack view to the question. Each view isolates a different kind of cost, and the answers do not transfer between them.

View Question it answers Use it when
Overall CPU cost stack Which Lua functions accumulate the most cost across the whole session Building the hotspot shortlist at the start
Specified-scene stack Which Lua functions dominate in one particular scene Cost differs by scene, and you want to target one
Single-frame cost stack Which Lua functions consumed time in the exact frame where cost peaked Explaining a specific spike or stutter

Three signals confirm that a function is a genuine target rather than noise:

  • It appears high in the reversed overall stack, meaning its own cost is large rather than inherited from children.
  • It reappears in the per-scene view for the scene that carries the memory or frame-time pressure.
  • It positions itself in the peak frame's stack, so the aggregate number and the visible symptom agree.

If a function only satisfies the first signal, you have found volume, not a bottleneck. If it only satisfies the third, you have found a one-off spike, not a pattern.

What Should You Check First?

  1. Open the Code Efficiency → CPU Time page and confirm Lua entries exist. If Lua does not appear in the top-20 logic cost list, this workflow has nothing to target yet.
  2. Start with the overall stack to build a shortlist. Do not optimize from this list; use it to pick candidates.
  3. Reverse the stack before judging any candidate. The entry with the biggest number in the default order is frequently the caller, not the cause.
  4. Record the X@Y:Z identifier for each candidate. File and line are what make the finding actionable in code review.
  5. Confirm the test ran on source, not bytecode. If every Z is 0, fix the test setup before drawing conclusions — the data is coarse by construction.
  6. Re-check the candidate in the scene view and the peak-frame view. A function that survives all three is a real target.

What Should You Optimize?

Optimize the leaf, then the path that reaches it.

  • The leaf function itself is where the self-cost sits. The reversed stack identifies it; the X@Y:Z identifier locates it.
  • The call frequency of that path decides whether the total cost is a problem. The per-frame stack shows what one call costs; the aggregate stack shows how often it happens. A cheap function on a hot path costs more than an expensive function called twice.
  • The scene where it concentrates tells you whether the fix is local (a scene-specific feature) or systemic (a shared utility used everywhere).

Each change should be re-measured with the same view that produced the finding. A fix that lowers aggregate cost but leaves the peak-frame stack unchanged has moved volume without removing the spike.

What Should You Avoid?

  • Do not optimize the top entry of the default stack. It inherits cost from everything beneath it; changing it usually means changing design, not code.
  • Do not profile bytecode builds and expect line numbers. Z = 0 is a test configuration result, not a report bug.
  • Do not expand the stack by hand to find the bottom. Toggle the reversed view instead; dozens of manual expansions is how bottlenecks get missed.
  • Do not treat an aggregate hotspot as a frame-time problem without checking the peak frame. Total cost and peak cost point at different code.

Practical Recommendations

Problem What to inspect How to judge What to change What to re-measure
Lua appears in the cost list but you cannot name the culprit Reversed overall stack Highest self-cost at the deepest level That leaf function Overall stack
Cost is concentrated in one scene Specified-scene stack Same function tops the scene view Scene-scoped logic Scene view plus overall
Cost peaks only in one frame Single-frame stack Function present in the peak frame The call path taken in that frame Peak-frame view
Line numbers are all 0 Test script delivery Z equals 0 across entries Run the test on Lua source Naming resolved to file and line
A candidate looks large but changes nothing when tuned Peak-frame view Function absent from the spike frame Investigate the actual spike frame Stutter metric, not total cost

Key Takeaways

  • Lua cost in a report is a list of functions, and the listed function is often the caller rather than the cause.
  • Reverse stack analysis surfaces the deep sub-function that actually holds the cost.
  • X@Y:Z — name, file, line — is the bridge from a profiler row to a code location.
  • Bytecode execution forces Z to 0. Test with source when line-level attribution matters.
  • Overall, per-scene, and per-frame stacks answer different questions; a real bottleneck shows up in the ones that match your symptom.

FAQ

What does the X@Y:Z format in a Lua stack entry mean?
X is the function name, Y is the file where the function is defined, and Z is the line number of its definition. If the name cannot be resolved, X becomes unknown.

Why is the line number always 0 in my Lua data?
Because the scripts are running as bytecode. Under bytecode execution the line value is always 0, so run the test with Lua source to get usable line-level attribution.

Should I use the overall stack or the single-frame stack?
Use the overall stack to find which functions accumulate cost across the session, and the single-frame stack to explain a specific spike or stutter. A function can be large in total while never appearing in the frame you are investigating.

Why does reversing the stack make the bottleneck easier to find?
The default order lists callers above callees, so entry points carry inflated totals. Reversed, the deepest callee with the highest self-cost appears first, which removes the need to expand dozens of levels manually.

Is a function that tops the overall cost list necessarily the one to optimize?
Not necessarily. It may simply be a caller that aggregates everything beneath it. Confirm that the self-cost is high and that it also appears in the scene or peak-frame view before treating it as a target.

title: A card issuer publishes four country lists, and they don't match. So I put them in a CSV.
description:
If you ask "does this crypto card work in my country?", the answer depends on which page you read.

RedotPay's help center has four separate restriction lists: account verification, card issuance, card delivery and app access. We read all four on 22 October 2026 and merged them into one table, with one column per list. The result is a small CC BY 4.0 dataset on GitHub, with a Zenodo DOI.

What the merged table shows

51 countries and regions appear on at least one list. The lists have different lengths:

List Places named
Account verification 41
Card issuance 47
Card delivery 47
App access 38

35 places are on all four. The other 16 are the interesting ones, because reading a single list gives you the wrong picture:

  • Singapore is only on the card issuance list.
  • Tanzania is only on the app access list.
  • Egypt, Tunisia and Palestine are only on the delivery list.
  • India is on the issuance and delivery lists, but not on the other two.

The United Kingdom isn't named on any of them, and neither is Nigeria. That doesn't prove a card works there, and the README says so: a country missing from all four lists isn't confirmed as supported. Only the app can confirm that.

Reproducing the counts

The CSV is plain enough that a few lines of standard-library Python get you the same numbers:

import csv
from collections import Counter

with open("data/redotpay-country-lists-20261022.csv") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

lists = [c for c in rows[0] if c.startswith("listed_")]
for c in lists:
    print(c, sum(r[c].lower() == "true" for r in rows))

on_how_many = Counter(sum(r[c].lower() == "true" for c in lists) for r in rows)
print(on_how_many)  # 4 lists: 35, 3: 6, 2: 5, 1: 5

The source table you can't scrape

The same repo has a second file: issuance, FX and ATM fees for 11 crypto debit cards. The fiddly part was RedotPay's fee table, which is an image on its help page, so a text extraction comes back empty. It had to be read from the image itself. Two of its articles also disagree: the fee table lists a 1,000,000 USD daily spending limit, and an older article says there is none. When sources conflict like that, we note it instead of quietly picking one.

Each fee record has a lastVerified date and an evidenceLevel, so you can see where a value came from and how old it is. These are snapshots and they go stale. The most recent check in the current file is 27 October 2026, and some records are older.

If you use it

Keep the snapshot date with any number you reuse, and check the issuer's app before relying on it. Corrections are welcome as GitHub issues, with a link to the source.

If you want to look something up without opening a CSV, there's a country checker built on the same data.

Disclosure: I run CryptoCard Insider, a crypto card comparison site, and we have a partner arrangement with RedotPay, so I may earn a commission if someone signs up through our links. This post was written by an AI agent working for me, and I approved it before publishing. The counts were recomputed from the CSV.

title: webdev, api, fintech, programming
description:
Weryfikacja europejskich numerów identyfikacji podatkowej (VAT-UE) w systemie VIES (VAT Information Exchange System) to kluczowy element każdego systemu e-commerce, platformy SaaS oraz oprogramowania finansowo-księgowego obsługującego transakcje transgraniczne (B2B) w Unii Europejskiej.

Zastosowanie preferencyjnej stawki 0% VAT przy Wewnątrzwspólnotowej Dostawie Towarów (WDT) lub procedury odwrotnego obciążenia (reverse charge) przy świadczeniu usług wymaga bezwzględnego potwierdzenia, że kontrahent posiada aktywny numer w rejestrze VIES.

Przed wysłaniem zapytania do unijnego API kluczowa jest lokalna walidacja składniowa. Poniżej przedstawiamy zestawienie struktur i algorytmów numerów VAT w poszczególnych państwach członkowskich UE.

Tabela formatów numerów VAT w Unii Europejskiej

Każde z 27 państw członkowskich stosuje własny standard tworzenia numeru identyfikacji podatkowej. Poniższa tabela przedstawia strukturę wymaganą przez unijną bazę VIES:

Państwo Kod kraju (Prefiks) Długość i format znaków Przykład struktury
Austria AT U + 8 cyfr ATU12345678
Belgia BE 10 cyfr (zaczyna się od 0 lub 1) BE0123456789
Czechy CZ 8, 9 lub 10 cyfr CZ12345678
Dania DK 8 cyfr DK12345678
Estonia EE 9 cyfr EE123456789
Finlandia FI 8 cyfr FI12345678
Francja FR 2 znaki (cyfry/litery) + 9 cyfr FRXX123456789
Grecja EL 9 cyfr (uwaga: prefiks EL) EL123456789
Hiszpania ES 9 znaków (litera na początku/końcu) ESX1234567X
Holandia NL 9 cyfr + B + 2 cyfry NL123456789B01
Irlandia IE 7 cyfr + 1-2 litery IE1234567T
Litwa LT 9 lub 12 cyfr LT123456789
Łotwa LV 11 cyfr LV12345678901
Niemcy DE Dokładnie 9 cyfr DE123456789
Polska PL Dokładnie 10 cyfr PL1234567890
Szwecja SE 12 cyfr (kończy się 01) SE123456789001
Włochy IT Dokładnie 11 cyfr IT12345678901

Kompletne zestawienie wszystkich 27 państw członkowskich oraz aktualną specyfikację techniczną udostępnia serwis viesvat, który pozwala zweryfikować dokładne reguły walidacji algorytmicznej dla poszczególnych jurysdykcji podatkowych.

Kluczowe pułapki implementacyjne

Programiści integrujący formularze zamówień i walidatory NIP najczęściej napotykają na następujące specyficzne wyjątki:

  1. Prefiks Grecji (EL zamiast GR):
    Zgodnie z unijną specyfikacją techniczną Grecja posługuje się kodem EL, podczas gdy międzynarodowy kod ISO państwa to GR. Formularz musi automatycznie mapować ten wyjątek.

  2. Litera U w numerze austriackim (ATU):
    Po prefiksie kraju w Austrii zawsze występuje wielka litera U, po której następuje 8 cyfr. Wpisanie samych cyfr jest najczęstszym błędem użytkowników.

  3. Francuski klucz kontrolny modulo 97:
    Dwa pierwsze znaki po prefiksie FR są wyliczane na podstawie algorytmu: [12 + 3 * (SIREN modulo 97)] modulo 97. Jeśli wynik jest mniejszy niż 10, prefiks uzupełnia się cyfrą zero lub literami.

  4. Wielka Brytania i Irlandia Północna:
    Po Brexicie numery z Wielkiej Brytanii (GB) nie podlegają walidacji w VIES. Wyjątkiem jest Irlandia Północna dla obrotu towarowego, która posługuje się prefiksem XI.

Walidacja wstępna (RegEx) w JavaScript

Aby zmniejszyć obciążenie sieciowe i ograniczyć liczbę zbędnych zapytań do zewnętrznych serwerów, dobrą praktyką jest wstępna walidacja wyrażeniem regularnym przed wysłaniem żądania API:


javascript
// Przykładowy słownik podstawowych formatów RegEx dla wybranych krajów UE
const vatPatterns = {
  PL: /^PL[0-9]{10}$/,
  DE: /^DE[0-9]{9}$/,
  AT: /^ATU[0-9]{8}$/,
  FR: /^FR[A-Z0-9]{2}[0-9]{9}$/,
  ES: /^ES[A-Z0-9][0-9]{7}[A-Z0-9]$/,
  IT: /^IT[0-9]{11}$/,
  NL: /^NL[0-9]{9}B[0-9]{2}$/
};

function validateVatFormat(countryCode, vatNumber) {
  const sanitized = vatNumber.replace(/[\s.-]/g, '').toUpperCase();
  const pattern = vatPatterns[countryCode];

  if (!pattern) {
    return false; // Nieobsługiwany kod kraju
  }

  return pattern.test(sanitized);
}

title: Gamma 5 Free Plan Review: I Turned One of My Articles Into a 10-Slide Deck
description:
Key takeaways

  • From pasted article to a finished 10-slide deck took about two and a half minutes in English, including one error that a page refresh fixed, and about three minutes in Chinese.
  • The results table came through with every number right in both languages. Elsewhere the agent added claims my article never made, such as "22x faster", and then told me it had added nothing.
  • Asking the agent to fix one slide worked: it changed only that slide, in under a minute, and showed the original and the edit side by side.
  • On the free plan a deck cost me about 130 to 140 of the 400 signup credits, Gamma stops at 10 slides per prompt, and every exported slide carries a "Made with Gamma" badge.

Tested on: Gamma 5 on the free plan, Standard effort, November 3, 2026, in Chrome on Windows 11. The PPTX export was opened in Microsoft PowerPoint.

I wanted to know whether Gamma could turn something I had already written into slides I would actually present, without me rewriting it first. So I gave it a real document: my ElevenLabs vs Qwen3-TTS test, with its methods, its seven-version results table and its caveats. Then I read every slide against the original.

I used a new account on the free plan. When I logged in, Gamma opened with an announcement for Gamma 5, which it calls its biggest update so far: an agent you chat with now plans, writes and designs the whole thing.

What I gave it

The home screen asks "What should we create together?" and offers Presentation, Document, Carousel, Image, Beautify and Import. A balance in the top corner showed 400 credits. Next to the prompt box is an effort setting with three levels: Lite, Standard and Max, where Max needs the Pro plan and more effort uses more credits. I left it on Standard.

I picked Presentation and pasted the article, about 4 KB of text with my instructions at the top: ten slides, keep every number and conclusion, add no facts that are not in the article, and give the results table its own slide. Gamma turned the long paste into an attachment called "Pasted text", so I added one line in the box itself: "Make a 10-slide presentation from the attached article. Keep all numbers as written."

The first try failed, the refresh worked

Sending it gave me a cat with a magnifying glass and "Couldn't open chat. Refresh the page to try again."

After a refresh the job was already running. The agent named the deck "ElevenLabs vs local TTS deck", showed "Creating Plan" and then "Creating your gamma".

Before it finished, it posted a note saying the first draft was done and it was going over it again, because a few lines were smaller than the text around them, one title didn't match the others and one panel sat off the margin. Then it reported that the deck was ready, that it had kept every number and conclusion as written, and that the results table was on slide 6. From pressing send to that message took about two and a half minutes, refresh included.

Checking the slides against the article

The style it chose is called Freeform: heavy black headlines, a decorative selection box with corner handles around the title, a cursor icon, a barcode, and glossy AI images of a blue glass microphone and yellow glass spheres. Every slide also repeats the full article title in tiny spaced capitals at the top, which looks odd at that length.

The results table is the slide I expected to break, and it was perfect. Every cell matched my table, and it highlighted the "Most natural" ranking and the preset voice's misread English name.

Slide 8 was wrong in two ways. It put the 176 to 184 seconds per take under the cloned voice, when that figure belongs to the preset voice; the clone's figure is 3 to 6 seconds of computing per second of speech. It also ended with "Cloud synthesis delivered 22x faster turnaround than the 14-core Intel laptop CPU". My article contains neither "22x" nor "14-core". The second is true of that processor, and the first is arithmetic the agent did on its own, but I had asked for no added facts, and the summary told me it had kept to the article.

Slide 7 had a layout problem: the three boxes on the right run into the edge of the slide. The agent's own note said it had left slide 7 as drafted. The other slides held up, apart from small additions such as an IPA spelling of "Muse".

Asking it to fix one slide

I told the agent what was wrong with slide 8, gave it the correct figure and asked it to change only that slide. It replied with its plan, and less than a minute later it was done. The clone's box now said 3 to 6 seconds of computing per second of speech, and both added claims were gone. It also corrected the slide's speaker notes, which had repeated the same mix-up, and confirmed that no other slides changed.

The panel then showed the original and the modified slide side by side, with the new one selected and a "Compare all edits" link. If the fix had been wrong, I could have picked the original back.

The same test in Chinese

My readers include Chinese speakers, so I ran the Chinese version of the article through the same steps. The agent replied in Chinese, named the deck 中文AI配音测评 and finished in about 175 seconds. Chinese text rendered cleanly in a different style, with soft 3D illustrations, and the results table was again correct.

It also hit the free plan's limit. The agent had planned 11 slides, the free plan creates at most 10, and the slide it dropped was the last one, "What I did not test". The agent said so plainly, and a banner offered an upgrade to finish the deck.

The Chinese deck added more than the English one. Slide 4 described a blind test with the seven audio files shuffled at random, when I had simply listened to them one after another. Slide 7 gained a "core conclusion" in bold that I never wrote, saying that realism in voiceover comes from the breathing room between punctuation marks. Slide 8 calculated a "22.5x" efficiency gap and said ElevenLabs runs on a cloud cluster. The agent's summary again said it had added nothing beyond the article.

Exporting to PowerPoint

The export panel offers PDF, PowerPoint, Google Slides and PNGs, at Basic, Standard or Detailed quality. "Hide Made with Gamma badge" is a Plus feature. The panel also suggests installing two fonts, Outfit and Urbanist, and warns that gradient text and frosted backgrounds fall back to simpler styles in PDF and PowerPoint.

The PowerPoint file took under half a minute and came to 2.36 MB. Inside were 10 slides of editable text, a real PowerPoint table on slide 6, speaker notes on every slide and the six font files embedded, so it displayed correctly in PowerPoint without installing anything.

Every slide had the "Made with Gamma" badge in the bottom right corner. The title wrapped differently from the web version, so the decorative box no longer lines up with the text.

On slide 8 the corrected sentence is longer than the original, and in PowerPoint its last word spills just below the box.

What the free plan gets you

The balance went from 400 to 270 after the English deck and the one-slide fix, then to 131 after the Chinese deck, so a 10-slide deck cost me 130 to 140 credits. That is about three decks from the signup credits. The credit panel says upgrading gets you credits that refresh monthly; according to Gamma's pricing page, the free plan's 400 come once, at signup.

On the pricing page on November 3, 2026, Plus cost $12 a month, or $9 a month billed yearly, for 1,500 credits a month, up to 100 slides per prompt and no Gamma branding. Pro cost $25, or $18 billed yearly, for 4,000 credits a month, better image models and custom branding.

Would I use it?

For a first draft of a deck from my own writing, yes. It took a long article and produced a structured, good-looking deck faster than I could pick a template, and the hardest slide, the table, was exact. The fix-one-slide request was the best part of the test.

What I wouldn't do is present it unchecked. In both languages it added numbers and conclusions I never wrote, and its own summary said it hadn't, so the summary is no substitute for reading every slide against the source. The free credits are enough to try that on two or three of your own documents before paying. I tested only the Presentation mode, Standard effort and one article in two languages.

Originally published on Hands-On AI Tools, where I test AI tools on real tasks. Cover: the title slide Gamma generated in this test; the images on it were made by Gamma.

title: How to Choose the Right Data Migration Strategy: Decision Criteria, Evaluation Frameworks, and Real-World Examples
description:
Every growing software application eventually faces a critical crossroad: migrating its data. Whether you are scaling up your infrastructure, cutting cloud costs, or moving away from legacy technologies, a poorly planned data migration can lead to corruption, extended downtime, or heavy financial loss.
To prevent these pitfalls, engineering teams need more than just migration tools—they need a structured approach. In this article, we will break down the essential decision criteria, evaluation frameworks, and real-world examples to help you execute a risk-free data migration.

  1. Software Data Migration Decision Criteria

Before writing any migration script or pipeline, your team must analyze four critical pillars to choose the right strategy:
• Downtime Tolerance: Can your business afford hours of a maintenance window, or do you require a near-zero downtime (live-sync) migration to protect user experience?
• Data Volume and Velocity: Is your database a few gigabytes, or are you moving multi-terabyte systems with thousands of concurrent live writes per second?
• Network Bandwidth: Do you have the pipeline speed to move data over the internet/cloud, or do you need offline physical transfer appliances (like AWS Snowball)?
• Team Expertise: Does your team have deep experience with complex change-data-capture (CDC) tools, or is a simpler, traditional approach safer for your skill level?

  1. Software Data Migration Evaluation Framework

An evaluation framework ensures you select the correct technical path based on your constraints. Here is a standard 4-step framework used by enterprise teams:
• Phase 1: Discovery & Profiling: Analyze the quality of source data. Identify anomalies, duplicate records, missing constraints, and outdated schemas that need cleaning before the actual shift.
• Phase 2: Strategy Selection: Evaluate which approach fits best:
• Big Bang Migration: Move all data in one single downtime window. It is simpler but carries higher risk if things go wrong.
• Trickle (Live) Migration: Run source and target systems in parallel, syncing data incrementally. It is highly reliable but more complex to build.
• Phase 3: Risk Assessment & Rollback: Map out single points of failure. Define clear metrics that trigger an immediate rollback plan if the migration fails mid-way.
• Phase 4: Post-Migration Audit: Formulate verification checklists using checksums, row count comparisons, and automated smoke tests to formally declare the migration successful.

  1. Real-World Software Data Migration Examples

Let’s look at how these frameworks and criteria apply in actual production environments:
• Example 1: Relational to Relational (Zero Downtime)
A high-traffic SaaS company outgrows its self-hosted PostgreSQL database. Because their primary criterion is zero downtime, they choose a Trickle Migration strategy. They use a Change Data Capture (CDC) tool to seamlessly sync data to a fully managed cloud database while the application remains live for global users.
• Example 2: Relational to Non-Relational (Schema Transformation)
A fast-growing e-commerce platform wants to migrate its unstructured product catalog from a rigid MySQL schema to a flexible MongoDB setup. Their primary decision criterion is schema flexibility. The team builds an intermediate ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) pipeline to map and transform tabular rows into JSON documents.
• Example 3: Lift-and-Shift (Big Bang Migration)
An internal corporate HR tool with a small 50GB database needs to move to a new cloud server. Since the tool is only used during weekdays, the team schedules a Big Bang migration over the weekend. They lock the source database on Friday night, copy the data directly, test it on Sunday, and point the app to the new cloud server before Monday morning.

Conclusion

Data migration shouldn’t be a guessing game. By clearly assessing your unique decision criteria and applying a concrete evaluation framework early on, you can eliminate the anxiety of data loss and ensure long-term system stability.

title: I built a bot that plays my Unreal game and files the bugs
description:
I'm making an indie game in Unreal Engine 5.8, and like most solo developers I have a testing problem: nobody walks the whole game after every change. I do it for ten minutes, see nothing wrong, and ship the build. So I wrote a bot to do the boring part, and I'm releasing it as open source. It is called PlayGoblin, and it is pre-release (0.1.0-dev), so please read the limits section before you get excited.

A real 150 s run on my game, shown as a 3x time-lapse of seconds 19 to 52 (overlay added by me). The full run walked 251 m and reached 19 waypoints, but covered only 12.0% of the 1137 walkable cells; it logged 1 confirmed and 12 unconfirmed stuck spots. Coverage in the overlay is derived from sampled positions. The goblin is not a speedrunner yet.

The problem

Unit tests check what you thought to assert. Recorded input replays only cover the path you recorded and break when the level changes. Manual QA is great, but it does not run at 3 a.m. after every commit. The gap I care about is "nobody walked there": a stuck spot behind a prop, a fall through a missing collision, a menu button wired to nothing, a TODO that made it into a title screen.

What PlayGoblin is

An engine-side component walks the game and writes a plain run folder: events.jsonl plus a summary. A Python CLI reads that folder and produces findings, an HTML report, and optionally GitHub issues. Each finding has evidence, meaning an event, a frame, or a log line. If the bot cannot show it, it does not report it.

There are engine sides for Unity (6000.4 tested) and Unreal (5.8.3 Win64 tested). Any other engine that can write the run-folder format (documented in docs/PROTOCOL.md) gets the same checks and reports. I tested that with a fake Godot-style run, not a real Godot game.

The bugs it found on my game

I ran it on my Unreal game this week. Three results are worth telling honestly.

The player could not move. The game had no input bound to move the pawn. The bot, which reads the game's own key and axis bindings and presses the keys that should move the player, never left the spawn point and reported "The player never moved" as critical.

A bug in the bot, found by the game. My game has a level-sized invisible blocking volume. It hid the ground from every floor probe, so the bot saw nothing walkable. That was a bug in PlayGoblin, not in the game, and the fix is that the bot now skips actors it starts inside and logs them. Real games are weirder than sample projects, and this is why I am asking for run folders from yours.

Grey-box look. It lists visible actors still using /Engine/BasicShapes meshes or the engine grid material and reports each as "Prototype look". It is a cheap way to see how much of a level is still placeholder art.

On the Unreal sample project, which has bugs I planted, it also finds a UMG "Options" button that does nothing and menu text reading "TODO: title". Another false positive taught me something: it flagged a pastel-pink game as missing-material pink. Now only pure magenta counts.

How it works

It plays through real input. In key mode (-PlayGoblinKeys) it presses the game's bound keys, turns with simulated mouse movement rather than setting the camera, taps action keys at irregular intervals, and tries a jump when stuck. If nothing moves the player, or the mouse does nothing after repeated probes, that is itself a finding (dead_input).

It crawls UMG menus. About every two seconds it finds visible widgets, reports placeholder text, and clicks each enabled button once. A button is dead if nothing observable changed within a second.

It explores on purpose. Instead of random destinations it heads for the nearest unvisited ground next to what it has already seen. On the sample project, same seed and 150 seconds, coverage went from 34% to 73% on one level and from 48% to 93% on the other. Every report prints coverage.

The checks have no LLM in them. Each check is a pure function: run folder in, findings out. The same events give the same findings every time, and there are 62 Python tests. A stuck spot only counts as confirmed once it repeats, so one unlucky run does not file a fake bug. An LLM can optionally write a summary paragraph, labelled as such.

Agents can drive it. There is an MCP server (playgoblin mcp) with five tools: status, run, report, findings and file_issues. The repo is also a Claude Code plugin with a skill that teaches an agent when to run it and how to read confidence. Filing GitHub issues is a dry run unless you explicitly confirm.


The HTML report: each finding links to its evidence.

Quickstart 

pip install "git+https://github.com/grloper/playgoblin#subdirectory=cli"   # Python 3.11+

Unreal: copy unreal/PlayGoblin into your project's Plugins/ and launch the game with the flag:

UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe MyGame.uproject -game -playgoblin -PlayGoblinSeconds=300 -PlayGoblinSeed=1 -PlayGoblinOut=D:/runs -PlayGoblinExit
playgoblin report D:/runs/<run id>     # report.html, report.md, findings.json

Unity: add the package from https://github.com/grloper/playgoblin.git?path=/unity, put the PlayGoblin Player component on your player, press Play, then playgoblin run --minutes 10 --runs 3.

The plugin does nothing unless -playgoblin is on the command line, so shipping with it enabled is harmless.

Honest limits

  • It is pre-release. Unity 6000.4 and Unreal 5.8.3 on Win64 are the only tested combinations.
  • Accuracy on real games is not measured. My samples were written by the people who wrote the checks, so treat them as regression tests. The Unreal plugin passed its sample (all 5 planted bugs, nothing on the clean twin) on one seed and one machine.
  • UMG buttons are clicked by broadcasting OnClicked, so Slate hit testing is not exercised; Enhanced-Input-driven and CommonUI-only menus are not covered.
  • It walks and clicks. It does not judge fun, balance, visuals or audio, and "no findings" never means bug free.

Try it, and help

The most useful contribution right now is running it on a game and telling me what it missed or got wrong, with the run folder attached. Open an issue at https://github.com/grloper/playgoblin. Roadmap items: more real-game runs with published precision numbers, other Unreal versions and Enhanced Input, Unity UI Toolkit and player builds, and a GitHub Action. If you build for another engine, the run-folder format is short; a writer for it is a good first contribution.

title: What is Unmounting in React?
description:
Unmounting is the process of removing a component from the screen.
When a React component is removed from the UI, it is called Unmounting.

Unmounting is useful for:

  • Clearing timers (setInterval, setTimeout).
  • Removing event listeners.
  • Cleaning up subscriptions.
  • Preventing unnecessary background operations.

Example using useEffect:

import React, { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

function App() {

const [show, setShow] = useState(true);

return (
    <div>
        <button onClick={() => setShow(!show)}>
            Show / Hide
        </button>

        {show && <Child />}
    </div>
);

}

function Child() {

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Component Mounted");

    return () => {
        console.log("Component Unmounted");
    };

}, []);

return <h1>Hello React!</h1>;

}

export default App;

How does it work?

Step 1: Initially, show = true.

Output:

Hello React!
Component Mounted

Click the Hide button:

  • show becomes false.
  • The Child component is removed from the screen.
  • Cleanup function executes.

Console:
Component Unmounted

Click the Show button again:

  • show becomes true.
  • Child component mounts again.
  • Mounting effect runs again.

Cleanup Function:

useEffect(() => {

console.log("Mounted");

return () => {
    console.log("Unmounted");
};

}, []);

The return function is called the Cleanup Function:

  1. When the component unmounts.
  2. Before the effect runs again when its dependencies change.

title: Your Code Has Bugs You Haven't Met Yet: A Friendly Deep Dive into SAST with SonarQube
description:
"An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure."
— Benjamin Franklin

The bug that waited six months

Let me tell you about a Friday night that went sideways.

A team I know shipped a tiny feature: a search box on an internal admin dashboard. Two lines of code built a SQL query by gluing the user's input straight into a string. It passed code review. It passed QA. It worked perfectly for six months.

Then someone typed ' OR '1'='1 into that box. Every customer record came back in one page.

Here's the painful part: nobody was careless. The reviewer was looking at business logic, not string concatenation. QA was testing whether search worked, not whether it could be abused. The bug wasn't hidden. It was sitting in plain sight, in a pull request, waiting.

A tool that reads code for exactly this kind of mistake would have flagged it in seconds, before the merge button was ever clicked.

That tool category has a name: SAST. And one of the most popular ways to do it is SonarQube.

If the pattern feels familiar, it should. Injection is still a headline category: it sits at #5 in the OWASP Top 10:2025 (it was #3 in 2021). It dropped because the industry got better at it, not because it went away.

The post at a glance

  • Reading time: about 14 minutes
  • Hands-on time: about 10 minutes, with Docker
  • You will learn: what SAST is, how taint analysis works, how SonarQube is built, how to gate pull requests, and how to keep a team from muting the tool
  • You need: Docker, a project with some code, and a coffee

Here's the road map:

  • What SAST actually is (and what it isn't)
  • How a machine can "read" your code and spot a vulnerability
  • What SonarQube does, and how its pieces fit together
  • Running it locally with Docker in about ten minutes
  • Wiring it into CI so bad code can't sneak into main
  • The honest stuff: false positives, noisy dashboards, and how to get your team to actually care

Grab a coffee. Let's go.

So what is SAST, really?

SAST (Static Application Security Testing) reads your source code without running it, and looks for patterns that lead to security holes.

Think of it like a spell-checker, but for danger. A spell-checker doesn't need you to say the sentence out loud to know "recieve" is wrong. SAST doesn't need your app to run to know that user input is flowing straight into a SQL query.

The word that matters most is static. The code is just text on disk. No server, no database, no test data. That's what makes SAST so useful: it can run the moment you write a line, long before anything is deployed.

Where SAST fits among its cousins

You'll hear a pile of acronyms in AppSec conversations. Here's the cheat sheet:

Approach What it looks at When it runs Great at catching Blind spots
SAST (static) Your source code While coding, on every PR Injection, hardcoded secrets, unsafe APIs, crypto misuse Runtime config, server setup, business logic
DAST (dynamic) Your running app, from outside Against staging or test environments Misconfigured headers, auth issues, real exploitable endpoints Can't point to the exact line of code
SCA (composition) Your dependencies (npm, Maven, pip) On every build Known CVEs in third-party libraries Bugs in your code
IAST (interactive) The app from inside, while tests run During QA and integration tests Confirmed, real-path vulnerabilities Only sees code paths your tests exercise

None of these replaces the others. But if you can only start with one, SAST gives you the best bang for the buck. It's cheap, fast, and it talks to developers in their own language: file name, line number, here's why, here's the fix.

The "shift left" argument

You've probably heard "shift left." It just means: find problems earlier in the timeline, where they're cheaper to fix.

A vulnerability caught in your editor costs you thirty seconds. The same vulnerability caught in a penetration test costs a ticket, a context switch, a re-review and a redeploy. Caught in production by an attacker? That's an incident report, a lawyer, and possibly a news headline.

The shape is the point: effort multiplies at every stage. The numbers are an illustrative model, not measured data.

SAST is the most "left" security check you can run. It lives right next to your code.

How does a tool "read" code?

A SAST engine turns your code into a structured model, then asks questions about how data moves through it. It's less magic than it sounds. Let's peel it open, one layer at a time.

Step 1: From text to a tree

To you, code is text. To a SAST tool, text is useless until it's parsed into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST): a tree where every node is a meaningful piece, like a function call, a variable, or a string.

Take this tiny snippet, shown in Python and Node.js:

name = request.args.get("name")
sql = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
cursor.execute(sql)

const name = req.query.name;
const sql = `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '${name}'`;
db.query(sql);

The tool no longer sees characters. It sees: a variable name assigned from request.args.get (or req.query), a string built by interpolation, and a call to execute (or query). Now it can reason.

Step 2: Simple rules (pattern matching)

The easiest checks just look at the tree's shape. "Is someone calling MD5 for password hashing?" "Is there a hardcoded string that looks like an AWS key?" "Is this catch block empty?"

These are fast and precise, but they only see one spot at a time.

Step 3: Following the data (taint analysis)

This is where SAST gets clever. Taint analysis tracks untrusted data as it travels through your program. It uses three ideas:

  • Source: where untrusted data enters. Think HTTP parameters, headers, file uploads, or message queues.
  • Sink: a dangerous place for that data to land. Think SQL queries, shell commands, file paths, or HTML output.
  • Sanitizer: something that makes the data safe on the way. Think parameterized queries, escaping, or strict validation.

The rule is simple: if tainted data reaches a sink without passing through a sanitizer, raise the alarm.

If the data passes a sanitizer, nothing is reported; if it reaches the sink untouched, you get a vulnerability.

In our snippet, request.args.get("name") (or req.query.name) is the source, cursor.execute(sql) (or db.query(sql)) is the sink, and nothing cleans the data in between. That's SQL injection, flagged before the code ever runs. And the real power is that the source and sink can live in different files, three function calls apart. A human reviewer looking at one diff would never connect them. The engine does.

The fix the tool will nudge you toward 

name = request.args.get("name")
sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"
cursor.execute(sql, (name,))
rows = cursor.fetchall()

const name = req.query.name;
const sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = $1";
const { rows } = await db.query(sql, [name]);

The parameterized query acts as the sanitizer. The data can still be anything, but it can no longer change the shape of the SQL.

The placeholder depends on your driver: ? for sqlite3 and mysql2, %s for psycopg2, $1 for node-postgres. The idea is identical: the value travels separately from the query text.

A quick reality check

Static analysis has a famous trade-off. Being exhaustive means more false positives (alarms that aren't real). Being conservative means more false negatives (real bugs it misses). Every tool picks a spot on that dial. We'll come back to how to live with this later.

"Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place."
— Brian Kernighan, The Elements of Programming Style

Meet SonarQube

SonarQube is a code quality and security platform from SonarSource that runs SAST (and much more) on every branch and pull request, and turns the results into a simple pass/fail signal. It's been around since 2007, and it's probably the tool your company's platform team has already heard of.

What makes it different from a pure security scanner is its scope. SonarQube cares about the whole health of your code: security vulnerabilities, yes, but also reliability bugs, maintainability problems, duplication and test coverage. Security people love it for the first part. Developers tend to love it for the rest.

The family, untangled

SonarSource renamed things in 2024–2025, so blog posts online can be confusing. Here's today's lineup:

Product What it is Who it's for
SonarQube for IDE (formerly SonarLint) A free plugin for VS Code, IntelliJ, Visual Studio and Eclipse Every developer, catching issues as they type
SonarQube Community Build (formerly Community Edition) Free, open-source, self-hosted; released on a regular cadence Learning, small teams, single-branch analysis
SonarQube Server (Developer, Enterprise, Data Center editions) Commercial, self-hosted; branch and PR analysis, deeper taint analysis Teams who need PR decoration and full security coverage
SonarQube Cloud (formerly SonarCloud) The SaaS version, hosted by Sonar Teams who don't want to run a server; has a free tier

Two things worth knowing before you choose:

  • Server versions now use calendar numbering, like 2025.1. Some releases are marked LTA (Long-Term Active), which is what you want for a stable production install.
  • The free Community Build analyzes one branch and doesn't decorate pull requests. The heavier security analysis, including cross-file taint tracking, lives in the commercial editions and SonarQube Cloud. For learning and for this tutorial, Community Build is perfect.

The four ideas you need to know

Once you understand these, the whole SonarQube UI makes sense:

  1. Rules. A single check, like "SQL queries should not be built from user input." SonarQube ships with thousands of them across 30+ languages.
  2. Quality Profiles. A named set of rules per language. The default is called "Sonar way", and it's a sensible starting point. You can copy it and tune it.
  3. Quality Gates. The pass/fail verdict. A gate is a set of conditions, like "no new vulnerabilities" and "coverage on new code is at least 80%." If any condition fails, the gate fails, and your pipeline can stop the merge.
  4. New Code. SonarQube's secret weapon. Instead of shouting about ten years of legacy debt, it focuses on code you changed recently. More on this in a moment.

How the pieces talk to each other

The architecture is simpler than it looks. The scanner runs where your code is (your laptop or a CI runner). It does the analysis and uploads a report. The server processes that report, stores results in a database, and shows them in the web UI.

The important bit: your source code never has to leave your CI runner. Only the analysis report travels to the server.

Hands-on: your first scan in about ten minutes

You need Docker and a project with some code in it. That's it. We'll run the free Community Build locally and scan a deliberately vulnerable snippet.

1. Start the server 

docker run -d --name sonarqube \
  -p 9000:9000 \
  sonarqube:community

Give it a minute or two to boot (it starts an Elasticsearch instance inside, so it's not instant). Then open http://localhost:9000 and log in with admin / admin. It'll ask you to change the password right away.

Heads up: this quick-start uses an embedded H2 database. It's fine for a demo, but never use it in production. For a real install, point SonarQube at PostgreSQL with a docker-compose.yml. On Linux you may also need sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=524288 for Elasticsearch to start.

2. Create a project and a token

In the UI:

  1. Click Create Project → Local project.
  2. Give it a key, for example my-first-scan.
  3. For the baseline, choose Previous version as the definition of "new code."
  4. Choose Locally as the analysis method and generate a token. Copy it somewhere safe; you'll see it only once.

3. Add some deliberately bad code

Let's give the scanner something to find. Save this as app.py in an empty folder:

import sqlite3
import hashlib
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)
AWS_SECRET = "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE"   # hardcoded credential

@app.route("/user")
def get_user():
    name = request.args.get("name")                # source
    conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
    query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
    return str(conn.execute(query).fetchall())     # sink

def hash_password(pw):
    return hashlib.md5(pw.encode()).hexdigest()   # weak hashing

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(debug=True)                            # debug in prod

Four problems, hiding in about twenty lines. Let's see how many get caught.

4. Run the scanner

The easiest way is the scanner's own Docker image, so you don't install anything:

docker run --rm \
  --network host \
  -e SONAR_HOST_URL="http://localhost:9000" \
  -e SONAR_TOKEN="<your-token>" \
  -v "$(pwd):/usr/src" \
  sonarsource/sonar-scanner-cli \
  -Dsonar.projectKey=my-first-scan

On macOS or Windows, swap localhost for host.docker.internal and drop --network host.

Projects you'll scan again and again deserve a config file. Drop a sonar-project.properties at the root:

sonar.projectKey=my-first-scan
sonar.projectName=My First Scan
sonar.sources=.
sonar.exclusions=**/tests/**,**/node_modules/**
sonar.python.version=3.12

Python projects use the scanner CLI or the Docker image above, with the sonar-project.properties file you just wrote. There's no build plugin to add, so the same command works on your laptop and in CI.

JavaScript and TypeScript projects can skip Docker and run the npm scanner directly, with no install step:

npx @sonar/scan   -Dsonar.host.url=http://localhost:9000   -Dsonar.token=<your-token>   -Dsonar.projectKey=my-first-scan

Without -Dsonar.projectKey, it takes the key from the name field in package.json.

5. Look at the dashboard

Refresh the project page. Expect the hardcoded secret, the weak MD5 hash and the Flask debug mode to show up, either as issues or as Security Hotspots depending on the rule and your version.

The SQL injection is the interesting one. It needs cross-function taint analysis, which lives in the commercial editions. On Community Build it may not be reported at all. That's not a bug in your test; it's the edition boundary, and it's a good reason to know what your tier can and can't see. The next section explains the hotspot idea.

Reading the report without panicking

Your first dashboard will probably show hundreds of issues. That's normal, and you don't have to fix them all. Let's decode what you're looking at.

Issue types, in human terms

SonarQube sorts findings by which quality of your software they hurt:

What you see What it means Example What to do
Vulnerability (Security) The tool is confident this is exploitable SQL built from request data, reaching execute() Fix it. Usually before merging.
Security Hotspot Security-sensitive code that needs a human to judge Using random(), a permissive CORS setting, a regex that could be slow Review it and mark it Safe or Fix
Bug (Reliability) Code that will likely misbehave Null dereference, unclosed resource, always-true condition Fix it; these become production incidents
Code Smell (Maintainability) Code that works but is hard to change 200-line function, duplicated blocks, deep nesting Fix when you touch that code

Each issue also carries a severity (Blocker, High, Medium, Low, Info) and a Clean Code attribute explaining why it matters. Click any issue and you'll get the exact line, a description of the risk, and usually a compliant code example. This is where developers actually learn something.

Not sure what to do with a finding? Follow the flow:

Every finding ends in one of three outcomes: fix it, justify it, or defer it on purpose.

Hotspots are not vulnerabilities

This trips up nearly everyone. A Vulnerability is SonarQube saying: "This is a problem." A Hotspot is SonarQube saying: "This could be a problem, and only you know the context."

Using a non-cryptographic random number is fine for shuffling a playlist. It's a disaster for generating a password reset token. The tool can't know which one you're doing, so it asks. Your job is to review hotspots, not ignore them.

The ratings

The dashboard grades Security, Reliability and Maintainability from A (best) to E. A single unresolved critical vulnerability can drag your Security rating to D or E. That's intentional: one real hole matters more than a thousand smells.

"Clean as You Code": the idea that saves your sanity

Imagine scanning a ten-year-old codebase for the first time. 4,000 issues. Your team will look at that number, sigh, and close the tab forever.

SonarQube's answer is a philosophy called Clean as You Code:

Don't try to fix the past. Just make sure every new change is clean.

It's the Boy Scout rule in a CI pipeline:

"Leave the campground cleaner than you found it."
— The Boy Scout rule, popularized in Clean Code by Robert C. Martin

The default Quality Gate, "Sonar way", only judges new code: the lines added or changed since your baseline. It checks roughly that new code has:

  • 0 new issues
  • 100% of new Security Hotspots reviewed
  • At least 80% test coverage
  • At most 3% duplication

The magic is that legacy code gets cleaner over time anyway, because every file you touch for a new feature gets held to the new standard. No "cleanup sprint" required. Old debt fades, new debt never arrives.

Putting it in your pipeline

A scan you run by hand is a scan you'll forget. The real value comes when every pull request is scanned automatically and the Quality Gate can block the merge.

Here's the flow we're building. A developer opens a PR, CI runs tests and the scanner, SonarQube judges the new code, and the result comes back as a status check on the PR.

The loop is the point: a red gate doesn't end the conversation, it just sends the change back for one more push.

GitHub Actions example

First, add two repository secrets under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions:

  • SONAR_TOKEN: a token generated in SonarQube (use a project analysis token, not your admin token)
  • SONAR_HOST_URL: your server's URL, like https://sonar.yourcompany.com

Then create .github/workflows/sonarqube.yml:

Python:

name: SonarQube Analysis

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

jobs:
  sonarqube:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # full history = accurate "new code" and blame data

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Run tests with coverage
        run: |
          pip install -r requirements.txt pytest pytest-cov
          pytest --cov=. --cov-report=xml

      - name: SonarQube Scan
        uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@v5
        env:
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
          SONAR_HOST_URL: ${{ secrets.SONAR_HOST_URL }}
        with:
          args: >
            -Dsonar.python.coverage.reportPaths=coverage.xml
            -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true

JavaScript (Node.js):

name: SonarQube Analysis

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

jobs:
  sonarqube:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # full history = accurate "new code" and blame data

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22

      - name: Run tests with coverage
        run: |
          npm ci
          npx jest --coverage --coverageReporters=lcov

      - name: SonarQube Scan
        uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@v5
        env:
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
          SONAR_HOST_URL: ${{ secrets.SONAR_HOST_URL }}
        with:
          args: >
            -Dsonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths=coverage/lcov.info
            -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true

A few lines deserve a closer look:

  • fetch-depth: 0 is the most-forgotten line in every SonarQube setup. Without the full Git history, SonarQube can't tell which lines are new, and "Clean as You Code" quietly breaks.
  • sonar.qualitygate.wait=true makes the job wait for SonarQube's verdict and fail if the gate fails. That red X is what stops the merge.
  • Coverage is generated by your tests, not by SonarQube. SonarQube only reads the report. No report, no coverage number.
  • The Python property reads Cobertura XML, which pytest-cov writes as coverage.xml. The JavaScript property reads LCOV, which Jest writes to coverage/lcov.info.

The @v5 above is an example. Newer major versions of the action exist, so check the releases page, pin to a release you've verified, and update it on purpose, not by accident.

Making the gate actually block merges

The workflow failing isn't enough on its own. Go to Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules for main, enable Require status checks to pass, and select the SonarQube job. Now a failed Quality Gate physically blocks the merge button.

On SonarQube Server Developer Edition and above, or SonarQube Cloud, you also get PR decoration: a comment on the pull request summarizing new issues, with links straight to the problem lines. Developers see the feedback where they already are, which matters more than you'd think.

Using GitLab, Jenkins or Azure DevOps?

Same idea, different syntax. SonarQube has official integrations for GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Bitbucket Pipelines and Jenkins (via the SonarQube Scanner plugin plus a waitForQualityGate step). The three essentials stay identical: full Git history, a coverage report, and waiting for the gate.

The honest part: false positives, noise, and people

The hardest part of SAST is not installing the tool. It's getting a team to trust it. A scanner that cries wolf gets muted. Here's how to avoid that fate.

Dealing with false positives

You will see findings that aren't real problems. When that happens, resist the urge to silence everything. Instead:

  • Mark it in the UI, not in code. In SonarQube, set the issue to False Positive or Accepted and leave a short comment explaining why. Future you, and your auditor, will thank you.
  • Use // NOSONAR sparingly. It suppresses every issue on that line, silently, forever. It's the duct tape of static analysis. Some teams ban it outright in code review.
  • Tune the Quality Profile if one rule is consistently wrong for your codebase. Copy "Sonar way", deactivate that rule, and document the decision. Never edit the built-in profile directly.
  • Exclude what isn't yours. Generated code, vendored libraries, migrations and test fixtures inflate the noise. Use sonar.exclusions and sonar.test.exclusions.

Common mistakes I see over and over

  1. Shallow clones in CI. No full history means broken "new code" detection. (Yes, again. It's that common.)
  2. Scanning before tests. Coverage shows 0% and the gate fails for the wrong reason.
  3. Gating on overall code instead of new code. The gate fails on day one for legacy reasons, and the team learns to ignore red.
  4. One shared admin token in every pipeline. Use project-scoped analysis tokens and rotate them.
  5. Treating SonarQube as the whole security program. It doesn't scan your dependencies for known CVEs the way a dedicated SCA tool does (newer commercial editions add SCA as an option), and it never sees your runtime config. Pair it with SCA, secrets scanning and DAST.
  6. Running H2 in production. It's for demos only. Use PostgreSQL.

Rolling it out to a real team

The rollout plan that works tends to look like this:

Four steps, and the gate only turns on in week 3, after people have had time to get curious.

  1. Week 1, observe. Turn on scanning in CI, but don't block anything. Let people look at the dashboard and get curious.
  2. Week 2, install the IDE plugin. Get every developer on SonarQube for IDE in connected mode, so their editor uses the same rules as the server. Catching issues while typing is far less annoying than catching them in CI.
  3. Week 3, enable the gate on new code only. Use "Sonar way" as-is. Announce it, explain Clean as You Code, and answer questions.
  4. Ongoing, review together. Spend fifteen minutes in a retro now and then looking at hotspots and false positives. Tune the profile as a team.

The pattern underneath: make the tool a teammate, not a cop. Developers adopt tools that make them better at their job. They route around tools that only make them slower.

Wrapping up

Remember that search box from the start? With SonarQube in the pipeline, that PR would have come back red in a few minutes, with the exact line and a fix example attached. No incident, no Friday night, no awkward meeting.

That's the whole promise of SAST: catch the boring, predictable, expensive mistakes while they're still cheap. Not because developers are careless, but because humans are bad at spotting the same pattern for the thousandth time, and machines are great at it.

"We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit."
— Will Durant, summarizing Aristotle

Your quick-start checklist

  • [ ] Run SonarQube Community Build locally with Docker
  • [ ] Scan one real project and skim the dashboard
  • [ ] Install SonarQube for IDE in your editor
  • [ ] Add the scanner to CI with fetch-depth: 0 and a coverage report
  • [ ] Turn on sonar.qualitygate.wait=true
  • [ ] Protect main so a failed gate blocks the merge
  • [ ] Gate on new code only, with "Sonar way"
  • [ ] Review hotspots; mark false positives with a reason
  • [ ] Pair it with dependency scanning (SCA) and secrets scanning

Over to you

Start small. Scan one repo this week. You'll almost certainly find something that makes you go "huh, how long has that been there?"

If this helped, drop a ❤️ or a 🦄, and tell me in the comments: what's the weirdest thing a static analysis tool has ever caught in your code? I read every reply.

Sources

  • SonarQube downloads and editions
  • Official SonarQube Docker image
  • SonarQube release announcements
  • SonarQube security-related rules
  • sonarqube-scan-action releases
  • OWASP Top 10:2025 introduction

title: Decision-Linked Development (DLD) 1.0 Released
description:
DLD Kit 1.0 (https://github.com/jimutt/dld-kit) is released. Here's a summary of what changed since the 0.x versions, mainly the move to an npm package.

If you missed the original post, DLD (Decision-Linked Development) is a set of skills that make your coding agent record the decisions behind your code, and read them again before it changes anything. It has been about eight months since I started building it, and it's now in use in a number of personal projects and repositories at my day job at Storytel. DLD takes a somewhat relaxed stance, in the sense that it doesn't try to reach for exhaustive specs, and its comment-based @decision annotations, which tie entries from the decision log to code, are its main distinguishing feature from other delta-oriented, spec-driven approaches.

Nowadays (as of November 2026) software factories and attempts to bridge more of the software development lifecycle in an agent-friendly way are on the tip of many people's tongues. DLD does not in its current shape offer much in that area. It has however been injected and used for the code implementation phase of such pipelines, and I'm experimenting in a separate repository with an optional DLD add-on that adds pipeline & orchestration-oriented features to DLD; some of it appears promising, but if integrated into core DLD, they'll likely be oriented more towards solo projects and smaller OSS projects rather than enterprise settings.

From copied skills to an npm package

Before I started releasing DLD as 1.0 release candidates, you'd install DLD by copying a bunch of skills into your repo (or through Tessl), and each skill carried its own bash scripts. It worked and I like the simplicity, but it was a bit clumsy. Bash scripts that need to run on everything from Linux to Windows are not something I want to maintain, and the test suite was turning into something that was not of the most readable kind.

Now DLD is distributed as npm package called dld-kit. In your repo, run:

npx dld-kit init

It asks which agent harnesses your team uses, writes the config, the skills and a short always-on rule, and you commit the result. Teammates don't have to install anything. To upgrade later it's npx dld-kit@latest update. If you'd rather not have the DLD "binary" (not really the correct term for an .mjs file) checked into the repo, you can gitignore it and use npx dld-kit@latest update to bring it in locally.

The bash scripts are gone as well. The skills now call a small Node CLI that's bundled into them, so everything runs the same way on every platform. You need Node.js 22+ and git.

If you're coming from 0.x, your decision records, config and index carry over untouched. There's an upgrade guide with the few manual steps.

Other harnesses than Claude Code

DLD started out as a Claude Code thing, but init now supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Pi and Antigravity. There's also a Claude Code plugin and plugins for Codex and Copilot CLI, and if you already manage your skills with npx skills or gh skill it works with those too. The always-on rule is now installed in the file each agent actually loads, instead of being tacked on to the end of CLAUDE.md.

What else is new

  • Decisions are drafts until they reach your main branch, in the sense that the agent will be less reluctant than earlier to adjust prose in non-accepted decisions as long as they haven't been integrated yet (in line with the general philosophy of DLD). decision_edits in the config decides how strict it is, and there's a command you can run in CI to enforce it.

  • /dld-snapshot only generates OVERVIEW.md now, since the old SNAPSHOT.md turned out to be redundant. It was never well thought through, and a number of end-to-end evaluations proved that it provided no measurable value for agents (contrary to INDEX.md and OVERVIEW.md which often improve agent decision recall & precision). You can still define your own generated documents in the config.

  • /dld-plan can have a subagent review the decisions it wrote, and you can pick which model the reviewers run on. There's also a dld.local.yaml for settings that are just for you and shouldn't be committed. Subagent reviews for the plan step are disabled by default. Enable them by setting plan_review: true.

A couple of smaller things. /dld-audit now notices most cases when a decision's text says it amends or supersedes another one but the link is missing from its metadata, and /dld-reindex commits the renames on top of your branch instead of squashing it, unless you ask for that.

From 1.0 on the versions follow semver, for everything a project builds on: the record format, annotations, config files, commands and the installed layout. So an update shouldn't break your setup unless the major version changes.

Try it 

npx dld-kit init

The README has the rest. And please open an issue in the GitHub repo if something doesn't work, or if you'd like to see support for another agent.

title: Check a CSV's missing-data contract before drawing a line
description:
A parser can read every row successfully and still pass the wrong meaning to a plotting step. Consider six time records with response values 2, 3, NA, 0, 4, 5. The third value is missing. The fourth is an observed zero. Replacing one with the other changes the scientific meaning; deleting the missing record can also change the continuity of a line plot.

This is a self-written synthetic teaching example, not a dataset from a study, a customer result, or the output of an installed research Skill. We are the RigorMed team. The calculation below was actually run locally with Python's standard library; it does not use a model, paid service, or production research task.

Freeze what the file means

For this file only, the schema is time_h,response_au. Time is in hours; response is in arbitrary units. The exact token NA means missing. Numeric zero means observed zero. Rows are in strictly increasing time order. They describe one sequence, so the number of rows is not automatically an independent sample size.

Those rules are declared inputs, not guesses learned by the parser. If a source uses -999, an empty field, or another code, confirm its meaning and change the contract explicitly. Do not extend this example into a universal CSV cleaner.

Inspect without rewriting the source

The code retains each original token alongside a parsed value. Missing values become None in the inspection structure; the source CSV remains unchanged. It also rejects non-finite numbers and time reversals under this particular declared schema.

import csv
import io
import math

raw = """time_h,response_au
0,2
1,3
2,NA
3,0
4,4
5,5
"""
reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(raw))
assert reader.fieldnames == ["time_h", "response_au"]
source_rows = list(reader)
checked = []
previous_time = None
for row in source_rows:
    t = float(row["time_h"])
    assert math.isfinite(t)
    assert previous_time is None or t > previous_time
    previous_time = t
    token = row["response_au"]
    value = None if token == "NA" else float(token)
    assert value is None or math.isfinite(value)
    checked.append((t, token, value))

missing_times = [t for t, token, value in checked if value is None]
observed = [value for t, token, value in checked if value is not None]
zero_times = [t for t, token, value in checked if value == 0]
assert len(source_rows) == 6
assert missing_times == [2.0]
assert zero_times == [3.0]
print({"records": len(checked), "observed": len(observed),
       "missing_times_h": missing_times, "zero_times_h": zero_times})

Actual local output:

{'records': 6, 'observed': 5, 'missing_times_h': [2.0], 'zero_times_h': [3.0]}

There are six records and five observed responses. Missingness occurs at hour two; the observed zero occurs at hour three. No row was imputed or deleted. Python assertions here are deliberately small teaching checks; a production validator should report explicit structured errors and must not rely on assertions that optimized execution can disable.

Pass the contract to the plotting step

Keep all six time coordinates. In the separate minimum Matplotlib teaching example used for today's video, the missing response is represented by a plotting NaN, so the line breaks at hour two. The zero stays on the response axis at hour three. A missingness marker sits in a separate strip; it must not masquerade as a measured response.

This behavior agrees with Matplotlib's documented masked-and-NaN example: removing a point can connect the remaining line, while masked or NaN values can leave a gap. A visible gap is a display choice bound to the data; it does not explain why the measurement is missing or establish that missingness is ignorable.

The handoff should include the original table, variable definitions, units, missing-code rule, exact plotting code and caption. Ask a reviewer to trace the count of records, the missing position and the observed zero back to the source. Do not add confidence intervals without an estimand, an appropriate sampling structure and an uncertainty method.
