Where the two recommended Skills fit

The K-Dense-AI public exploratory-data-analysis source provides an inspection-oriented task, while scientific-visualization addresses figure production and export. Both source files reviewed on 2026-11-04 identify version 1.4. The tabular core requires Python 3.11 or later; other formats and plotting/export dependencies need checking for the actual task.

Neither recommended Skill was installed or run for this article. Our CSV check and minimum plot are separate local teaching work, not evidence that either complete Skill installation succeeds, and not a RigorMed integration. Source review, an individual Python calculation, a figure export and a complete workflow acceptance test are different states.

For an authorized research-material task, you can describe the materials and required reviewable output in the RigorMed browser workspace. This article does not claim the two third-party Skills are available there; actual model use follows the displayed credit terms.

Sources and scope

  • Python standard library, csv and math: the executable example above uses DictReader, isfinite and ordinary collection operations.
  • Matplotlib, Plotting masked and NaN values, source reviewed with the day's plotting package.
  • K-Dense-AI exploratory-data-analysis source and scientific-visualization source, reviewed on 2026-11-04; version statements refer to those files.

The example does not estimate a treatment effect, validate a measurement method, perform inference, or recommend a missing-data analysis strategy. It checks a declared material contract before drawing a figure.

title: How I Clone My Own Voice on a Laptop With No GPU (Qwen3-TTS)
description:
Key takeaways

  • A laptop with no GPU can run Qwen3-TTS voice cloning. Expect 3 to 6 seconds of computing per second of speech.
  • Use reference clips of 7 to 15 seconds. About 30 seconds in total was enough for me.
  • If your reference is casual talking, use x-vector only mode, or the clone will copy your hesitations.
  • Generate 3 to 5 takes per line and pick by where the pauses fall.

Tested on: Windows 11 laptop, Intel Core i9-13900H, 32 GB RAM, integrated graphics only (no NVIDIA GPU). Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base, qwen-tts 0.1.1, Python 3.11.

I post short animated videos that explain AI topics, narrated in Chinese. Recording the narration was the slowest part of every video. I stumble, re-record, and takes from different days don't sound the same. I wanted to type the script and get narration in my own voice.

Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, set this up on my laptop. I described what I wanted, listened to the results and made the calls. You can skip the code blocks; the settings that mattered are explained in plain words.

What I used

The model is Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base, an open-source text-to-speech model from Alibaba's Qwen team (Apache-2.0 license, code at github.com/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS). The "Base" version is the one that clones voices. I downloaded the weights from ModelScope, which was by far the fastest source where I live.

It runs through the qwen-tts Python package, version 0.1.1, in a Python 3.11 virtual environment. My system Python was newer than the machine-learning packages supported, so a separate 3.11 environment saved a lot of trouble.

Everything runs on the CPU in float32, with no CUDA and no NVIDIA card.

Step 1: Reference audio from a recording I already had

I didn't record anything new. I had a long screen recording where I was talking, and I cut three clips from it, about 33 seconds in total.

Longer clips sounded more like me. Clips of 7 to 15 seconds gave a clearly closer match than 4-second clips.

If there is music or noise behind your voice, remove it first. On my CPU, the BS-Roformer separation model needed about two hours for three minutes of audio. The Kim_Vocal_2 model in the audio-separator package did the same job in about three minutes.

Step 2: The setting that decides whether it sounds fluent

Qwen3-TTS Base can clone a voice in two ways:

Mode What you give it What it copies
ICL (the default) One clip plus its exact transcript Your voice and the way you spoke in that clip
x-vector only One or more clips, no transcript Only the sound of your voice

I started with ICL because it's the default. The problem was my reference clip: unscripted talking, with hesitations and uneven pace. The clone copied that too. Every line came out with the same stop-start rhythm, and it didn't sound fluent.

Switching to x-vector only mode fixed it. The model keeps my voice but uses its own steadier pacing, which is what narration needs. Since no transcript is needed, I could also feed it several clips at once.

If your reference is clean read-aloud speech, ICL may be fine. If it's casual talking, try x-vector first.

This is a simplified version of the script on my laptop:

import numpy as np, soundfile as sf, torch
from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel

torch.set_num_threads(14)  # how many CPU threads to use

model = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained(
    "models/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base", device_map="cpu", dtype=torch.float32
)

# Join a few clips of my voice (mono WAV) with a short silence between them
voice, sr = sf.read("my_voice.wav", dtype="float32")
gap = np.zeros(int(0.25 * sr), np.float32)
clips = [(12.0, 23.5), (61.0, 72.7), (130.2, 141.1)]  # start, end in seconds
parts = []
for start, end in clips:
    parts += [voice[int(start * sr):int(end * sr)], gap]
ref = np.concatenate(parts)

# x-vector only: copy the voice, not the rhythm. No transcript needed.
prompt = model.create_voice_clone_prompt(
    ref_audio=(ref, sr), ref_text=None, x_vector_only_mode=True
)

wavs, out_sr = model.generate_voice_clone(
    text=["大家好，今天聊聊怎么用 AI 给视频配音。"],
    language=["Chinese"],
    voice_clone_prompt=prompt,
)
sf.write("line01.wav", wavs[0], out_sr)

For ICL mode you pass one clip, its exact transcript as ref_text, and x_vector_only_mode=False.

Step 3: Make several takes and keep the best one

The same line comes out a little different every time. Some takes pause in the right places, some rush through a comma. So I generate every line 3 to 5 times and pick one.

What I listen for: does it pause at the commas, and does it avoid long gaps in the middle of a phrase. That matters more than small differences in tone.

With twenty-odd lines and several takes each, listening to everything gets tiring. So a script ranks the takes first:

  • It transcribes each take with a speech recognizer (Paraformer, for Chinese) and compares it with the script, to catch swallowed or wrong words.
  • It measures how close the voice is to a separate sample of my real voice that wasn't used for cloning (CAM++ speaker verification).
  • It counts the pauses and compares them with the commas in the line.

Then I only listen to the top few.

How fast is it on a CPU?

From my logs, generating up to six lines per batch: roughly 3 to 6 seconds of computing for each second of speech. One batch produced 37 seconds of speech in 127 seconds; another produced 24 seconds in 147 seconds.

For a two-minute narration that means about 7 to 12 minutes per take, or roughly half an hour for three takes. It's slow, but it runs in the background. Loading the model also takes time, so I generate all the lines in one run.

Smaller things that helped

Some Chinese characters have more than one pronunciation, and the model sometimes picks the wrong one. When that happens I swap in a same-sounding character in the text sent to the model and keep the correct word in the subtitles. For example, 长连接 became 常连接, and 回调 became 回掉.

Not every video needs my voice, either. For quick news videos I use a preset voice from the CustomVoice version of the same model, which needs no reference audio.

Only clone voices you have permission to use

Clone your own voice, or a voice whose owner has agreed. Don't publish a cloned voice of anyone else.

Would a paid service be easier?

Probably. Hosted services such as ElevenLabs need no setup. I have since run the same script through ElevenLabs' free plan, and its stock Mandarin voices sounded more natural than my clone: ElevenLabs free plan vs a local open-source model.

Originally published on Hands-On AI Tools, where I test AI tools on real tasks. Cover: official Qwen3-TTS introduction graphic from the Qwen team's GitHub repository.

title: Handling Fatal Errors in Production: Lessons from Incident Investigation Protocols
description:
Handling Fatal Errors in Production: Lessons from Incident Investigation Protocols

When Systems Fail: Building Resilience Into Critical Workflows

The recent investigation into an on-field medical incident reminds us that some failures demand immediate, thorough response protocols. While the context is sports medicine, the operational lesson applies directly to fintech and payment systems: when a critical transaction or event fails, your investigation and recovery process can determine whether trust survives.

In payment systems, a "fatal error" isn't death—it's a failed ACH transfer, a reversed payout, or a settlement that never completed. Like a medical investigation, a payment incident requires:

  1. Immediate detection – Did the system know failure occurred?
  2. Root cause analysis – Which component failed, and why?
  3. Stakeholder notification – Who needs to know, and when?
  4. Recovery procedure – What's the next valid state?

ACH Return Codes as Incident Signals

When an ACH payout fails, NACHA return codes (R01–R85) are your incident classification system. Each code signals a specific failure mode:

Code Meaning Recovery Action
R01 Insufficient funds Retry after balance check; notify user
R03 No account/unable to locate Route to alternate payment method
R10 Unauthorized Verify authorization; escalate to compliance
R29 Corporate account closed Update account status; halt future attempts

Unlike a manual investigation, your code must detect and classify these codes automatically. A developer who treats all ACH returns as identical failures will lose customer trust faster than any single transaction.

Building an Incident Response Flow

Here's a production pattern for handling ACH returns without breaking your payout engine:

def handle_ach_return(return_code, payout_id, recipient_id):
    """
    Classify ACH return and route to appropriate recovery.
    """

    # Permanent failure: no recovery possible
    permanent_codes = ['R03', 'R04', 'R29', 'R31']

    # Temporary failure: safe to retry
    retryable_codes = ['R01', 'R09', 'R16', 'R20']

    # Requires manual review
    escalation_codes = ['R10', 'R37', 'R51']

    if return_code in permanent_codes:
        # Mark recipient account as invalid
        mark_account_invalid(recipient_id)
        notify_user(payout_id, "Account no longer valid. Please update.")
        return 'FAILED_PERMANENT'

    elif return_code in retryable_codes:
        # Schedule retry after 2 business days
        schedule_retry(payout_id, delay_days=2, max_attempts=3)
        return 'SCHEDULED_RETRY'

    elif return_code in escalation_codes:
        # Flag for compliance review
        escalate_to_support(payout_id, reason=return_code)
        return 'ESCALATED'

    else:
        # Unknown code: safe default is escalation
        log_unknown_return(payout_id, return_code)
        escalate_to_support(payout_id, reason=f"Unknown: {return_code}")
        return 'ESCALATED'

Timing and Notification

ACH returns arrive 1–5 business days after the original transfer attempt. Your system must:

  • Poll or subscribe to return notifications from your ACH provider (most offer webhooks or SFTP feeds)
  • Correlate returns to original payouts using trace numbers
  • Notify affected users within 24 hours of detecting the return
  • Avoid double-processing if a retry is scheduled

A developer who waits for a user to report a failed payout has already failed the incident response test.

The Broader Pattern

Whether investigating a medical incident or an ACH return, the principle is identical:

  1. Detect the failure signal immediately
  2. Classify it into a known category
  3. Route to the appropriate handler (retry, escalate, or terminal fail)
  4. Notify all stakeholders
  5. Log for audit and learning

In payment systems, this discipline isn't optional—it's the difference between a payout platform customers trust and one they abandon.

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: 评审意见别只写感想：/review 的 5 条硬规则
description:
说明：本文是整理，不是新实测。内容来自完整版 commands/review.md 原文与 /review 公开 Gist。/review 是 Lite 版 3 条命令之一（Lite 版免费就有 /review、/commit、/test），完整版同款命令，另含其余 7 条命令与三套模板、速查表。本文只讲 /review 这一条，不编造新实测。

1. 先读全再下判断，不确定的意图标 [推测]

/review 的第一步不是给意见，是把涉及的文件读完、理解意图后再说问题。不确定的意图标 [推测]，不按推测扣分。

没读全就评，评出来的多半是“这段代码为什么这样写”而不是“这段代码有什么问题”。接手一段陌生代码时这条尤其重要：先搞清它想干什么，再说它哪里不对。

2. 只说五个维度的真问题，不凑数

五个维度是：正确性（边界、空值、异常路径、并发）、安全（注入、敏感信息、权限、资源未释放）、可读性（命名、函数长度、注释是否说清“为什么”）、性能（只说明显的数量级问题，如 N+1、重复计算、大对象拷贝）、测试（关键分支是否有用例覆盖）。

每个维度只说真问题，某个维度没问题就空着，不为凑齐五个维度硬找。凑出来的意见接手的人改不动，还会把真正的问题淹没。

3. 分级输出，[必须改] 只留 bug 和安全问题

分三级：[必须改]（bug 或安全）/ [建议改]（可读性、性能）/ [可忽略]（个人偏好，最多 2 条）。

风格之争（单引号还是双引号）不在评审里讨论，用 linter 解决；“只想听夸奖”也不要用这个命令，它只说真话。分级的作用是让接手的人先改会出事的，再改可以更好的，最后才看个人偏好。

4. 每条意见固定四段式，给代码片段不只给方向

格式：文件:行号 — 问题一句话 — 为什么这是问题 — 改法建议（给代码片段，不只说“建议优化”）。

示例取自命令自带示例：orders.py:8 — 文件打开后未关闭，异常时泄漏句柄 — 用 with open(...) 包裹：

with open(path) as f:
return json.load(f)

没有“为什么”和“改法”，意见就落不了地；没有文件:行号，意见就找不到位置。评审结论也只有一句话：可合并 / 需修改后合并 / 建议重构。

5. 上限 10 条，超了先重构再评审

超过 10 条说明代码需要重构而不是评审：直接说“建议先重构再评审”并给出重构方向，不要把 30 条意见一次性倒出来。

同样，超过 500 行的大文件不要一次性评审，先拆小、按模块分次评审；代码还没写完、自己都知道是草稿的，先写完再评，半成品评审浪费双方时间。

不用 /review 的场景

  • 代码还没写完、自己都知道是草稿：先写完再评。
  • 只想听夸奖：这个命令只说真话。
  • 超过 500 行的大文件一次性评审：先拆小，按模块分次评审。
  • 风格之争：用 linter 解决，不在评审里讨论。

价格与链接

完整版中文 AI 编程 CLI 工作流包：早鸟 ¥9.90（限前 100 份），正式 ¥19.90。/review 本身在 Lite 版免费版中已有，完整版是 10 条命令全量。

  • Lite 版公开仓：https://github.com/alapha888/cn-ai-coding-workflow-lite
  • 爱发电商品页：https://afdian.com/item/8c9c0932bd7711f19eb852540025c377
  • /review 命令原文 Gist：https://gist.github.com/alapha888/bfad6db24e0971d4cbf87e778758615b

title: I built an AI assistant to understand GitHub codebases
description:
I built an AI assistant to help developers understand GitHub codebases

When I join an unfamiliar project, I often spend a lot of time searching through files just to understand how things fit together. I wanted to build a tool that could make exploring a codebase easier.

So I built CodeRAG Assistant.

What it does

CodeRAG Assistant lets you:

  • Index a GitHub repository and search its code by meaning or keywords.
  • Ask questions about the codebase in plain English.
  • See relevant source files alongside answers, so you can verify the context.
  • Generate an architecture and onboarding report for a public repository.

What I learned

Building this taught me that answering a question is only part of the experience. It also matters to show where the answer came from, make repository setup straightforward, and handle the small-screen experience carefully.

I’m still improving the product and would love feedback on what feels useful, confusing, or missing.

Try it

  • Live demo: https://coding-assistant-hazel.vercel.app/

I’m the creator of CodeRAG Assistant. If you try it, please let me know what you think!

title: How to Build an MCP Server in NestJS: Streamable HTTP, Guards and DI (Tested)
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

To build an MCP server in NestJS, install the official MCP TypeScript SDK (@modelcontextprotocol/server and @modelcontextprotocol/node), build one createMcpHandler inside an injectable service, and call it from a @Post('mcp') controller method that takes @Req() and @Res(). Put a Nest guard in front for the bearer token and Origin check, pass req.body to the handler, and your tools can use any provider through normal dependency injection.

I built exactly that on November 4, 2026 and tested it end to end: with curl, the MCP Inspector CLI, and 8 e2e tests that use the official MCP client against both protocol versions. Below is the full code, how the pieces fit, and five problems I hit that most tutorials skip, including one that turns every request into a Parse error.

Is there an official NestJS MCP module?

No. There is no @nestjs/mcp package: the npm registry returned 404 for it on November 4, 2026. You have two real options:

  • Wire the official SDK yourself, which is what this guide does. It came to about 180 lines across a provider, a service, a guard, a controller and two modules, and you control auth, scopes and errors.
  • Use the community module @rekog/mcp-nest (MIT, version 2.0.9, about 384,000 npm downloads in the week of October 27 to November 2, 2026). Its README describes it as a NestJS microservice transport strategy: tools are @Tool() methods on @McpController() classes, so Nest guards, pipes, interceptors and filters apply, and it serves Streamable HTTP and STDIO. It peer-depends on the same v2 SDK packages and isn't maintained by the NestJS team.

Hand-wiring is worth understanding even if you end up on the module, because the gotchas below come from how Nest and the SDK share one Express request.

What I tested

Everything ran on one Linux VM (8 vCPUs) on Node.js 24.22.1:

  • NestJS 12.3.2 with @nestjs/platform-express (Express 5.3.0)
  • @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.4.0 and @modelcontextprotocol/node 2.1.2, the v2 SDK
  • @modelcontextprotocol/client 2.4.0 for the e2e tests, MCP Inspector 2.13.0 for manual calls
  • Zod 4.6.7, TypeScript 6.0.3, tests on node:test

The demo is a small notes API: a NotesService provider, a search_notes tool any token can call, and a create_note tool only a write-scoped token can see. If you're new to the SDK itself, my guide on building an MCP server in Next.js covers tools, schemas and the v1 to v2 changes in more depth.

Step 1: Install the packages 

npm install @nestjs/common @nestjs/core @nestjs/platform-express reflect-metadata rxjs \
  @modelcontextprotocol/server @modelcontextprotocol/node zod
npm install -D typescript @types/node @types/express @nestjs/testing @modelcontextprotocol/client

NestJS 12 ships as ES modules ("type": "module" in @nestjs/core), so set "type": "module" in your package.json and use .js extensions in relative imports. The tsconfig.json I used:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "target": "ES2023",
    "experimentalDecorators": true,
    "emitDecoratorMetadata": true,
    "strict": true,
    "strictPropertyInitialization": false,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "outDir": "dist",
    "rootDir": "."
  },
  "include": ["src", "test"]
}

Step 2: A normal Nest provider for your data

The tools should call the same services your REST controllers already use. Here an in-memory store stands in for a Prisma or TypeORM repository:

// src/notes/notes.service.ts
import { Injectable } from "@nestjs/common";

export interface Note { id: number; title: string; body: string; owner: string; createdAt: string }

@Injectable()
export class NotesService {
  private notes: Note[] = [];
  private nextId = 1;

  search(owner: string, q?: string): Note[] {
    const needle = q?.toLowerCase();
    return this.notes.filter(
      (n) => n.owner === owner && (!needle || `${n.title} ${n.body}`.toLowerCase().includes(needle)),
    );
  }

  create(owner: string, title: string, body: string): Note {
    const note = { id: this.nextId++, title, body, owner, createdAt: new Date().toISOString() };
    this.notes.push(note);
    return note;
  }
}

Export it from a NotesModule (providers: [NotesService], exports: [NotesService]) like any shared provider.

Step 3: The MCP service (handler, tools and DI)

This is the core. createMcpHandler takes a factory that returns a fresh McpServer, and the SDK's HTTP guide says the factory runs once per HTTP request and receives the request context, including authInfo. That gives you two things in Nest:

  1. The factory is an arrow function inside an @Injectable() class, so every tool handler can use this.notes or any other injected provider.
  2. You can register a different set of tools per caller. A token without the write scope never sees create_note in tools/list. 
// src/mcp/mcp.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy } from "@nestjs/common";
import { createMcpHandler, McpServer, type McpRequestContext } from "@modelcontextprotocol/server";
import { toNodeHandler } from "@modelcontextprotocol/node";
import * as z from "zod/v4";
import { NotesService } from "../notes/notes.service.js";

@Injectable()
export class McpService implements OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(McpService.name);

  // Built once. The factory runs once per HTTP request, so every request gets a fresh McpServer.
  private readonly handler = createMcpHandler((ctx) => this.createServer(ctx), {
    responseMode: "json",
    onerror: (err) => this.logger.warn(err.message),
  });
  readonly node = toNodeHandler(this.handler);

  constructor(private readonly notes: NotesService) {}

  private createServer({ authInfo }: McpRequestContext): McpServer {
    const owner = authInfo?.clientId ?? "anonymous";
    const scopes = authInfo?.scopes ?? [];
    const server = new McpServer({ name: "notes", version: "1.0.0" });

    server.registerTool(
      "search_notes",
      {
        title: "Search notes",
        description: "Search the caller's notes by a word in the title or body. Returns at most 20.",
        inputSchema: z.object({ q: z.string().max(200).optional().describe("Text to match; omit to list all") }),
        annotations: { readOnlyHint: true },
      },
      async ({ q }) => {
        const hits = this.notes.search(owner, q).slice(0, 20);
        return { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(hits) }] };
      },
    );

    // Only tokens with the write scope ever see this tool in tools/list.
    if (scopes.includes("notes:write")) {
      server.registerTool(
        "create_note",
        {
          title: "Create note",
          description: "Save a new note for the caller.",
          inputSchema: z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(120), body: z.string().max(5000) }),
          outputSchema: z.object({ id: z.number(), title: z.string() }),
        },
        async ({ title, body }) => {
          const note = this.notes.create(owner, title, body);
          const out = { id: note.id, title: note.title };
          return { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(out) }], structuredContent: out };
        },
      );
    }
    return server;
  }

  async onModuleDestroy() {
    await this.handler.close();
  }
}

Notes on the choices:

  • toNodeHandler from @modelcontextprotocol/node adapts the fetch-style handler to Node's (req, res, parsedBody), which is what Express (and so Nest) gives you.
  • responseMode: "json" answers modern requests with one JSON body. The SDK prints a console warning when you set it, because progress and log notifications sent before the result are dropped. Leave it out if your tools stream progress.
  • handler.close() in onModuleDestroy aborts in-flight requests when Nest shuts down. Call app.enableShutdownHooks() so the hook runs on SIGTERM.
  • The owner comes from authInfo, not from tool arguments. The model can't ask for someone else's notes by passing a different user ID.

Step 4: A guard for the bearer token and Origin

The SDK checks no tokens and no Origin header on its own: authInfo is pass-through. A Nest guard is the natural place for both. The MCP transport spec says servers must validate Origin to stop DNS rebinding, and the SDK exports validateOriginHeader for that.

// src/mcp/mcp-auth.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, ForbiddenException, Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from "@nestjs/common";
import { createHash, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";
import { validateOriginHeader, type AuthInfo } from "@modelcontextprotocol/server";
import type { Request, Response } from "express";

const sha = (s: string) => createHash("sha256").update(s).digest();
const same = (a: string, b: string) => timingSafeEqual(sha(a), sha(b));

// token -> who it belongs to and what it may do. Load from env or a DB in a real app.
function tokenTable(): Array<{ token: string; clientId: string; scopes: string[] }> {
  return [
    { token: process.env.MCP_READ_TOKEN ?? "", clientId: "reader", scopes: ["notes:read"] },
    { token: process.env.MCP_WRITE_TOKEN ?? "", clientId: "writer", scopes: ["notes:read", "notes:write"] },
  ].filter((t) => t.token.length >= 32);
}

const ALLOWED_ORIGINS = (process.env.MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS ?? "localhost,127.0.0.1").split(",");

@Injectable()
export class McpAuthGuard implements CanActivate {
  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const http = ctx.switchToHttp();
    const req = http.getRequest<Request & { auth?: AuthInfo }>();

    // DNS rebinding / CSRF: a browser Origin must be on the list. No Origin (CLI, agents) passes.
    const origin = validateOriginHeader(req.headers.origin, ALLOWED_ORIGINS);
    if (!origin.ok) throw new ForbiddenException(origin.message);

    const m = /^Bearer\s+(\S+)$/i.exec(req.headers.authorization ?? "");
    const hit = m && tokenTable().find((t) => same(m[1], t.token));
    if (!hit) {
      http.getResponse<Response>().setHeader("WWW-Authenticate", 'Bearer realm="mcp"');
      throw new UnauthorizedException("Invalid or missing bearer token");
    }

    req.auth = { token: m[1], clientId: hit.clientId, scopes: hit.scopes };
    return true;
  }
}

The guard sets req.auth, and toNodeHandler reads exactly that property and hands it to your factory as authInfo. That one line is the bridge between Nest's auth and the MCP server. Hashing both tokens before timingSafeEqual keeps the comparison constant-time even when lengths differ, and tokens shorter than 32 characters are ignored so an empty env var can't open the endpoint. For OAuth instead of static tokens, see the MCP authorization spec and my notes on MCP security.

Step 5: The controller 

// src/mcp/mcp.controller.ts
import { All, Controller, Header, HttpCode, Post, Req, Res, UseGuards } from "@nestjs/common";
import type { Request, Response } from "express";
import { McpAuthGuard } from "./mcp-auth.guard.js";
import { McpService } from "./mcp.service.js";

@Controller("mcp")
export class McpController {
  constructor(private readonly mcp: McpService) {}

  @Post()
  @UseGuards(McpAuthGuard)
  async handle(@Req() req: Request, @Res() res: Response): Promise<void> {
    // With @Res() the SDK writes the response itself, so set headers on res directly.
    res.setHeader("Cache-Control", "no-store");
    // Pass req.body: Nest's JSON parser has already read the stream.
    await this.mcp.node(req, res, req.body);
  }

  // Stateless server: no GET stream, no DELETE session.
  @All()
  @HttpCode(405)
  @Header("Allow", "POST")
  notAllowed() {
    return { error: "Method not allowed" };
  }
}

Then the module and main.ts:

// src/mcp/mcp.module.ts
import { Module } from "@nestjs/common";
import { NotesModule } from "../notes/notes.module.js";
import { McpController } from "./mcp.controller.js";
import { McpService } from "./mcp.service.js";

@Module({ imports: [NotesModule], controllers: [McpController], providers: [McpService] })
export class McpModule {}

// src/main.ts
import "reflect-metadata";
import { NestFactory } from "@nestjs/core";
import type { NestExpressApplication } from "@nestjs/platform-express";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module.js";

const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);
// Express's JSON parser defaults to 100kb; the MCP SDK itself allows 4 MiB.
app.useBodyParser("json", { limit: "4mb" });
app.enableShutdownHooks();
await app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000), "127.0.0.1");
console.log(`MCP endpoint: ${await app.getUrl()}/mcp`);

AppModule just imports McpModule. Build with tsc, start with two tokens, and the endpoint is http://127.0.0.1:3000/mcp.

Step 6: Test it (curl, Inspector, e2e)

First the cheap checks with curl. Against my running server:

Request Result
POST /mcp with no token 401, WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="mcp"
POST /mcp with Origin: https://evil.example 403 Invalid Origin: evil.example
GET /mcp 405
tools/list with the read token search_notes only
tools/list with the write token search_notes, create_note

Then a real tool call with the MCP Inspector CLI. It takes the bearer token through --header:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://127.0.0.1:3000/mcp \
  --transport http --header "Authorization: Bearer $MCP_WRITE_TOKEN" \
  --method tools/call --tool-name create_note --tool-arg title=Hello --tool-arg body=From-inspector

It printed "structuredContent": { "id": 1, "title": "Hello" }.

For CI, boot the real Nest app on a random port with @nestjs/testing and drive it with the official client. This is a trimmed version of my test file; the full one has 8 tests and all passed:

// test/mcp.e2e.test.ts
import "reflect-metadata";
import { after, before, describe, it } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { randomBytes } from "node:crypto";
import { Test } from "@nestjs/testing";
import type { INestApplication } from "@nestjs/common";
import { Client, StreamableHTTPClientTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/client";

process.env.MCP_READ_TOKEN = randomBytes(24).toString("hex");
process.env.MCP_WRITE_TOKEN = randomBytes(24).toString("hex");
const { AppModule } = await import("../src/app.module.js");

let app: INestApplication;
let url: URL;

async function connect(token: string, mode: "auto" | "legacy" = "auto") {
  const client = new Client({ name: "e2e", version: "1.0.0" }, { versionNegotiation: { mode } });
  await client.connect(
    new StreamableHTTPClientTransport(url, { requestInit: { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } } }),
  );
  return client;
}

describe("NestJS MCP endpoint", () => {
  before(async () => {
    const mod = await Test.createTestingModule({ imports: [AppModule] }).compile();
    app = mod.createNestApplication({ logger: false });
    await app.listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
    url = new URL(`${await app.getUrl()}/mcp`.replace("[::1]", "127.0.0.1"));
  });
  after(() => app.close());

  for (const mode of ["auto", "legacy"] as const) {
    it(`scopes the tool list per token (${mode} handshake)`, async () => {
      const reader = await connect(process.env.MCP_READ_TOKEN!, mode);
      const writer = await connect(process.env.MCP_WRITE_TOKEN!, mode);
      assert.deepEqual((await reader.listTools()).tools.map((t) => t.name), ["search_notes"]);
      assert.deepEqual((await writer.listTools()).tools.map((t) => t.name).sort(), ["create_note", "search_notes"]);
      await reader.close(); await writer.close();
    });
  }

  it("runs tools through Nest DI and keeps data per caller", async () => {
    const writer = await connect(process.env.MCP_WRITE_TOKEN!);
    const reader = await connect(process.env.MCP_READ_TOKEN!);
    const created = await writer.callTool({ name: "create_note", arguments: { title: "Deploy notes", body: "rotate MCP tokens" } });
    assert.deepEqual(created.structuredContent, { id: 1, title: "Deploy notes" });
    const theirs = await reader.callTool({ name: "search_notes", arguments: { q: "rotate" } });
    assert.equal(JSON.parse((theirs.content as any)[0].text).length, 0);
    await writer.close(); await reader.close();
  });
});

The auto client negotiated protocol 2026-07-28 (the modern era) and the legacy client 2025-11-25, and the same factory served both. If you want the testing side in more depth (in-memory transport, Vitest, snapshots of tools/list), I wrote a separate guide on how to test an MCP server.

Five things that broke (and the fixes)

1. Forgetting req.body gives -32700 Parse error. Nest's JSON body parser reads the request stream before your controller runs. When I called this.mcp.node(req, res) without the third argument, every request got 400 with {"code":-32700,"message":"Parse error: Invalid JSON"}, because the SDK found an empty stream. Always pass req.body.

2. Nest's 100kb body limit answers before the SDK does. A 200 KB tools/call got 413 request entity too large from Express, not from the MCP server, so the client sees a plain HTTP error instead of a JSON-RPC one. The SDK's own default limit is 4 MiB (maxRequestBodySize). If your tools accept documents, raise Nest's limit with app.useBodyParser("json", { limit: "4mb" }). With that change, the same oversized call reached the SDK and came back as a normal tool error from Zod (q: Too big: expected string to have <=200 characters).

3. responseMode: "json" only shapes modern traffic. I logged the responses from both client modes. The 2026-07-28 client made two POSTs and got application/json both times. The 2025-11-25 client got text/event-stream for its requests even with responseMode: "json", plus a 202 for the initialized notification and a GET that my controller answered with 405. That's documented in the option's type comments: legacy traffic is served by a stateless fallback transport. Don't put a proxy in front that breaks SSE, or old clients fail.

4. @Header() is the wrong tool on the MCP route. With @Res(), the SDK calls writeHead itself. I set Cache-Control: no-store on res before handing it over: modern JSON responses kept it, but on legacy SSE responses the SDK's own Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform replaced it. Both stop caching, so it's fine, but set headers on res, not with decorators.

5. A hidden tool is a protocol error, not a tool error. When the read token called create_note, the client threw Tool create_note not found rather than returning an isError result. That's what you want for scoping: the tool doesn't exist for that caller. Bad arguments are different: an empty title came back as a normal result with isError: true and Input validation error: ... title: Too small, so the model can fix the call and retry.

How fast is a per-request MCP server in NestJS?

Fast enough to ignore. I made 500 sequential search_notes calls from one connected client after 50 warm-up calls, three runs per protocol mode, on localhost:

Mode p50 p95 p99
2026-07-28 (modern) 1.36 to 1.69 ms 1.94 to 2.73 ms 2.97 to 5.56 ms
2025-11-25 (legacy) 1.39 to 1.71 ms 2.05 to 2.97 ms 2.94 to 5.27 ms

The ranges are the lowest and highest of the three runs. That's the whole round trip: Nest routing, the guard, a fresh McpServer from the factory, Zod validation, the tool and the response. Your database call will dominate. A fresh server per request is how the SDK's HTTP guide says createMcpHandler works, and I covered the trade-offs of that stateless design in stateless MCP servers.

Should you use @rekog/mcp-nest instead?

Use the community module if you want decorators: tools declared as @Tool() methods on @McpController() classes, with Nest pipes and interceptors around them, and STDIO as well as HTTP. Hand-wire the SDK, as above, if you want per-token tool lists, your own guard and error format, or fewer dependencies between you and SDK updates. The SDK's v2 line only went stable in July 2026 (@modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0), so expect changes; with the hand-wired version I upgrade two packages and rerun my e2e tests. Either way, connect clients the same way: my guide on adding a remote MCP server to Cursor, Claude Code and VS Code shows the config for each.

FAQ

Is there an official NestJS MCP package?

No. As of November 4, 2026 the npm registry has no @nestjs/mcp package. You can wire the official MCP TypeScript SDK into a Nest controller yourself, or use the community module @rekog/mcp-nest (MIT, version 2.0.9), which is not maintained by the NestJS team.

Can I use NestJS dependency injection inside MCP tools?

Yes. Create the handler with createMcpHandler inside an @Injectable() service and register tools in a factory method on that class. Tool handlers then call injected providers through this, like any other Nest service. The factory runs once per HTTP request.

How do I add authentication to a NestJS MCP server?

Use a Nest guard on the POST /mcp route. Verify the bearer token, reject bad Origin headers with 403, and set req.auth to an object with token, clientId and scopes. The @modelcontextprotocol/node adapter passes req.auth to your server factory as authInfo, so you can scope data and tools per caller.

Why does my NestJS MCP endpoint return Parse error -32700?

Nest's JSON body parser has already consumed the request stream. Pass the parsed body as the third argument: toNodeHandler(handler)(req, res, req.body). Without it the SDK reads an empty stream and answers 400 with Parse error: Invalid JSON.

Does a NestJS MCP server work with older MCP clients?

Yes. createMcpHandler serves 2025-era clients through a stateless fallback by default. In my tests one endpoint answered a 2026-07-28 client with JSON and a 2025-11-25 client over SSE. Set legacy: "reject" if you only want the modern protocol.

title: pnpm vs npm Security in 2026: Install Scripts and Release Age, Tested
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Most npm malware runs the moment you install it, through a postinstall script, and it usually ships as a fresh patch release that gets pulled within hours or days. So the two package-manager settings that matter most for supply chain security are: does it run dependency install scripts by default, and will it install a version that was published an hour ago. I tested both on pnpm vs npm tonight with a harmless canary package and a real package that had just shipped a release. The defaults are not what most people assume, and they differ between npm 11 and npm 12.

pnpm vs npm security: results with default settings

Tested November 3, 2026 on Linux with Node 26.13.0.

npm 11.20.0 (bundled with Node 26.13) npm 12.2.1 (latest) pnpm 12.16.1
Dependency postinstall script ran, with a warning blocked, with a warning blocked, install exits with an error
Installs a version published 17 hours ago yes yes no (waits 1 day)
Approve a package's scripts npm approve-scripts <pkg> npm approve-scripts <pkg> allowBuilds in pnpm-workspace.yaml
Release-age setting min-release-age (days, off by default) min-release-age (days, off by default) minimumReleaseAge (minutes, default 1440)

Node 24.22.2 bundles npm 11.19.1, which has the same script settings as 11.20. If you use the npm that came with Node, you're on npm 11.

Test 1: does the install script run?

I made a local package whose only job is to write a file when its postinstall runs:

{
  "name": "install-canary",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "scripts": {
    "postinstall": "node -e \"require('fs').writeFileSync('/tmp/canary','ran')\""
  }
}

Then I packed it with npm pack and installed the tarball into an empty project with each tool, deleting /tmp/canary before each run.

npm 11.20.0 printed a warning and then ran the script anyway. /tmp/canary existed afterwards:

npm warn install-scripts 1 package has install scripts not yet covered by allowScripts:
npm warn install-scripts   install-canary@1.0.0 (postinstall: node -e "...")
npm warn install-scripts Run `npm install-scripts ls` to review, or `npm install-scripts approve <pkg>` to allow.

npm 12.2.1 printed a similar warning, but worded as "had install scripts blocked", and the canary file was not created.

pnpm 12.16.1 didn't run the script and exited with code 1:

× adding a new package
╰─▶ Ignored build scripts: install-canary@file:../canary/install-canary-1.0.0.tgz
help: Run "pnpm approve-builds" to pick which dependencies should be allowed to run scripts.

The packages were still written to node_modules, but the failing exit code means CI stops instead of quietly continuing. pnpm's docs call this strictDepBuilds, and it's on by default.

I got the same pattern with esbuild@0.28.2, a real package with a legitimate postinstall: npm 11 ran it with a warning, npm 12 blocked it, and pnpm blocked it and failed.

Allowing the scripts you trust

With npm (11.19+ and 12), approve per package. The approval is pinned to the exact version:

npm approve-scripts esbuild
node -p "JSON.stringify(require('./package.json').allowScripts)"
# {"esbuild@0.28.2":true}

Because the approval is pinned, a new esbuild release will be flagged again, which is exactly when you want to look.

With pnpm, list trusted packages in pnpm-workspace.yaml:

allowBuilds:
  esbuild: true

With that file in place, pnpm add esbuild@0.28.2 finished with exit code 0. pnpm approve-builds gives you an interactive picker for the same thing.

Test 2: will it install a brand-new release?

The ai package published 7.0.162 at 01:19 UTC on November 3, about 17 hours before I ran this. The previous releases were 7.0.161 and 7.0.160 on November 2, and 7.0.159 on October 30.

Command Installed
npm i ai (npm 11.20.0) 7.0.162
npm i ai (npm 12.2.1) 7.0.162
npm i ai --min-release-age=1 (npm 11.20.0) 7.0.159
pnpm add ai (pnpm 12.16.1, defaults) 7.0.159

Both npm versions installed the newest release by default. pnpm skipped everything younger than 24 hours because minimumReleaseAge defaults to 1440 minutes, as described in pnpm's supply chain security docs. npm's min-release-age does the same once you set it, but it's measured in days and is off by default.

Note that the cooldown cuts both ways. A real security fix published today also waits. Both tools let you exempt packages: min-release-age-exclude in npm, minimumReleaseAgeExclude in pnpm. With minimumReleaseAgeExclude: [ai] in pnpm-workspace.yaml, pnpm installed 7.0.162 straight away.

Recommended settings for each

npm

In the project's .npmrc:

min-release-age=3
strict-allow-scripts=true

Then approve the few packages that genuinely need install scripts with npm approve-scripts <pkg>, and commit the allowScripts field in package.json. If you're still on npm 11, upgrading to npm 12 gets you blocking by default: npm i -g npm@12.

pnpm

In pnpm-workspace.yaml:

minimumReleaseAge: 4320        # 3 days, in minutes
trustPolicy: no-downgrade      # refuse a version with weaker publish provenance than earlier ones
allowBuilds:
  esbuild: true
  sharp: true

Script blocking, strictDepBuilds and blockExoticSubdeps (no git or tarball URLs deep in the tree) are already on by default.

Both

  • Commit the lockfile and install with npm ci / pnpm install --frozen-lockfile in CI. The release-age window matters when versions get resolved, which is when the lockfile changes, so review lockfile diffs in pull requests.
  • Don't run installs with secrets in the environment. If a script does slip through, it can read whatever env vars the install step has.
  • Build Docker images from the lockfile. My Next.js Dockerfile installs from the lockfile in a separate deps stage.

If you write server code that fetches user-supplied URLs, SSRF protection in Node.js covers the other half of keeping a Node app safe.

So, is pnpm more secure than npm?

With default settings, yes, in both tests: pnpm blocked the install script and failed the install, and it refused a 17-hour-old release. npm 12 now blocks install scripts by default too, but still installs brand-new releases unless you set min-release-age. npm 11, which is what ships with Node 24 and Node 26 today, only warns about install scripts. Configured properly, npm 11.19+ and npm 12 can match pnpm on both points. The difference is what you get if you never touch the config.

FAQ

Does pnpm run postinstall scripts?

Not for dependencies, unless you allow them. pnpm 12.16.1 skipped my canary's postinstall and exited with Ignored build scripts. Allow trusted packages with allowBuilds in pnpm-workspace.yaml or by running pnpm approve-builds.

Does npm block install scripts by default?

npm 12 does: version 12.2.1 blocked my canary's postinstall. npm 11.20.0, the version bundled with Node 26.13.0, only printed a warning and ran the script. Set strict-allow-scripts=true or upgrade to npm 12.

What is minimumReleaseAge in pnpm?

It's the number of minutes a version must have been published before pnpm will install it. It defaults to 1440 (one day). In my test, pnpm installed ai@7.0.159 instead of the 17-hour-old 7.0.162.

What is min-release-age in npm?

An npm config option, measured in days, that makes npm ignore versions published more recently than that. It's off by default. npm i ai --min-release-age=1 installed 7.0.159 instead of the 17-hour-old 7.0.162.

Is pnpm safer than npm?

With default settings, pnpm blocked more in my tests: it refused to run dependency install scripts and refused a release under 24 hours old. npm can be configured to do both with strict-allow-scripts and min-release-age.

title: What is Mounting in React?
description:
Mounting is the first phase of a React component's lifecycle.
When a component is created and displayed on the screen for the first time, it is called Mounting.

  1. Mounting steps
  2. Component Function Runs – React executes the component.
  3. DOM Creation – React prepares the UI.
  4. DOM Update – React displays the UI on the screen.
  5. useEffect Runs – The effect runs after the component is displayed.

Example:

import React, { useEffect } from 'react';

function App() {

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Component Mounted");
}, []);

return (
    <h1>Hello React!</h1>
);

}

export default App;

Output:

Hello React!

Console:

Component Mounted

title: I Built a RAG Assistant That Explains Your Electricity Bill — Without Letting the AI Invent Numbers
description:
Pakistani electricity bills are hard to read even when you're technical. The total jumps month to month, and the bill itself doesn't really explain why — slabs, categories, rates, and surcharges all blur together. Most people just pay it and move on.

I built BijliCheck at a hackathon to attack that confusion directly: a Bill Checker web app with an "Ask about your bill" AI assistant box. You check your bill, then you ask it questions about it in plain English — "why did my bill jump so much?", "how do I avoid this next time?" — and it answers using your actual numbers, not generic advice.

How it works

There are two halves, and the order matters.

First, the Bill Checker. You open the site, fill in your usage, and click "Check my bill." That produces your computed bill numbers: units, category, rate, and total. Nothing about the assistant works without this step, because the assistant's job is to explain these numbers — not to guess at bills in general.

Second, the assistant. It uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), in three steps:

  1. Retrieve. Your question is matched against a small local knowledge base of slab rules and billing facts, using keyword-based matching. This runs instantly in the browser — no API call for this step at all.
  2. Augment. The matched facts are combined with your computed bill numbers (units, category, rate, total) into a single prompt.
  3. Generate. That prompt goes to a free LLM (Groq), which writes a plain-English answer grounded in what was retrieved and your numbers.

The user sees the retrieved reference facts listed first, then the generated answer. That ordering is deliberate: you can see what the answer is based on before you read the answer itself.

The design decision that matters most

The assistant is not allowed to invent tariff numbers that were not given to it. That's the whole point of the RAG setup here. A plain chatbot asked about electricity bills will happily produce confident-sounding rates that may be wrong — and a wrong number on a bill is worse than no answer at all. By forcing every answer through retrieved facts plus the user's own computed numbers, the system trades fluency for grounding. The answer might be less smooth than a free-form chat, but it can't hallucinate a slab rate.

There's a second, quieter lesson in the retrieval step: RAG doesn't have to mean a vector database. For a small, well-understood set of facts — slab rules and billing facts — keyword matching over a local knowledge base is fast, free, and runs entirely in the browser. The fancy version of a technique is not always the right version. Match the retrieval method to the size of your knowledge base.

The architecture is deliberately boring

The whole thing is HTML and JavaScript — no framework — hosted on Vercel for free, connected directly to the GitHub repository. The one piece that isn't static is a single tiny serverless function in the api/ folder. It exists for one reason: the API key has to stay secret, and a purely static host can't keep a secret. So the browser does the retrieval, and the serverless function makes the one call that needs the key.

Total setup cost: $0, on Groq's free tier, in about 15 minutes. If the Ask box ever says "offline mode," it means that serverless endpoint isn't reachable — usually the API key wasn't set or the deployment wasn't redeployed after adding it. That's a deployment detail, but it's the kind of thing that eats an hour at a hackathon if you don't know where to look.

Three lessons I'd pass on

  1. Ground the model before you prompt it. Retrieval first, generation second. The order is the safety mechanism.
  2. Show your sources. Listing the retrieved facts before the answer lets the user judge the answer instead of just trusting it.
  3. Keep the demo shippable. A static frontend, one serverless function, and a free-tier model got a working hackathon demo live at zero cost. Complexity can come later, after the idea is proven.

BijliCheck started as a hackathon demo, but the pattern generalises: any domain where the model must not invent numbers — bills, tariffs, schedules, policies — benefits from the same shape. Compute the real numbers first, retrieve the real rules, and only then let the model talk.

Malik Ali Hassan — .NET & full-stack developer, final-year Software Engineering student. I build Python automation, AI assistants, and web apps.

title: A Vitest test that fails when anyone types one of our prices
description:
We run BaseAcross, a site for founders outside the US forming US companies. A price on a site like ours shows up in more places than you'd guess: the landing page, the pricing table, the checkout total, guides, FAQ answers, glossary entries, emails, JSON-LD offers and the llms.txt file. On 29 October 2026 our founder said our pricing didn't look consistent across pages.

So we audited it. We fetched all 516 URLs in the sitemap and checked 16,540 dollar amounts against the catalogue. No page printed a wrong number for a product we were selling. The inconsistency he saw was real, and it came from three other places:

  1. Plans we no longer sold still had prices on the site, including JSON-LD offers on three pages. A reader who clicked through would find a different plan at a different price on the order form.
  2. An add-on that was switched off was still priced in one guide.
  3. One state charges an LLC and a corporation different yearly amounts. Both totals were correct, and different pages showed different ones without saying which was which.

The audit also counted state fees typed by hand into prose: 69 Wyoming and Delaware fee figures across 16 files, each one right on the day it was typed. Each of them would stay put the next time the state changed its fee.

What follows is the setup we built after it: one home for every figure, tokens for prose, and a test that walks every string in src/ looking for a price somebody typed.

The catalogue is the only place a price may live

Plans, add-ons and the state fees we pass on live in src/lib/data/catalog-picks.ts and a short list of product modules beside it. Public pages read plansOnSale, a filtered view of the catalogue, and a page that names one plan goes through a helper that throws for a retired one:

export const plansOnSale: PlanPick[] = planPicks.filter((plan) => plan.onSale);

/** A plan by key, for a page that names one: throws for a retired plan. */
export function planOnSale(key: PlanKey): PlanPick {
  const plan = plansOnSale.find((p) => p.key === key);
  if (!plan) throw new Error(`Plan ${key} is not on sale.`);
  return plan;
}

The arithmetic gets the same treatment. Whether a plan includes the state's filing fee is decided in one function, and everything that adds a state fee to a plan price calls it:

/**
 * Everything that adds a state fee to a plan price goes through here, so the
 * figure on the pricing table, the one in the wizard's running total, the one
 * on the review and the one Stripe charges cannot disagree again.
 */
export function stateFeeFor(plan: Pick<PlanPick, "coversStateFee">, state: { stateFee: number }) {
  return plan.coversStateFee ? 0 : state.stateFee;
}

Formatting has one home too. money() prints whole amounts without cents and keeps cents only when an amount has them, because a page showing a rounded figure next to a card charge with cents looks like a mistake even when it's a rounding choice:

export function money(value: number, options: Intl.NumberFormatOptions = {}) {
  const places = Number.isInteger(value) ? 0 : 2;
  return new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", {
    style: "currency", currency: "USD",
    minimumFractionDigits: places, maximumFractionDigits: places,
    ...options,
  }).format(value);
}

Prose gets tokens instead of template literals

Code was already reading the catalogue. The 69 typed fees were all in prose, and they were typed for a plain reason: writing ${money(DE.annualCost)} in the middle of a long guide paragraph is clumsy, so people typed the number. The fix had to keep plain strings for the people writing them.

So prose now writes a token, and prices() swaps it for the catalogue's figure when the module that holds the text loads:

const TOKEN = /\{((?:price|fee|addon|total)\.[A-Za-z0-9.]+)\}/g;

export function prices(text: string): string {
  return text.replace(TOKEN, (_, name: string) => {
    const amount = PRICE_TOKENS[name];
    if (amount === undefined) throw new Error(`Unknown price token {${name}}`);
    return money(amount);
  });
}

A sentence in a guide reads like this (an illustration in the shape our data files use):

a: prices("Launch is {price.launch} a year, and Delaware then charges {fee.DE.annual.llc} for an LLC."),

PRICE_TOKENS is built from the catalogue: plan prices, add-ons, every state fee field, and a few totals such as a plan plus the state's filing fee. Three properties fall out of that.

  • A typo like {fee.DE.anual.llc} throws when the module loads, so it fails the build and never reaches a reader.
  • A retired plan has no token, so its price can't be written into a page. prices("{price.build}") is a test case that must throw.
  • The regex only matches the four token families, so the add-on blurbs' own {state} and {turnaround} placeholders pass through for their own filler.

The test reads every string in src/

Tokens only help if people use them. src/lib/price-literals.test.ts checks that they do. It builds the set of every amount the catalogue charges or passes on, formatted by money(), then parses every .ts and .tsx file with the TypeScript compiler API and looks at string literals, template literals and JSX text:

if (ts.isStringLiteral(node) || ts.isNoSubstitutionTemplateLiteral(node)) {
  words = node.text;
  context = words;
} else if (ts.isJsxText(node)) {
  words = node.text;
  context = node.parent.getText();
}
// … template expressions are read with their ${} holes blanked out

for (const m of words.matchAll(AMOUNT)) {
  if (!guarded.has(m[0])) continue;   // not one of our figures
  if (!OURS.test(context)) continue;  // not next to our words
  // … allow-list check, then report file:line and the words around it
}

We parse instead of grepping so that comments are never read. A comment can explain where a figure came from without failing the build. Code that computes a figure from the catalogue isn't text, so it passes too.

A failure prints file:line $X | the 80 characters either side, so it shows the sentence as well as the line.

Keeping false positives down

A site about company formation is full of dollar figures that aren't ours: other providers' prices, other states' fees, worked examples of a payment. The test filters in layers.

  • AMOUNT matches a whole figure, so a larger amount that starts with the same digits isn't read as one of ours.
  • Only figures equal to one we charge or pass on count.
  • Only figures in a string that also contains one of our words count: a state we form in, a plan name, "state fee", or "we" and "our".
  • The catalogue modules themselves are exempt, along with the token resolver.
  • Anything left goes on an allow-list, and the allow-list is held to its own rules: 
const ALLOW: { file?: RegExp; near?: RegExp; amounts?: string[]; reason: string }[] = [
  { file: /^lib\/site\/data\/competitors\.ts$/, reason: "Rivals' prices, as each publishes them." },
  { file: /^lib\/site\/sources\.ts$/, reason: "The source's own words, which the source check looks for." },
  { near: /authori[sz]ed shares|…/, amounts: ["$…"], reason: "Delaware's authorised-shares franchise tax, not a certificate fee." },
  // …
];

it("keeps the allow-list small, each entry with its reason", () => {
  expect(ALLOW.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(12);
  for (const a of ALLOW) {
    expect(a.reason.length).toBeGreaterThan(10);
    if (a.near) expect(a.amounts?.length, a.reason).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  }
});

The last rule matters most. An entry matched by nearby words has to name the exact amounts it lets through, so a second figure typed into the same sentence still fails.

What it doesn't catch

The guarded set is today's catalogue. If a price changes and an old figure is still typed somewhere, that old figure no longer matches anything and the test passes. The test catches a literal at the moment it's written, while it still equals a real price. The literals that were already there had to be found by the audit and converted by hand.

Retired plans needed their own tests for the same reason. One asserts that only the two plans on sale are on sale. One checks that structured data offers only those plans. One serialises the add-on pages, guides, glossary and FAQ and fails on a retired plan's name or price. That last matcher needed care, because one retired plan was called "Build", which is also a verb, so it only matches the name in plan-shaped phrases like "on Build" or "Build plan".

Beyond that, the test only knows dollar-sign figures, and "we" and "our" are a blunt way to decide whose number it is. We'd rather take the occasional allow-list entry than miss a real one. The audit found 69 typed fees, each right on the day it was typed; the test's own header says it exists so the 70th is caught when it's written.

Drafted with AI assistance and checked against our code and the sources it cites.

title: How to Build a Super-Agent Like DeepSeek's: Router, Workers and Triggers Explained
description:
To build a super-agent like the one DeepSeek Harness describes, split your agent into two layers: one long-lived Router session that talks to humans and dispatches work, and many isolated Worker sessions that each run one task with full tools. Feed both from event Triggers (chat, GitHub, CI), route follow-ups by Thread, and add a separate Watchdog that checks on everything.

Try Apidog today

This guide turns DeepSeek Harness's design essay, "Exploring Super-agent Design", into a build order. One caveat: the essay describes architecture, not a shipped feature. Parts of it live in a prototype plugin called dsh-superagent-prototype, which the authors say is "not an official DeepSeek product." Every code sketch below is illustrative, not DeepSeek's code.

What is a super-agent?

A super-agent is a single, always-online AI teammate that receives events from many channels (chat, pull requests, CI), runs many tasks in parallel in isolated sessions, and replies to people as one consistent identity.

The problem: agent sessions are isolated, and "a person can usually follow only 3 to 5 active sessions at once." A single task is limited by the model. Multi-tasking is limited by human attention. The super-agent targets the second limit.

It has four traits:

  • Continuous: one agent across IM and GitHub. You discuss Plan A in chat, switch to Plan B in a PR comment, and it follows.
  • Productive: it runs tasks in parallel and takes your next instruction before the last one finishes.
  • Proactive: it watches events and stays quiet unless something needs it.
  • Persistent: it's always online and recovers on its own.

If you're new to the harness itself, start with what DeepSeek Harness is and how it compares with Claude Code.

Super-agent architecture: the five modules

The essay has five modules. Here they are with the step where you'd build each:

Module What it does Build step
Two-level architecture Router dispatches, Workers execute 1
Event-driven Triggers Turn chat, GitHub and CI events into agent input 2
Full-duplex, multi-channel Async tools, channel-aware replies 4
Compute, state, environment split Stateless loop, state in a DB, machines stay put 5
Watchdog Separate session that checks progress and errors 6

Step 1: Split the Router from the Workers

The Router is one long-lived session. It handles all human interaction and all dispatch, and it never executes tasks itself. It can run without a Bash tool, and a lighter, cheaper model is enough. When several Triggers arrive during one Router turn, they're batched into the next call: long input, short output, merged in prefill.

Each Worker is one isolated session per task. It gets full tools and the strongest model you can afford. It never talks to humans; it reports back to the Router. A Worker can itself use subagents, or be a whole agent team.

Don't confuse this with an agent team. A team lead decomposes one coupled task; the Router only dispatches independent tasks. You can stack them.

# Illustrative sketch, not DeepSeek's code
class Router:
    def on_events(self, batch):              # triggers arriving mid-turn are batched
        plan = self.llm_light.decide(batch)  # dispatch, reply, or ignore
        for task in plan.new_tasks:
            Worker.spawn(task, model="strongest", tools="all", report_to=self)
        for msg in plan.replies:
            self.channels.send(msg)          # only the Router speaks to humans

Step 2: Turn events into Triggers

Every input to a super-agent is a Trigger: a chat message, a GitHub webhook event, a Slack Events API payload or a CI callback. Most of them shouldn't reach a model at all, so the essay filters in two passes.

  1. Fast path, in code. Filter by source, group, and user or bot allowlists. Each source gets a mode: "respond only to explicit requests," "candidate," or "ignore."
  2. Slow path, with an LLM. Candidates go to a model that applies policies written as prompts, such as "reply when someone reports a bug in this channel."

Your intake endpoint should acknowledge fast and work later. GitHub's webhook best practices ask you to respond with a 2XX within 10 seconds, which a model call can't promise. Return 202 Accepted, queue the Trigger, and let the Router pick it up. Our guide to designing reliable webhooks covers retries and idempotency for this layer.

Step 3: Route follow-ups by Thread

A Thread is a run of consecutive events on one PR, one IM topic or one email chain. The Worker created for a Thread's first event subscribes to it. Follow-up events then pass straight to that Worker, with no Router call.

The mapping is many-to-many. If two Workers touch the same PR, both receive its events, and they can resolve conflicts through the PR itself without messaging each other directly.

Skip this step and you pay: in the essay's experiment, removing pass-through made the Router take about 30% more decisions and raised token use by about 37%.

Step 4: Treat context as a cache and make tools async

The Router can't hold everything, so the essay treats context like a cache:

  • Inline what's likely needed: IDs, short summaries, neighboring messages.
  • Spill the rest: truncate it and leave a pointer the agent can follow.

Stable IDs on Triggers, Threads and Workers form a reference graph the authors call a "Chain of Recall." The agent hops from a Trigger to its Thread to the Worker that handled it, which gives it multi-hop recall without a giant prompt.

Then go full-duplex. Replace a blocking run() tool with async start() and stop(). start() returns "Started" right away, and the result arrives later as a new event. That's what lets the agent take your next instruction while the last one is still running. The essay says DeepSeek Harness implements this but doesn't enable it by default.

Finally, make replies channel-aware. Their tested rule caps IM replies at 100 words, while GitHub, email and docs get structured, dense write-ups.

It also enables speculative execution: in their user group, a "silently reproduce and fix" policy delivers only a confirmed simple fix and otherwise stays quiet.

Step 5: Separate compute, state and environments

Run the agent loop in stateless cloud containers and keep session state in a database. Environments stay where they are: each machine runs a lightweight daemon, which the essay calls BYOM (Bring Your Own Machine). A crashed loop restarts anywhere and reloads its state, while repos stay on their machines.

The essay points to Anthropic's "Scaling Managed Agents: Decoupling the brain from the hands" as the same idea, aimed at managed sandboxes rather than your own machines.

Step 6: Add a Watchdog

The Watchdog is a separate session on a schedule, outside the main system. It handles API errors and asks a model whether each Worker is making progress or drifting. Maintainers can also ask it directly why something failed. Keep it outside the Router's process so a stuck Router can't take its monitor down.

What the experiments showed

The authors ran about 300 chat and CI messages containing about 20 work requests, simulated the coding with a timer, and ran each setup 5 times. They call the results "indicative only."

Setup p50 (min) p95 (min) Cache-read tokens per run
Super-agent 12.4 15.7 23.2M
Without Thread pass-through 12.6 15.5 31.8M
Single session + subagent tool, neutral prompt 20.4 29.5 6.1M
Single session, delegation-first prompt 13.8 29.0 10.8M

Two findings stand out. With a neutral prompt, the single session never delegated in 5 runs, so its p95 was nearly double the super-agent's. A delegation-first prompt fixed the median but not the tail. The super-agent costs more tokens than a single session, so you're trading tokens for latency and attention.

A second test loaded the Router alone. As Triggers rose from 1 to 40 per minute, batch size grew from 1.0 to 2.8 and time per request went from 2.5 s to 3.9 s, while time per decision fell from 6.4 s to 1.6 s. Batching is what keeps a single Router from becoming the bottleneck early.

Test your Trigger intake with Apidog CLI

Every Trigger starts life as an HTTP request hitting your intake endpoint, so that endpoint is the first thing worth testing. If it drops a PR comment or assigns a new thread_id to each event, Thread routing breaks and every follow-up goes back through the Router. Let your coding agent write and run that test with Apidog CLI.

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog auth login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Then give your agent one [REDACTED PROMPT]
In Apidog project , create POST /triggers/github for a GitHub
pull_request_review_comment webhook. Add a test case that sends two
comments on the same PR and asserts: status 202, a trigger_id in the
body, and the same thread_id both times. Run it against staging and
summarize any failures.


The agent reads each payload schema, validates its JSON, writes the endpoint and the case, and runs it:


bash
apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create
apidog cli-schema validate endpoint-create --file endpoint.json
apidog endpoint create --project --file endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project --file case.json
apidog run --test-case --project -e -r cli,json




The same `apidog run` call with `-r junit` drops into your pipeline; see [Apidog CLI in CI/CD](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-cli-ci-cd-pipeline?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). If your agent is DeepSeek Harness itself, follow [this setup guide](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-cli-in-deepseek-harness?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation); for Claude Code, use [this one](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-cli-in-claude-code?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Apidog's Free plan covers up to 4 users.

## Open problems

The essay lists what isn't solved:

- **Scaling the Router** and choosing a Worker topology as load grows.
- **Long-term memory** beyond the Chain of Recall.
- **UX without sessions:** steering an agent with no single chat window.
- **Context boundaries and agent-to-agent protocols**, where [A2A](http://apidog.com/blog/what-is-agent2agent-a2a?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) is one candidate.
- **Security.** A prompt injection that reaches the cloud loop could reach every connected machine, and credentials in context can leak. The authors want agents to use credentials without ever seeing them.

## FAQ

**Is the super-agent a DeepSeek Harness feature I can turn on?** No. The essay describes architecture. Parts exist in the `dsh-superagent-prototype` plugin, which the authors say is not an official DeepSeek product. Full-duplex tools are implemented but off by default.

**Why does the Router use a lighter model?** It only dispatches and talks to people; it never executes tasks or needs Bash. Workers do the heavy reasoning with the strongest model.

**How is a super-agent different from an agent team?** A team lead splits one coupled task into parts. The Router dispatches independent tasks. A Worker can run its own agent team inside the super-agent.

**What is Thread pass-through?** Follow-up events on a PR, IM topic or email chain go straight to the Worker that owns that Thread, skipping the Router. Removing it raised token use by about 37% in their test.

**Does a super-agent save tokens?** Not against a single session. It used 23.2M cache-read tokens per run versus 6.1M to 10.8M, in exchange for a p95 of 15.7 minutes instead of about 29.

title: Prompt Caching, Explained: How Claude Reuses Your Prompt Prefix — and When It Doesn't Pay Off
description:
If you build anything that talks to Claude more than once — a chatbot, a coding agent, a document Q&A tool — you are probably paying to process the same text over and over again. Every API request is stateless: the model re-reads your system prompt, your tool definitions, and the whole conversation history each time. Prompt caching is Anthropic's answer to that waste. It lets the API reuse a previously processed prefix of your prompt instead of processing it again.

This is not a different model or a new endpoint. It is a way of marking part of your request as reusable. Here is how it works, what it costs, and where it quietly stops working.

What gets cached: a prefix, not a paragraph

A cache entry covers the start of your request, up to a breakpoint you mark. Anthropic's docs describe the prefix as being built in a fixed order: tool definitions first, then the system prompt, then the message history. Everything from the very first token up to and including your breakpoint becomes one cacheable unit.

That ordering is the whole design discipline. Put the content that rarely changes at the beginning — your tools, your system instructions, your background documents, your few-shot examples — and put the thing that changes every request at the end. If the variable part sits inside the cached prefix, the prefix is different on every request and nothing is ever reused.

Two ways to turn it on

Automatic caching is the simplest start: add a single cache_control field at the top level of your request, and the system places the breakpoint on the last cacheable block for you. As a multi-turn conversation grows, the breakpoint moves forward automatically, so each new request reads the earlier turns from cache and writes only the newest exchange.

Explicit breakpoints give you finer control. You place cache_control directly on individual content blocks — for example, one breakpoint after your system prompt and another after a large reference document that updates daily. You can define up to 4 breakpoints in a request, which also helps when a long conversation grows past the 20-block lookback window the docs describe: each breakpoint gets its own backward search for a prior cache entry.

Breakpoints themselves cost nothing. You pay only for cache writes, cache reads, and the uncached tokens in each request.

What it costs

By default, a cache entry lives for 5 minutes, and reading it refreshes that lifetime at no extra charge. The lifetime is measured from the start of the request that writes or reads the entry, not from the end of the response — so a response that takes 4 minutes to stream leaves only about 1 minute for the follow-up to reuse the same prefix.

The price structure, per Anthropic's documentation:

  • Cache writes (5-minute TTL) cost 25% more than base input tokens.
  • Cache reads cost 10% of the base input price for most models, with exceptions: 0.025x for Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and 0.05x for Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • A 1-hour TTL is available at 2x the base input price for writes.

A concrete example from the pricing table: for Claude Sonnet 4.6, base input is $3 per million tokens, a 5-minute cache write is $3.75, a 1-hour write is $6, and a cache read is $0.30. So the second request that reuses a large prefix is dramatically cheaper than the first — but the first request is slightly more expensive than it would be without caching. Caching only pays off when the prefix is actually reused.

The minimums and the traps

Not every prompt is eligible. There is a minimum cacheable prompt length, which varies by model — for example, 1,024 tokens for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Sonnet 4.5, and 512 tokens for newer models such as Claude Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Haiku 5.5. A short system prompt will simply never be cached, silently.

The most common failure mode is documented with unusual clarity: a breakpoint placed on a block that changes every request — say, a message containing a fresh timestamp — produces a different prefix hash each time. The lookback walks backward looking for entries that prior requests actually wrote, and since no prior request wrote an entry at an earlier position, there is no hit. You pay for a fresh cache write on every request and never get a read. The fix is to move the breakpoint to the last block that stays identical across requests.

Two more rules worth knowing:

  • The cache is per model. Switching models mid-conversation starts cold.
  • Automatic and explicit breakpoints can conflict. If the last block already has an explicit breakpoint with a different TTL, the API returns a 400 error, and if 4 explicit breakpoints already exist there is no slot left for automatic caching.

A practical checklist

  1. Order your request: static content first, varying content last.
  2. Start with automatic caching — one top-level cache_control field — unless you have sections that change at different frequencies.
  3. Put explicit breakpoints at the end of each stable section, never on a block containing a timestamp or per-request data.
  4. Check that your stable prefix clears the model's minimum token threshold; otherwise nothing is cached at all.
  5. If your turns are long, add a second breakpoint so a growing conversation does not push the last cache write outside the 20-block lookback window.
  6. Choose the 5-minute TTL for active conversations and the 1-hour TTL only when gaps between requests are long enough to justify the 2x write price.

Prompt caching does not make the model smarter, and it does not change what the model outputs. It just stops you from paying full price to re-read the same instructions for the hundredth time. Used with the prefix discipline above, that is one of the cheapest wins available in a production LLM app.

All pricing and behavior details in this article are from Anthropic's prompt caching documentation: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching — re-check the page before relying on a number, since pricing and minimums change.
