title: 2,000 TripAdvisor reviews in 62 seconds for one cent: what one Times Square hotel's guests actually complain about
description:
TripAdvisor shows a hotel's all-time score at the top of the page. For an old hotel with 18,000 reviews, that number mostly describes stays from years ago. If you want to know what guests say now, you need the recent reviews themselves, in a table.

So we pulled them. One run of our TripAdvisor Reviews Scraper on Apify, pointed at the Hotel Edison Times Square, asking for 2,000 reviews:

  • Time: 62 seconds.
  • Cost: $0.0096 of compute on our side. A user pays $0.50 per 1,000 reviews on the Starter tier, so this run is $1.00 for anyone else.
  • Coverage: 2,000 reviews from 12 Dec 2024 to 3 Nov 2026, plus one row for the hotel itself.

Every number below comes from that one run. Reviews are written by members of the public, so this post shows counts only: no reviewer names and no quotes from reviews.

The input 

{
  "startUrls": [
    { "url": "https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g60763-d93437-Reviews-Hotel_Edison_Times_Square-New_York_City_New_York.html" }
  ],
  "maxReviewsPerPlace": 2000
}

Any TripAdvisor review page works the same way: hotels, restaurants and attractions, on any TripAdvisor country site. Filters are optional: ratings (for example only 1 and 2 stars), reviewsSince, languages, tripTypes (family, couples, solo, business, friends), reviewsContaining and sortBy.

From Python:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("locaihost/tripadvisor-reviews").call(run_input={
    "startUrls": [{"url": "https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g60763-d93437-Reviews-Hotel_Edison_Times_Square-New_York_City_New_York.html"}],
    "maxReviewsPerPlace": 2000,
})
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
reviews = [r for r in rows if r["type"] == "review"]

Each review row has the rating, title, full text, language (and whether TripAdvisor machine-translated it), published date, travel month, trip type, sub-ratings when given, helpful votes, photo count and the hotel's reply. Reviewer names are off by default. The place row carries the address, coordinates, all-time rating and histogram, sub-scores, the "#169 of 529 hotels" ranking, amenities, and three numbers computed from the reviews you collected: owner reply rate, average reply lag and the rating over the last 90 days.

Finding 1: the all-time score hides two good years

Reviews Average 5 stars
All time (TripAdvisor's own histogram) 18,836 3.9 40%
Latest 2,000 (Dec 2024 to Nov 2026) 2,000 4.43 71%

The headline 3.9 is dragged down by older stays: 2,482 of the hotel's one and two-star reviews are in the all-time histogram, and only 176 of them are in the last two years. Month by month, the recent average sits between 4.18 (September 2026) and 4.67 (April 2025), with no trend down.

If you compare hotels by their all-time score, an older property that has improved looks worse than it is. A 90-day or 12-month average from the raw reviews is fairer, and it's one column in the output (ratingLast90d: 4.35 over 250 reviews here).

Finding 2: who is happiest

Trip type Reviews Average
Solo 93 4.78
Friends 256 4.68
Family 620 4.58
Couples 262 4.47
Business 124 4.34
Not given 645 4.14

Business travellers rate it lowest of the groups that say why they came. Reviewers who don't pick a trip type are the least happy of all, which is common: an angry reviewer fills in fewer optional fields.

Finding 3: what the bad reviews are about

We split the reviews into 176 low (1 or 2 stars) and 1,701 high (4 or 5 stars) and counted how many in each group mention a word at least once (whole words only):

Mentioned Low reviews High reviews
noise / noisy 23% 7%
bathroom 26% 8%
old / dated / outdated 20% 5%
check-in 17% 8%
window 16% 1%
price / expensive / overpriced 18% 6%
rude 12% 0%
fee / fees 11% 1%
air conditioning / AC 11% 2%
dirty 9% 0%
staff 44% 54%
location 34% 54%
clean 15% 33%

The pattern is clear even with simple word counts. Happy guests talk about the staff and the location. Unhappy guests talk about the room itself (bathroom, noise through the windows, an old building, the air conditioning) and about the front desk (check-in, rude, fees). "Staff" shows up in both groups, because staff are the reason for both the best and the worst reviews.

This is the cheapest version of the analysis. With the full text in a dataframe, the next step is an embedding or topic model over the 176 low reviews, which takes a few seconds on a laptop.

Finding 4: the hotel answers almost everything

1,991 of the 2,000 reviews have a reply from the hotel (99.6%), including 175 of the 176 low ones, and the average reply comes 4.6 days after the review. That's a well-run reply process. For a competitor analysis, reply rate and reply lag are two of the most telling columns: they show which hotels have someone watching their reviews.

What it doesn't do

  • It reads what a logged-out visitor can see. A list stops at about 10,000 reviews; for bigger places, run it per star rating to go deeper.
  • Machine-translated reviews are marked (machineTranslated). 161 of these 2,000 were translations; filter them out with languages if you only want originals.
  • It doesn't name staff. Names in the hotel's replies are replaced with [name removed].

Try it

The Actor is locaihost/tripadvisor-reviews on the Apify Store: $0.50 per 1,000 reviews and $1 per 1,000 places on the Starter tier, cheaper on the higher tiers, and links that aren't a TripAdvisor place are never charged. It also works from AI agents through Apify's MCP server, so "pull the last 500 reviews of these 10 hotels and tell me what the one-star ones have in common" is one tool call away.

If you run it and something looks wrong, open an issue on the Actor page and we'll fix it the same day.

title: A worked example with @cai.com: from signup to first hosted-action payment to a stored vault credential
description:
A worked example with @cai.com — from signup to first hosted-action payment to a stored vault credential

A worked example, end to end. About six minutes from cai.com/app to a working agent that has an @cai.com email, a funded wallet, a stored vault credential, and an installed MCP server. This post walks through every step with the actual commands and the actual API calls.

Step 1 — Sign up

Go to cai.com/app. Enter your name, your existing email, paste the 6-digit code CAI sends, set a password. Done. About 2 minutes.

What you have at the end: an @cai.com email, an empty wallet, an empty vault, and an API key with the read scopes.

Step 2 — Receive your first @cai.com email

Forward a test mail to your new address from your old email. It arrives in the CAI inbox. Send a reply to your old address from @cai.com — through the dashboard's compose UI, or via the API:

curl -X POST https://api.cai.com/functions/v1/send-email \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ***" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "to": "you@youroldaddress.com",
    "subject": "Hello from @cai.com",
    "body": "Testing the new address."
  }'

The send goes through. The reply arrives in your old inbox. The @cai.com address is live.

Step 3 — Top up the wallet

Open the account dashboard, click "Add funds," pick a chain. Base is fastest for testing. Pick a token — USDC is the default. Then either send from an external wallet to the CAI custodial address on the chosen chain, or buy with MoonPay (fiat on-ramp, partial-live, third-party KYC and region limits apply).

Your wallet has a $200/day auto-limit while CAI completes its security audit. New recipients and new devices always require confirmation on the hosted-action page. Think of it like cash in your pocket — perfect for daily spending. The vault product (multi-sig, time-locks) is coming for larger balances.

After the deposit confirms, check the balance:

curl -X POST https://api.cai.com/functions/v1/get-wallet-balances \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ***" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"chains": ["base"], "tokens": ["USDC"]}'

The response includes the new balance. About 2 minutes for the deposit to confirm on Base.

Step 4 — Confirm a hosted-action payment

Now the agent side. The agent (or you, via curl) initiates a transfer:

curl -X POST https://api.cai.com/functions/v1/wallet-custodial-transfer \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ***" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "to_address": "0xYourOtherAddress",
    "amount": "1.00",
    "chain": "base",
    "token": "USDC"
  }'

The response includes a hosted-action URL. Open the URL on your phone. The page shows the recipient, the amount, the chain. Tap "Confirm." The transfer executes.

After the user confirms, the agent checks the activity feed for the receipt:

curl -X GET https://api.cai.com/functions/v1/wallet-activity-list \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ***"

The response includes the completed transfer with its on-chain tx hash and status. The agent can then show the receipt to the user.

Step 5 — Store a site credential in the vault

Open the account dashboard, click "Vault," add a credential for a site you use often. The form is (site, username, password). The credential is encrypted at rest.

The agent can now list saved credentials:

curl -X GET https://api.cai.com/functions/v1/user-site-credentials \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ***"

The response shows the metadata for each saved credential. The actual credential value is delivered through the user-confirmation hosted-action flow when the agent needs to use it.

Step 6 — Install the MCP server (optional)

The final step is the agent side. Install the MCP server:

npm i -g @cailab/mcp

Add the server to your MCP host (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Cursor). The config is:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cai": {
      "command": "cai-mcp",
      "env": {
        "CAI_API_KEY": "your-api-key-from-the-dashboard"
      }
    }
  }
}

Restart the host. The CAI tools appear in the agent's tool surface. The agent can now call get_identity, get_wallet_balances, wallet_custodial_transfer, vault_get_site_credential, and the rest of the CAI surface — without you pasting a private key in chat.

Total time

Six minutes from signup to a working agent. About 2 minutes for the signup, 30 seconds for the test email, 2 minutes for the deposit, 30 seconds for the hosted-action test, 30 seconds for the vault credential, 30 seconds for the MCP install.

Apply at cai.com/app. The contract is cai.com/skill.md. The npm package is @cailab/mcp.

If you ran the end-to-end walkthrough above and a step failed

Comment below with:

  1. What you ran — the install command, the request, the MCP host config. Copy the actual command or request.
  2. What you expected — one sentence.
  3. What you got — the error message, the empty response, the unexpected behavior. Paste it verbatim.
  4. Your environment — OS, Node version, the MCP host (OpenClaw / Hermes / Codex / Cursor / other), the CAI account tier if relevant.

Every comment on this article gets read. Bug reports will be replied to within 24 hours. Friction points shape what we document next.

Documentation: cai.com/skill.md · cai.com/developers.html · cai.com/app to sign up.

title: Your Best Dunning Email Is Worthless in the Spam Folder
description:
Developers who work on billing recovery will debug everything: retry intervals, decline-code mapping, webhook idempotency, the card-update page's mobile layout. Then the recovery email — the artifact the whole system exists to deliver — goes out from a subdomain nobody warmed, with a subject line that reads like a phishing attempt, and lands in spam. The retry logic was perfect. The customer never saw it.

Dunning email has a deliverability problem that ordinary product email does not. It talks about money, failed payments, and updating card details, which is precisely the vocabulary spam filters and cautious humans are trained to distrust. It is also sent disproportionately to your least-engaged customers — the ones who have not opened anything in months — which is exactly the sending pattern that drags a domain's reputation down. Every unopened dunning email makes the next one more likely to be filtered. The failure compounds in the worst direction.

The fixes are mostly unglamorous infrastructure, and they are checkable. Send billing mail from a dedicated subdomain so its reputation is not hostage to your marketing sends, and authenticate it properly: SPF, DKIM, and a DMARC policy that is actually enforced rather than parked at monitor-only. Keep the from-name and from-address boringly consistent with what the customer saw at signup; a payment email from a name they do not recognize is a delete, or worse, a spam report. Put the card-update link on your real domain, never a shortener. And write subject lines that a bank would write — "Your payment didn't go through" survives filters and humans; "URGENT: action required on your account!!" survives neither.

Then instrument it like the revenue surface it is. Track delivery, bounces, and spam complaints per send, not per month. A hard bounce on a dunning email is diagnostic gold: it often means the account's contact email is dead, which means the subscription behind it is unrecoverable by email and should route to another channel immediately instead of burning four more sends. A complaint spike after a copy change is a rollback signal, not a rounding error.

For the full working list — authentication setup, subdomain strategy, copy patterns that stay out of the filter, and the per-send metrics worth alerting on — a deliverability checklist for dunning email that lands in the inbox lays it out in implementation order, written for the person who owns the sending pipeline rather than the person who owns the brand book.

Bounce policy deserves its own paragraph because billing teams routinely get it backwards. A hard bounce — the address does not exist — should end email attempts to that address immediately and reroute the account to whatever second channel exists, even if that channel is only a banner the customer sees at next login. Soft bounces, the full mailbox and the temporary server refusal, earn a short, bounded retry of the message itself, and then the same rerouting. What neither should trigger is the marketing team's usual reflex, suppressing the contact entirely: a suppressed billing contact is an account you have decided to let die silently. Keep the billing suppression list separate from the marketing one, review it like a failure queue in its own right, and treat every address on it as a small mystery worth one human look — a mistyped domain at signup accounts for more of them than anyone expects, and it is fixable in a single apologetic email to the corrected address.

Recovery systems are usually judged on retry intelligence. Fair enough. But a retry the customer never learns about is only half a recovery, and the other half lives or dies in the inbox. That is why Swipe Again's recovery work treats the email itself — its authentication, its timing, its plain-spoken copy — as part of the retry, not as the notification stapled to it.

title: I Wrote a Python Script That Cleans Up Any Messy Folder — and It Never Deletes Anything by Default
description:
Everyone has that one folder. Downloads, Desktop, some project directory — hundreds of files, no structure, and the thought of sorting it by hand is so dull you just... don't.

I wrote a small Python script that does it for you. It sorts a folder's files into subfolders by type, and the important part is in the title: by default, it changes nothing. It only shows you what it would do. You have to explicitly tell it to move files.

What it does

Point it at a folder and it sorts every file into one of six categories:

Folder Extensions
Images .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .gif, .webp, .svg
Documents .pdf, .doc, .docx, .txt, .md
Spreadsheets .csv, .xls, .xlsx, .ods
Archives .zip, .tar, .gz, .rar, .7z
Code .py, .js, .html, .css, .json
Others anything else

No dependencies beyond the standard library — just argparse, shutil, and pathlib. No install step at all.

Usage 

python file_organizer.py ~/Downloads            # dry run, no changes
python file_organizer.py ~/Downloads --apply    # actually move files

The dry run prints lines like would move: report.pdf -> Documents/ and finishes with a count. Only --apply performs the moves.

How it works

The whole script is built around one mapping and one function:

CATEGORIES = {
    "Images": {".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".gif", ".webp", ".svg"},
    "Documents": {".pdf", ".doc", ".docx", ".txt", ".md"},
    "Spreadsheets": {".csv", ".xls", ".xlsx", ".ods"},
    "Archives": {".zip", ".tar", ".gz", ".rar", ".7z"},
    "Code": {".py", ".js", ".html", ".css", ".json"},
}

def category_for(path):
    """Return the category folder name for a file's extension."""
    for name, extensions in CATEGORIES.items():
        if path.suffix.lower() in extensions:
            return name
    return "Others"

Extensions are lowercased before matching, so Photo.JPG and photo.jpg land in the same folder. Anything unknown falls into Others rather than being skipped silently — a file you can't find is worse than a file in a misc folder.

The organising function keeps the dry-run and apply paths in one place, so they can never drift apart:

def organize(folder, apply=False):
    folder = Path(folder)
    if not folder.is_dir():
        print(f"error: {folder} is not a folder", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    moved = 0
    for path in sorted(folder.iterdir()):
        if not path.is_file():
            continue  # never touch subfolders
        target_dir = folder / category_for(path)
        target = target_dir / path.name
        if apply:
            target_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
            shutil.move(str(path), str(target))
            print(f"moved: {path.name} -> {target_dir.name}/")
        else:
            print(f"would move: {path.name} -> {target_dir.name}/")
        moved += 1
    mode = "moved" if apply else "would move (dry run — use --apply to move)"
    print(f"{moved} file(s) {mode}")
    return 0

Three safety decisions are doing the quiet work here:

  1. Dry run is the default. The destructive action requires an explicit flag. If you run it by accident, nothing happens — you just get a preview.
  2. It never touches subfolders. Only files directly in the folder are moved. Your existing structure stays intact.
  3. It never deletes. Files are moved, not removed. If a category looks wrong, everything is still there, one folder away.

Three lessons I'd pass on

  1. Make the safe behaviour the default. A script that moves files should have to be talked into it. Dry-run-first is a design decision, not a feature — and it's the reason I'd trust this on a real Downloads folder.
  2. Small scripts beat small apps. This is about 70 lines and has no dependencies. It doesn't need a GUI, a config file, or a scheduler to be useful.
  3. Print what you're doing. Every move gets a line of output, and the run ends with a count. When a script touches your files, silence is a bug.

This is the second tool in my Python Automation Toolkit — the first scrapes a catalogue into a clean Excel report, and this one tidies the folder that report lands in. Next, I'll write about the project that taught me the most: a RAG-powered assistant that answers questions about Pakistani electricity bills.

title: Shopify Webhooks Will Fail Silently — Build for That From Day One
description:
Shopify Webhooks Will Fail Silently — Build for That From Day One

Shopify webhooks are "at least once" delivery, not guaranteed, and not ordered. Most custom integrations we see built for the first time assume the opposite, and it's invisible until a webhook silently never arrives.

❌ The Assumption That Breaks Things

Treating a webhook as a reliable, ordered event stream — assuming inventory-updated always arrives before order-created for the same product, or that every webhook sent is a webhook received — causes bugs that only show up under real production load, not in testing.

🔁 The Fix: Reconciliation, Not Just Listening

Pair webhook listeners with a periodic reconciliation job that pulls current state via the API and corrects drift. Webhooks become the fast path; reconciliation becomes the safety net that catches what webhooks missed.

🔒 Idempotency Is Not Optional

Because delivery can duplicate, every webhook handler needs to be safe to run twice on the same event — check a processed-event log before acting, not after. This single habit prevents most of the double-charge and double-fulfillment bugs we've debugged for clients.

Originally published on the KLYX blog.

title: How to Solve the Cloudflare 5-Second Challenge in Python for Automated Testing
description:
You already have Cloudflare Turnstile handled. But then you hit a different wall: instead of a widget inside the page, the entire page is replaced by a full-screen "Verifying you are human" interstitial that never resolves for your script. That is the Cloudflare challenge page (the "5-second challenge" in a browser), and it needs a completely different API call than Turnstile does.

This walkthrough shows how to solve it with Kaptra's captcha API using the AntiCloudflareTask type: what parameters it needs, what comes back, and how to replay the result so your requests actually get through.

Widget vs full-page: know which one you are facing

These two Cloudflare defenses get confused all the time, and the fix for one does not work on the other:

  • Turnstile: an embedded widget in a form. You collect a sitekey from the page, send it with the URL, and receive a token to submit with the form.
  • The challenge page: the page itself is swapped for an interstitial. There is no sitekey anywhere. The solver has to pass the interstitial and return the resulting cookies, and those cookies are bound to the IP that earned them. That binding is exactly why this task type requires you to pass your own proxy.

Quick diagnostic: if your response body is mostly a "Just a moment..." page, it is the second case. Read on.

What the solved task hands you

When polling completes, solution contains cookies: the clearance material for that protected page. The flow from there:

  1. Create an AntiCloudflareTask with the protected URL and your HTTP proxy.
  2. Poll getTaskResult until status is ready.
  3. Attach solution["cookies"] to your session and send your real requests through the same proxy from step 1. The clearance was issued for that IP, so keep using it.

Full Python example 

import time
import requests
# ---
BASE_URL = "https://api.kaptra.ai"
API_KEY = "YOUR_KAPTRA_API_KEY"
# ---
def solve_cloudflare_challenge(website_url: str, proxy: str) -> dict:
    # 1. create the task; proxy is required for this type (HTTP only)
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{BASE_URL}/createTask",
        json={
            "clientKey": API_KEY,
            "task": {
                "type": "AntiCloudflareTask",
                "websiteURL": website_url,
                "proxy": proxy,
            },
        },
    ).json()
    if resp.get("errorId"):
        raise RuntimeError(f"createTask failed: {resp.get('errorCode')}")
    task_id = resp["taskId"]
    # 2. poll every 1-2s, max 120 queries per task
    for _ in range(120):
        result = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/getTaskResult",
            json={"clientKey": API_KEY, "taskId": task_id},
        ).json()
        status = result.get("status")
        if status == "ready":
            return result["solution"]  # {"cookies": ...}
        if status == "failure":
            raise RuntimeError(f"task failed: {result.get('errorCode')}")
        # processing (or CAPTCHA_NOT_READY): keep polling
        time.sleep(1.5)
    raise TimeoutError("gave up after 120 polls")
# ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    my_proxy = "http://USER:PASS@HOST:PORT"
    solution = solve_cloudflare_challenge(
        "https://www.example.com/protected", my_proxy
    )
    print(solution["cookies"])
    # 3. attach these cookies to your session and keep
    #    sending requests through that same proxy

Same client skeleton as the Turnstile flow: createTask, then poll every 1 to 2 seconds with a ceiling of 120 queries. CAPTCHA_NOT_READY means the worker is still on it; status settles at ready or failure.

Gotchas worth knowing before you ship

HTTP proxies only. The docs state it plainly: a public HTTP proxy is required and SOCKS is rejected. If your stack is SOCKS-only, front it with HTTP or use a different provider for these tasks.

Failure handling. Average solve time is under 10 seconds, so 120 polls at 1.5 second intervals is a wide margin. A failure surfaces as ERROR_CAPTCHA_UNSOLVABLE; retrying once with the same parameters is the normal move, because billing is per solved task.

Cost. $1.20 per 1,000 successful solves, nothing for failures or timeouts, no monthly fee, no expiring balance. New Kaptra accounts start with $10 in test credit, enough to validate the whole flow before you commit.

HTTP codes carry no signal. Every response is HTTP 200. The verdict lives in errorId (0 or 1) and errorCode in the JSON. If your code already speaks that envelope, nothing to change.

Summary

Widget: sitekey in, token out, submit with the form. Challenge page: your HTTP proxy in, cookies out, replay through that proxy. Different inputs, different outputs, same create-then-poll loop underneath.

  • Site: kaptra.ai
  • AntiCloudflareTask docs: kaptra.ai/docs

The companion piece on Turnstile (the widget) is worth reading alongside this one. Questions or a task type you want covered next? The team answers tickets in Discord.

title: Chat memory as a 41.9 MB file: building on MemT-1.0-Nano's save and reload
description:
Most chat backends resend the whole transcript to the model on every turn. MemT-1.0-Nano, an open model from MemTensor whose base model is the Qwen team's Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, works on a different contract. Turns you flag are folded into a block of numbers that never grows, and that block can be written to disk. In the test, a saved memory was loaded into a new session holding zero messages, and the model got all nine recall questions right. Every saved file weighed 41,944,024 bytes.

The tables and setup are in the full MemT-1.0-Nano memory file write-up on inferencekey.com; here is what you would build around it.

Your code chooses what the model keeps

The session API in MemTensor's modeling_memt.py treats remembering as an explicit call. Pass enable_memory=True and that turn is committed into the memory state and its text discarded. Other turns stay in the session as ordinary text. Shortened from the model card:

session.chat("<facts to remember>", enable_memory=True, enable_thinking=False)
session.save_state("dana.safetensors")
restored = model.create_session(tokenizer, state="dana.safetensors")
print(len(restored.messages))  # 0

Which turns deserve the flag is product logic you write. Tokens are the word pieces a model reads, and in the restored session the input for each question went from 27 tokens to 210 over four questions, because the questions themselves were never flagged and piled up as text. Flag nothing and the transcript is back.

By default save_state will not overwrite an existing file, so plan your naming.

Disk gets worse, rereading gets better

As text on disk, the made-up bakery owner's history in the test was 107 tokens, a few hundred bytes. The memory file is 41.9 MB no matter what.

It competes instead with the working memory a regular model rebuilds from the whole history and holds on the GPU while the session is open. According to the storage arithmetic in the MemT-1.0-Nano research post, the fixed file only beats it once the history passes roughly 2,000 tokens, and at 128K tokens it is about 64 times smaller. For speed, MemTensor's paper has Nano losing on short histories, breaking even near 32,000 tokens and pulling ahead by about 1.86 times at 128K. The test measured neither.

On one A100 80 GB, loading took 1.35 to 1.99 seconds and saving 0.66 to 1.02. Generating was slow: answering a "remember" turn with 128 tokens took about 13 seconds on the stock Hugging Face code, without the optional faster GPU components and with no tuning.

Two traps worth knowing first

Compressing to 8 bits does not get you onto a smaller GPU. The weights normally run in bf16, a 16-bit number format. With the A100 limited to what a 48 GB card offers, the 8-bit load ran out of memory after asking for about 64 GiB. With the limit removed it loaded, and the first "remember" call then died with a dtype (number type) mismatch. The cause is in the architecture. Each layer holds 256 experts (sub-networks the model picks between per token), stored as fused 3D parameters rather than nn.Linear layers, so the bitsandbytes 8-bit library skips them and the saving is about 2 GiB. The 48 GB case was emulated with a cap, and no other shrinking method was tried. With no official compressed release, budget for an 80 GB GPU.

Load by repo id, not from the Hugging Face cache folder. trust_remote_code lets Transformers, the Hugging Face Python library, run the model's own Python files. Pointing it at the downloaded snapshot directory fails with "file not found": Transformers follows the modeling_memt.py symlink into blobs/ and looks for the relative import there. Loading by repo id with a pinned revision avoids it.

Behind an API, the state file will not fit a result payload capped at 8 MB. In the InferenceKey backend it stays on the worker's disk (the worker is the program running the model on the GPU machine), and the API returns its size and sha256.

Two licenses, two answers

The Nano weights carry Apache-2.0, which permits commercial use. MemTensor's own code on GitHub, the two-GPU memt-sglang server included, is under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0. The test ran the Apache-2.0 code from the Hugging Face repo, the slow path.

What a pilot should measure

Every recall question in the test asked for a short fact given to the model moments earlier. That shows the round trip works, not memory over months. MemTensor is open about this: text-based memory systems still lead, above all on long histories where a precise detail has to be found. On the LongMemEval-S benchmark the paper puts Nano at 32.6, while sending the whole conversation scores 76.8. On your own data, check:

  • Exact details from early in long histories, compared with a text store.
  • Whether many memory writes over time push older facts out. Nobody has tested it.
  • Behavior with several sessions at once. The test sent one request at a time.

The hosted InferenceKey endpoint was not tested either: the run used a local test copy of InferenceKey and a worker on a GPU on our cloud.

Credit goes to MemTensor for the model, the trained memory block, the session API and the MemT-1.0 paper, to the Qwen team for the base model, and to Hugging Face Transformers for running the custom code. We found the model through the AI Search news video and an r/LocalLLaMA thread. We wrote the custom backend, found the load fix and ran the tests. To repeat the round trip on your own NVIDIA machine, the SDK example for the MemT-1.0-Nano backend runs it end to end.

The GPU memory results, every timing, the paper's benchmark numbers and the open issues are in the MemT-1.0-Nano research article on inferencekey.com.

title: A heartbeat that goes quiet when the route is dead: signed presence records with a short TTL
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code.

Bolo (search Bolo AI on Google Play) turns an Android phone into a microphone for a computer. On the same Wi-Fi the phone finds the PC directly. Away from it, the PC's Node.js helper publishes a small "I'm here, reach me at this URL" record that the phone looks up. This post covers src/presence.js, the 146-line module behind that record, and four decisions in it.

1. Sign the record, don't trust the transport

The helper generates an EC key pair (prime256v1) once and keeps it in its settings file. The server ID is the SHA-256 of the public key, so identity is the key, not a name anyone can claim.

Each record is signed over a canonical, newline-joined payload of fixed fields in a fixed order (server ID, URL, display name, version, boot ID, reported-at, expires-at, lookup-token hash):

record.signature = crypto.sign(
  'sha256',
  Buffer.from(canonicalPresencePayload(record), 'utf8'),
  identity.privateKey
).toString('base64');

Signing a canonical string instead of JSON.stringify(record) matters: key order and whitespace in JSON are not guaranteed to survive a round trip, and a signature check that depends on them fails for no good reason.

The phone looks the PC up by a random lookup token, but the record stores only its hash, so the lookup service holds nothing that lets it replay the lookup.

2. Short TTL, steady heartbeat

Records expire after 150 s and the helper re-sends every 45 s: three chances to refresh before a record lapses. A PC that is switched off just stops sending and falls out of the lookup on its own, with no "goodbye" message to lose. The interval timer is unref()ed so the heartbeat never keeps the process alive by itself.

3. Publish only while the route works

This is the fix that taught me the most. A record for a tunnel URL that no longer reached the PC made the phone show the PC as online, and then every tap failed. The refresh now asks a health check first:

async function publishPresence() {
  if (!currentTunnelUrl || !currentVersion) return false;
  if (!routeHealthy()) return false;
  ...
}

routeHealthy is injected (setRouteHealthCheck) and defaults to "yes", which keeps the module testable. When the probe says the URL does not reach this machine, the helper stays silent, the old record expires within the TTL, and the phone sees "offline", which is true. Absence of a record is more honest than a stale one.

4. Say who said no

A rejected refresh now logs who rejected it. The service answers with JSON; an edge bot-challenge answers with HTML. So the log line is either proxy: {...} or edge (cf-mitigated=..., ray=...). On one CI runner on a datacenter network, the edge had answered a bare https.request with a bot challenge while fetch from the same machine got a 200. Home networks passed both. The module now uses fetch with a 10 s AbortSignal.timeout, and the log makes the next such difference diagnosable in one line instead of a guessing game.

Takeaways

  • Make identity a key; sign a canonical string, not serialized JSON.
  • Short TTL plus a faster heartbeat beats explicit "I'm gone" messages.
  • Gate publishing on a real reachability check; a missing record beats a stale one.
  • Log which layer rejected you.
  • Inject the health check so the module stays testable.

Bolo is on Google Play (search Bolo AI): https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ashwar.bolo. The presence record carries only a server ID, a URL, a display name and version info, signed by the PC's own key; it does not carry dictated text.

title: I Built a Scraper That Turns 1,000 Book Listings Into a Clean Excel Report — Here's How
description:
Most "learn web scraping" tutorials stop at printing a few titles to the terminal. That never felt like a finished tool to me, so I built one that goes all the way: scrape a catalogue, clean the data, and hand over a formatted Excel report someone could actually use.

The stack is plain Python: requests, BeautifulSoup, pandas, and openpyxl. No frameworks, no paid APIs. The target is books.toscrape.com, a site built specifically for practising scraping — so everything here is on a public practice page, not a real store.

What you end up with

Running two scripts produces:

  • data/books_raw.csv — the raw scrape, one row per book
  • data/books_clean.csv — the same data, cleaned
  • data/books_clean.xlsx — a formatted Excel report: bold headers, filters, a frozen top row, and sensible column widths

The full run collects 1,000 books, and the cleaned report's average price comes out at £35.07.

Step 0: Setup 

pip install requests beautifulsoup4 pandas openpyxl

Three files: scraper.py (collect), clean_export.py (clean + export), and a data/ folder for the outputs.

Step 1: Scrape every page, not just the first one

A catalogue scraper that only reads page 1 is a demo, not a tool. The real job is walking the pagination until there is no "next" link left. The core loop does exactly that:

def scrape(max_pages=None):
    all_books = []
    page = 1
    while True:
        url = CATALOGUE_URL.format(page)
        response = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=20)
        response.raise_for_status()
        response.encoding = "utf-8"
        books, has_next = parse_page(response.text, url)
        all_books.extend(books)
        if not has_next:
            break
        page += 1
        if max_pages and page > max_pages:
            break
        time.sleep(0.2)  # be polite to the server
    return all_books

Each page is parsed with one function that pulls five fields out of every book card:

def parse_page(html, page_url):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
    books = []
    for article in soup.select("article.product_pod"):
        title = article.h3.a["title"].strip()
        price_text = article.select_one("p.price_color").get_text(strip=True)
        rating_word = article.select_one("p.star-rating")["class"][1]
        availability = article.select_one("p.instock").get_text(strip=True)
        rel_url = article.h3.a["href"]
        books.append({
            "title": title,
            "price": price_text,
            "rating": rating_word,
            "availability": availability,
            "url": urljoin(page_url, rel_url),
        })
    has_next = soup.select_one("li.next a") is not None
    return books, has_next

Three details worth calling out, because each one bit me or would have:

  1. The £ encoding gotcha. This site doesn't declare its charset, so requests guesses Latin-1 and corrupts the £ sign. The pages are actually UTF-8, so one line — response.encoding = "utf-8" — fixes it before parsing. If your scraped prices ever look like Â£51.77, this is almost certainly why.
  2. Be polite. A 0.2 second sleep between pages and an honest User-Agent (python-automation-toolkit/1.0 (learning project)) cost nothing and keep you from hammering someone else's server. Scraping fast is not a skill; scraping without getting blocked is.
  3. Relative URLs. Book links on the page are relative, so urljoin(page_url, rel_url) turns them into full URLs you can actually click later.

Run it with python scraper.py (or --pages 5 for a quick test run), and you get data/books_raw.csv with 1,000 rows.

Step 2: Clean the data before anyone sees it

Raw scraped data is never report-ready. Prices are strings with currency symbols (£51.77), ratings are words (Three), and availability is a sentence fragment. The cleaning step turns all of that into typed, analysable data:

RATING_MAP = {"One": 1, "Two": 2, "Three": 3, "Four": 4, "Five": 5}

def clean(df):
    df = df.copy()
    # "£51.77" -> 51.77 (drop anything that is not a digit or a dot)
    df["price"] = df["price"].astype(str).str.replace(r"[^0-9.]", "", regex=True)
    df["price"] = pd.to_numeric(df["price"], errors="coerce")
    df = df.dropna(subset=["price"])
    # "Three" -> 3
    df["rating"] = df["rating"].map(RATING_MAP)
    # "In stock" -> True, anything else -> False
    df["in_stock"] = df["availability"].str.contains("In stock", na=False)
    df = df.drop(columns=["availability"])
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["title", "url"])
    return df

The pattern here is worth stealing for any scrape: strip, convert with errors="coerce" (bad values become NaN instead of crashing the run), drop the rows that didn't convert, and drop duplicates on a sensible key — here, title + URL.

Step 3: Export an Excel file a human would enjoy opening

A CSV is fine for machines. If a person is going to read the report, formatting matters — and it's only a few lines with openpyxl:

def write_excel(df, path):
    with pd.ExcelWriter(path, engine="openpyxl") as writer:
        df.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Books", index=False)
        sheet = writer.sheets["Books"]
        for cell in sheet[1]:
            cell.font = Font(bold=True)
        sheet.auto_filter.ref = sheet.dimensions
        sheet.freeze_panes = "A2"
        widths = {"title": 55, "price": 10, "rating": 10,
                  "in_stock": 10, "url": 60}
        for idx, col in enumerate(df.columns, start=1):
            sheet.column_dimensions[get_column_letter(idx)].width = (
                widths.get(col, 20)
            )

Bold headers, filters, a frozen top row, columns wide enough for the content. That's the difference between "here's a file" and "here's a report."

python clean_export.py also prints a short summary: book count, average price, how many are in stock, and the rating mix.

The result

Output Contents
books_raw.csv 1,000 books, raw strings
books_clean.csv 1,000 books, typed and deduplicated
books_clean.xlsx Same data, formatted and filterable

Average price across the catalogue: £35.07.

Three lessons I'd pass on

  1. Scrape practice sites to learn. Real sites have terms of service, rate limits, and anti-bot measures. Learn the mechanics on a site built for it, and only scrape public pages with permission when real data is involved.
  2. The pipeline is the project. Scraping is the easy third. Cleaning and presenting the data is where a script becomes a tool someone would pay for.
  3. Small, polite, honest scripts beat clever ones. A 0.2 second delay and a real User-Agent never got anyone blocked; pretending to be a browser did.

The full code is in my Python Automation Toolkit project, and the same scrape → clean → report pattern works for any tabular listing: products, jobs, or prices. Next, I'll write about the other half of the toolkit — a file organiser that tidies a messy downloads folder without ever deleting anything by default.

title: Reverting Git Won’t Undo Your Database Migration
description:
A release introduces an application bug. You revert the deployment configuration, and the previous container image starts successfully.

But requests still fail.

The application has returned to its previous version. The database has not.

For stateful applications, a deployment rollback and a recovery plan cover different things.

A simple column rename can break rollback

Consider an application that reads this column:

SELECT customer_name FROM orders;

A new release renames it:

ALTER TABLE orders
RENAME COLUMN customer_name TO billing_name;

The new application expects billing_name. The previous application expects customer_name.

If the release fails after the migration, deploying the previous image leaves it querying a column that no longer exists.

The same compatibility problem can appear during a rolling deployment, while old and new application instances run together.

This is an illustrative example. The locking and operational impact of schema changes depend on the database engine and workload.

Separate schema evolution into stages

The expand, migrate, contract pattern spreads a breaking change across compatible steps. GitLab documents this approach for changes that must work across application versions. GitLab's compatibility guide

For this example, a staged approach could look like:

1. Expand

Introduce the new column while keeping the existing one.

Old application instances can continue using the original schema.

Adding a column still needs operational review: defaults, constraints, table size and database behavior can affect deployment safety.

2. Migrate

Introduce application behavior that supports the transition.

Define how both representations stay consistent while older instances remain active. A one-time backfill is insufficient if ongoing writes can immediately make the columns disagree.

Backfill existing records in controlled batches where appropriate. Make progress observable and retries safe.

Check completeness and consistency before switching reads.

3. Contract

Remove the old representation only after its consumers have stopped using it and the intended rollback window has closed.

Consumers may include background workers, reports, integrations and scheduled jobs—not just web application instances.

Once the old column is removed, an older application version may no longer be a valid recovery target.

Keep GitOps reconciliation in the recovery plan

A manual change to a running Deployment can conflict with the desired state maintained by a GitOps controller.

Decide how recovery changes the authoritative configuration, and how reconciliation behaves during the incident.

Also distinguish a Git revert from the deployment tool's rollback operation. They are separate mechanisms with their own behavior and constraints. Check the documentation for your deployed version, such as Argo CD's automated sync policy.

Neither operation inherently reverses database writes or external side effects.

Test the previous application against the migrated database

A useful compatibility test is:

Create representative starting data
    → Apply the proposed migration
    → Run the previous application version
    → Exercise important reads and writes
    → Run the new application version
    → Verify transition behavior

For a rolling release, also test the period when both versions operate concurrently.

A successful migration command proves that the database accepted the change. It does not prove application compatibility.

Write down where rollback stops being safe

Before release, answer:

  • Which application versions support the resulting schema?
  • Can migration jobs resume safely after interruption?
  • What happens to writes made during the transition?
  • At what step does recovery require a forward fix?
  • If restoration is necessary, what happens to data written since the backup?

The recovery target is a compatible application-and-data state.

How does your team define the rollback window for releases that change the database?

title: RagLeap Physical: A Simulation-First Safety Bridge for AI Agents
description:
What should happen when an AI agent proposes an action that affects a physical-system simulation?

At RagLeap, we're exploring a controlled workflow:

AI proposes → Human approves → Safety limits are checked → Simulator verifies

RagLeap Physical is an open-source, pre-alpha Python project built around this idea.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/tree/main/packages/ragleap-physical

What it does

RagLeap Physical provides a simulation-first bridge between AI agents and physical-system simulators.

The project includes:

  • Safety envelopes
  • Exact-proposal approval
  • Dry runs
  • Runtime monitoring
  • Stop functionality
  • Audit logs
  • AI-facing tools
  • MCP server
  • Optional MuJoCo adapters
  • Workspace limits
  • Runnable simulation demos

The focus is not unrestricted AI control. It is controlled, observable interaction.

Release journey

v0.0.1 — Core bridge

The first release introduced the safety bridge, exact-proposal approval, runtime monitoring, audit logs, MCP tools, MuJoCo adapters, workspace limits, and simulation examples.

v0.0.2 — Operator console

The second release added a human operator console.

A named person can review pending proposals, approve the exact digest, apply the action, and stop.

The console is loopback-only, uses one token per person, and is not an AI tool.

v0.0.3 — Two-link workspace demo

The latest release adds:

examples/two_link_workspace_demo.py

The demo shows a two-link arm with one accepted workspace move and one refused move.

It also includes package metadata improvements and a fix for request handling in the operator console and MCP server.

Install 

pip install ragleap-physical==0.0.3

Optional extras:

pip install "ragleap-physical[mujoco]"
pip install "ragleap-physical[test]"
pip install "ragleap-physical[interop]"

Testing

The v0.0.3 release reports:

  • 255 tests passed with MuJoCo and the MCP SDK installed in Colab
  • GitHub CI on Python 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12

The Windows refusal-fix behavior is not yet verified.

Important limitations

This is pre-alpha and simulation-only.

It does not control real hardware. No real-robot or real-machine validation, safety certification, or regulatory compliance is claimed.

MuJoCo results are repeatable within one installed environment only. The wear-study and machine-tool numbers are invented.

Contribute

We welcome feedback and contributions from developers working on AI agents, simulation, robotics, MCP, and safety engineering.

Explore the package:

https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/tree/main/packages/ragleap-physical

Install:

pip install ragleap-physical==0.0.3

AI proposes. Humans approve. The system verifies.

title: datapatch Fails in sqlpatch.pm: Fixing a Corrupted PDB$SEED Tempfile in Oracle 19c
description:
The symptom

datapatch -verbose stopped with:

Unsupported named object type for bind parameter at $ORACLE_HOME/sqlpatch/sqlpatch.pm line 6153.

That message says very little. The useful clue was in the database alert log at the same time:

Read of datafile '/u01/oradata/CDB1/pdbseed/temp01<timestamp>.dbf' (fno 202) header failed with ORA-01206
ORA-01122: database file 202 failed verification check
ORA-01206: file is not part of this database - wrong database id
PDB$SEED(2): Cannot re-create tempfile /u01/oradata/CDB1/pdbseed/temp01<timestamp>.dbf, the same name file exists

What the alert log is telling you

  • ORA-01206 (wrong database id): the header of the PDB$SEED tempfile belongs to a different database.
  • "Cannot re-create tempfile... the same name file exists": when PDB$SEED opened, Oracle tried to rebuild the bad tempfile on its own. It couldn't, because a file with that name was already on disk.
  • The datapatch error: datapatch needs a working temporary tablespace in every container, including the seed. With none available, it hit an unhandled exception in sqlpatch.pm.

Likely cause

The tempfile name carries a timestamp from 2024, but PDB$SEED had already been patched successfully in an earlier cycle, so the header problem probably appeared after that, for example following a storage-level copy or a refresh of the database files between patch cycles. I can't prove when or how it happened, so treat this as the most likely explanation, not a confirmed one.

This is a useful lesson in itself: a seed that patched fine once can still break later.

The fix

I replaced the bad tempfile in PDB$SEED with a new one. This uses a hidden parameter, so read the cautions below first.

sqlplus / as sysdba

-- allow changes to the seed (session level only)
ALTER SESSION SET "_oracle_script" = TRUE;

ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB$SEED CLOSE IMMEDIATE;
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB$SEED OPEN READ WRITE;

ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = PDB$SEED;

-- remove the corrupted tempfile
ALTER DATABASE TEMPFILE '/u01/oradata/CDB1/pdbseed/temp01<timestamp>.dbf' DROP INCLUDING DATAFILES;

-- add a clean one
ALTER TABLESPACE TEMP ADD TEMPFILE '/u01/oradata/CDB1/pdbseed/temp01.dbf'
  SIZE 100M AUTOEXTEND ON NEXT 10M MAXSIZE 2G;

-- put the seed back as it was
ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = CDB$ROOT;
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB$SEED CLOSE IMMEDIATE;
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB$SEED OPEN READ ONLY;

EXIT;

Then rerun datapatch:

$ORACLE_HOME/OPatch/datapatch -verbose

Verify

After the fix, the rerun patched all three containers, including the seed:

$ORACLE_HOME/OPatch/datapatch -verbose
SQL Patching tool version 19.32.0.0.0 Production

Installation queue:
  For the following PDBs: CDB$ROOT PDB$SEED <PDB_NAME>
    The following interim patches will be rolled back:
      37847857 (OJVM RELEASE UPDATE: 19.28.0.0.250715)
    Patch 39472050 (Database Release Update : 19.32.0.0.260721):
      Apply from 19.28.0.0.0 to 19.32.0.0.0
    The following interim patches will be applied:
      39222882 (OJVM RELEASE UPDATE: 19.32.0.0.260721)

Patch installation complete.  Total patches installed: 9

Patch 37847857 rollback (pdb CDB$ROOT): SUCCESS
Patch 39472050 apply (pdb CDB$ROOT): SUCCESS
Patch 39222882 apply (pdb CDB$ROOT): SUCCESS
Patch 37847857 rollback (pdb PDB$SEED): SUCCESS
Patch 39472050 apply (pdb PDB$SEED): SUCCESS
Patch 39222882 apply (pdb PDB$SEED): SUCCESS
Patch 37847857 rollback (pdb <PDB_NAME>): SUCCESS
Patch 39472050 apply (pdb <PDB_NAME>): SUCCESS
Patch 39222882 apply (pdb <PDB_NAME>): SUCCESS

Then check the tempfiles across all containers:

SELECT con_id, file_id, file_name, tablespace_name, status
FROM cdb_temp_files ORDER BY con_id;

CON_ID 2 (the seed) should show the new temp01.dbf. Confirm the seed is back in its normal state:

SELECT name, open_mode, restricted FROM v$pdbs;

Finally, check that the patch was recorded:

SELECT patch_id, action, status, description
FROM dba_registry_sqlpatch ORDER BY action_time;

Cautions

  • _oracle_script is an underscore parameter. Oracle's own scripts use it, but using it by hand to change the seed is not something I'd do without a backup and a check of the relevant My Oracle Support note. In production, I'd raise a Service Request first.
  • I set it at session level only. ALTER SESSION means it was gone when I exited and never touched the spfile.
  • Take a backup first and try this in a non-production database.
  • Read-only afterwards. Always put PDB$SEED back in READ ONLY once you're done.

What I learned

  • A Perl-level error can hide a storage problem. When datapatch fails inside sqlpatch.pm, read the alert log at the same moment.
  • Check the seed's tempfile, not just the root. A bad tempfile in PDB$SEED can block patching even when everything else looks healthy.
  • Open your PDBs before running datapatch. It only patches PDBs that are open, and it skips closed ones.
  • Files can change between patch cycles. A seed that patched fine before can still break after copies or refreshes, so it's worth checking tempfile headers before a patching window.

Have you seen this error after patching a cloned or refreshed CDB? I'd like to hear whether the cause matched.

Kumaran Murugan is an Oracle Apps DBA and OCI Cloud Administrator with 5+ years of experience in Oracle E-Business Suite, database migrations, and OCI infrastructure. Connect on LinkedIn.

title: Dunning Compliance Is a Code Review Problem
description:
Most dunning compliance advice is written for lawyers and read by nobody. Meanwhile the actual decisions — how many texts you may send, what the email must say, when consent was recorded and where that record lives — get made by whoever writes the retry job. If compliance lives in a PDF nobody opens, it does not live anywhere. It has to survive as checks in the codebase and fields in the schema.

Start with consent, because everything else hangs off it. For email, the rules are comparatively forgiving: a transactional notice about a failed payment to an existing customer sits on solid ground in most jurisdictions, provided it is actually about the payment and carries working identification and opt-out mechanics where the law requires them. SMS is stricter everywhere. In the US, marketing texts need express written consent; transactional texts still need a defensible consent record, a recognizable sender, and a functioning STOP path — and “the customer gave us a number at checkout” is a thinner record than most teams assume. Store the consent event like you store a payment event: timestamp, surface, exact language shown, and the number it applied to. If you cannot query it, you do not have it.

Second: frequency is a compliance surface, not just a UX one. Several regimes and carrier rules treat repeated automated messages as a category problem regardless of content. Cap your sequences in code, per channel, per customer, with the caps visible in one config file a reviewer can read. A dunning flow that can send nine touches because three separate jobs each think they own three is a bug with legal consequences.

Third: content constraints are checkable. No threats you cannot carry out (“your account will be deleted tonight” when it will not be), no invented deadlines, no fees described that the contract does not support, and in the EU and UK, consumer-protection rules on top of the privacy ones. Write these as lint rules for templates: banned phrases fail the build, required elements (business identity, a real reply path, the actual amount) are asserted present. Templates change often; the checks should run every time they do.

Fourth: data handling. Card-update links should be tokenized, single-purpose, and expiring; logs should never carry full card data (they should not carry it at all — that is what your processor’s vault is for); and retention needs a number, in days, that somebody chose on purpose. “Forever” is not a retention policy, it is an accident in progress.

None of this is exotic. It is the same discipline as idempotency keys and webhook signature checks — boring, testable, and much cheaper before the first regulator or carrier asks than after. If you want the whole thing as a pass/fail list you can work through with your own stack open beside it, a compliance checklist for dunning that a developer can actually implement covers consent records, channel rules, content constraints, and data handling in implementation order.

Finally, build the audit drill before anyone asks for it. Once a quarter, pull a random sample of twenty dunning sends across channels and reconstruct each one’s paperwork from the system’s own records: the consent event behind the number or address, the frequency cap in force at send time, the template version that produced the copy, and the suppression checks that ran. Time the exercise. If a single send takes an afternoon to document, the records exist on paper but not in practice, and that gap — not any individual rule — is the real compliance risk. The drill has a side benefit engineers appreciate: it is a standing test of the logging nobody otherwise exercises until an incident, and it turns “we keep good records” from an assertion into a measured retrieval time.

Treat the checklist like a test suite: run it when the flow changes, not when someone remembers. That habit — compliance as a maintained property of the system rather than a document about the system — is the core of Swipe Again’s recovery work, and it is available to any team willing to write the checks down.

title: Designing a real AI kill switch: capability absence vs middleware gates
description:
"Which guardrail framework should I use?" is the wrong question for a kill switch. The best interceptor in the world still intercepts something that exists.

Quick disclosure before the code: I work on KarmaBox, where agent permissions are enforced exactly the way this article recommends, so I'm arguing my own book. Three things keep this checkable: the pattern below is ~40 lines of dependency-free Python you can run and attack yourself; every news fact carries its outlet and date; and the last section lists what this pattern does not solve — including the part my employer hasn't solved either.

Why this is worth your evening this particular week: on November 3, Google announced that schools disabling its AI features lose Google Search entirely, because — per its education VP — "Search and AI are deeply integrated" (TechCrunch, November 3, 2026). Set aside the politics. As engineers, read it as an architecture confession: they built the off switch into a layer where flipping it takes down the building. This article is about not building that.

The definition, before the code

A real kill switch removes a capability. It does not hide it, intercept it, or instruct the model to decline it — it makes the capability unreachable, for every caller, through every path. If "off" is implemented anywhere the capability can still be invoked, what you have is a gate: a thing that says no while the wiring behind it stays live.

The distinction matters because gates and absences fail in opposite directions. A gate that crashes, gets misconfigured, or gets argued past fails open — the capability runs. An absence cannot fail open, because there is nothing on the other side of the switch to run. At 2 a.m., that's the whole difference.

Two architectures for "off"

Most agent stacks implement "off" as middleware: the tool stays registered, and a policy layer intercepts calls.

# Architecture A: middleware gate
agent → tool_call("send_email") → policy middleware → [allow? deny?] → send_email()

# Architecture B: registry absence
agent → tools_for(role)  →  send_email was never in the list

In Architecture A, send_email exists in the agent's tool list. The model can see it, plan around it, and attempt it; a middleware decides at call time. In Architecture B, the tool surface is assembled per role from a registry, and a capability that is off was simply never assembled in. The model cannot call what it cannot see, and neither can a prompt injection riding in on a document.


The failure-mode comparison, side by side:

One row deserves emphasis because this week made it concrete: the audit story. Google's announcement also claims schools can toggle each service individually — but two months from now, the only way a district can verify what was actually off is whatever the console shows. A switch you can't independently audit is a promise with a UI. Registries make the audit cheap: the assembled list is the ground truth.

The pattern in ~40 lines

Dependency-free, three permission tiers: direct (runs), approval (runs after a human approves), absent (not assembled at all).

# registry.py — capability registry with three tiers
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable

TIERS = ("direct", "approval", "absent")

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Capability:
    name: str
    fn: Callable
    tier: str  # one of TIERS

class Registry:
    def __init__(self):
        self._caps: dict[str, Capability] = {}

    def register(self, name, fn, tier):
        if tier not in TIERS:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown tier: {tier}")
        self._caps[name] = Capability(name, fn, tier)

    def tools_for(self, role_policy: dict[str, str]) -> dict[str, Capability]:
        """Assemble the tool surface for one role.
        A capability whose tier is 'absent' is NOT in the result.
        There is no gate to bypass — it simply isn't mounted."""
        surface = {}
        for name, tier in role_policy.items():
            cap = self._caps.get(name)
            if cap is None or tier == "absent":
                continue  # never mounted
            surface[name] = Capability(name, cap.fn, tier)
        return surface

    def audit(self, role_policy: dict[str, str]) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
        """Export the effective capability list — this is the audit artifact."""
        mounted = self.tools_for(role_policy)
        return sorted(
            (name, mounted[name].tier if name in mounted else "absent")
            for name in role_policy
        )

def dispatch(surface, name, approver=None, **kwargs):
    cap = surface.get(name)
    if cap is None:
        raise LookupError(f"{name}: not a capability of this role")  # fail closed
    if cap.tier == "approval":
        if approver is None or not approver(name, kwargs):
            raise PermissionError(f"{name}: approval required, none given")
    return cap.fn(**kwargs)

Notes on the load-bearing lines. tools_for is where "off" happens: an absent capability is skipped at assembly, so the model's tool list — the thing you serialize into the API call — never contains it. dispatch fails closed on anything outside the surface: an unknown or absent tool raises, it doesn't fall through to a default handler. And audit exists because the Google story's quiet lesson is that consoles and reality drift; your auditor gets the assembled list, not a screenshot of settings.

Three tests, and what it means when each fails 

def test_absent_is_unreachable(registry):
    surface = registry.tools_for({"send_email": "absent"})
    assert "send_email" not in surface
    try:
        dispatch(surface, "send_email", to="x@y.z")
        assert False, "dispatch must raise"
    except LookupError:
        pass

If this fails: your "off" is a gate, not an absence — somewhere a fallback path still resolves the tool. This is the test that separates the two architectures; everything else is decoration.


def test_approval_blocks_without_human(registry):
    surface = registry.tools_for({"post_public": "approval"})
    try:
        dispatch(surface, "post_public", body="hi")  # no approver passed
        assert False, "must require approval"
    except PermissionError:
        pass

If this fails: your approval tier silently degraded into the direct tier — the exact drift the middleware column of the table predicts. Expect to find a "temporary" default-approver someone added during an incident.

def test_audit_matches_surface(registry, role_policy):
    audit = dict(registry.audit(role_policy))
    surface = registry.tools_for(role_policy)
    for name, tier in audit.items():
        assert (name in surface) == (tier != "absent")

If this fails: your audit artifact lies. That's worse than having no audit, because people will trust it. Fix this before fixing anything it reports.

The audit endpoint

Expose registry.audit(role_policy) as an internal endpoint or a CLI command and snapshot it on every deploy. Go one step further and make the snapshot a CI artifact: a job that diffs the assembled surface against the last release and fails the build on any unreviewed widening — a capability moving from absent to anything, or a new tool appearing in a role. Narrowing can auto-pass; widening needs a human's name on it. Now "what could the agent do on March 12" is a git log question, not an archaeology project. When a vendor tells you a capability "can be disabled," this is the artifact to ask them for — the effective capability list, not the settings screenshot. (For schools asking Google that question right now: per the November 3 reporting, the answer for Search-AI is that no such list will ever show it off while Search is on. The wiring is the policy.)

One more direction worth knowing about, published the same day: Anthropic released FlashProve, open-source research toward cryptographic proof of which model produced an output — fingerprints published per model, no weights revealed, verifiable locally (TechCrunch, November 3, 2026). Registry audit tells you which capabilities were mounted; provable inference points at the next layer — proving which model sat behind them. Research status, no deployments; but that's the end state audits are crawling toward.

Migrating an existing stack: the strangler path

Nobody gets to rewrite their agent platform this sprint, so here is the incremental path we'd actually recommend — the classic strangler pattern, applied to tool surfaces. Four stages, each shippable on its own.

Stage one: inventory the gates. Grep for wherever tool calls get intercepted today — middleware, decorators, the if-statement graveyard inside your dispatcher. Each interception point is a capability that believes it has an off switch. List them with their current default behavior on error: you will find at least one that fails open, and finding it is the first win of the migration.

Stage two: wrap, don't replace. Introduce the registry in front of the existing gates. The registry assembles the tool surface; the old gates stay exactly where they are, now guarding capabilities that were already filtered upstream. Nothing can break, because nothing was removed — you've added a second, stricter filter.

Stage three: dual-run with a mismatch alarm. For a few weeks, log every case where the old gate blocked something the registry had mounted, or — the interesting direction — where the registry excluded something the gate would have allowed. Each mismatch is either a policy bug or an undocumented dependency. We'd treat the second kind exactly like the accounting-filters discovery in this week's sysadmin threads: evidence of load-bearing coupling nobody wrote down.

Stage four: flip per role, then delete. Move one role at a time to registry-only enforcement, lowest-risk role first. Delete the gates last, not first — dead code that can't be reached through the registry is annoying; a gate deleted before the registry covered it is an incident.

Two objections that always come up, answered honestly. Latency: effectively none — assembly happens once at session start, not per call; tools_for is a dictionary filter. Operational cost: yes, changing a capability now requires a deploy instead of a config flip. That is not a drawback to minimize; it is the entire point. A capability change that produces a diff, a reviewer, and a rollback path is the audit trail — the config flip that skips all three is how the middleware column of the failure table happens.

What this pattern does not solve

Honesty section, including against my employer. The registry pattern does not solve judgment: deciding which capability belongs in which tier is a human call, and a wrong call with perfect enforcement is still wrong. It does not solve data already sent: a capability you unmount today did whatever it did last quarter. It does not solve indirect effects: a direct-tier tool can still be misused within its scope (a search tool can exfiltrate by querying; the registry won't see it). And it does not give you cryptographic verification — my audit endpoint is logs you have to trust; the FlashProve direction is the eventual fix, and nobody ships it yet, including the product I work on.

The question worth taking back to your own stack: for each tool your agent can currently see — if the policy service died at 2 a.m., which way does it fail?

Sources

  1. TechCrunch (Aisha Malik), Google will let schools disable its AI tools, but not without sacrificing Search, November 3, 2026

  2. TechCrunch (Russell Brandom), Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models' identity, November 3, 2026 FlashProve is research with published code, no deployment.

  3. Code in this article: illustrative, dependency-free, written for this post — run it, break it, tell me where.

title: How to Audit Any Trading Indicator Before You Trust It With Real Money
description:
Most traders spend more time picking which indicator to buy than they spend checking whether it actually does what the sales page claims. That is backwards. A $40 indicator that quietly repaints its last three signals, or one that was curve-fit to eighteen months of trending price action, can cost you a lot more than $40 once you start sizing real positions around it.

This isn't a pitch for any specific tool. It's a walkthrough of the questions you should be asking before you add any indicator — free, paid, subscription, or one-time purchase — to your chart. If you've never run this kind of check before, it will take about twenty minutes the first time and five minutes after that, once it becomes a habit.

Why Most Traders Never Actually Vet Their Tools
There's a simple reason indicator due diligence gets skipped: it's not fun. Buying a new tool feels like progress. Testing whether it lies to you feels like homework. So traders install, glance at a few pretty signals on the chart, and move on to actually trading — which is exactly the order that gets people hurt.

There's also a confidence problem. A lot of retail traders assume that because an indicator is sold on a marketplace, or has a slick landing page with backtest screenshots, someone else has already checked it. Nobody has. Script marketplaces host thousands of public and invite-only scripts with no vetting process beyond "does it compile." A backtest screenshot on a sales page proves the author ran a backtest once. It proves nothing about how that backtest was constructed.

The fix isn't paranoia — it's a short, repeatable checklist you run on anything before it touches your trading decisions. That's what the rest of this piece gives you.

The Three Layers of Indicator Risk
Every indicator carries risk at three distinct layers, and they require different checks:

Code risk — what the script is mathematically doing on each bar, and whether it changes its mind retroactively.
Claims risk — the gap between what the marketing says and what an independent test would show.
Context risk — whether the tool, even if honest and well-built, actually fits your market, timeframe, and trading style.
An indicator can pass one layer and fail another. A perfectly honest trend-following overlay can still be the wrong tool for a scalper trading five-minute charts on a chop-heavy index. Treat all three as mandatory, not optional.

Layer One: What the Code Is Actually Doing
This is the layer most traders skip entirely, usually because they can't read Pine Script and assume they don't need to. You don't need to be a programmer to run the three checks below — you need about fifteen minutes and TradingView's own replay tool.

Check for repainting
Repainting is when a signal that appeared on a historical bar changes or disappears once price action has moved past it. It is the single most common way an indicator's backtest looks far better than its live performance, because the indicator is quietly "seeing" information it would not have had in real time.

There are three common ways this happens: future data leakage inside the script logic (using request.security calls without the right lookahead setting), signals that are only finalized after a bar closes but get drawn as if they fired mid-bar, and adaptive lookback windows that silently recalculate historical values as new bars arrive. Any one of these can make a strategy look profitable in a screenshot and lose money the moment you trade it live.

The fastest way to catch it yourself: open TradingView's Bar Replay mode, step forward bar by bar through a period you haven't looked at before, and watch whether signals that already printed move, vanish, or change color after the fact. If they do, you've found repainting — full stop, regardless of what the sales copy says. It's worth building this into a standing habit any time you evaluate a new script; traders who search specifically for non-repainting indicators before buying are doing exactly this kind of check, just from the buyer's side rather than by testing the code themselves.

Check for smoothing and lag disguised as "AI"
A lot of modern indicator marketing leans on "AI-powered" or "adaptive" language. Sometimes that genuinely means parameters that adjust to current volatility (a real, useful property). Sometimes it means a moving average with an extra smoothing pass, relabeled. The test is simple: does the indicator's signal timing change meaningfully as you switch between a high-volatility period and a quiet one? If the lag is constant regardless of market conditions, "adaptive" is marketing language, not a mechanism.

Read the Pine Script, even badly
If the script is open-source (many are, even paid ones, since TradingView's invite-only model still requires publishing readable or at least partially commented code), skim it for request.security calls, barstate.isconfirmed checks, and any variable that gets reassigned inside a loop over historical bars. You don't need to understand the math — you need to see whether the author bothered to guard against lookahead bias at all. Scripts that never reference bar confirmation state are worth a second look.

Layer Two: Marketing Claims vs Verifiable Performance
Every indicator seller has an incentive to show you their best quarter. That's not necessarily dishonest — it's just marketing — but it means you need to separate three categories of claim:

1. Win Rate / Backtest Screenshot
How verifiable: Low — unknown data range, unknown slippage, and unknown curve-fitting.

What to do with it: Treat it as a hypothesis, not evidence. Re-test yourself on out-of-sample data.

2. "Non-Repainting" or "Lag-Free"
How verifiable: High — directly testable with TradingView Bar Replay.

What to do with it: Verify before you believe it. This is the cheapest check on the list.

3. Named Customer Reviews with Specifics
How verifiable: Medium — can't confirm identity, but detail and consistency over time are useful signals.

What to do with it: Give more weight to consistent, specific, long-term reviews than one-off five-star reviews with no supporting details.

4. "Institutional-Grade" / "Proprietary Algorithm"
How verifiable: Low — these are unfalsifiable marketing terms.

Layer Three: Context Fit
An honest, well-built indicator can still be wrong for you. Three context questions matter more than most buyers realize:

Instrument fit. An indicator tuned and tested on BTC/USD 15-minute candles may behave completely differently on an equity index or a forex pair with different volatility regimes and session structure.
Timeframe fit. A tool designed to confirm swing entries on daily charts will generate noise if you force it onto a 1-minute scalping chart, and vice versa.
Workflow fit. Does the signal give you enough lead time to actually act on it given your execution method (manual, alert-triggered, or automated)? A signal that fires and expires within one bar is useless if you're trading manually off a phone.
Ask any vendor directly what instrument and timeframe their internal testing used. A vague answer is itself useful information.

A Five-Step Audit You Can Run in 20 Minutes

Bar Replay test. Step through 100+ historical bars and watch for signals that move or vanish after printing.
Screenshot-vs-live comparison. Take a screenshot of the current chart with signals visible, wait 24–48 hours, and compare against the same period later. Any discrepancy on already-closed bars is a repaint.
Ask for the methodology, not the results. A vendor who can describe how their signal logic locks values at bar close is giving you something checkable. A vendor who only shows you the P&L screenshot is not.
Run it on an instrument it wasn't marketed for. If performance collapses completely outside the marketed use case, that tells you how narrow — and how curve-fit — the design actually is.
Paper trade for at least two full weeks before funding it. This is the only step that tests execution lag, alert reliability, and your own discipline following the signal, none of which a backtest can show you.
Always paper trade a new indicator or signal source before committing real capital to it. No amount of due diligence substitutes for watching a tool behave in live, forward-looking conditions with money you haven't risked yet.

Red Flags That Should End the Conversation
The vendor cannot explain, in plain language, why their indicator doesn't repaint — or dodges the question.
Every testimonial is generic ("Changed my trading forever!") with no specifics about instrument, timeframe, or what actually improved.
The backtest period conveniently starts right before a strong trending market and ends right before it reversed.
Pricing pressure tactics — countdown timers, "only 10 spots left," artificial urgency on a digital product with zero inventory constraint.
No visible documentation, demo, or public track record you can inspect before paying.

A Walkthrough: Auditing a Momentum Overlay
Here's how this plays out in practice. Say you're a swing trader considering a momentum overlay indicator marketed for daily-chart equity trades.
