You open the free trial, flip on Bar Replay, and step through six months of a mid-cap stock. Three of the overlay's "buy" arrows on older bars have quietly disappeared compared to where they were when you first loaded the chart — a clear repaint. That alone is enough to walk away, but suppose it had passed: your next move is to check whether the vendor publishes any description of how signals finalize. Some providers document this explicitly — in the non-repainting indicator space, for example, QuantZee's product pages describe signals as locking at bar close and never shifting retroactively, which is the kind of mechanism-level claim you can actually go verify yourself with the replay test above, rather than just take on faith.

From there, you'd run the instrument-fit check: load the same overlay onto a volatile small-cap and a slow-moving large-cap index, and see whether signal frequency and quality hold up or whether it only "works" on the exact ticker used in the marketing screenshots. Only after all of that would a two-week paper-trading window make sense.

What Pricing Structure Tells You About Risk
Pricing model isn't just a cost decision — it's a signal about how the vendor is incentivized to treat you. A monthly subscription with no annual option and heavy discounting on "upgrade now" pop-ups usually means the business model depends on constant new-customer acquisition rather than long-term retention from satisfied users. That's not proof of a bad product, but it does change how much weight you should put on retention-based signals like "thousands of happy subscribers," since churn can be high even while new signups look healthy.

A one-time purchase model flips the incentive the other way: the vendor only gets paid once per customer, so there's no recurring revenue to hide a declining user base behind. That makes public reviews, documentation quality, and demo transparency more informative, because the vendor has less ongoing leverage over you after the sale — they either earned trust at the point of purchase or they didn't. It also means you should scrutinize the return policy more carefully: source-code products that email you the actual script on purchase typically can't offer refunds in good faith, because the code can't be un-sent once delivered. A strict no-refund policy on a source-code product is not automatically a red flag; it's often just an honest acknowledgment of what a digital, non-returnable good actually is. The red flag is the opposite — a vendor promising money-back guarantees on something that can be copied the moment it's delivered.

Either model can be run honestly or dishonestly. The point isn't to prefer one over the other; it's to understand what incentives the pricing structure creates, and adjust how much weight you give to the vendor's own retention claims accordingly.

Where Vendors Hide Weak Claims in Plain Sight
A surprisingly common tactic is burying a weak or qualified claim inside a strong-sounding sentence. "Our proprietary algorithm analyzes over 40 market variables" sounds impressive and is almost always unfalsifiable — you have no way to check the number 40, no way to know if "analyzes" means anything more than reading 40 price-derived inputs into a single weighted average. Compare that to a specific, checkable claim: "signals lock at bar close and do not recalculate on historical bars," which you can directly test with the Bar Replay method above. The difference between the two sentence types is the difference between marketing copy and an engineering claim. Train yourself to notice which one you're reading.

The same pattern shows up in comparison pages across the industry — a page claiming to be "the most accurate indicator on TradingView" with no named benchmark, no stated accuracy metric, and no methodology is making a claim that cannot be checked by definition. That doesn't necessarily mean the product is bad; it means the page gave you zero information you can act on, and you need to go find the checkable claims elsewhere (documentation, code, or a trial).

A Short Note on Backtest Mechanics Worth Asking About
If a vendor does share backtest results, three questions separate a credible test from a decorative one:

**What slippage and fee assumptions were used? **A backtest with zero slippage on a scalping strategy is not a backtest of anything you could actually trade.

Was the test run on the same parameters shown on the sales page, or were parameters optimized after seeing the result? Optimizing parameters on the same data you're reporting results from is curve-fitting by definition, even if nobody involved intended to mislead anyone.

Is there an out-of-sample period — data the strategy was never tuned against — and does performance hold up there? This is the single most informative question you can ask, and the one vendors answer least often, simply because most never ran one.
You don't need the full dataset to ask these questions. A vendor's willingness (or refusal) to answer them tells you most of what you need to know.

Building This Into a Standing Habit
The traders who get burned repeatedly by indicator marketing aren't unintelligent — they just never built a repeatable process, so every new tool gets evaluated from scratch, under time pressure, usually right after a losing week when they're most tempted to buy a solution. Put the five-step audit above into a note you can reuse. Treat every new tool, free or paid, the same way: replay test first, methodology question second, context fit third, paper trade fourth. The habit costs you twenty minutes. Skipping it costs a lot more when the tool fails in exactly the way a twenty-minute check would have caught.

**How to Verify a "Non-Repainting" Claim Yourself, Step by Step
**Most of this guide has described the Bar Replay test in general terms. It's worth walking through the exact mechanics once, because the value of the test comes entirely from doing it correctly, not from knowing it exists.

Load the indicator on a liquid instrument with at least six months of history — enough historical bars that the script has had to recalculate across multiple volatility regimes.
Open the Bar Replay toolbar and set the replay start point roughly four months back. Starting further back than that mostly wastes time; starting too close to "now" leaves too few bars to judge signal stability.
Step forward in small increments — five to ten bars at a time — and take a mental or literal screenshot of every signal that has already printed. The habit that matters here is actively watching the already-drawn signals, not just the newest one appearing at the playhead.
When you reach the point where you started, compare your screenshot against the chart as it now stands with all bars confirmed. Any signal that has moved to a different bar, changed direction, or disappeared entirely between your first look and your second is a repaint — confirmed by direct observation rather than taken on the vendor's word.
Repeat the exact same process on a second, unrelated instrument. A result that holds on one chart but not another often points to repainting that's data-dependent rather than present in every case, which is still disqualifying but worth noting precisely.

This is the same basic method professional quant researchers use when auditing a third party's signal generation before trusting it in production — load historical data, step through it deterministically, and compare snapshots. The retail version just runs on a chart instead of in a dataframe.

Common Mistakes Traders Make Even After Running the Audit
Running the checklist once isn't the same as building immunity to bad tools forever. A few mistakes show up repeatedly even among traders who know better:

Re-testing a tool once, then trusting every future update blindly. Vendors ship updates.A version that passed your replay test in March can be modified in June in ways that reintroduce lookahead bias, especially if the change touches the underlying calculation rather than just the UI. Spot-check again after any meaningful version update, not just at first purchase.
Letting a winning streak suspend the checklist.Three or four profitable trades in a row with a new tool feels like validation, and it quietly turns off the skepticism that got you through the due-diligence process in the first place. A short winning streak on a small sample size is not evidence of anything — it's noise, in either direction.
Confusing "it's free" with "it's low-risk." A free indicator that repaints and leads you into a bad position costs you exactly as much as a paid one that does the same thing. Price has nothing to do with code correctness.
Skipping the paper-trading window because the audit "looked clean." A clean code and marketing audit tells you the tool isn't lying to you. It doesn't tell you whether the signal frequency, lead time, and false-positive rate actually fit how you trade day to day. Only live forward testing with no money at risk answers that.
None of these are complicated to avoid. They just require treating indicator evaluation as an ongoing discipline rather than a one-time gate you pass through on the way to a purchase.

FAQ

Is repainting always a dealbreaker?
For any indicator you intend to trade off directly, yes. A small amount of redraw on indicators explicitly built as lagging confirmation tools (where the vendor is upfront about it) is different from a signal-generation tool that silently repaints its entries — but when in doubt, treat repainting as disqualifying.
Can a free TradingView built-in indicator repaint?
Generally no for the standard built-ins (RSI, MACD, moving averages) when used in their default, non-security-request form — they calculate off confirmed historical data by construction. Custom scripts built on top of them can still introduce repainting through how they're coded.
How long should I paper trade a new indicator before funding it?
Two weeks is a reasonable minimum for anything used on intraday to swing timeframes — long enough to see several full signal cycles, including at least one losing stretch.
Do one-time-purchase indicators get less scrutiny than subscriptions?
If anything they deserve more upfront scrutiny, since there's no ongoing relationship or renewal decision forcing a re-evaluation later — you're committing to the tool as-is at purchase.
What does "repainting" actually mean in plain terms?
It means a signal that already appeared on your chart, on a bar that has already closed, changes or vanishes later — as if the indicator went back in time and edited history. In live trading you never get that privilege, so a backtest built on repainted signals is testing a version of the market that never existed.

title: TypeScript `globalThis` Typing in 2026: Safely Adding Properties to the Global Scope Without `any`
description:
TypeScript globalThis Typing in 2026: Safely Adding Properties to the Global Scope Without any

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Why globalThis Typing Still Matters in 2026

The global scope remains the path of least resistance for quick hacks. Developers drop variables onto globalThis to share state across modules, expose debug hooks to the browser console, or bridge third-party scripts that expect global names. TypeScript sees these assignments and defaults to any, erasing type safety at the exact boundary where typos and runtime crashes cluster.

The broken pattern looks innocent: globalThis.featureFlags = { darkMode: true } compiles without complaint, but every access to globalThis.featureFlags surrenders type checking. When another engineer misspells darkMode as darkmode three modules away, the compiler stays silent and the test suite passes until production traffic hits the undefined code path.

Declaration merging solves this. TypeScript permits extending the globalThis interface with new properties, restoring autocomplete and type errors for every global access. The corrected pattern uses an ambient declaration to teach the compiler about the new global without changing runtime behavior.

This pattern matters when a codebase has already committed to global state and rewriting it would delay shipping features. The technique also bridges legacy constraints: third-party analytics scripts, browser extensions that inject globals, or Node.js test runners that expose assertion libraries on global. Knowing when each variant (globalThis, window, global) breaks prevents silent failures in cross-environment builds.

Key Takeaways

  • TypeScript allows extending the globalThis interface via declaration merging, restoring full type safety for global properties without runtime overhead.
  • The declare global block works only in module files; script files can declare directly on interface globalThis but lose module isolation.
  • The window, global, and globalThis identifiers reference different objects depending on the runtime environment, causing subtle breakage when the wrong one is typed.
  • Proper cleanup between test suites requires explicit delete statements, as TypeScript type declarations do not remove runtime properties.
  • Most use cases have better alternatives: environment variable objects, dependency injection, or module-scoped constants avoid global namespace pollution entirely.

The Problem: Adding Properties to globalThis Without any

A common scenario surfaces when integrating analytics libraries. The vendor provides a snippet that assigns a tracker instance to the global scope:

globalThis.analytics = {
  track: (event, properties) => {
    // implementation
  },
  identify: (userId, traits) => {
    // implementation
  }
};

TypeScript infers the type of globalThis.analytics as any because globalThis is a predefined global with a fixed type that does not include an analytics property. Every subsequent access to globalThis.analytics.track bypasses type checking. The engineer who writes globalThis.analytics.trak("click") will not receive an error until runtime.

TypeScript globalThis without proper typing

Attempting to add a type annotation at the assignment site fails:

globalThis.analytics = {
  track: (event: string, properties: Record<string, unknown>) => {},
  identify: (userId: string, traits: Record<string, unknown>) => {}
} as AnalyticsClient;
// Error: Property 'analytics' does not exist on type 'typeof globalThis'

The error reveals the core issue: TypeScript has a preexisting interface definition for globalThis that does not include an analytics member. Adding the property at runtime does not change the compile-time type.

The compiler blocks the assignment because it cannot verify that adding arbitrary properties to a global object is safe. The solution requires teaching TypeScript about the new property through declaration merging.

Declaration Merging: The Official TypeScript Pattern

Declaration merging extends an existing interface by declaring it again with additional members. TypeScript combines all declarations of the same interface into a single definition. For globalThis, this means adding a new interface declaration that specifies the custom property:

// types/global.d.ts
declare global {
  interface globalThis {
    analytics: {
      track: (event: string, properties: Record<string, unknown>) => void;
      identify: (userId: string, traits: Record<string, unknown>) => void;
    };
  }
}

export {};

The declare global block is necessary when the file is a module (contains an import or export statement). The empty export {} at the end forces TypeScript to treat the file as a module, which activates the declare global requirement. Without this, the declaration would apply to the module's local scope instead of the global scope.

After adding this declaration, the original assignment compiles without error:

globalThis.analytics = {
  track: (event, properties) => {
    console.log(event, properties);
  },
  identify: (userId, traits) => {
    console.log(userId, traits);
  }
};

Type checking now works across the entire codebase. Accessing globalThis.analytics.track provides autocomplete for the method signature, and misspelling the method name triggers a compile error:

// Autocomplete suggests: track, identify
globalThis.analytics.track("pageview", { path: "/home" });

// Error: Property 'trak' does not exist on type
globalThis.analytics.trak("click");

The declaration can reference custom types for cleaner definitions:

// types/global.d.ts
interface AnalyticsClient {
  track: (event: string, properties: Record<string, unknown>) => void;
  identify: (userId: string, traits: Record<string, unknown>) => void;
}

declare global {
  interface globalThis {
    analytics: AnalyticsClient;
  }
}

export {};

This pattern works for any property type. Complex nested objects, function signatures, and generic constraints all merge correctly. The TypeScript compiler released version 3.4 with explicit support for typing globalThis, as documented in the TypeScript 3.4 release notes.

globalThis vs window vs global: When Each Pattern Breaks

The JavaScript language provides three identifiers for the global object: globalThis, window, and global. Each identifier works in specific environments, and typing the wrong one causes silent failures.

Identifier Browser Node.js Web Worker When it breaks
globalThis ✓ ✓ ✓ Never (ES2020+)
window ✓ ✗ ✗ Node.js and Worker environments throw ReferenceError
global ✗ ✓ ✗ Browser and Worker environments have no global

Typing window creates code that compiles for browser targets but crashes in Node.js:

// types/global.d.ts
declare global {
  interface Window {
    analytics: AnalyticsClient;
  }
}

export {};

// runtime.ts
window.analytics = { /* ... */ };
// ReferenceError: window is not defined (in Node.js)

The same issue occurs when typing global for Node.js projects that later run in a browser:

// types/global.d.ts
declare global {
  namespace NodeJS {
    interface Global {
      analytics: AnalyticsClient;
    }
  }
}

export {};

// runtime.ts
global.analytics = { /* ... */ };
// ReferenceError: global is not defined (in browser)

The globalThis identifier solves this. Introduced in ES2020, globalThis references the global object in all environments. Browsers alias it to window, Node.js aliases it to global, and Web Workers provide it directly. Code that uses globalThis runs unchanged across all targets.

TypeScript's type definitions for globalThis live in lib.es2020.d.ts. Projects targeting ES2020 or later automatically include these definitions. For older targets, developers must add "lib": ["ES2020"] to tsconfig.json or include a polyfill that backfills the globalThis identifier at runtime.

Module vs Script Context: Why declare global Sometimes Fails

TypeScript distinguishes between module files and script files based on the presence of import or export statements. This distinction changes how global declarations work.

A script file has no import or export statements. Its declarations apply to the global scope by default:

// types/global.d.ts (script file)
interface globalThis {
  analytics: AnalyticsClient;
}

This works without the declare global wrapper. TypeScript merges the interface directly into the global globalThis type. However, the file lacks module isolation. Any types defined here pollute the global namespace and can conflict with types in other files.

A module file contains at least one import or export statement. Module files have their own scope, so declarations do not affect the global scope unless wrapped in declare global:

// types/global.d.ts (module file)
export {};

interface globalThis {
  analytics: AnalyticsClient;
}
// This declaration applies to the module scope, not the global scope

The globalThis interface above creates a local type that shadows the global globalThis. Accessing globalThis.analytics in another file still returns any because the global type has not changed.

The correct pattern for a module file uses declare global:

// types/global.d.ts (module file)
declare global {
  interface globalThis {
    analytics: AnalyticsClient;
  }
}

export {};

The export {} forces the file to be a module while exporting nothing. This preserves module isolation while allowing the declare global block to modify the global scope.

Projects that use ES modules (.mts extension or "type": "module" in package.json) default to module context. Adding a global type declaration to such a project without declare global produces no effect, and the compiler offers no warning about the mistake.

Real-World Patterns: Environment Variables, Feature Flags, and Runtime Config

Three scenarios drive most globalThis typing: environment variables exposed by bundlers, feature flags controlled by remote config, and runtime configuration injected by server-side rendering.

Environment Variables

Bundlers like Vite expose environment variables through import.meta.env. TypeScript does not know which variables the bundler will inject, so accessing import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL returns string | undefined. Declaring the variables restores specificity:

// env.d.ts
interface ImportMetaEnv {
  readonly VITE_API_URL: string;
  readonly VITE_ENABLE_ANALYTICS: string;
}

interface ImportMeta {
  readonly env: ImportMetaEnv;
}

This pattern extends ImportMeta instead of globalThis, but the principle is identical. The declaration merges into the existing interface, and all accesses to import.meta.env gain type safety.

Some projects assign environment variables directly to globalThis for access in non-module code:

// runtime-env.ts
declare global {
  interface globalThis {
    ENV: {
      API_URL: string;
      ENABLE_ANALYTICS: boolean;
    };
  }
}

globalThis.ENV = {
  API_URL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
  ENABLE_ANALYTICS: import.meta.env.VITE_ENABLE_ANALYTICS === "true"
};

export {};

This approach centralizes the boolean parsing logic and provides a single typed object for environment configuration.

Feature Flags

Remote configuration services deliver feature flags as JSON. The consuming application receives an object with boolean properties:

// feature-flags.d.ts
declare global {
  interface globalThis {
    featureFlags: {
      enableDarkMode: boolean;
      enableBetaFeatures: boolean;
      maxUploadSizeMB: number;
    };
  }
}

export {};

// init.ts
fetch("/api/feature-flags")
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(flags => {
    globalThis.featureFlags = flags;
  });

Components that check flags receive autocomplete and type errors:

if (globalThis.featureFlags.enableDarkMode) {
  document.body.classList.add("dark");
}

// Error: Property 'enableDrakMode' does not exist
if (globalThis.featureFlags.enableDrakMode) {
  // typo caught at compile time
}

The risk here is runtime shape mismatch. If the API response changes and removes enableDarkMode, the application will read undefined at runtime despite the TypeScript type claiming a boolean. Adding runtime validation with a library like Zod or writing a manual assertion function mitigates this.

TypeScript globalThis feature flags pattern

Server-Side Rendering Config

Frameworks like Next.js inject configuration into the initial HTML payload. The server renders a `tag that assigns towindow`:

`html

window.INITIAL_STATE = {
user: { id: "123", name: "Alice" },
cart: []
};

`

The client-side code reads this state before making API calls:

`typescript
// initial-state.d.ts
declare global {
interface Window {
INITIAL_STATE: {
user: { id: string; name: string };
cart: Array<{ productId: string; quantity: number }>;
};
}
}

export {};
`

`typescript
// hydrate.ts
const initialState = window.__INITIAL_STATE__;
renderApp(initialState);
`

This pattern works only in browser environments. Server-side code that references window.__INITIAL_STATE__ will crash. Conditional checks guard the access:

`typescript
const state = typeof window !== "undefined"
? window.__INITIAL_STATE__
: getDefaultState();
`

The type system does not enforce this check. Developers must remember to add it, or the build will succeed and production will fail when server-side rendering tries to reference window.

Testing and Cleanup: Avoiding Pollution Between Test Suites

Global state persists across test files when a test runner executes all files in a single process. A test that assigns globalThis.featureFlags = { enableBeta: true } leaves that property set for subsequent tests. The next test suite that checks if (globalThis.featureFlags.enableBeta) will read the previous value instead of the expected undefined, causing false passes or failures.

The TypeScript declaration does not remove runtime properties. Deleting the type does not reset the global:

`typescript
// This does not work:
declare global {
interface globalThis {
featureFlags: undefined; // only affects compile-time type
}
}
`

Proper cleanup requires explicit delete statements in an afterEach hook:

`typescript
// test-setup.ts
afterEach(() => {
delete globalThis.featureFlags;
delete globalThis.analytics;
delete globalThis.ENV;
});
`

TypeScript will still report errors if code accesses the deleted property, because the type declaration remains in scope. Wrapping the delete in a type guard silences this:

`typescript
afterEach(() => {
if ("featureFlags" in globalThis) {
delete globalThis.featureFlags;
}
});
`

Alternatively, setting the property to undefined instead of deleting it preserves the type shape:

`typescript
afterEach(() => {
globalThis.featureFlags = undefined as any;
});
`

This approach requires changing the type declaration to allow undefined:

`typescript
declare global {
interface globalThis {
featureFlags?: {
enableDarkMode: boolean;
enableBetaFeatures: boolean;
};
}
}
`

Now every access requires an optional chain or existence check:

`typescript
if (globalThis.featureFlags?.enableDarkMode) {
// safe access
}
`

The choice between deletion and undefined depends on whether the codebase prefers explicit existence checks or assumes the property is always present during normal operation.

When NOT to Use globalThis: Better Alternatives for Most Use Cases

Typing globalThis addresses a tactical problem but does not solve the strategic issue of global state. Most applications benefit from alternatives that avoid polluting the global namespace.

Module-Scoped Constants

Configuration that never changes at runtime belongs in a module:

`typescript
// config.ts
export const config = {
apiUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
enableAnalytics: import.meta.env.VITE_ENABLE_ANALYTICS === "true"
};
`

This provides the same centralized access without touching globalThis. TypeScript infers the exact types, and tree shaking can remove unused properties in production builds. For more patterns around modern TypeScript library configuration, see Create a Modern TypeScript/JavaScript Library for 2023.

Dependency Injection

Services like analytics clients belong in dependency containers:

`typescript
// services.ts
export class Analytics {
track(event: string, properties: Record): void {
// implementation
}
}

export const analytics = new Analytics();
`

`typescript
// component.ts
import { analytics } from "./services";

analytics.track("pageview", { path: "/home" });
`

This supports testing through mock injection and avoids singleton globals. The pattern scales to complex applications without namespace conflicts.

Context Objects

React, Vue, and other frameworks provide context mechanisms for shared state:

`typescript
// feature-flags-context.tsx
const FeatureFlagsContext = createContext({
enableDarkMode: false,
enableBetaFeatures: false
});

export function FeatureFlagsProvider({ children }) {
const [flags, setFlags] = useState(defaultFlags);

useEffect(() => {
fetch("/api/feature-flags")
.then(res => res.json())
.then(setFlags);
}, []);

return (

{children}

);
}

export const useFeatureFlags = () => useContext(FeatureFlagsContext);
`

Components consume flags through the hook, and the framework handles the scoping. This eliminates global pollution and simplifies testing by allowing test wrappers to provide mock values.

When globalThis Is Actually Correct

The pattern remains valid for:

  • Integrating third-party scripts that expect global names (analytics vendors, error trackers)
  • Exposing debug utilities to the browser console during development
  • Bridging module code and legacy non-module scripts in a migration period
  • Polyfilling missing global APIs in older environments

If the global property ships to production, the declaration should include comments explaining why alternatives were rejected:

`typescript
declare global {
interface globalThis {
/**
* Segment analytics instance.
* Global assignment required by vendor SDK.
* See: https://segment.com/docs/connections/sources/catalog/libraries/website/javascript/
*/
analytics: SegmentAnalytics;
}
}
`

This prevents future engineers from assuming the global was added carelessly. For guidance on structuring cross-cutting concerns like correlation IDs in distributed systems, see Correlation IDs in AI Agent Architectures.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I declare multiple properties on globalThis in separate files?

Yes. TypeScript merges all declarations of the same interface across files. Each file can extend globalThis with different properties, and the compiler combines them into a single type. This works as long as the properties do not conflict.

Why does my globalThis declaration not work in a .ts file?

The file likely has no import or export statements, making it a script instead of a module. Script files cannot use declare global. Add export {} to force module context, or move the declaration to a .d.ts file.

How do I prevent accidental writes to typed global properties?

Use readonly in the declaration:

`typescript
declare global {
interface globalThis {
readonly featureFlags: {
enableDarkMode: boolean;
};
}
}
`

This prevents assignment after initialization:

`typescript
globalThis.featureFlags = newFlags; // Error: Cannot assign to 'featureFlags'
`

Does globalThis typing work with strictNullChecks enabled?

Yes. The compiler enforces nullability based on the declared type. If the declaration does not include undefined, TypeScript assumes the property is always present. If runtime code might delete the property, add ? to the declaration or union with undefined.

What happens if two libraries declare the same global property with different types?

TypeScript reports an error when merging incompatible types. If library A declares globalThis.config: { timeout: number } and library B declares globalThis.config: { retries: number }, the compiler cannot merge them. The developer must declare a combined type that satisfies both libraries or file a bug with the library maintainers.

Conclusion

Declaration merging makes globalThis properties type-safe without runtime cost. The pattern works across all environments when using globalThis instead of window or global, and it integrates with existing toolchains without configuration changes. The technique fills a narrow gap: code that already relies on global state and cannot migrate to module-scoped alternatives.

Most new code should avoid globalThis entirely. Module exports, dependency injection, and framework context APIs provide better isolation and testability. When globals are unavoidable, proper TypeScript declarations prevent the most common failure mode: silent any types that surrender error checking at the exact boundary where runtime bugs cluster. For broader context on modern TypeScript tooling ecosystems, see Biome vs oxlint Comparison 2026.

title: Out of Postgres Connections? Find the Limit You Hit and Get Back In
description:
"No connections left" is not one symptom. It is at least four different limits with four different fixes, and picking the wrong one makes things worse. I filled a Nano-sized Supabase lab on purpose and worked through the recovery steps one at a time, with the real error text and real timings.

Three things I did not expect: when the database is full, postgres cannot connect either; terminating idle backends recovers it in milliseconds; and raising the pool size made throughput worse for one of the two query shapes I tested.

How this was made: I wrote this with Claude's help: it drafted, and I ran every step, edited the text, and checked the results. The mistakes are mine.

The companion piece — how connections are counted in the first place, and why they multiply: https://dev.to/tomozilla/supabase-connection-budgets-pool-size-roles-modes-and-limits-4lc8
The code: https://github.com/tomozilla/connection-budget-en-demo

What I did and did not do

  • Everything new here ran in a local lab: a Supabase CLI stack with max_connections 90, pooler pool size 15, client cap 200 — Nano-like limits where going past a limit hurts nobody. Cost: $0.
  • I never filled a hosted database. It is shared infrastructure. So every "while full" result below is from the lab.
  • The hosted numbers I reuse (the client-cap scope, the live pool-size change, the Micro → Small upgrade) were measured on a throwaway Pro project that I created and deleted the same day, in the companion article.
  • Each experiment ran a few times at most.

1. First, read the error text

This is the step people skip. "Out of connections" covers at least four separate limits, and the fix differs for each.

What you see Which limit First move
(EMAXCONN) max client connections reached, limit: 200 the pooler's client cap, per role shrink the per-copy pool, or run fewer copies (§6)
(EMAXCONNSESSION) max clients reached in session mode the session-mode pool move to transaction mode if you can
(ECHECKOUTTIMEOUT) ... after 60000ms in Transaction mode the transaction pool is full, and you waited 60 s §7 — and read it before you raise the pool size
FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute (53300) max_connections itself §2–§4. This is the heavy one
(EAUTHQUERY) authentication query failed the pooler can't even open a connection to check your login same cause: max_connections is full
504 PGRST003 the Data API's own pool hunt the slow query
too many connections for role "..." a role's CONNECTION LIMIT check it is at least pool size + 1 (§8)
no error at all, just slow queueing §7. Watch p95, not the error count

→ The first three are inside the pooler; your database may still have room. The fourth means the database itself is full. Those are different emergencies.

Don't skip the last row. In the companion article, going from 5 clients to 100 changed throughput not at all — only the wait, from 0.1 s to 0.6 s — with zero errors the whole time.

2. When it is full, you cannot get in — not even as postgres

This surprised me most, and it changes what "preparation" means.

I filled max_connections with idle connections on one role, then tried to log in as several roles.

filled: 51 connections held, 39 refused
  remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute
Role I tried to connect as Result
r1 (the app's role) refused, 53300
r2 (another app role) refused, 53300
postgres refused, 53300
supabase_admin connected, 3 ms

→ postgres is refused too, because on Supabase it is not a superuser and cannot use the reserved slots (superuser_reserved_connections, which is 3 on both hosted and the lab). The role you normally administer with is unavailable exactly when you need it.

That makes this a preparation problem, not a recovery step:

  • Decide before the incident how you will get in. Searching for a way while it is down is too late.
  • The dashboard's SQL editor reaches the database by a different path than a client connection. Mine worked when the database was not full; I did not test it against a full database, so I can't promise it.
  • PostgreSQL 17 has reserved_connections: set it, grant a role pg_use_reserved_connections, and that role still connects when full. It worked in the lab. I have not confirmed you can set it on a hosted project (the hosted value was 0), so do not build your plan on it.
  • In practice, knowing who can open the dashboard is the reliable answer.

3. See what is actually holding the connections

Once you are in, count before you act.

select usename,
       application_name,
       state,
       count(*) as n,
       max(now() - state_change)::interval(0) as longest_in_state
from pg_stat_activity
where backend_type = 'client backend'
group by 1, 2, 3
order by n desc;

Three columns matter. usename tells you whether one role dominates, or whether it is a Supabase service (supabase_auth_admin, supabase_storage_admin). application_name tells you the route: Supavisor means through the pooler, PostgREST 14.x means the Data API, empty usually means a direct connection. And then state:

state What it means How to read it
active running a query right now genuinely busy — go to §7
idle connected, doing nothing holding a seat — §4 clears these
idle in transaction stopped mid-transaction the dangerous one — §8

→ Lots of idle is a connection problem. Lots of active is a query problem. Skip this distinction and §7 will send you the wrong way.

4. Stop the bleeding: terminate

If idle is the culprit, kill those backends.

-- In a real incident, always filter by age so you don't kill connections that just opened
select pg_terminate_backend(pid)
from pg_stat_activity
where backend_type = 'client backend'
  and usename = 'r1'
  and state = 'idle'
  and now() - state_change > interval '1 minute';

From a full database in the lab:

Step Result
a normal connection while full refused, 53300
pg_terminate_backend on that role's idle backends 51 terminated in 12 ms
the same connection attempt, right after connected, 3 ms

→ Recovery is effectively instant. The slow part of an incident is deciding to do this, not doing it.

Two cautions. Drop state = 'idle' from that query and you will terminate running queries too, rolling back whatever they were writing. And what the killed client sees depends on the library: node-postgres' Pool crashed the process without an error handler (Unhandled 'error' event), recovered from the next query with one, and through the pooler produced no event at all.

Terminating does not fix the cause. The same app will reopen the same connections within minutes, so continue to §8.

5. Stop the bleeding: change the pool size (no restart)

If the pooler is the bottleneck, the pool size is the dial. The question I actually cared about was whether changing it forces a restart, because a restart during an incident is its own problem.

Measured on a hosted project: the same load — 10 clients each holding an 8-second query — run twice, changing only the pool size in the dashboard between runs.

Pool size Backends opened Time for all 10 queries Errors
3 4 25.3 s 0
15 10 9.3 s 0

→ It took effect immediately, with no restart. It works downward too: if one role is hogging the database, lowering the pool size hands capacity back to the others.

Before you reach for "raise it", though, read §7.

6. Stop the bleeding: split roles — but only for EMAXCONN

If you hit the client cap, this is different, because that cap is per role. Measured on a hosted project, with idle connections and no queries at all:

Attempt Result
215 clients on one role exactly 200 connect, the rest get (EMAXCONN) ... limit: 200
150 clients on each of two roles (300 total) all 300 connect, zero refusals

→ A second role really does buy another 200 client slots. As a stopgap for EMAXCONN, it works.

Now the catch. While those 300 clients were connected, the database held:

300 clients (2 roles)  ->  2 backends

→ Two. One per role, because nothing was running a query. Adding a role buys client slots and zero backend slots. If those 300 clients all start querying, you have moved the queue to max_connections, not removed it.

7. "Just raise the pool size" is half right

This is the part I got wrong before measuring.

Remember state from §3. Whether raising the pool helps depends entirely on whether the backends are waiting or burning CPU. To separate the two I used queries that both take about 100 ms for opposite reasons:

  • wait: pg_sleep(0.1) — the backend is idle, waiting (think an external API call or a lock).
  • cpu: count(*) over 2,000,000 rows — the backend is saturating a core (think a heavy aggregate).

60 concurrent clients, closed loop, pool size 15 vs 30:

Query Pool 15 (16 backends) Pool 30 (31 backends) Effect
wait 154/s, p50 409 ms 295–300/s, p50 204 ms throughput nearly doubled, latency halved
cpu 48–51/s, p50 1149–1230 ms, p95 1328–1465 ms 38–44/s, p50 1235–1493 ms, p95 1456–2160 ms throughput dropped, p95 got worse

→ The same change that nearly doubled one workload made the other measurably worse. The cpu row was 38, 44 and 44/s across three runs, against 48–51/s at pool 15.

The reason is obvious in hindsight: raising the pool does not add CPU. Thirty-one backends contending for the same cores each run slower, and the extra context switching costs more than it returns. Queries that are merely waiting have nothing to contend over, so they scale cleanly.

So the procedure is:

  1. Look at state (§3).
  2. Mostly idle or waiting → raising the pool size is worth it (§5, and it applies live).
  3. Mostly active → raising the pool makes it worse. Fix the query: pg_stat_statements, an index, fewer rows returned. If you can't, go to §9.

8. Remove the cause, or it comes back

A leaked transaction: idle in transaction

If §3 showed idle in transaction, fix that first. The connection never comes back on its own, and it blocks vacuum on the tables it touched.

I opened a transaction and did nothing:

state: idle in transaction, held: 2 seconds (and counting, indefinitely)

The fix is a timeout the client cannot wait out:

alter role r1 set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5s';

→ The server killed it at 5.0 s: terminating connection due to idle-in-transaction timeout.

Fixing the application bug is the real answer, but this setting is a seatbelt you can fasten today, before you find the bug.

One role starving everyone

Per-role limits work, but the value matters. With pool size 15 and 40 clients running 5-second queries:

connection limit Backends Queries that failed
15 (same as pool size) 15 25 of 40, immediately
16 (pool size + 1) 16 0 (the rest waited)

→ Set it to at least pool size + 1. At exactly the pool size, the 16th backend is refused and clients that could have waited turn into errors instead. (Supavisor's transaction mode opens pool size + 1; that is measured in the companion article.)

Apply this to a role you created, not to authenticator (it would stop the Data API) and not to postgres.

A backstop the client cannot remove

statement_timeout is not a guardrail, because any role can change its own: a client can run SET statement_timeout = 0, and on the transaction pooler that zero is then inherited by the next client. Permissions do not stop this.

So the backstop has to live outside the session:

select cron.schedule('cancel-long-queries', '5 seconds', $$
  select pg_cancel_backend(pid)
  from pg_stat_activity
  where usename = 'batch_user'          -- scope it to a role you created
    and state = 'active'
    and now() - query_start > interval '6 seconds'
$$);

→ A client that had removed its own timeout and started a 30-second query was cancelled after 10–11 s (6 s plus the job interval).

Expect connections to linger

Closing clients does not free the slots at once: about 2 minutes in my measurements, and the docs say up to 5. Budget for 5. During an incident, "I stopped it and nothing freed up" is expected, not a second fault.

9. Last resort: a bigger instance

If §7 put you in the active column, this is where you end up. I upgraded the throwaway project to see what actually changes:

Micro Small
max_connections 60 90
pooler client cap 200 400
default pool size 15 15, unchanged
price shown in the dialog $9.68/mo $14.83/mo

→ Connections and client slots both grow, but your pool size does not. A bigger instance does not widen the pool for you — raise it yourself (§5), or you will have paid for headroom you aren't using.

One more thing worth knowing: moving to a paid plan buys no connections at all. Nano (free) and Micro (smallest paid) both have 60. Only compute size moves that number. Compute is billed hourly and is not covered by the Spend Cap.

A checklist for when it is quiet

  1. Decide who can get in when it is full. postgres cannot (§2).
  2. Keep the §3 query somewhere you can paste it, with the three meanings of state.
  3. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout on your roles now (§8).
  4. Set each pooled role's connection limit to pool size + 1 or more (§8).
  5. Put a query-killing backstop outside the session (§8).
  6. Alert on p95 latency, not on error count — the failure mode is silence (§1).
  7. Run the budget equation from the companion article against your current setup.

Takeaways

  • "Out of connections" is four different limits. Read the error text before acting (§1).
  • When the database is full, postgres cannot connect — only supabase_admin could. Arrange access in advance (§2).
  • state in pg_stat_activity decides your next move: idle → terminate, active → fix the query, idle in transaction → top priority (§3).
  • Terminating idle backends is instant: 51 in 12 ms, a normal connection 3 ms later (§4).
  • Pool size changes apply live, no restart: the same work took 25.3 s at pool 3 and 9.3 s at 15 (§5).
  • Splitting roles buys client slots and no backend slots: 300 clients held 2 backends (§6).
  • Raising the pool size helped waiting queries (154 → 295/s) and hurt CPU-bound ones (48 → 44/s). Check state first (§7).
  • statement_timeout can be removed by the client; the backstop must live outside the session (§8).
  • A bigger instance raises max_connections and the client cap but leaves the pool size at 15 (§9).
  • Every "while full" result here is from a local lab. I did not fill a hosted database.

The lab scripts for all of this are in the repo: https://github.com/tomozilla/connection-budget-en-demo

title: Go 1.27 Drains Unread Response Bodies for You. Past 256 KB, the Connection Still Dies
description:
• Book: The Complete Guide to Go Programming
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

100 sequential status-only GETs to index.golang.org, forced onto HTTP/1 with GODEBUG=http2client=0, took about 710 ms on Go 1.26 and about 150 ms on Go 1.27 on the author's machine. That is the benchmark in the Go team's post Better HTTP/1 connection reuse, published 14 October 2026 by Nicholas Husin and Damien Neil. The program itself didn't change. The standard library started doing something Go developers had been told to do by hand for years.

You know the habit. Every code review that touches an HTTP client eventually gets a comment asking for io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body) before resp.Body.Close(), so the connection goes back to the pool. Go 1.27 moved that into net/http.Transport. It also put limits on it, and the limits are where your connections still die.

What Go 1.26 did with a body you didn't finish

HTTP/1 sends responses back to back on one TCP connection. The client can't send the next request on that connection until it has consumed the current body to its end, as the Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header defines it. If you closed the body early, Go 1.26 and earlier gave up on the connection and dialed a new one, with a fresh TCP handshake and, for HTTPS, a fresh TLS handshake.

The blog post points out how easy this is to trigger by accident. A json.Decoder can stop reading right before the trailing newline of a JSON body. One unread byte, and the connection is gone.

Go 1.27 changes Close. The release notes say HTTP/1 Response.Body "now automatically drains any unread content upon being closed, up to a conservative limit." The work was tracked in golang/go#77370, which spells the limit out: "up to a limit of 256k bytes, or 50 milliseconds, whichever one is reached first." HTTP/2 is not affected, because its streams are multiplexed and an unread body on one stream doesn't block the others.


Small, fast leftovers go down the drain. Anything bigger or slower takes the connection with it.

The exact rule, from transport.go

"256 KB" sounds like "the first 256 KB of whatever is left." It isn't. In transport.go on the 1.27 release branch, the decision to try a drain is one line:

tryDrain := alive && resp.ContentLength <= maxPostCloseReadBytes

maxPostCloseReadBytes is 256 << 10 and maxPostCloseReadTime is 50 * time.Millisecond. Four things follow from that code:

  1. The check uses the declared Content-Length of the whole response, not the bytes you left unread. A 300 KB body is never drained, even if you read all but the last 100 bytes.
  2. A response with no length (chunked) has ContentLength -1, so it passes the check. The drain then copies at most 256 KB + 1 byte in a goroutine and only keeps the connection if it hits EOF.
  3. The drain gives up after 50 ms. A server that pauses mid-body costs you the connection.
  4. If the request or the response says Connection: close, alive is already false and no drain runs.

One more detail matters for measuring this. The read loop lets Close return before the drain starts. The related fix is tracked as CL 741222, "prevent blocking when draining response body after it has been closed," linked from the same issue. Your Close call doesn't wait. The drain happens behind it.

A demo that counts connections from the server's side

The cleanest way to see reuse is to count new connections where they arrive. http.Server.ConnState is called with StateNew once per accepted connection, and httptest keeps your hook when it wraps the server. The program below runs 100 GETs against a local server, reads -read bytes of each body, closes it, and prints how many connections the server accepted.

package main

import (
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "sync/atomic"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    size := flag.Int("size", 4<<10, "body size in bytes")
    read := flag.Int64("read", 0, "bytes the client reads")
    chunked := flag.Bool("chunked", false, "no Content-Length")
    stall := flag.Duration("stall", 0, "pause mid-body")
    flag.Parse()

    body := strings.Repeat("x", *size)
    half := *size / 2

    h := func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        if !*chunked {
            w.Header().Set("Content-Length",
                strconv.Itoa(*size))
        }
        if *chunked || *stall > 0 {
            w.(http.Flusher).Flush()
        }
        io.WriteString(w, body[:half])
        if *stall > 0 {
            w.(http.Flusher).Flush()
            time.Sleep(*stall)
        }
        io.WriteString(w, body[half:])
    }

    var newConns atomic.Int64
    srv := httptest.NewUnstartedServer(http.HandlerFunc(h))
    srv.Config.ConnState = func(c net.Conn, s http.ConnState) {
        if s == http.StateNew {
            newConns.Add(1)
        }
    }
    srv.Start()
    defer srv.Close()

    client := srv.Client()
    for i := 0; i < 100; i++ {
        resp, err := client.Get(srv.URL)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, resp.Body, *read)
        resp.Body.Close()
    }
    fmt.Println("new connections:", newConns.Load())
}

The Flush before the first write in chunked mode matters. The ResponseWriter.Write docs say the server adds Content-Length automatically when the output is under a few KB "and there are no Flush calls." Flushing first sends the headers without a length, so the body goes out chunked.

Save it as main.go, then run it under both toolchains. If you have 1.27 installed, GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.0 go run main.go fetches and uses 1.26 for the comparison run. I haven't run these myself; the expectations below come straight from the code quoted above.

go run main.go                         # 4 KB, read nothing
go run main.go -size 300000 -read 299900
go run main.go -chunked -size 100000
go run main.go -chunked -size 400000
go run main.go -stall 100ms


Count connections where they're accepted, not where they're requested.

What each run should show

Run one, 4 KB with nothing read: on 1.26 every Close is early, so expect 100 new connections. On 1.27 the drain picks up the 4 KB and the connection goes back to the pool, so the count should drop to a small number. It may not be exactly 1. Because Close returns before the drain finishes, the next Get can find no idle connection and start a dial, and on loopback a dial is fast enough to win that race sometimes.

Run two, 300,000 bytes with all but 100 read: declared length is over 262,144, so 1.27 never tries. Expect about 100 on both versions. This is the case where "it drains for you" is most misleading.

Run three, chunked 100,000 bytes: ContentLength is -1, the drain reads the rest within 256 KB + 1 and hits EOF, so 1.27 should reuse.

Run four, chunked 400,000 bytes: the drain copies 256 KB + 1 without reaching EOF and drops the connection. Back to about 100.

Run five, a 100 ms pause mid-body: the 50 ms timer fires before the second half arrives. About 100 on both, and each server handler is still sleeping when the client hangs up.

What to do with the drains already in your code

If your module only builds with Go 1.27 or later, delete the io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body) lines and keep defer resp.Body.Close(). That follows the blog's advice to just close the body. An unbounded io.Copy was always a liability anyway: point it at a multi-gigabyte download you meant to abandon and it reads the whole thing on your goroutine. The release notes list no GODEBUG setting for this change, so the behavior comes with the 1.27 standard library.

If you still support 1.26 or earlier, keep a drain but bound it. The blog's version caps bytes at 256 KB. The standard library copies 256<<10 + 1 bytes instead. If exactly 256 KB is left, a copy capped at 256 KB stops without reading EOF, and the transport only reuses a connection whose body reached EOF. The extra byte tells "exactly 256 KB" apart from "more".

func drainAndClose(body io.ReadCloser) {
    io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10+1)
    body.Close()
}

Run it as go drainAndClose(resp.Body) if you don't want the caller to wait on a slow peer. The blog also describes adding a timer that calls body.Close after 50 ms to interrupt the copy.

For responses you know you'll abandon and that are large, a drain won't help on any version. Avoid fetching what you don't need: a HEAD request, a Range header, or a paginated endpoint. When you will read a status line and walk away from a big body, set req.Close = true. The transport sends Connection: close, skips the drain, and the server knows not to keep the connection open for you. The blog notes that for large bodies a new connection can be cheaper than draining, which is why the limits exist.

For slow peers, the 50 ms drain timer protects connection reuse, not your own reads. Keep a Client.Timeout or a context deadline on the request.

The one setup this can make slower

The release notes call out a case that gets worse. Programs that were "improperly allowing an excessive amount of idle connections to linger," usually by setting Transport.MaxIdleConns to 0 or by using different Clients for different requests, may now see degradation, because connections that used to die early now survive into the idle pool. The fix they give is Transport.DisableKeepAlives = true if you truly don't want reuse. They add that this usually points to improper configuration or usage of Transport or Client in the first place, and that a deeper look would likely be beneficial. In practice, the common repair is sharing one Client instead of building a new one per request.

If this was useful

This change is a good example of why it pays to know what net/http does underneath Close: the rule lives in one line of transport.go, and it decides whether your client handshakes once or a hundred times. The Complete Guide to Go Programming is where I cover the standard library at that level, along with the runtime and the concurrency model that goroutine-based drains like this one sit on.

title: Supabase Connection Budgets: Pool Size, Roles, Modes, and Limits
description:
Your connection budget is three equations, and most "too many connections" surprises come from one of them being a multiplication you did as an addition. I rebuilt a Nano-sized Supabase limit set on my laptop, pushed past every limit, and wrote down what failed, in what order, and with which error text. Some checks ran on a hosted Free project at tiny scale, and a few that only a paid plan exposes ran on a throwaway Pro project I created and deleted the same day. Scripts, numbers and a calculator are in the repo. Everything is from my runs on 2026-11-03 and 2026-11-04; prices and versions change, so numbers carry dates.

The most serious finding is not about capacity: on the transaction pooler, a setting left behind by one client leaked rows (through an RLS policy) and an admin role's privileges to the next client (section 10).

How this was made: I wrote this with Claude's help: it drafted, and I ran every step, edited the text, and checked the results. The mistakes are mine.

The non-technical version (database "seats"): https://medium.com/p/a7f0cb1df4d4
The code: https://github.com/tomozilla/connection-budget-en-demo

Before the numbers, one map. Every term in this article is somewhere in this picture: where a request enters, which pool it lands in, and what else is already holding connections.

The bottom band is the part I kept underestimating: even with zero traffic of your own, the Data API, Auth, Realtime, Storage and the health checker each take connections out of the same total. Section 5 has the measurements.

Why I measured this

I started with a question I couldn't answer: "pool size 15, but 30 backends?" Listing library defaults wouldn't explain it, so I rebuilt the limits locally, where going past a limit hurts nobody, and ran one experiment per term of the budget. Where a claim needed a hosted check, I kept it tiny.

What I did and did not do

  • Local lab (most of it): a local Supabase CLI stack with Auth, Storage, Realtime, Studio and PostgREST running (no Edge Runtime or logs), max_connections 90, pooler pool size 15, 200 max clients. Cost: $0. Supavisor 2.9.12, PostgREST 16.2, Postgres 17. Scripts re-run from a clean copy of the repo.
  • Hosted, at tiny scale: on the Free demo project I set the pooler pool size to 3 (Database settings), used a handful of clients for seconds to a minute with a throwaway role, then dropped the role and put the pool size back to 15. I also read the idle connection list once, with no load. Hosted results are marked "hosted" below.
  • A throwaway Pro project (Micro), created and deleted on 2026-11-04. Some questions only a paid plan can answer: what Micro's limits actually are, how many connections Auth and Storage hold under load, and what the dedicated pooler's settings page says. I created one project, ran small read-only probes and two 40-request bursts, then deleted it. Cost: about $0.02 (Micro is $0.01344 per hour per the docs, 2026-11-04). Creating a Pro project requires the organization to be on a paid plan ($25/month).
  • Not verified: Rails, Edge Functions with postgres.js, Npgsql / pgx / HikariCP defaults, hosted PostgREST pool settings, the platform's request limits. I could not connect to the hosted dedicated pooler either: it is IPv6-only by default and my network is IPv4, which would need the IPv4 add-on ($4/month), so I only read its settings page. I also did not fill a hosted database — that is shared infrastructure — so every "what fails first" result below is from the lab. Each experiment ran a few times at most; the latency table is one 6-second run per cell.

1. The budget, as three equations 


backends in use = direct connections
                + sum over every (role, database, mode) pool of min(clients of that pool, pool size)
                  (a transaction-mode pool holds pool size + 1)
                + the dedicated pooler's backend connections, if you run both poolers
                  (the pool size setting applies to each pooler independently)
                + the Data API's own pool (10, plus one LISTEN connection = 11)
                + Auth, Storage, Realtime and the health checker, each with a pool of its own
must stay <= max_connections - superuser_reserved_connections - reserved_connections
                                                    (Nano / Micro: 60 - 3 - 0 = 57; reserved_connections is PostgreSQL 17, default 0, it was 0 on hosted Nano)

clients = running copies of the app x the library's pool size
must stay <= the pooler's client cap (Nano / Micro: 200), counted per pool (role x mode) -- measured on hosted

busy backends = queries per second x seconds per query   (Little's law)

That last line is the one I used to wave at. The Pooling and limits page lists the same sharers explicitly: "Supabase services hold their own connections, including Auth, Storage, PostgREST, and the health checker, and those come out of the same total." And those are not fixed numbers — some of them grow when used and then keep what they took (section 5).

The docs' rule of thumb (Connection management): pool size under about 40% of max_connections with heavy Data API use, up to about 80% without. That is 24 or 48 on Nano. Reading it as a budget for all pools together is not my inference — the Supavisor FAQ says it directly: "if you're using the DB REST API or multiple app-based 'user+db+mode' combinations, try to keep the pooler's usage under 40% of available connections." With two roles and two modes you have four pools.

3. The client cap is exact, and per role in my lab

201 node-postgres clients on the pooler:

connected 200
client 201: (EMAXCONN) max client connections reached, limit: 200   (0.5 s)

No waiting. With node-postgres' default Pool of 10, 21 serverless copies reach it. Is the 200 shared across roles? The FAQ only says the limit comes from the tenant's default_max_clients or a per-user max_clients. So I connected 150 clients each on r1 and r2:

2 roles x 150 clients: connected 300, refused none
3 roles x 70 clients:  connected 210, refused none

In my lab the cap applied per role. I didn't connect hundreds of clients to a hosted project; I read the source instead (Supavisor main on 2026-11-03; I did not diff it against the lab's 2.9.12). Manager.check_client_limit looks up the pool by its id (tenant, user, mode, database and so on), takes the size of that pool's client table, and compares it with max_clients (the user's setting or the tenant's default_max_clients) in transaction mode, or with pool_size in session mode. So the counting unit is the pool (role x mode), which matches the lab.

The docs read the other way, which is why I went and measured it. The Pooling and limits page describes client connections as "how many clients can connect to a pooler at the same time", set by "your compute size's max pooler clients limit" — no mention of roles. The Max client connections reached error is described as exceeding "the allowed limit of your compute add-on". The Pro project's settings page says: "This value is fixed at 200 based on your compute size of Micro and cannot be changed." All project-shaped.

So I tested it on a hosted project (throwaway Pro/Micro, 2026-11-04, idle connections only — not a single query):

attempt result
215 clients on one role exactly 200 connected; the rest got (EMAXCONN) max client connections reached, limit: 200
150 clients on each of two roles (300 total) all 300 connected, zero refusals

The cap is per role on hosted too, matching the lab. The settings page's "fixed at 200" is the value of one pool's cap, not a project-wide total.

Don't celebrate too early, though. While those 300 clients were connected, the database held 2 backend connections — one per role — because nothing was running a query:

300 clients (2 roles)  ->  2 backends

Adding a role buys client slots. It buys zero backend slots, and equation 1 (57 usable on Nano/Micro) is the one that actually bites. Splitting across roles is a legitimate fix for EMAXCONN, but it moves the queue rather than removing it: if those 300 clients all start querying, they are contending for the same 57.

4. Pools are per (role, mode), and transaction mode holds one extra

The docs changed under me while I was writing this, in late October 2026, and the change is in my favour. The sentence I used to quote — that the pool size is shared between ports 5432 and 6543 — is no longer there. What the Connection management page says now:

This pool size applies per database user (role), not as a single total for the whole project. Each distinct role that connects through a pooler gets its own pool of up to this many direct Postgres connections, so the total connections poolers can open scale with the number of roles in use.

The "shared" axis moved from between modes to between poolers: "The pool size applies to both the shared pooler (Supavisor) and the dedicated pooler (PgBouncer)", and they "read the same setting but apply it independently, so raising it raises the ceiling for both." If you run both, add the second pooler's backends to equation 1.

Three granularities still coexist, which is worth knowing when you size: Connection management says per role, the Supavisor FAQ says per user, database and mode combination, and the dashboard's own help text says "per user+db combination". Everything I measured says mode counts too, so size with the largest reading (user x database x mode).

5. A full database stops whatever needs a new connection first

Three roles at full pool, 87 of 87 used. I probed the other services with the lab's publishable key only:

while full result
new direct connection FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute (53300)
new login through the pooler (EAUTHQUERY) authentication query failed: connection to database not available (the pooler needs a connection to check your login)
Auth sign-in / sign-up 500: Database error querying schema, Database error finding user
Data API (rpc/ping) 200 (its pool already held open connections)
Storage upload and list 200 (same reason)

The rule is whatever needs a new connection fails first. In my lab Auth held no idle connection, so its sign-in broke first; the Data API and Storage kept working because the connections they already held were enough. That is not a guaranteed order:

  • In a separate run that filled the database with two roles only, a Data API call that needed a new connection got 503 PGRST000. So neither "full means 503" nor "full means Auth first" is a rule.
  • This round I measured the hosted side, and it changes the reading. On the fresh Pro / Micro project, Auth and Storage both hold zero connections until something uses them. So I sent 40 concurrent sign-in attempts, and separately 40 concurrent public-object requests, and counted by usename:
service idle right after the burst later
Auth (supabase_auth_admin) 0 9 to 10 back to 0 within about a minute (10 at t+46 s, 0 at t+61 s)
Storage (supabase_storage_admin) 0 8 still 8 fourteen minutes later

So hosted Auth keeps a warm pool of about ten once it has been used, while my lab's Auth held none. Sign-in was first to break in my lab, for that reason. On a hosted project Auth has about ten connections in hand and should ride out the moment the database fills. I did not fill a hosted database, so that last part is inference, not measurement — the point is that you cannot carry my lab's ordering over to production.

Storage matters differently: it took 8 and kept them. That is 8 of the 57 usable connections on Nano or Micro, permanently, once you serve a file. Put it in equation 1.

One caveat on Storage: the Supavisor FAQ says "the Storage server also uses Supavisor as a unique 'user+db+mode' combination, so the pool size you set for your general application will apply to it, too." On the project I measured, those connections had application_name of Supabase Storage API, not Supavisor — they looked direct, not pooled. One project, one observation; I am not generalising from it.

After the heavy clients stopped, sign-in stayed at 500 for about a minute (it came back at t+62 s, when the pooler released one backend).

One role using too much can take out other roles, the pooler's logins and Auth. I did not probe Studio.

6. Waiting, refusing, and the timeout ladder

Past the pool, one role, pool 15:

  • Transaction mode: 18 clients holding 30 s each: 16 ran, 2 waited, all done at 60 s. 17 clients holding 65 s: the waiting one fails at exactly 60 s with (ECHECKOUTTIMEOUT) unable to check out connection from the pool after 60000ms in Transaction mode. Hosted, pool size 3, 5 clients holding 65 s: 4 ran (3 + 1), the fifth failed at 61 s with the same error.
  • Session mode: 18 clients: 3 refused at once, (EMAXCONNSESSION) max clients reached in session mode - max clients are limited to pool_size. The FAQ says session mode "can queue clients for up to a minute"; in my lab (and on the hosted pooler) it refused instead.

A prediction, tested. A closed-loop client (finishes, then sends the next) waits about (clients - backends) / backends x query time. With 199 clients and 16 backends, queries averaging over roughly 5 seconds should push the wait to the 60-second limit. Role r1, transaction mode, 100 seconds per run:

query time predicted wait (time in the queue) measured p50 (wait + run time, successful requests only) outcome
4.5 s 51.5 s 54.1 s (about 49.6 s wait + 4.5 s) 551 succeeded, no errors
5.5 s 62.9 s 60.6 s 464 succeeded, 46 failed with ECHECKOUTTIMEOUT (46 of 510 requests, about 9%)

The p50 includes the query's own run time, so the 4.5 s row compares 51.5 s of predicted wait plus 4.5 s of work (about 56 s) with the measured 54.1 s. At 5.5 s the predicted wait is past 60 s, and the clients that waited that long were refused at 60 s; the ones that succeeded got their turn just before it. The prediction that the edge sits near 5 seconds held.

A client that runs BEGIN and stalls holds its backend as idle in transaction. With idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5s' on the role, Postgres ended it after 5 seconds (terminating connection due to idle-in-transaction timeout).

Open loop. A closed loop politely waits and hides overload; real traffic keeps arriving. New connection per request (serverless style), 100 ms queries:

100 per second: p50 105 ms, no errors
200 per second (capacity about 150):
  sec 0: p50 232 ms   sec 1: 494   sec 2: 767   sec 3: 1030
  sec 4 on: p50 about 1260 ms, and about a quarter of arrivals refused with (EMAXCONN)

After 4 seconds 200 client connections were in flight, so the cap started refusing; the p50 of the accepted ones plateaued near 200 / 16 x 0.1 s.

Many waits stack. The shortest one fires first:

The role defaults are rungs on the same ladder. Per the docs: anon 3 s, authenticated 8 s, service_role none (falls back to authenticator's 8 s), and postgres has no role timeout, "capped by default global timeout to be 2min". If you are upgrading from Prisma 6, this is the row to read. The 10-second safety net (pool_timeout) is gone by default with the pg adapter, so a saturated pool waits forever. Pass connectionTimeoutMillis to PrismaPg.

The Django last row came from a bug in my own test: my first script never called connection.close() and everything but four threads timed out. A web request closes at its end, so this bites long-lived threads (background workers).

9. What breaks on the transaction pooler

I rewrote this section, because the docs caught up. What I used to present as an undocumented trap is now spelled out on the Connecting to Postgres page:

Query pipelining isn't supported: transaction mode returns a connection to the pool as soon as it sees one reply finish, even if the client already queued more queries on it.

Caution: postgres.js pipelines queries by default, so this combination can hang queries or return mismatched rows.

Read that before my experiments. What I hit was the hang.

postgres.js 4.0.0 hung with 20 concurrent queries. Setting prepare: false and max_pipeline: 1 together fixes it, so I tried them one at a time:

setting lab, transaction hosted, transaction, pool 3 direct
default hang hang ok
prepare: false only hang hang
max_pipeline: 1 only ok (1.0 s) ok
both ok ok

The cause is pipelining (several queries queued on one connection; postgres.js defaults to 100), not prepared statements. "Transaction mode has no prepared statements" is true, and the docs tell you to turn them off for your library, and prepare: false is the usual postgres.js fix. It didn't fix this hang in my runs.

Does that mean prepare can stay on with max_pipeline: 1? Prepared-statement bugs only show on repetition (see psycopg below), so I repeated the same query: 200 and 3000 queries over 10 connections.

max_pipeline: 1 only (prepare on): no errors, 3000 queries x 2 runs
default, or prepare: false only: hang
session port, direct: ok

No prepared-statement failure with postgres.js here.

One suggestion was that postgres.js might be retrying silently: its source (GitHub main) does catch the "prepared statement does not exist" error (26000), re-prepare and retry. So I counted what the client sends (25-postgresjs-retry.mjs counts Parse messages and errors). Same 3000 queries, 10 connections:

setting result Parse messages sent errors
direct ok 10 none
pooler, max_pipeline: 1 only (prepare on) ok (0.2 s) 10 none
pooler, prepare: false and max_pipeline: 1 ok (0.3 s) 3000 none
pooler, default hang (10 sent, then stuck)
pooler, prepare: false only hang (about 1400 sent, then stuck)

With only max_pipeline: 1, Parse went out once per connection (10), not more; a retry path would have added more. The Postgres log and the pooler log had no prepared statement or 26000 lines either. So here it is not a hidden retry; the error does not occur. I don't know why (the pooler may handle it on its side; I didn't check). Through the same pooler, psycopg and Prisma did fail.

Do the mismatched rows show up?

The docs warn about two failures, and I had only chased the hang. So I went after the other one: every query sends a unique marker and must get that marker back.

setting (pooler, transaction) 300 queries / 10 connections mismatched rows
default hang (69 of 300 finished in that run; where it stops varies) —
prepare: false only hang (144 of 300 in that run) —
max_pipeline: 1 only ok (58 ms) 0
prepare: false and max_pipeline: 1 ok (38 ms) 0
(control) direct, default ok (15 ms) 0

I then ran 1000 queries over 20 connections three more times with max_pipeline: 1: not one mismatched row. In my environment it hangs before it can mismatch. "I couldn't reproduce it" is not "it doesn't happen" — trust the docs' warning over my runs here.

Does max_pipeline: 1 break sql.begin()?

This is the question I should have answered before recommending the setting. The Postgres.js page says:

postgres.js has no working option to turn pipelining off directly: max_pipeline: 0 breaks sql.begin() transactions instead, a known upstream bug.

It talks about 0. I recommend 1, which is a different thing, so I tested it with real transactions: two queries inside each sql.begin(), checking (a) that each query gets its own marker back and (b) that both ran on the same backend (pg_backend_pid()), i.e. the transaction never moved to another connection mid-flight.

setting (pooler, transaction mode) result wrong values split transactions
default ok (16 ms) 0 0
max_pipeline: 1 ok (18 ms) 0 0
prepare: false and max_pipeline: 1 ok (17 ms) 0 0
max_pipeline: 0 error: 42P05 prepared statement "..." already exists — —
prepare: false and max_pipeline: 0 ok, but 2029 ms 0 0

max_pipeline: 1 ran transactions cleanly, repeated three times at 8 to 30 concurrent transactions.

max_pipeline: 0 behaved differently from the docs' description. The upstream issues that match that claim were closed as completed on 2026-10-29, and postgres.js 4.0.0 was published the same day. On 4.0.0 I did not get UNSAFE_TRANSACTION; I got a prepared-statement collision (42P05), which prepare: false clears — at the price of being more than 100x slower (19 ms to 2029 ms), because switching pipelining fully off serialises every query.

So in my environment max_pipeline: 1 (plus prepare: false if you want it) was the clean option. It is not the documented fix, so if you adopt it, run this same check against your own queries and transactions.

Prisma 6 without ?pgbouncer=true 22 of 30 failed: prepared statement "sN" does not exist no errors

10. Session state leaks between clients, and a leaked setting becomes a leaked row

This is a safety issue, not a capacity one, and it is the part of this article that goes furthest past what the docs say.

The docs describe transaction-mode session state like this:

Session-level state is lost between transactions. This covers set and reset, session-level advisory locks, listen and notify, and temporary tables.

"Lost" sounds like an availability problem: your setting disappears, your code breaks, you fix it. What I measured is the other failure mode — the state is not lost, it stays on the backend and the next client inherits it. That turns it from an availability bug into a disclosure bug.

Same role, clients one after another:

action pooler (transaction) direct
set_config('app.user','alice', false) (session-wide) leaked into the next client, 8 of 8 0 of 8
set_config(..., true) (transaction-local) did not leak did not leak
SET statement_timeout = 0 the next client also had 0 (a guardrail silently removed) did not leak
session advisory lock still held after the client left released
named prepared statement prepared statement "q1" already exists ok
LISTEN / NOTIFY no notification works

A setting is only a setting until an RLS policy trusts it. Role r_app, policy owner = current_setting('app.user', true), and r_app allowed to SET ROLE r_admin (which bypasses RLS):


transaction pooler:
  A (alice, set_config(..., true))     sees: alice
  B afterwards                         sees: (none)       <- safe
  A (alice, set_config(..., false))    sees: alice
  B (forgot to set the user)           sees: alice        <- leaked row
  A (admin task: SET ROLE r_admin)     sees: alice, bob
  B (ordinary request)                 runs as r_admin, sees: alice, bob   <- leaked privilege
direct: B sees nothing in all three cases

For contrast, the Data API: PostgREST applies per-request settings inside the request's transaction. With two users (alice, bob) from the local Auth (publishable key only) and 40 mixed concurrent requests, nobody received someone else's data: 0 of 40, and an anonymous call right after a user's call saw nothing.

Fix: on transaction pooling, don't use session-level SET; use set_config(..., true) inside a transaction you open per request.
