12. Failure and lingering

Killing 5 idle pooled connections with pg_terminate_backend:

  • node-postgres Pool, direct, no error handler: the process crashed (Unhandled 'error' event). With a handler: 5 error events, next 6 queries fine.
  • Through the pooler: no event, queries fine (the pooler replaced the backend).
  • SQLAlchemy: first query after the kill failed without pool_pre_ping, worked with it.

The Supavisor FAQ makes three specific claims about how long backends stick around:

In transaction mode, once a direct connection is established, the pooler will keep it available for reuse for another client. However, if the connection remains unused for 5 minutes, the pooler will close it to free up database resources. In session mode, the connection will be immediately closed.
If a client is connected to the pooler, then at least 1 hot connection will be sustained, even if no client needs it.

I tested all three.

claim what I measured
transaction mode closes unused backends after 5 minutes Lab: about 2 minutes (present at 105 s, gone at 120 s; two runs). Hosted Pro: 6 backends at 106 s, 0 at 122 s. Both about 2 minutes, not 5
at least 1 hot connection while a client is connected Hosted Pro, one idle transaction-mode client: exactly 1 backend held, still there at 137 s — past the ~2 minute close. Confirmed
session mode closes immediately Hosted Pro, one session-mode client connected then disconnected: the backend stayed over 3 minutes and was reused by a later client. It went away around 4 to 5 minutes idle. Not "immediately"

My measurement is shorter than the documented 5 minutes, so size with 5 minutes, the larger number: I measured one project a handful of times. Either way, run short tests back to back and you will see slots occupied with nobody using them.

13. Guardrails: one role should not starve everyone

Local lab:

  • Per-role connection limit. alter role r1 connection limit 10: r1 held 10 backends, 10 of 20 queries failed at once with too many connections for role "r1", and r2 was unaffected. It fails fast, so plan for retries. For a role that goes through the pooler, set the limit to pool size + 1 or more. Transaction mode, pool 15, 40 clients running 5 s queries at once:

| connection limit | r1 backends | failed queries |
|---|---|---|
| 15 (equal to the pool size) | 15 | 25 of 40 (immediately) |
| 16 (pool size + 1) | 16 | 0 (the rest wait) |

A limit equal to the pool size refuses the 16th backend and turns clients that could have waited into errors.

  • Per-role timeouts. alter role r1 set statement_timeout = '2s' cancelled a 4-second query at 2.0 s. But any role may change its own statement_timeout, so the client could run SET statement_timeout = 0, and through the transaction pooler the next client then saw 0. Permissions don't stop it. The backstop has to live outside the session. One example is a scheduled job: a pg_cron job every 5 seconds that calls pg_cancel_backend on r1's active queries older than 6 seconds. A client that had run SET statement_timeout = 0 and started a 30-second query was cancelled after 10 to 11 seconds (6 s plus the job interval) with canceling statement due to user request (18-guardrails.mjs cron).
  • A monitoring role. With PostgreSQL 17's reserved_connections = 3, a normal role was refused when full (remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with privileges of the "pg_use_reserved_connections" role) while a role granted pg_use_reserved_connections connected. If you use it, subtract it in equation 1. I haven't tried that on a hosted project (supabase_admin isn't mine to use); the hosted Nano value was 0.

14. Costs (docs, 2026-11-04)

  • My experiments cost about $0.02 in total. Nearly all of it was local Docker ($0) plus a Free project for the tiny hosted checks; the throwaway Pro project (Micro) ran for roughly 1.5 hours at $0.01344 per hour, and I deleted it afterwards.
  • Nano: free. Smallest paid compute is Micro, about $10 a month, with the same limits as Nano (60 direct, 200 pooler clients, pool 15). I verified that on the paid project: max_connections 60, and the settings page saying the client limit is "fixed at 200". Small about $15 (90 / 400), Medium about $60 (120 / 600), XL about $210 (240 / 1000).
  • Large is listed as about $110 on the Compute and disk page and about $111 on the Manage your usage / Compute page. Both quote $0.1517 per hour, so it is a rounding difference (0.1517 x 730 = $110.74). Cite whichever page you are reading.
  • The Pro plan is $25 a month and includes $10 of compute credit per organization, which covers one Micro project. Upgrading the plan alone buys no connection headroom; a bigger compute size does.
  • Compute is billed by the hour and is not covered by the Spend Cap (docs).
  • Reaching the dedicated pooler needs IPv6. From an IPv4-only network you need the IPv4 add-on at $4 a month, which I did not buy — hence no dedicated-pooler measurements here.

15. What I would do next (untested)

  • Budget from the equation: (roles x modes) x (pool + 1), plus Data API and other services, under max_connections minus reserved.
  • Compare app copies x library pool with the per-role client cap. Serverless especially.
  • Line up the waits: Supavisor 60 s, PostgREST 10 s, anon 3 s, Prisma 6 10 s, libraries 30 s, with your own timeouts. Prisma 7 with the pg adapter and node-postgres wait forever by default: set connectionTimeoutMillis.
  • Per-role connection limit (pool size + 1 or more), statement_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout; a scheduled job as the backstop a client can't undo; set_config(..., true) only; check each library's prepared-statement setting.
  • Make sure a monitoring role can log in when the database is full.
  • On a throwaway project: the client-connection chart, the PostgREST pool setting, and whether the "+1" holds in other regions.

Takeaways

  • Three equations: backends <= max_connections minus reserved, clients <= the pooler cap, busy = qps x seconds per query.
  • Pools are per (role, database, mode), and transaction mode holds pool size + 1: multiply. The 200-client cap is also per role — measured on hosted: 200 on one role, 300 across two. But 300 idle clients held only 2 backends, so extra roles buy client slots and no backend slots.
  • Equation 1 has to include Auth, Storage, Realtime, the health checker, and the dedicated pooler's backends if you run both. Measured on hosted Pro: Auth takes about 10 once used and releases them in about a minute; Storage takes 8 and keeps them.
  • A full database stops whatever needs a new connection first. Auth sign-in went first in my lab because its Auth held nothing — hosted Auth keeps about ten warm, so don't assume the same order.
  • Waits have limits (60 s pooler, 10 s PostgREST, 2 min for postgres) and slow can look like "no errors": watch p95. The arithmetic predicted the 60 s failure. Prisma 7's pg adapter has no default wait limit.
  • Library defaults change with versions; run them and count.
  • On transaction pooling, session state does worse than the documented "lost": it stays for the next client, turning a setting into a leaked row or privilege. Use set_config(..., true).
  • The postgres.js hang is pipelining — now documented, along with mismatched rows. max_pipeline: 1 fixed it and did not break sql.begin() in my tests; I never reproduced a mismatched row.
  • Backends lingered about 2 minutes in both the lab and hosted, but the docs say up to 5: budget for 5. Session mode did not close "immediately" either.
  • A role's connection limit must be at least pool size + 1; statement_timeout can be undone by the client, so add a backstop outside the session.
  • Micro has the same 60 max_connections as Nano — a paid plan alone buys no connections (verified on a paid project).

The repo has the lab scripts, the results table and the calculator: https://github.com/tomozilla/connection-budget-en-demo

title: Python List Methods Explained with Simple Examples
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

Python list methods are built in functions you call on a list to add, remove, find, sort or copy items without writing long code yourself. The most useful ones are append, extend and insert for adding items, remove, pop and clear for removing items, index and count for searching, sort and reverse for ordering, and copy for making a safe duplicate. In this guide, you will learn each method with a short, working example you can try right away.

What Are Python List Methods?

A list in Python is an ordered collection that can hold numbers, strings, or even other lists. Lists can change after you create them, which is why they are called mutable. List methods are the tools Python gives you to work with that changing data. You call a method with a dot after the list name, like this: my_list.append(10).

Most list methods change the original list in place and return None. If you write new_list = my_list.sort(), your new variable will hold None, not a sorted list. The sorting worked, but it happened on the original list itself.

The official Python Tutorial on data structures lists these methods completely, and it is worth reading after this guide.

Adding Items: append, extend and insert

Use append() to add one item at the end of a list. Use extend() to add all items from another list, one by one. Use insert() when you need an item at a specific position, because it takes an index and a value.

fruits = ["apple", "banana"]
fruits.append("cherry")
print(fruits)  # ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']

fruits.extend(["mango", "orange"])
print(fruits)  # ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry', 'mango', 'orange']

fruits.insert(1, "grapes")
print(fruits)  # ['apple', 'grapes', 'banana', 'cherry', 'mango', 'orange']

Notice the difference between append and extend. If you pass a list to append, that whole list becomes a single nested item. If you pass a list to extend, each item joins the main list separately. Think of append as one guest joining a party, and extend as a whole group joining.

Removing Items: remove, pop and clear

The remove() method deletes the first matching value you give it. The pop() method removes an item by its index and returns that item, so you can use it somewhere else. The clear() method empties the whole list while keeping the list itself alive and ready for new items.

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 20, 40]
numbers.remove(20)
print(numbers)  # [10, 30, 20, 40]

last = numbers.pop()
print(last)     # 40
print(numbers)  # [10, 30, 20]

numbers.clear()
print(numbers)  # []

Be careful with remove. If the value is not in the list, Python raises a ValueError and your program stops. Check with the in keyword first, like if 20 in numbers: before calling remove. Popping from an empty list also raises an IndexError, so check first.

Note that pop(0) removes the first item instead of the last.

The official Python Tutorial, chapter 5 "Data Structures", listing the list methods on docs.python.org.

Finding Items: index and count

When you need to know where something is, use index(). It returns the position of the first matching item, starting from zero. When you need to know how many times a value appears, use count(). It returns how many times the value appears, or zero if it is not there.

colours = ["red", "blue", "green", "blue", "red"]
print(colours.index("green"))  # 2
print(colours.count("blue"))   # 2
print(colours.count("yellow")) # 0

Like remove, index raises a ValueError if the item is missing, so check first or handle the error. Count is the polite one of the pair, it never complains, it just tells you zero and moves on. These methods pair nicely with loops, and if loops still feel new, our guide on Python loops, for vs while loop, explains them with the same simple style.

Sorting and Reversing: sort and reverse

The sort() method orders a list from smallest to largest, or from A to Z for strings. Add reverse=True inside the brackets if you want the opposite order. The reverse() method is different: it does not sort anything, it simply flips the current order, so first becomes last and last becomes first.

scores = [45, 12, 88, 30]
scores.sort()
print(scores)  # [12, 30, 45, 88]

scores.sort(reverse=True)
print(scores)  # [88, 45, 30, 12]

names = ["Zara", "Amit", "John"]
names.reverse()
print(names)  # ['John', 'Amit', 'Zara']

Sorting mixed types, like numbers and strings in the same list, will raise a TypeError, because Python cannot decide which one is bigger. Sorting strings is case sensitive too, so capital letters come before small letters. You can fix that by passing key=str.lower to sort. The full rules are covered in the Python documentation on built in types, in the section on sequence types.

If you need a sorted copy without changing the original, use the built in sorted() function instead.

Copying a List: copy

The copy() method creates a new list with the same items. This solves a very common bug. When you write list_b = list_a, you do not make a copy at all. Both names point to the same list, so changing one changes the other, and your program starts behaving like it has a mind of its own. It does not, you are just editing the same list twice.

original = [1, 2, 3]
backup = original.copy()
backup.append(4)
print(original)  # [1, 2, 3]
print(backup)    # [1, 2, 3, 4]

Copy makes a shallow copy. The new list is separate, but if your list contains other lists inside it, those inner lists are still shared. For most beginner projects, a shallow copy is exactly what you need. Once you are comfortable here, the natural next step is Python list comprehension explained, which shows a shorter way to build new lists from old ones.

Quick Comparison Table

The table below sums up all eleven methods from this guide. Keep it nearby while you practise, and soon you will stop needing it at all.

Method What it does Returns
append(x) Adds one item at the end None
extend(list) Adds each item from another list None
insert(i, x) Adds an item at a given index None
remove(x) Removes the first matching value None
pop(i) Removes an item by index The removed item
clear() Removes every item None
index(x) Finds the first position of a value The index number
count(x) Counts how often a value appears The count number
sort() Sorts the list in place None
reverse() Reverses the current order None
copy() Makes a shallow copy A new list

Only pop, index, count and copy give you a value back. The rest change the list and return None.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

First, do not save the result of a method that returns None, like result = my_list.append(5), because result will hold None, not the list. Second, do not change a list while looping over it, because items shift and some get skipped. Loop over a copy if you plan to remove items. Third, check a value exists before using remove or index.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between append and extend in Python?

Append adds one whole item at the end of a list, even if that item is itself a list. Extend adds each item from another list one by one, so the new items become part of the main list directly.

Does sort return a new list in Python?

No, sort changes the original list in place and returns None. If you need a new sorted list while keeping the original unchanged, use the built in sorted() function instead.

How do I remove an item from a list by its value?

Use remove() with the value, like my_list.remove(20). It deletes the first matching item. If the value is not in the list, Python raises a ValueError, so check with the in keyword first.

What does pop do in a Python list?

Pop removes an item by its index and returns that item. With no index, it removes and returns the last item, which makes it useful when you need both the value and a shorter list.

Conclusion

You now know the eleven list methods that cover almost everything a beginner does with lists: adding with append, extend and insert, removing with remove, pop and clear, searching with index and count, ordering with sort and reverse, and staying safe with copy. Pick three, write small examples of your own, and add the rest during the week. Small daily practice beats one long reading session. Happy coding.

title: How to Prepare for a Junior Backend Developer Interview Using One Project
description:
Preparing for your first backend developer interview can become overwhelming very quickly.

One job description asks for REST APIs, another mentions SQL, and a third expects knowledge of authentication, deployment, and testing.

It's tempting to keep learning new technologies until you feel ready.

But there's another approach: take one project you already understand and use it to prepare for multiple technical interview topics.

A well-built project can help you demonstrate not just what you've learned, but how you think as a developer.

1. Choose a Project You Can Explain Clearly

You don't need a complicated application with dozens of features.

A task management API, expense tracker, inventory system, or simple booking backend can be enough if you've built it properly.

For example, imagine you've developed a task management API using Node.js, Express, and PostgreSQL.

Your project allows users to:

  • Create an account.
  • Sign in securely.
  • Create and update tasks.
  • View their saved tasks.
  • Delete tasks they no longer need.

This simple application already gives you several areas to discuss during an interview.

2. Understand the Request-to-Response Flow

Suppose an interviewer asks:

"What happens when a user creates a task?"

You should be able to explain the process in your own words.

For example:

  1. The frontend sends an HTTP POST request.
  2. The backend checks whether the user is authenticated.
  3. The request data is validated.
  4. The server creates a record in the database.
  5. The API returns an appropriate response.

Understanding this flow is more useful than memorizing a textbook definition of REST APIs.

You should also know why your application uses specific HTTP methods and status codes.

3. Review Your Database Decisions

A backend interview may include questions about your database structure.

Be prepared to explain:

  • Why you selected SQL or NoSQL.
  • How your tables or collections are organized.
  • How users and tasks are connected.
  • What happens when a database query fails.
  • How indexes might improve certain queries.

You don't need to pretend your first database design was perfect.

Being able to explain what you would improve is valuable.

4. Prepare for Authentication Questions

If your project includes login functionality, understand how it works.

For example:

  • How are passwords stored securely?
  • How does the server verify a user's identity?
  • How are protected routes secured?
  • Can one user access another user's tasks?
  • What happens when a token expires?

These questions help demonstrate that you've considered how your application behaves beyond a successful login.

5. Practice Debugging Your Own Application

Take one feature and deliberately test it with unexpected inputs.

What happens if:

  • A required field is missing?
  • The user sends invalid data?
  • The database becomes unavailable?
  • Someone requests a task that doesn't exist?
  • A user tries to access another user's record?

Document the issue, investigate the cause, and explain the solution.

This is useful interview preparation because real development work involves handling failures, not just implementing features.

For a structured approach to troubleshooting, you can also read my earlier article: Debugging Your First JavaScript Project: A Repeatable Checklist

6. Turn Your Project Into Interview Questions

Create a short document with questions based on your application.

For example:

Question: Why did you choose PostgreSQL?

Question: How do you handle errors in your API?

Question: What would happen if 1,000 users accessed the application simultaneously?

Question: How would you test an endpoint before deployment?

Question: What would you improve if you had another month to work on the project?

Practice answering these questions without reading your source code.

If you struggle with an answer, that gives you a clear topic to revisit.

7. Explain Your Contribution Honestly

If you followed a tutorial or used AI tools while developing the project, make sure you understand the implementation.

You should be able to modify the application, explain the decisions behind the code, and identify its limitations.

Avoid presenting tutorial code as an entirely original solution if it isn't.

Your goal is to demonstrate understanding, not to make your project sound more complicated than it is.

For more interview preparation guidance, see Preparing for Your First Software Developer Interview: What Actually Matters

Final Thoughts

For junior backend interviews, one thoroughly understood project can be more useful than five incomplete applications.

Start with something manageable. Test it, improve it, document your decisions, and practice explaining how it works.

The important part isn't having the most impressive technology stack.

It's being able to explain what you built, why you built it that way, and what you learned in the process.

What backend project are you currently using to prepare for interviews?

title: Magic Link Email Sessions: Audit Log Evidence for Edtech Revocation
description:
Short answer: moving email login off a managed provider transfers responsibility for session revocation to your application, so make single-use email verification, refresh-token rotation, and a durable revocation decision part of the migration contract before moving users. A delivered magic link proves neither that verification succeeded nor that a stolen session stopped working. For an education platform, the acceptance test is concrete: after revoking one learner's compromised session, its refresh tokens must stop producing credentials, and protected requests must obey the documented access-token revocation policy.

What page fired when the stolen session kept working?

Consider this hypothetical production exercise: I am reviewing a migration for a learning platform, a learner reports a stolen session, and the responder revokes it while an attacker holds its refresh token. This is a scenario to test, not a report of an observed incident. The learner requests another email login while the attacker attempts a refresh. The question for the postmortem is whether those operations share an enforceable session boundary, including during the period when the old issuer and the new issuer both accept credentials.

Name the page.

A green authentication dashboard is weak evidence here. It can show successful login traffic while saying nothing about the specific authorization decision that matters: can the revoked session still access course records? The useful page would identify a protected request accepted after the session's revocation became effective under the declared policy. Its evidence needs a session identifier, the revocation decision time, the authorization decision time, and the enforcing component. A refresh replay alert answers a different question: someone reused a credential that should already have been consumed. Both events deserve investigation, but their meanings should remain distinct.

The invariant is that every credential derived from a session must remain subject to that session's lifecycle. A fresh email login can create a separate session; it must not silently resurrect the revoked one. For refresh tokens, RFC 9700 describes rotation and retention of the relationship between tokens so reuse can reveal compromise. For access tokens, the enforcement design determines how quickly revocation takes effect. An incident report that merely says “we rotated the token” leaves that second boundary unanswered.

How should an email code create a session and audit log?

The reader looking for a Node.js magic-link or email-code example needs the same lifecycle contract as any other application server. The implementation below is in Go, but the storage boundary belongs behind the Node.js request handler too: accept a submitted proof, consume its challenge once, create a session, and commit the corresponding audit event. Changing runtimes doesn't remove the concurrency problem.

Keep the email challenge separate from the session credential. Generate an unpredictable challenge, bind it to its intended purpose and account, store a protected representation, and give it a bounded lifetime. An email code has a smaller guessing space than a long random token, so verification needs attempt limits as well as request throttling. OWASP's authentication guidance supports generic authentication responses and defenses against automated attacks; those controls matter before successful verification, when a request can otherwise disclose account existence or turn the mail sender into an abuse channel.

Consumption must be atomic.

Two requests presenting the same valid proof should not create two sessions because both read an unused challenge before either writes its used marker. The transaction should check expiry and attempt policy, consume the challenge, create the session, and record the security event together. A failed commit must leave no issued credential that the durable session record cannot explain. If audit events are exported elsewhere, an outbox committed with the transaction can preserve the local event until export succeeds; that is a design choice, with its own queue monitoring and retention work.

Email delivery sits outside that transaction. Record separate milestones for request accepted, message submitted, delivery feedback received when available, challenge verified, and session created. SMTP delivery status doesn't establish that the intended person read the message, and a missing verification event alone cannot diagnose an inbox-placement problem. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC address sender authentication and policy; none promises inbox placement. During migration, check the sending domain configuration and correlate message identifiers with challenge identifiers without recording the challenge secret itself.

There's another trap: making a link visit itself perform the security mutation. Automated link inspection can make a visit an unreliable signal of human intent. Design the landing page and explicit verification action so their semantics are clear, then test the actual mail path used by the platform. Keep tokens out of analytics, referrer exposure, and application logs. A useful audit trail records what happened without becoming a second credential store.

Rotate under the same lock that enforces revocation

The critical path is refresh, because it can prolong access after the original login has disappeared from operational attention. The following Go fragment is a storage contract sketch, not a complete authentication server. It deliberately leaves token generation, digest construction, HTTP responses, and database implementation outside the example so the transaction requirements are visible. Its strings describe internal event names, not API routes.

package sessions

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var ErrDenied = errors.New("refresh denied")

type Session struct {
    ID      string
    Revoked bool
}

type Refresh struct {
    SessionID string
    Used      bool
    ExpiresAt time.Time
}

// Every operation runs inside one database transaction.
// LockRefreshAndSession also locks the shared session row.
// ConsumeRefresh must reject an already consumed credential.
type Tx interface {
    LockRefreshAndSession(context.Context, []byte) (Refresh, Session, error)
    RevokeSession(context.Context, string) error
    ConsumeRefresh(context.Context, []byte) error
    InsertRefresh(context.Context, string, []byte, time.Time) error
    Audit(context.Context, string, string) error
}

// RotationStep returns allowed=false, err=nil for a policy denial.
// Commit before interpreting allowed; roll back on any error.
// The caller supplies a newly generated secret's protected digest.
func RotationStep(
    ctx context.Context, tx Tx, presented, replacement []byte,
    now, replacementExpiry time.Time,
) (allowed bool, err error) {
    if len(presented) == 0 || len(replacement) == 0 ||
        !replacementExpiry.After(now) {
        return false, ErrDenied
    }
    token, session, err := tx.LockRefreshAndSession(ctx, presented)
    if err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    if token.SessionID != session.ID {
        return false, ErrDenied
    }
    if session.Revoked {
        return false, tx.Audit(ctx, session.ID, "refresh_denied_revoked")
    }
    if token.Used {
        if err := tx.RevokeSession(ctx, session.ID); err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        return false, tx.Audit(ctx, session.ID, "refresh_reuse_revoked")
    }
    if !now.Before(token.ExpiresAt) {
        return false, tx.Audit(ctx, session.ID, "refresh_denied_expired")
    }
    if err := tx.ConsumeRefresh(ctx, presented); err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    if err := tx.InsertRefresh(ctx, session.ID, replacement, replacementExpiry); err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    if err := tx.Audit(ctx, session.ID, "refresh_rotated"); err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    return true, nil
}

The awkward return contract is intentional. If reuse causes revocation, the application must commit that revocation even though authentication is denied. Returning an ordinary authentication error to a transaction wrapper that automatically rolls back would erase the very security action the responder needs. Commit the transaction first, then issue credentials only when allowed is true; on any storage or commit error, issue none. Map unknown tokens and other denials to an appropriate generic external response rather than exposing storage details.

An explicit session-revocation operation must acquire the same session lock, and every refresh path must check that row. Retain enough consumed-token lineage to recognize reuse; deleting the old record immediately defeats that detection. Set a deliberate retention boundary and document what happens after it expires. Digest handling and random-secret generation need their own review. This fragment doesn't establish either. In a race, the serialization order matters: if refresh commits before revocation, its replacement belongs to the session that revocation subsequently disables; if revocation commits first, refresh must observe the revoked state and deny issuance. Neither outcome establishes that an already issued access token stopped working, because that depends on the protected request's enforcement policy. Test both orders against the real database implementation rather than treating the interface as proof of isolation.

The interface isn't evidence.

Now consider a legitimate browser sending 2 refresh requests concurrently. Strict single-use rotation can interpret the second request as reuse and revoke the session, which is secure but disruptive during a lesson. Serialize refresh attempts in the client and test retries after a lost response. A retry grace policy can reduce disruption, but it changes the replay boundary and needs an explicit threat model; adding an unexamined grace window merely moves uncertainty into incident response.

Migration changes who can enforce the decision

A reference session checked on protected requests gives the application a direct revocation decision, at the cost of state lookup and an availability dependency. A locally validated access token can reduce that dependency, but an offline validator doesn't learn that its session was revoked simply because the refresh store changed. Short access-token lifetimes bound one form of exposure; online session checks or introspection can provide a different enforcement boundary. Choose the boundary before claiming immediate revocation.

Enforcement choice Revocation boundary Operational trade-off
Session lookup on protected requests The session check can observe committed revocation Lookup availability and caching policy affect enforcement
Offline access-token validation An issued token may remain usable until expiry Fewer online checks, but delayed containment without another control
Online token introspection The authorization decision uses the introspection result Endpoint availability and cached results need an explicit policy

During overlap with a managed issuer, write down who validates each credential and who owns revocation for each session. A successful revoke request against one issuer doesn't demonstrate enforcement by another. RFC 7009 defines token revocation behavior, but migration still requires checking which token types and related credentials the particular integration invalidates. Don't assume that exporting account profiles exports usable session state or token-family relationships. Those are separate migration questions.

A staged cutover can require existing users to authenticate again while directing new email challenges to the new implementation. That trades classroom interruption for a smaller period of credential overlap. Preserving existing sessions instead requires an explicit bridge: issuer-specific validation rules, traceable session ownership, and a tested revocation path across the overlap.

Rollback must preserve revocation decisions too.

Restoring an older session snapshot without reconciling later revocations can undo the security action the migration was supposed to preserve.

The operating cost is more than token storage. Someone must own the mail queue, sender configuration, challenge cleanup, abuse controls, audit retention, and the refresh transaction's database contention. That work can justify keeping an existing boundary while the team develops the missing operational capability. A migration decision should include the responder's ability to investigate and revoke a session, not just the developer's ability to complete a login demo.

Prove containment before moving the classroom

Use a synthetic learner account and an isolated test mail path. Test a challenge submitted twice, an expired code, an unknown account request, and a delivery failure; each needs a distinguishable internal outcome without leaking account existence externally. Then race refresh against refresh and refresh against revocation. Include a commit failure and a response lost after commit, because those cases expose the difference between database truth and what the client believes happened. These are proposed acceptance tests, not reported measurements.

For the stolen-session exercise, preserve a timeline of issuance, consumption, revocation, and protected-request decisions. Keep raw email proofs, refresh tokens, access tokens, and session cookies out of the log. Prefer opaque identifiers and restrict access to the audit store. OWASP's logging guidance is useful here: authentication events are valuable evidence, while logging secrets can create another incident.

A dashboard needs a falsifiable claim.

“No accepted protected request after the declared revocation boundary in this exercise” is something the test can establish. “The login service is healthy” cannot establish containment. Alert on a violation of the former and retain enough evidence to investigate it.

This advice has limitations. A browser application using only server-side sessions may have no refresh-token family to rotate; it still needs atomic session revocation and safe cookie handling. Email-only verification also depends on mailbox control and doesn't supply phishing resistance or an independent authentication factor. For sensitive educator actions or student-record access, assess assurance requirements separately using authentication guidance.

Move the classroom only when the team can explain which credential stopped working, where the decision was enforced, and how the audit trail proves it. The migration is ready when a responder can answer those questions during a stolen-session report.

References

The authentication guidance informs generic errors, throttling, and assurance boundaries. The OAuth specifications define refresh-token protection and revocation semantics; the logging and session guidance support the evidence and lifecycle requirements. Email standards explain sender authentication, not a delivery guarantee.

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • RFC 9700, Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html
  • RFC 7009, OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7009.html
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208.html
  • RFC 6376, DomainKeys Identified Mail: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6376.html
  • RFC 7489, Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489.html

Sources

  • Authentication controls: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • Refresh-token replay protection: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html#section-4.14
  • Revocation behavior: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7009.html#section-2.1

title: How to Build an IT Asset Lifecycle Management System with Node.js and PostgreSQL
description:
Managing company equipment sounds simple until you have dozens of laptops, monitors, phones, and other devices moving between employees, departments, and locations.

A spreadsheet might tell you which laptop belongs to whom today. But can it tell you who previously held that laptop, when it went for repair, whether its warranty has expired, or why it was retired?

Those questions become important as an organization grows.

In this tutorial, we'll build the foundation of an IT asset lifecycle management system using Node.js, Express, and PostgreSQL. Rather than creating another basic CRUD application, we'll focus on asset states, controlled transitions, transaction safety, and historical records.

By the end, you'll understand how to structure a backend that keeps track of equipment throughout its lifecycle.

1. Understanding the IT Asset Lifecycle

An IT asset lifecycle describes the stages an asset passes through, from acquisition to final disposal.

A typical lifecycle looks like this:

Stage Description
Procurement Equipment is purchased or ordered
Registration Asset information is recorded
Available Equipment is ready for assignment
Assigned Equipment is issued to an employee
Maintenance Equipment is being inspected or repaired
Returned Equipment is received back and assessed
Retired Equipment is permanently removed from active use

There is an important distinction here: not every business event needs to become a permanent asset status.

For example, returned is often better modeled as an event. Once a laptop is returned and inspected, its current state might become available or maintenance.

This avoids building an unnecessarily complicated state machine.

For our implementation, we'll use four operational states:

  • available
  • assigned
  • maintenance
  • retired

We'll record procurement and registration details separately, while assignment, return, repair, and retirement actions will create historical events.

2. Choosing the Technology Stack

We'll use three main technologies:

Technology Responsibility
Node.js JavaScript runtime
Express HTTP API and routing
PostgreSQL Relational database and transaction management

PostgreSQL is particularly useful here because equipment records have relationships, constraints, and consistency requirements.

Consider a laptop assignment. We need to update its current holder and record the assignment event. Either both operations should succeed or neither should be committed.

That's where database transactions become essential.

Project Setup

Create a project:

mkdir asset-lifecycle-api
cd asset-lifecycle-api

npm init -y

npm install express pg dotenv

Enable ES modules in package.json:

{
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node server.js"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "dotenv": "^17.0.0",
    "express": "^5.0.0",
    "pg": "^8.0.0"
  }
}

The version ranges above are illustrative; use currently maintained compatible releases and commit your generated lockfile.

Create a .env file:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:password@localhost:5432/asset_db
PORT=3000

Replace the example credentials with your local database credentials. Never commit .env files or real secrets to source control.

Create the database:

CREATE DATABASE asset_db;

We'll run our schema against that database next.

3. Designing the PostgreSQL Database

A common mistake in asset tracking applications is storing everything in one table.

That approach makes the current inventory easy to display, but historical information becomes difficult to reconstruct.

For this example, we'll use two tables:

  1. assets — the current state of each asset.
  2. asset_events — the history of lifecycle actions.

This gives us a practical separation between current state and historical events.

Create the Assets Table 

CREATE TABLE assets (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,

    asset_tag TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    serial_number TEXT UNIQUE,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,

    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'available'
        CHECK (status IN (
            'available',
            'assigned',
            'maintenance',
            'retired'
        )),

    assigned_to TEXT,

    purchased_on DATE,
    warranty_expires_on DATE,

    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),

    CONSTRAINT valid_assignment CHECK (
        (status = 'assigned' AND assigned_to IS NOT NULL)
        OR
        (status <> 'assigned' AND assigned_to IS NULL)
    )
);

The valid_assignment constraint prevents an asset from remaining assigned to someone while its status says available, maintenance, or retired.

This is useful because database constraints protect data even when an application bug bypasses expected validation.

In a larger system, assigned_to should normally reference an employee or user record through a foreign key. We're using text here to keep the example focused.

Create the Asset Events Table 

CREATE TABLE asset_events (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,

    asset_id BIGINT NOT NULL
        REFERENCES assets(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,

    event_type TEXT NOT NULL
        CHECK (event_type IN (
            'registered',
            'assigned',
            'returned',
            'sent_to_maintenance',
            'maintenance_completed',
            'retired'
        )),

    from_status TEXT,
    to_status TEXT NOT NULL,

    performed_by TEXT NOT NULL,
    details JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,

    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE INDEX idx_asset_events_history
ON asset_events (asset_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);

The event table records what happened, when it happened, and which application identity performed the action.

For example:

Event Previous State New State
Registered — Available
Assigned Available Assigned
Returned Assigned Available
Sent for repair Available Maintenance
Repair completed Maintenance Available
Retired Available Retired

An event history is useful for troubleshooting, compliance evidence, and understanding equipment movement.

However, an ordinary database table is not automatically a tamper-proof audit log. Stronger audit requirements may need restricted permissions, append-only enforcement, external log retention, or additional integrity controls.

4. Connecting Node.js to PostgreSQL

Create db.js:

import 'dotenv/config';
import pg from 'pg';

const { Pool } = pg;

export const pool = new Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  max: 10,
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 5000,
  idleTimeoutMillis: 30000,
});

A connection pool lets your application reuse database connections instead of opening a new connection for every request.

For ordinary independent queries, pool.query() is convenient.

For transactions, we'll acquire a dedicated client from the pool.

This distinction matters because all statements in a PostgreSQL transaction must run through the same database connection.

5. Implementing Controlled Lifecycle Transitions

Instead of allowing arbitrary status updates, we'll define which changes are permitted.

Our state-transition rules are:

const transitions = {
  available: {
    assign: 'assigned',
    send_to_maintenance: 'maintenance',
    retire: 'retired',
  },

  assigned: {
    return: 'available',
  },

  maintenance: {
    complete_maintenance: 'available',
    retire: 'retired',
  },

  retired: {},
};

An assigned laptop cannot be directly assigned to somebody else using this simplified workflow. It must first be returned.

Similarly, a retired asset cannot be reactivated accidentally.

Different organizations may need additional rules, such as direct reassignments, lost equipment, quarantine, or disposal approval.

For now, we want a small state machine with predictable behavior.

6. Building the Lifecycle REST API

Create server.js:

import express from 'express';
import { pool } from './db.js';

const app = express();
app.use(express.json({ limit: '100kb' }));

const transitions = {
  available: {
    assign: 'assigned',
    send_to_maintenance: 'maintenance',
    retire: 'retired',
  },
  assigned: {
    return: 'available',
  },
  maintenance: {
    complete_maintenance: 'available',
    retire: 'retired',
  },
  retired: {},
};

const eventNames = {
  assign: 'assigned',
  return: 'returned',
  send_to_maintenance: 'sent_to_maintenance',
  complete_maintenance: 'maintenance_completed',
  retire: 'retired',
};

function getAssetId(value) {
  if (!/^[1-9]\d*$/.test(value)) return null;

  const id = Number(value);

  return Number.isSafeInteger(id) ? id : null;
}

// Demo identity only. Replace with authenticated
// authorization context before production.
function getActor() {
  return 'demo-operator';
}

app.post('/assets', async (req, res) => {
  const { assetTag, name } = req.body ?? {};

  if (
    typeof assetTag !== 'string' ||
    !assetTag.trim() ||
    typeof name !== 'string' ||
    !name.trim()
  ) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      error: 'Valid assetTag and name are required',
    });
  }

  const client = await pool.connect();

  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');

    const result = await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO assets (asset_tag, name)
       VALUES ($1, $2)
       RETURNING *`,
      [assetTag.trim(), name.trim()]
    );

    const asset = result.rows[0];

    await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO asset_events
       (asset_id, event_type, to_status, performed_by)
       VALUES ($1, 'registered', 'available', $2)`,
      [asset.id, getActor()]
    );

    await client.query('COMMIT');

    return res.status(201).json(asset);
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');

    if (error.code === '23505') {
      return res.status(409).json({
        error: 'Asset tag already exists',
      });
    }

    throw error;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
});

app.post('/assets/:id/transition', async (req, res) => {
  const id = getAssetId(req.params.id);
  const { action, assignedTo } = req.body ?? {};

  if (!id || typeof action !== 'string') {
    return res.status(400).json({
      error: 'Invalid asset ID or action',
    });
  }

  if (
    action === 'assign' &&
    (typeof assignedTo !== 'string' ||
      !assignedTo.trim())
  ) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      error: 'assignedTo is required',
    });
  }

  const client = await pool.connect();

  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');

    const result = await client.query(
      'SELECT * FROM assets WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE',
      [id]
    );

    const asset = result.rows[0];

    if (!asset) {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');
      return res.status(404).json({
        error: 'Asset not found',
      });
    }

    const nextStatus = transitions[asset.status]?.[action];

    if (!nextStatus) {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');

      return res.status(409).json({
        error: 'Invalid lifecycle transition',
      });
    }

    const holder =
      action === 'assign' ? assignedTo.trim() : null;

    const updated = await client.query(
      `UPDATE assets
       SET status = $1,
           assigned_to = $2,
           updated_at = NOW()
       WHERE id = $3
       RETURNING *`,
      [nextStatus, holder, id]
    );

    await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO asset_events
       (asset_id, event_type, from_status,
        to_status, performed_by, details)
       VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6::jsonb)`,
      [
        id,
        eventNames[action],
        asset.status,
        nextStatus,
        getActor(),
        JSON.stringify(
          action === 'assign'
            ? { assignedTo: holder }
            : {}
        ),
      ]
    );

    await client.query('COMMIT');

    return res.json(updated.rows[0]);
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');
    throw error;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
});

app.get('/assets/:id/history', async (req, res) => {
  const id = getAssetId(req.params.id);

  if (!id) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      error: 'Invalid asset ID',
    });
  }

  const result = await pool.query(
    `SELECT event_type, from_status, to_status,
            performed_by, details, created_at
     FROM asset_events
     WHERE asset_id = $1
     ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC`,
    [id]
  );

  res.json(result.rows);
});

app.use((error, req, res, next) => {
  console.error(error);

  res.status(500).json({
    error: 'Internal server error',
  });
});

app.listen(process.env.PORT || 3000, () => {
  console.log('Asset lifecycle API is running');
});

This example demonstrates the core workflow. It is not a complete production authentication or authorization implementation.

Why Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE?

Imagine two IT administrators trying to assign the same available laptop at almost the same time.

Without proper concurrency control, both requests might read the asset as available before either update completes.

PostgreSQL's FOR UPDATE acquires a row-level lock inside the transaction.

The second transaction must wait for the first to finish. It then reads the updated status and can reject an invalid transition.

This is one way to prevent conflicting changes to an asset's current state.

Why Keep Updates and Events in One Transaction?

Suppose the application successfully changes an asset to assigned but fails to write the assignment event.

Now the system shows a current holder without a corresponding historical record.

By wrapping both operations in a transaction, we ensure they are committed together or rolled back together.

That is essential when the asset history needs to remain consistent with operational changes.

7. Testing the Asset Lifecycle API

Start the server:

npm start

Register an Asset 

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/assets \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "assetTag": "LAP-001",
    "name": "Dell Latitude Laptop"
  }'

The response will contain the newly registered asset, initially marked as available.

Assign the Asset

Replace 1 with the ID returned during registration if necessary.

curl -X POST \
  http://localhost:3000/assets/1/transition \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "action": "assign",
    "assignedTo": "employee-101"
  }'

The asset now moves from available to assigned.

The assignment also creates a historical event.

Return the Asset 

curl -X POST \
  http://localhost:3000/assets/1/transition \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "action": "return"
  }'

After a valid return, its current status becomes available, and the previous holder is cleared.

View Lifecycle History 

curl http://localhost:3000/assets/1/history

A typical response includes:

[
  {
    "event_type": "returned",
    "from_status": "assigned",
    "to_status": "available",
    "performed_by": "demo-operator",
    "details": {},
    "created_at": "..."
  },
  {
    "event_type": "assigned",
    "from_status": "available",
    "to_status": "assigned",
    "performed_by": "demo-operator",
    "details": {
      "assignedTo": "employee-101"
    },
    "created_at": "..."
  }
]

This is much more useful than knowing only the asset's latest status.

It gives the IT team a chronological record of important activities.

8. Adding Warranty Tracking

Asset lifecycle management is not just about assignment and return.

IT departments also need visibility into warranty expiry, service contracts, and maintenance schedules.

Our assets table already includes warranty_expires_on.

We can query warranties expiring within the next 30 calendar days:

SELECT
    id,
    asset_tag,
    name,
    warranty_expires_on
FROM assets
WHERE status <> 'retired'
  AND warranty_expires_on >= CURRENT_DATE
  AND warranty_expires_on <= CURRENT_DATE + 30
ORDER BY warranty_expires_on ASC;

A scheduled job could run this query daily and notify the responsible team.

For production, the notification system should also keep delivery records to avoid repeatedly sending identical alerts.

A simple notification_log table with an appropriate uniqueness rule can help prevent duplicate reminders.

You should also distinguish between equipment warranties and software subscription renewals. They may involve different records, owners, and renewal policies.

9. Preparing the System for Production

The API we've created demonstrates state management and transaction safety, but several additional controls are necessary before using it with real company data.

Authentication and Authorization

Our example uses a fixed demo-operator identity.

A production system must replace that with verified identity information from its authentication layer.

Permissions should distinguish between users who can view equipment, assign assets, approve transfers, manage maintenance, and retire equipment.

Do not trust an identity or permission value simply because it appears in an incoming HTTP request.

Input Validation

Validate request bodies with a schema validation library such as Zod or another maintained solution.

Examples include:

  • Enforcing valid asset identifiers
  • Limiting string lengths
  • Rejecting unsupported actions
  • Validating dates and serial numbers
  • Applying consistent error responses

Tenant Isolation

If multiple organizations use the same application, add organization ownership to relevant tables.

Every operation must then enforce organization-level access controls. For stronger isolation, consider PostgreSQL row-level security with correctly scoped database roles and policies.

Transaction Safety

Always release database clients, even when an operation fails.

Use parameterized SQL queries to separate untrusted values from query text.

For higher availability and resilience, consider connection limits, transaction timeouts, retry strategies for appropriate transient failures, and graceful shutdown.

Auditing

A useful audit record should capture:

  • Who performed the action
  • What changed
  • When it changed
  • Which asset was affected
  • Relevant business context

For stronger accountability, preserve the previous assignee, current assignee, approved request, and reason for each handover.

Other Production Requirements

A complete implementation should also include:

  • Database migrations
  • Automated tests for valid and invalid transitions
  • Pagination for event history
  • Backup and recovery procedures
  • Error monitoring and structured logging
  • Idempotency for retried commands
  • Asset reconciliation and periodic audits
  • Secure equipment disposal procedures
  • Protection of historical events from unauthorized changes

An important test case is sending two simultaneous assignment requests for the same device and confirming that only one succeeds.

10. Build Your Own or Use an Existing Platform?

Building an asset management backend is a useful engineering project.

But maintaining a complete IT asset management platform involves more than storing equipment records.

Real organizations often need QR code scanning, signed handovers, employee offboarding, maintenance workflows, location tracking, reports, and role-based access.

If your goal is to learn backend architecture, building the system yourself is an excellent exercise.

If your goal is operational asset management, it may be more practical to evaluate an existing solution.

For example, Stackroom's IT asset management platform provides equipment assignment, custody records, and lifecycle visibility as part of a broader asset management workflow.

The right choice depends on whether you're solving a software engineering problem or an equipment management problem.

11. Final Thoughts

An effective IT asset lifecycle management system needs more than an assets table and a few CRUD endpoints.

The most important architectural decisions are often the less visible ones:

  • Keeping current state separate from historical activity
  • Defining valid lifecycle transitions
  • Using database transactions for consistent updates
  • Preventing conflicting assignments
  • Enforcing constraints at the database level
  • Preserving meaningful operational history

Node.js and PostgreSQL provide a solid foundation for implementing these patterns.

The same principles also apply to equipment checkout systems, inventory services, rental platforms, and other applications where resources move between people or operational states.

Start with a small, reliable lifecycle model. Add workflows as your actual business requirements become clear.

A system that accurately answers "Who has this asset, and how did it get here?" is already solving one of the most important problems in equipment management.

References and Further Reading

  • PostgreSQL Documentation — Constraints
  • node-postgres — Transactions
  • node-postgres — Parameterized Queries
  • Express — Production Security Best Practices
