title: If You Think React Is Free to Use, You Are Wrong.
description:
React Is Not Free. Let’s Clarify This.

When you use an abstraction over a complex task, it gives you convenience by moving complexity into a framework, which you learn through another mental model present in your mind.

This adds more concepts, like React mental model complexity, component/state complexity, and reconciliation/runtime complexity.

That’s why I say it: you move complexity into the mental model that is present in the mind.

Another trade-off is control.

You get maximum control when you work directly with DOM manipulation.

But in the case of React, control is given to React.

React manages all the operations, like insertion and deletion of DOM elements and updates to the DOM.

Now, you don’t have direct access to the DOM.

You exchange control for complexity.

If you lose control, then you lose ownership.

Now React becomes the owner of the rendering process.

It becomes a middleman between your application and the browser.

It creates the necessity to understand React’s rules.

That’s it.

Ummmm, really, don’t.

Another big trade-off is runtime overhead and memory.

Assume that React has some work pending to do.

Now, the question is: does React directly hand over this work to the browser?

Really, don’t.

It creates a virtual DOM, then uses reconciliation and updates the Fiber tree before reflecting the updates.

This can make the application slower due to runtime overhead.

Maintaining the React Fiber tree requires additional memory, which is not required in a vanilla JavaScript application due to its limited framework state.

In the case of React, it is not free to use.

You pay the cost through these trade-offs and mental models.

title: Custom Node.js OTP Service: 3 Recovery Rules for Secure SMS Validation
description:
Build a custom Node.js service for secure OTP generation and validation around one rule: keep the same challenge across retries of an external SMS API request. Decide who owns the message template first. An edtech signup has two separate proofs: the email link verifies access to an email address; an SMS OTP verifies access to a phone number. Neither should silently satisfy the other.

Template and challenge ownership Options to evaluate Recovery trade-off
Application owns both Custom Node.js service with Amazon SNS for SMS delivery You control wording and validation, and own expiration, attempt limits, and duplicate prevention.
Provider manages the verification flow Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify Evaluate their verification workflows and template controls before committing the signup experience to them.
Application owns the signup policy behind a capability contract Infrai A consistent API boundary can reduce provider-specific integration work; inspect the chosen capability's schema and retry contract.

TL;DR: Build generation and validation in Node.js when template ownership is a product requirement. Use cryptographic randomness, expiring server-side challenge records, bounded guesses, and atomic consumption. Treat SMS sending as a separate delivery operation. For a solo edtech founder who wants to retain signup policy while changing the vendor behind delivery, try Infrai for that delivery boundary: the capability contract stays put when the vendor behind it changes. Its public, self-describing request and response schemas also help check the integration before writing recovery code.

That recommendation has a boundary. A managed verification specialist deserves the first evaluation if handing over the challenge lifecycle matters more than owning it. Revenue per hour is the useful lens: how much engineering time should signup messaging take away from the next lesson feature?

Ship weekly. Outsource the undifferentiated.

Infrai also uses a single API key and one bill across its backend capabilities. For a founder integrating signup email alongside phone verification, that reduces separate credential rotation and billing reconciliation work. It doesn't remove the need to own the signup policy.

Who owns the signup message and its verification state?

Start with the link. For this edtech signup, the application creates a verification link for the learner's email address. If the product also requires a phone check, the application opens a separate SMS challenge tied to that learner and purpose. Sending a phone code is not an equivalent fallback for confirming an email address; changing the channel changes what the application has established. Keep the email confirmation requirement explicit.

Template ownership is more than editing a sentence. It includes the approved wording, locale, link destination, expiration language, and which version a retry uses.

Store a template version with the delivery intent.

If the team changes the welcome copy while a send is waiting, the worker should still know which version belongs to that signup attempt. Otherwise an apparently harmless deployment can make a support investigation ambiguous.

Keep the distinction sharp.

The challenge record owns the security decision: learner ID, verification purpose, destination binding, verifier, expiration, attempt count, and consumed state. The delivery record owns the transport decision: template version, logical send ID, provider reference, and current delivery state. A message reaching a handset does not mean the learner entered the code. A learner entering the code does not confirm the email link.

For a custom service, generate the OTP with Node.js crypto. Store its verifier and expiration metadata in the backend database. A keyed verifier is useful for short numeric codes because a plain hash leaves a small search space to an attacker who obtains the database. Keep the key outside that database, and keep raw codes out of logs. The minimal example below uses a process-local store to make this boundary visible; persistence and concurrency need a database implementation.

Recover the signup attempt before resending its message

A timeout is ambiguous.

The sender may have accepted the request before the connection disappeared. Creating a fresh challenge on every retry can invalidate the code the learner is already typing, while sending the same challenge without delivery deduplication can produce multiple messages. Choose the recovery policy before adding a retry loop. Persist the challenge and its delivery intent together, using a database transaction and an outbox worker. Assign a stable logical ID to that delivery intent. Reuse it for retries of the same operation wherever the selected API supports idempotency; an intentional resend needs its own recorded policy. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention, with a default deduplication window of 24 hours. Check the individual capability's idempotency declaration before relying on it. A transport deduplication window never defines how long a login code remains valid.

For an HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present. Otherwise use bounded exponential backoff with jitter. Keep a maximum attempt count and a deadline, and stop trying once the challenge expires. Surface other response errors with enough context to distinguish a rejected template from a request that needs a later retry. Do not treat every unsuccessful response as permission to resend.

Recovery also needs an application-level record of uncertainty. Separate pending, accepted, and confirmed states rather than labeling a transport timeout as either delivered or failed. Store the request ID and provider reference when available. Infrai's native response metadata specifies request_id, vendor, and latency_ms, which can help connect an individual send to a support investigation. Those fields are context, not evidence that the learner received or used the OTP.

If the signup journey requires immediate delivery-event callbacks, make that a provider-selection requirement and test the event contract. For a polling-based recovery design, bound the polling window and stop it when the challenge expires. Separately, the application should enforce signup throttles, destination cooldowns, geographic restrictions, and spending cutoffs. These are business rules; a consistent transport API does not choose them for an edtech product.

How should a custom Node.js service secure OTP generation and validation?

This TypeScript example starts with an Infrai discovery request to locate the SMS OTP capability, then demonstrates the local security boundary. Run it with a TypeScript-capable Node.js runtime. Discovery is public; the example accepts an optional INFRAI_API_KEY environment variable to show the authentication convention used for subsequent integration. The request is read-only and does not send a message.

The local checks create a six-digit challenge for a learner and prove that consuming it twice fails. A lifetime of 5 minutes and a limit of 5 attempts are example policy choices, not provider defaults.

import {
  createHmac,
  randomBytes,
  randomInt,
  randomUUID,
  timingSafeEqual,
} from "node:crypto";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";

async function inspectSmsCapability() {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  const headers: Record<string, string> = key
    ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` }
    : {};
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", {
      method: "GET",
      headers,
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
    });
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = response.headers.get("Retry-After");
      const seconds = retryAfter === null ? NaN : Number(retryAfter);
      const date = retryAfter === null ? NaN : Date.parse(retryAfter);
      const waitMs = Number.isFinite(seconds)
        ? Math.max(0, seconds * 1000)
        : Number.isFinite(date)
          ? Math.max(0, date - Date.now())
          : 500 * 2 ** attempt + randomInt(0, 250);
      await response.body?.cancel();
      // Leave long waits to a durable worker rather than an in-process timer.
      if (waitMs > 30_000) throw new Error("Retry deferred beyond demo budget");
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Discovery HTTP ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    const manifest = await response.json();
    const capabilities = typeof manifest.capabilities === "string"
      ? JSON.parse(manifest.capabilities)
      : manifest.capabilities;
    if (!Array.isArray(capabilities)) throw new Error("Invalid discovery manifest");
    const capability = capabilities.find((item) => item.path === "/v1/sms/otp");
    if (!capability) throw new Error("SMS OTP capability not found");
    return capability;
  }
  throw new Error("Discovery retry budget exhausted");
}

const capability = await inspectSmsCapability();
console.log("Located capability:", capability.id);

type Challenge = {
  learnerId: string;
  purpose: "signup-phone";
  verifier: Buffer;
  expiresAt: number;
  attempts: number;
};

// Demo only: production needs a persistent key and atomic database operations.
const verifierKey = randomBytes(32);
const challenges = new Map<string, Challenge>();
const lifetimeMs = 5 * 60 * 1000;
const maxAttempts = 5;

function digest(id: string, code: string): Buffer {
  return createHmac("sha256", verifierKey)
    .update(JSON.stringify([id, code]))
    .digest();
}

function issue(learnerId: string, now = Date.now()) {
  const id = randomUUID();
  const code = randomInt(0, 1_000_000).toString().padStart(6, "0");
  challenges.set(id, {
    learnerId,
    purpose: "signup-phone",
    verifier: digest(id, code),
    expiresAt: now + lifetimeMs,
    attempts: 0,
  });
  // Give the raw code only to the trusted delivery worker.
  return { id, code };
}

function verify(
  id: string,
  learnerId: string,
  candidate: string,
  now = Date.now(),
): boolean {
  const record = challenges.get(id);
  if (!record || record.learnerId !== learnerId) return false;
  if (now >= record.expiresAt || record.attempts >= maxAttempts) {
    challenges.delete(id);
    return false;
  }

  record.attempts += 1;
  const valid = /^\d{6}$/.test(candidate)
    && timingSafeEqual(record.verifier, digest(id, candidate));
  if (valid || record.attempts >= maxAttempts) challenges.delete(id);
  return valid;
}

const learnerId = "learner-demo";
const challenge = issue(learnerId);
assert.equal(verify(challenge.id, learnerId, "invalid"), false);
assert.equal(verify(challenge.id, learnerId, challenge.code), true);
assert.equal(verify(challenge.id, learnerId, challenge.code), false);

const expired = issue(learnerId, 0);
assert.equal(verify(expired.id, learnerId, expired.code, lifetimeMs), false);
console.log("Challenge checks passed; no OTP values logged.");

The Map deliberately keeps the demonstration small. It loses its contents on restart and cannot coordinate multiple workers. In production, check expiration, increment the attempt count, compare the verifier, and consume the challenge within one transaction that locks the challenge row. Two concurrent correct requests must produce one successful consumption. Bind that operation to the authenticated signup session and the stored destination as well as the learner ID. The demo's learner ID argument is not authentication.

There is another persistence trap: an outbox worker needs access to the code to send it after the request handler finishes, but the verifier cannot reconstruct it. Persist a separately encrypted, short-lived delivery payload under a key kept outside the database, and delete that payload after its delivery or expiration policy allows. Storing the raw OTP next to its verifier defeats the point of storing a verifier.

Attach the external SMS adapter after this boundary. Use the selected provider's documented request schema, keep credentials in environment variables, and give its worker the stable delivery ID. If the provider manages generation and verification instead, replace the local challenge lifecycle deliberately. Do not generate one code locally and ask a managed service to validate a different challenge.

When is a direct provider the better choice?

Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify are the relevant comparisons when you want a managed verification workflow. Evaluate their template controls against the exact signup copy and locales you need, then test expiration, wrong-code handling, and resend behavior. Delegating verification can be a good trade for one founder, provided the product can accept that ownership boundary.

Amazon SNS belongs in a different comparison: SMS transport for an application that already owns generation, storage, validation, and recovery. It deserves an evaluation when that application control is intentional. The trade is the amount of security and operational code the team keeps. Compare the implementation burden against the managed verification options rather than treating all three products as interchangeable send buttons.

Infrai fits between those decisions when the useful abstraction is a stable delivery capability contract. Its discovery schemas help inspect that boundary, but the application still needs a clear policy for template versions, signup abuse, and challenge consumption. If a specialist's template workflow or delivery-event integration matches your operating requirements better, choose the specialist. Owning an abstraction has value only if it removes work you would otherwise maintain.

Before shipping, exercise four recovery cases: a send times out after acceptance, a learner requests another message, two valid submissions arrive together, and the worker restarts with a pending delivery. Check the stored state after each case. No benchmark is needed to discover that an expired code must stay expired.

References

  • Node.js cryptographic randomness, HMAC, and timing-safe comparison
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify documentation
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation

If this delivery boundary fits your signup flow, start with the capability schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc

title: Building an MBTI Cognitive Functions Test in JavaScript: Data Model and Scoring
description:
An mbti cognitive functions test is one of those projects that looks like a form full of radio buttons until you sit down to write the scoring. This post builds the data layer for one in plain JavaScript: a model of the eight functions, rule-based derivation of each type's four-function stack, a scorer that ranks all sixteen types, tie handling, and unit tests. One caveat shapes everything below: a self-report measures how strongly you agree with statements written from a theory. It does not observe your functions. With that settled, an mbti cognitive functions test is a genuinely fun engineering problem.

What an MBTI cognitive functions test actually measures

Start with vocabulary. Jung described sensing, intuition, thinking and feeling, and as MBF on type dynamics puts it, "Jung called the processes functions." Attach an attitude — extraverted or introverted — and you get eight functions: Se, Si, Ne, Ni, Te, Ti, Fe and Fi. Type dynamics arranges four per type as Dominant, Auxiliary, Tertiary and Inferior. The fourth letter names the process you extravert: J extraverts judging (T or F), P extraverts perceiving (S or N). Extraverts use the dominant in the outer world; introverts show the auxiliary outwardly. Every mbti cognitive functions test is downstream of those rules.

Jung also wrote that "all the basic psychological functions seldom or never have the same strength or grade of development in one and the same individual" — as a rule, one predominates (Jung, Psychological Types, Ch. X). Hence stack-position scoring in this mbti cognitive functions test. But be precise about what any mbti functions test does: it asks how much you recognize yourself in descriptions of Ni or Se. A cognitive functions mbti test scores agreement with a taxonomy, not cognition itself, and an mbti cognitive functions test that claims more in its copy is overclaiming.

Data model for an mbti cognitive functions test

Three pieces carry the whole mbti cognitive functions test: the function list, statements that each target one function, and a scorer producing comparable numbers. Here is the skeleton I would start any jungian cognitive functions test with. Every later piece of the mbti cognitive functions test reads from it:

// Eight Jungian functions: a process (S, N, T, F) plus an attitude (e or i)
const FUNCTIONS = ['Se', 'Si', 'Ne', 'Ni', 'Te', 'Ti', 'Fe', 'Fi'];

// Each item measures one function on a 1-5 scale; 4 items per function, 32 total
const items = [
  { id: 1, fn: 'Ni', text: 'I often know where something is heading before I can explain why.' },
  { id: 2, fn: 'Se', text: 'I notice small changes in a room as soon as I walk in.' },
  // ...
];

function scoreFunctions(answers) {            // answers: { [itemId]: 1..5 }
  const totals = Object.fromEntries(FUNCTIONS.map(f => [f, 0]));
  const counts = Object.fromEntries(FUNCTIONS.map(f => [f, 0]));
  for (const item of items) {
    const a = answers[item.id];
    if (a == null) continue;                  // skipped items don't count
    totals[item.fn] += a - 3;                 // center the scale: -2..+2
    counts[item.fn] += 1;
  }
  return Object.fromEntries(FUNCTIONS.map(f =>
    [f, counts[f] ? totals[f] / (2 * counts[f]) : null]));  // -1..+1, or null
}

Answers are centered on 3, so disagreement pushes a function negative, and dividing by twice the number of answered items clamps each score into -1..+1. Skipped items are ignored, and a function with no answered items returns null rather than a polite zero. On a jungian functions test, an unanswered item is missing data, not neutrality. Four statements per function is demo-sized; a production mbti cognitive functions test would use more items without changing this shape. Since the mbti cognitive functions test scores agreement, keep statement wording behavioral ("I notice…") rather than identity claims.

Deriving MBTI function stacks from a four-letter code

No lookup table needed: the mbti function stack falls straight out of the type-dynamics rules. J means you extravert your judging process, P your perceiving one. An extravert leads with that extraverted process; an introvert leads with the other pair turned inward and shows the auxiliary to the world. The tertiary is the opposite process of the auxiliary, though its attitude is debated — the Foundation's answer is basically "You decide from your own experience!" — and the inferior is the dominant's opposite in every way. That is all an mbti cognitive functions test needs to build every stack on the fly.


const OPP = { S: 'N', N: 'S', T: 'F', F: 'T' };
const flip = a => (a === 'e' ? 'i' : 'e');

function stackFromCode(code) {                // e.g. 'INFJ'
  const [ei, sn, tf, jp] = code.toUpperCase().split('');
  // The last letter names the process you extravert: J -> T/F, P -> S/N
  const outward = jp === 'J' ? tf : sn;
  const inward = jp === 'J' ? sn : tf;
  const dom = ei === 'E' ? outward + 'e' : inward + 'i';
  const aux = ei === 'E' ? inward + 'i' : outward + 'e';
  const ter = OPP[aux[0]] + dom[1];           // one convention; the tertiary's attitude is debated
  const inf = OPP[dom[0]] + flip(dom[1]);     // opposite of the dominant in every way
  return [dom, aux, ter, inf];
}
// stackFromCode('INFJ') -> ['Ni', 'Fe', 'Ti', 'Se']
// stackFromCode('ENFP') -> ['Ne', 'Fi', 'Te', 'Si']

One comment in that code is doing honest work: the tertiary's attitude is a convention here, not scripture. The rules also have a satisfying symmetry — every function is dominant for exactly two types. Ni leads INFJ and INTJ, Se leads ESTP and ESFP, Fi leads ISFP and INFP, and so on. That symmetry is trivial to assert in a unit test, and an mbti cognitive functions test built on these rules gets it for free. Because mbti function stacks are derived rather than stored, the mbti cognitive functions test never carries a stale table someone could mistype.

Scoring a Myers Briggs cognitive functions test

Now the scoring step of the mbti cognitive functions test: compare the answer profile against every type's stack, with the dominant counting most and the inferior least. I use weights 4/3/2/1 and a 0.25 tie band — both are design choices for this mbti cognitive functions test, not a standard, so print them next to the results.

const WEIGHTS = [4, 3, 2, 1];                 // dominant .. inferior (a design choice)
const TYPES = ['ISTJ', 'ISFJ', 'INFJ', 'INTJ', 'ISTP', 'ISFP', 'INFP', 'INTP',
               'ESTP', 'ESFP', 'ENFP', 'ENTP', 'ESTJ', 'ESFJ', 'ENFJ', 'ENTJ'];

function rankTypes(fnScores, tieBand = 0.25) {
  const ranked = TYPES.map(code => ({
    code,
    fit: stackFromCode(code).reduce((s, fn, i) => s + WEIGHTS[i] * (fnScores[fn] ?? 0), 0),
  })).sort((a, b) => b.fit - a.fit);
  const top = ranked.filter(t => ranked[0].fit - t.fit <= tieBand);
  return { ranked, top };                     // top.length > 1 means "show the tie"
}

A worked example with illustrative scores: Ni +0.75, Fe +0.50, Ne +0.50, Ti +0.25, Se -0.50, everything else 0. INFJ computes as 4(0.75) + 3(0.50) + 2(0.25) + 1(-0.50) = 4.5. Here are the top five, which is the table an mbti cognitive functions test should show:

Type Stack Fit
INFJ Ni Fe Ti Se 4.5
ENTP Ne Ti Fe Si 3.75
ENFJ Fe Ni Se Ti 3.5
ESFJ Fe Si Ne Ti 3.25
INTP Ti Ne Si Fe 3.0

This table is where an mbti cognitive functions test earns or loses trust, and it surprised me the first time I ran it. ENTP comes second, ahead of ENFJ, even though ENTP shares neither of INFJ's lead functions. It collects points from Ne in first place and Fe in third, and nothing in its stack is negative. ENFJ shares Ni and Fe with INFJ in reverse order, but it pays for Se sitting in third place. That is the mbti cognitive functions test's weighted sum doing exactly what it was told, and a reminder that the weights are an opinion. The 0.75 gap to second place sits outside the tie band, so top holds one type here. If you're building a function test MBTI fans will actually trust, show this arithmetic instead of only the winner. For a contrasting philosophy, compare a Jung-inspired test that openly skips function stacks — its page states it does not measure the eight cognitive functions and that no self-report preference quiz can. That's a refreshing thing to read on a quiz page.

Ties and unit tests for your mbti cognitive functions test

With only four items per function, near-ties are common, so ties get first-class handling in any mbti cognitive functions test and the rules get tests. Three cover what breaks silently:

import { test, expect } from 'vitest';

test('INFJ stack follows the type-dynamics rules', () => {
  expect(stackFromCode('INFJ')).toEqual(['Ni', 'Fe', 'Ti', 'Se']);
});

test('each function is dominant for exactly two types', () => {
  const doms = TYPES.map(t => stackFromCode(t)[0]);
  for (const fn of FUNCTIONS) expect(doms.filter(d => d === fn)).toHaveLength(2);
});

test('all-neutral answers produce a full tie, not a type', () => {
  const answers = Object.fromEntries(items.map(i => [i.id, 3]));
  expect(rankTypes(scoreFunctions(answers)).top).toHaveLength(16);
});

The first locks the mbti cognitive functions test to a known stack. The second asserts that symmetry from earlier: each function is dominant for exactly two of the sixteen types. The third is my favorite — if every answer is neutral, all sixteen types tie and top comes back with sixteen entries, forcing the UI to show a tie instead of inventing a winner. An mbti cognitive functions test that returns a confident type from all-neutral input is broken somewhere in its centering, and this catches it loudly.

What I would not ship in an mbti cognitive functions test

Three rules I hold before shipping any mbti cognitive functions test:

  • No "accuracy %". Nothing here was validated against anything, so a percentage would be theater. Show the fit numbers and the tie band instead.
  • No unstated weights. Fixed weights like 4/3/2/1 are fine; shipping them silently turns the mbti cognitive functions test into a black box. Print them.
  • Show ties. If top.length > 1, render every tied type. Forcing one letter out of a quarter-point difference is where an mbti cognitive functions test starts lying.

I took a slower pass at the preference-pair side of this in How to build a personality test in JavaScript, which covers neutral answers and the same test-first habits. The mbti cognitive functions test in this post is the layer underneath. If there is a lesson, it is that an honest mbti cognitive functions test is careful plumbing plus a refusal to overclaim.

Editor's note from Nico: I help out with PersonalityTest, so I'm biased toward quizzes that admit their limits. This is a scoring exercise, not a claim that a self-report can see your functions.

To see that philosophy running, try the free MBTI-style test: 32 original statements, scored entirely in the browser, answers never uploaded, no account or email gate — and when a pair lands near the middle it says "balanced" and shows neighboring codes instead of forcing a letter. It is the same honesty the mbti cognitive functions test above is aiming for.

PersonalityTest is unofficial and not affiliated with The Myers-Briggs Company or the Myers & Briggs Foundation. The code here was written for this article.

title: A college notice board in React: a first project for web design students
description:
If you're a student learning web design and you've just finished HTML, CSS and some JavaScript, React can feel like a big jump. The best way across is a small project that you'd actually use. Here's one we give students: a college notice board.

What it does

  • Shows a list of notices (title, department, date).
  • Lets you filter by department.
  • Lets you add a notice through a form.
  • Saves notices in localStorage so they survive a refresh.

That's enough to touch components, props, state, events, forms, lists and effects, without a backend.

Step 1: Set up 

npm create vite@latest notice-board -- --template react
cd notice-board
npm install
npm run dev

Step 2: Model the data 

const starter = [
  { id: 1, title: "Mid-sem exams start 18 Nov", dept: "CSE", date: "2026-11-04" },
  { id: 2, title: "Placement talk in Seminar Hall", dept: "All", date: "2026-11-05" },
];

Step 3: State that persists 

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function useNotices() {
  const [notices, setNotices] = useState(() => {
    const saved = localStorage.getItem("notices");
    return saved ? JSON.parse(saved) : starter;
  });
  useEffect(() => {
    localStorage.setItem("notices", JSON.stringify(notices));
  }, [notices]);
  return [notices, setNotices];
}

Step 4: Components

Split it into NoticeList, NoticeCard, DeptFilter and NoticeForm. Pass data down as props, and pass functions like onAdd down so the form can update the list.

function NoticeCard({ notice }) {
  return (
    <article className="card">
      <h3>{notice.title}</h3>
      <p>{notice.dept} · {notice.date}</p>
    </article>
  );
}

Step 5: The filter 

const visible = dept === "All"
  ? notices
  : notices.filter(n => n.dept === dept || n.dept === "All");

Step 6: Make it look good

Use CSS Grid for the card layout and a single media query for mobile. Check it on your phone. Most people who view your portfolio will.

Stretch goals

  • Sort by date, newest first.
  • Mark notices as "important" with a badge.
  • Deploy it and put the live link on your CV.
  • Later, replace localStorage with a small API.

What this teaches

By the end you have used every core React idea a junior interview asks about, and you have something finished to show. That matters more than a long list of half-done tutorials.

We teach this project in the React module of our web designing course for students in Mohali and Chandigarh. The full module list is on the Dzimark Training course page.

title: Zoho Integration Services in Node.js: Upsert Without Duplicates
description:
A webhook retries, and your Node.js worker creates a second Account in Zoho CRM for the same customer. Sales now has two half-histories, and finance invoices the wrong one. This failure appears in how Zoho integration services handle retries and identity in production, usually after a timeout or a duplicate event from the source system. Teams hit it first in order-to-cash flows, where a duplicate Account later reaches invoicing. The cause is rarely the API call. It is a missing identity rule: nothing tells Zoho which record is which. This article shows how to fix that with an idempotent upsert client, bounded retries, and a review queue.

Context and Setup

Zoho integration services connect Zoho apps to outside systems, and the hard part is consistency when messages repeat. In the scenario below, a source system sends events to a Node.js service that writes Accounts into Zoho CRM.

Prerequisites: Node.js 18 or later (for global fetch), a Zoho OAuth client with a refresh token, and a custom Account field named Organization_Number holding a legal identifier. The scale of the problem is well documented. According to MuleSoft’s 2025 Connectivity Benchmark Report, the average enterprise runs 897 applications and integrates only 29 percent of them.

Building Zoho Integration Services with Idempotent Upserts
An idempotent write gives the same result whether it runs once or five times. Zoho CRM’s upsert endpoint provides that when you pick the right match field.

Step 1: Pick the match key
Match on an identifier the business already enforces, such as an organization number. Names and emails drift, so they make weak keys.

Add a custom field for the legal identifier to the Accounts module.
Normalize it before sending (strip spaces and punctuation).
Pass it as duplicate_check_fields so Zoho decides between insert and update.

Step 2: Write the upsert client for Zoho integration services
js
// Node 18+: global fetch, no dependencies
const ZOHO_API = "https://www.zohoapis.com/crm/v6"; // Why: region specific (.eu, .in elsewhere)

async function upsertAccount(record, token, attempt = 1) {
const res = await fetch(${ZOHO_API}/Accounts/upsert, {
method: "POST",
headers: {
Authorization: Zoho-oauthtoken ${token},
"Content-Type": "application/json",
},
body: JSON.stringify({
data: [record],
// Why: a retry updates the existing record instead of creating a duplicate
duplicate_check_fields: ["Organization_Number"],
}),
});

// Why: only transient errors deserve a retry; a 4xx means the payload is wrong
if ((res.status === 429 || res.status >= 500) && attempt <= 3) {
const delay = 2 ** attempt * 500; // exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay));
return upsertAccount(record, token, attempt + 1);
}

const body = await res.json();
const item = body.data?.[0];
if (res.ok && item?.code === "SUCCESS") {
return { id: item.details.id, action: item.action }; // "insert" or "update"
}
// Why: fail loudly so the caller can route the record to a review queue
throw new Error(Zoho rejected record: ${JSON.stringify(item ?? body)});
}
Step 3: Weigh the trade-offs
We retry a fixed number of times, then send the record to a queue with a named owner. This costs reviewer time, so the queue stays short only if the match rule is strict.

Batching is the other lever. Zoho’s CRM API limits documentation (reviewed November 2026) allows up to 100 records per insert, update, or upsert call and caps the deduction for such a call at 10 credits. Credits run on a rolling 24-hour window, so batch non-urgent syncs.

Real-World Application

In one of our Zoho integration projects at Oodles, Devinco AS, a Norwegian provider of integrated mobile solutions, needed its course platform connected to Zoho CRM. The goal was tracking sales, accounts, and contacts without manual entry.

We built a trigger that creates a Won Deal on each sale, with separate pipeline stages for paid and free courses. Account matching uses organization numbers, and a new account is created only when no match exists. Contact lookup runs on email with duplicate prevention, and Deal Contact Roles separate course orderers from attendees.

Key Takeaways

An upsert keyed on a business identifier makes retries safe, because repeats update instead of clone.
Retry only 429 and 5xx responses, with exponential backoff, since 4xx errors fail identically every time.
Batch up to 100 records per call to cut credit use, and keep single-record calls for time-sensitive events.
Route rejected records to an owned review queue so failures are visible, not silent.

Questions about your own sync design? Share them in the comments, or talk with us about Zoho integration services.

What are Zoho integration services?
Zoho integration services connect Zoho apps to each other and to external systems such as ERP, billing, and e-commerce platforms. The work includes data mapping, trigger design, retry and error handling, and monitoring so records stay consistent.

How do you avoid duplicate records in Zoho CRM from Node.js?
Use the Upsert Records endpoint with duplicate_check_fields set to a stable identifier, such as an organization number. Zoho then updates the matching record instead of inserting a second one, which makes webhook retries safe.

How do you authenticate to the Zoho CRM API?
Register a server-based client in the Zoho API Console, complete the OAuth 2.0 grant once for a refresh token, then exchange it for short-lived access tokens sent in an Authorization: Zoho-oauthtoken header.

What happens when Zoho API credits run out?
Zoho rejects further calls until credits free up on the rolling 24-hour window, and admins can add credits. Batch records and queue non-urgent syncs so real-time flows keep their credits.

Should Zoho integration services use webhooks or polling?
Use webhooks for event-driven flows such as a closed deal, because they avoid spending credits on empty polls. Reserve scheduled reads for backfills and daily reconciliation, where comparing record counts catches silent mismatches.

title: Responsive Iframes in Chrome 154: Auto-Height in 3 Steps
description:
Originally published on ExtensionBooster.

Responsive iframes are finally a platform feature: since Chrome 154 hit Stable on September 22, 2026, an iframe can grow to fit its content with no script in the parent page. The WHATWG request for this has been open since January 2016, and the classic Stack Overflow question about auto-height iframes has passed 1.5 million views. Here is the three-step setup, what you can delete, and how to ship it without breaking Firefox and Safari.

Why this matters

An iframe is a fixed viewport (300×150 px unless you size it). Taller content means a second scrollbar inside your page. For a decade the fix has been a two-sided protocol: the child measures itself, postMessage()s the height, and the parent sets style.height.

Chrome 154 replaces that with a double opt-in: a CSS property on the embedding side and a meta tag on the embedded side. It ships on desktop, Android and WebView, and the spec lives in the CSS Sizing Level 4 working draft.

The 3 steps

1. Embedder: set frame-sizing.

.embed {
  width: 100%;
  frame-sizing: content-height;
  max-height: 80vh; /* optional guard against runaway embeds */
}

Available values: auto (default, old behavior), content-height, content-width, and the logical content-block-size / content-inline-size. For horizontal writing modes, content-height is the one you will use.

2. Embedded document: agree to share its size.

<meta name="responsive-embedded-sizing"
      content="allow-origins=https://publisher1.example https://publisher2.example">

This tag must be in the HTML the server delivers. Google is explicit that it can't be injected after load, so a React head manager won't cut it. Use allow-origins=* only if any site may embed you.

3. Call requestResize() when content changes.

Sizing happens once, at load. That one-shot model is deliberate: it prevents the resize → reflow → resize loop. After you load more comments or expand an accordion, ask for a re-measure:

function render(items) {
  list.replaceChildren(...items.map(toListItem));
  if ('requestResize' in window) window.requestResize();
}

Call it once after the DOM update finishes. Don't wire it to a ResizeObserver that fires every frame.

What you can delete (and what you can't)

Concern postMessage resizer frame-sizing
Parent code Listener + height logic One CSS declaration
Child code Measure + postMessage Meta tag + requestResize()
Origin checks Manual, easy to botch Declarative allow-origins
Jitter / loops You debounce it Avoided by design
Support Every browser Chrome 154+

One more reason to look at this: iframe-resizer v5 moved to GPL v3 or a paid commercial license (4.x was MIT), so closed-source teams have been pinning old versions or writing their own.

What you can't delete yet: Firefox and Safari haven't published a position. Keep the fallback and gate both paths:

.widget { width: 100%; height: 500px; }

@supports (frame-sizing: content-height) {
  .widget { height: auto; frame-sizing: content-height; }
}

if (!CSS.supports('frame-sizing', 'content-height')) {
  window.addEventListener('message', onHeightMessage); // legacy path
}

Also watch Core Web Vitals. Google warns the late resize can shift content, so give embeds a realistic min-height and avoid auto-sized embeds above the fold.

The extension angle

Browser extensions often inject an extension page as an iframe from a content script so the host page can't restyle or read the UI. Height was always the pain point. Now the pattern is:

  1. List panel.html in web_accessible_resources with matches limited to the sites where the panel actually appears.
  2. Put the meta tag in the panel's static HTML entry (not a component, whether you use WXT, Plasmo or CRXJS). The embedder origin is the website, not your extension.
  3. From the content script, set frame-sizing with !important (the iframe lives in the host DOM, so page CSS can target it), and fall back to a fixed height elsewhere: 
const frame = document.createElement('iframe');
frame.src = chrome.runtime.getURL('panel.html');
if (CSS.supports('frame-sizing', 'content-height')) {
  frame.style.setProperty('frame-sizing', 'content-height', 'important');
  frame.style.setProperty('max-height', '80vh', 'important');
} else {
  frame.style.setProperty('height', '420px', 'important');
}
document.body.append(frame);
  1. Call requestResize() inside the panel after each render.

Chrome hasn't documented any special case for chrome-extension:// documents, so test on a real target site in Chrome 154+ before removing your old resizer.

Security note: height is data. The explainer warns that a page observing an iframe's laid-out size can learn things about the cross-origin document. If your panel's height depends on login state or result counts, any allowed embedder can read that. Scope allow-origins tightly, keep matches narrow, add frame-ancestors CSP on regular sites, and don't let a sensitive panel's size reflect private data before the user interacts.

Key takeaways

  • frame-sizing: content-height + a server-rendered meta tag = auto-height iframes in Chrome 154+.
  • Sizing is one-shot; call window.requestResize() after dynamic updates.
  • Firefox and Safari have no signal yet, so ship behind @supports and keep your resizer.
  • Reserve min-height to limit layout shift.
  • For extensions, treat iframe height as leakable state and scope origins narrowly.

The original article also covers iframe vs Shadow DOM trade-offs and other Chrome 154/155 changes, so read the full guide to responsive iframes and frame-sizing in Chrome 154 for the details. If you build extensions, ExtensionBooster's growth tools for Chrome extension developers can help after you ship.

Are you keeping your postMessage resizer as a fallback, or has iframe-resizer's license change already pushed you to roll your own? Tell me in the comments.

title: Three Correlations Passed Validation. The Matrix Was Impossible.
description:
A risk dashboard can look completely convincing while displaying numbers from a model that should never have accepted its inputs.

Imagine a UI with three correlation sliders:

  • Asset A and asset B: +0.90
  • Asset A and asset C: +0.90
  • Asset B and asset C: -0.90 Every input fits the permitted range. The diagonal of the resulting matrix is 1. The matrix is symmetric. A naïve form validator gives it a green checkmark.

And yet no three random variables can have all three of those pairwise correlations at once.

This isn't a report of a production failure. It's a failure mode we explicitly designed against while building a browser-based portfolio-risk visualization. The surprising part is that the bug can live entirely in the inputs, before any rendering code runs.
The matrix that looks valid

Our three sliders produce:

A      B      C

A [ 1.00, 0.90, 0.90 ]
B [ 0.90, 1.00, -0.90 ]
C [ 0.90, -0.90, 1.00 ]

The following check is necessary, but insufficient:

const correlations = [0.9, 0.9, -0.9];
const inRange = correlations.every(
  value => Number.isFinite(value) && value >= -1 && value <= 1
);

It returns true. That proves only that individual cells are in range.

A correlation matrix has to describe a jointly possible system. Its entries are constrained by one another.

There is a geometric intuition: if B closely follows A, and C also closely follows A, then B and C cannot simultaneously behave as almost exact opposites. The three statements conflict.

Why the determinant exposes the contradiction

For a symmetric three-asset correlation matrix with off-diagonal entries a, b, and c, its determinant is:

det(R) = 1 + 2abc - a² - b² - c²

In this example, a = 0.9, b = 0.9, and c = -0.9, so:

det(R) = 1 + 2(0.9)(0.9)(-0.9) - 3(0.9²)
= -2.888

A real correlation matrix must be positive semidefinite (PSD): for every vector x, the quadratic form xᵀRx must be nonnegative. That is what makes it possible to interpret the matrix as correlations coming from a covariance matrix.

This particular matrix has eigenvalues -0.8, 1.9, and 1.9. A negative eigenvalue is enough to show it is not PSD.

Here's another way to see it. Take x = [-1, 1, 1]. Then xᵀRx = -2.4. If R were a covariance matrix of unit-variance variables, that would claim a linear combination has negative variance. That's impossible.

One nuance: a bad correlation matrix does not necessarily produce a negative variance for every long-only portfolio. It is invalid globally, even if one portfolio happens to produce a nonnegative result. That's why validating only the final variance is not enough.

You can also derive the allowable third correlation when the first two are fixed:

ab - sqrt((1 - a²)(1 - b²))
   ≤ c ≤
ab + sqrt((1 - a²)(1 - b²))

For a = b = 0.9, the range is 0.62 ≤ c ≤ 1.00. A value of -0.9 is nowhere near feasible.

Changing c to +0.8 creates a valid matrix with determinant +0.036. But an application should not silently change a user's assumption. Fixing or projecting a matrix is a modeling choice that deserves an explanation.

A tiny JavaScript engine you can run

The example below deliberately has three assets so the PSD test fits in one formula. It is a self-contained teaching implementation, not a copy of our production module and not a generic validator for matrices of any size.

It also demonstrates a second engineering invariant: the sum of Euler volatility contributions must equal portfolio volatility whenever that quantity is defined.

Create risk-matrix.mjs:

// Standalone educational example for the DEV article.
// Three assets, decimal inputs, no dependencies, no price feed.
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { resolve } from 'node:path';

const EPS = 1e-10;

export function validateCorrelation3(R) {
  if (!Array.isArray(R) || R.length !== 3 ||
      R.some(row => !Array.isArray(row) || row.length !== 3)) {
    throw new RangeError('Expected a 3 x 3 matrix');
  }

  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
      const r = R[i][j];
      if (!Number.isFinite(r) || r < -1 || r > 1) {
        throw new RangeError('Correlations must be finite and in [-1, 1]');
      }
      if (i === j && Math.abs(r - 1) > EPS) {
        throw new RangeError('Diagonal entries must be 1');
      }
      if (Math.abs(r - R[j][i]) > EPS) {
        throw new RangeError('Matrix must be symmetric');
      }
    }
  }

  const a = R[0][1], b = R[0][2], c = R[1][2];
  // For a symmetric 3x3 unit-diagonal matrix, with |a|,|b|,|c| <= 1,
  // all principal minors are nonnegative iff this determinant is >= 0.
  const determinant = 1 + 2 * a * b * c - a*a - b*b - c*c;
  if (determinant < -EPS) {
    throw new RangeError(`Not positive semidefinite; det=${determinant.toFixed(3)}`);
  }
  return determinant;
}

export function portfolioRisk3({ weights, vols, correlations }) {
  validateCorrelation3(correlations);
  if (!Array.isArray(weights) || weights.length !== 3 ||
      weights.some(w => !Number.isFinite(w) || w < 0 || w > 1) ||
      Math.abs(weights.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) - 1) > EPS) {
    throw new RangeError('Long-only weights must sum to 1');
  }
  if (!Array.isArray(vols) || vols.length !== 3 ||
      vols.some(v => !Number.isFinite(v) || v < 0)) {
    throw new RangeError('Volatilities must be nonnegative decimals');
  }

  const cov = correlations.map((row, i) =>
    row.map((rho, j) => vols[i] * rho * vols[j]));
  const sigmaW = cov.map(row =>
    row.reduce((sum, element, j) => sum + element * weights[j], 0));
  const variance = weights.reduce((sum, w, i) => sum + w * sigmaW[i], 0);
  if (variance < -EPS) throw new RangeError('Negative portfolio variance');

  const volatility = Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, variance));
  // The Euler attribution is undefined at zero volatility; don't fake shares.
  const contributions = volatility > 0
    ? weights.map((w, i) => w * sigmaW[i] / volatility)
    : null;
  return { volatility, contributions };
}

export const IMPOSSIBLE = [
  [ 1,   0.9,  0.9 ],
  [ 0.9, 1,   -0.9 ],
  [ 0.9,-0.9,  1   ],
];

export const POSSIBLE = [
  [ 1,   0.9, 0.9 ],
  [ 0.9, 1,   0.8 ],
  [ 0.9, 0.8, 1   ],
];

if (process.argv[1] && fileURLToPath(import.meta.url) === resolve(process.argv[1])) {
  try {
    validateCorrelation3(IMPOSSIBLE);
  } catch (error) {
    console.log('Rejected:', error.message);
  }
  const out = portfolioRisk3({
    weights: [0.4, 0.35, 0.25],
    vols: [0.3, 0.2, 0.15],
    correlations: POSSIBLE,
  });
  console.log('Portfolio volatility:', `${(100 * out.volatility).toFixed(3)}%`);
  console.log('Risk contributions:', out.contributions.map(x => `${(100 * x).toFixed(3)}pp`));
  console.log('Sum:', `${(100 * out.contributions.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0)).toFixed(3)}pp`);
}

Run it with Node.js (tested with Node 22.16.0):

node risk-matrix.mjs

Expected output (rounded for display):

Rejected: Not positive semidefinite; det=-2.888
Portfolio volatility: 21.938%
Risk contributions: [ '11.856pp', '6.637pp', '3.444pp' ]
Sum: 21.938pp

Nothing here calls an API or downloads price data. The weights, volatilities, and correlations are hypothetical decimals, not historical estimates or investment recommendations.
The important part is what we test
For risk software, a nice-looking result isn't an acceptance test. We want a handful of invariants that can fail loudly:

  • The impossible matrix is rejected before pricing or rendering.
  • A valid matrix is accepted with its determinant unchanged.
  • Risk contributions sum to the same volatility computed by the covariance model.
  • Singular PSD matrices can be valid, but zero-volatility risk shares are undefined rather than an invented 0% / 0% / 0% chart.
  • Unnormalized long-only portfolio weights are rejected.
  • A negative individual Euler risk contribution can be legitimate when an asset hedges the rest. Don't automatically clip it to zero. Create risk-matrix.test.mjs: 
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import {
  validateCorrelation3, portfolioRisk3, IMPOSSIBLE, POSSIBLE,
} from './risk-matrix.mjs';

const close = (actual, expected, tolerance = 1e-12) =>
  assert.ok(Math.abs(actual - expected) < tolerance,
    `Expected ${actual} ≈ ${expected}`);

test('rejects pairwise-valid but jointly impossible correlations', () => {
  assert.throws(() => validateCorrelation3(IMPOSSIBLE), /Not positive semidefinite/);
});

test('accepts a valid 3-asset correlation matrix', () => {
  close(validateCorrelation3(POSSIBLE), 0.036);
});

test('risk contributions add up to portfolio volatility', () => {
  const out = portfolioRisk3({
    weights: [0.4, 0.35, 0.25],
    vols: [0.3, 0.2, 0.15],
    correlations: POSSIBLE,
  });
  close(out.volatility, 0.2193769586807147);
  close(out.contributions.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0), out.volatility);
});

test('accepts singular PSD matrices but does not invent zero-risk shares', () => {
  const perfectOpposites = [
    [1, -1, 0],
    [-1, 1, 0],
    [0, 0, 1],
  ];
  const out = portfolioRisk3({
    weights: [0.5, 0.5, 0],
    vols: [0.2, 0.2, 0.2],
    correlations: perfectOpposites,
  });
  close(out.volatility, 0);
  assert.equal(out.contributions, null);
});

test('invalid weights never reach the model', () => {
  assert.throws(() => portfolioRisk3({
    weights: [0.5, 0.5, 0.5],
    vols: [0.2, 0.2, 0.2],
    correlations: POSSIBLE,
  }), /weights must sum to 1/);
});

test('negative Euler contributions can be legitimate', () => {
  const hedge = [
    [1, -0.9, 0],
    [-0.9, 1, 0],
    [0, 0, 1],
  ];
  const out = portfolioRisk3({
    weights: [0.05, 0.8, 0.15],
    vols: [0.2, 0.2, 0.2],
    correlations: hedge,
  });
  assert.ok(out.contributions[0] < 0);
  close(out.contributions.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0), out.volatility);
});

Then run:

node --test risk-matrix.test.mjs

Result: six tests pass on the code above. The valid example uses weights 40% / 35% / 25%, individual annualized volatilities 30% / 20% / 15%, and pairwise correlations 0.9 / 0.9 / 0.8. It calculates 21.938% modeled portfolio volatility. Its contributions are 11.856, 6.637, and 3.444 volatility percentage points—not three independent asset volatilities.

The units matter: 0.20 means 20% annualized volatility; 0.20 is not 0.20 percentage points. Errors here can be just as misleading as a bad matrix.
This is a UI architecture problem, too
In MarketDeck's Risk Constellation, the live public educational lab models four fictional assets. It calculates covariance, portfolio volatility, and Euler risk contributions in a numerical engine rather than inferring them from how far a line stretches on screen. Its public equal-correlation slider is constrained to a safe 0...1 range; you cannot paste the impossible three-asset matrix into that public UI.

The engineering lesson is still useful for any application that accepts independently edited pairwise assumptions:

  1. Validate the complete mathematical object, not individual form fields. For bigger matrices, use a tested PSD eigenvalue or factorization method, with an explicit numerical tolerance.
  2. Don't let a renderer own the answer. The chart, table, tooltip, and accessible text should all read the same verified result.
  3. Reject or explain invalid edits. If you choose a nearest-correlation-matrix repair, show the changed assumptions. Don't silently manufacture a different experiment.
  4. Make undefined states explicit. Zero portfolio volatility doesn't produce meaningful proportional risk shares.
  5. Test identities, not screenshots alone. The equality sum(risk contributions) ≈ portfolio volatility is a stronger regression check than a beautiful SVG. The nearest-correlation-matrix problem is a serious numerical-analysis problem in its own right; Nicholas Higham's paper is a good starting point if you want to investigate careful projection algorithms rather than simply rejecting an input. One last challenge Try replacing the valid matrix's third correlation, 0.8, with 0.61. The entry is still between -1 and 1, yet the complete matrix should fail the PSD test. Then try 0.62, the singular boundary, and see why a zero determinant does not automatically mean an invalid correlation matrix.

It's a small experiment, but it carries a general engineering lesson:
A set of individually plausible inputs is not necessarily a mathematically possible system.

That's true in finance, numerical simulation, ML feature engineering, and many applications where relationships are entered pair by pair.

References: Higham, Computing the Nearest Correlation Matrix, Node.js built-in test runner.

Disclosure: This article and its illustrative code were drafted with substantial AI assistance. The mathematical definitions were checked against the MarketDeck model and numerical references, and the included JavaScript example was executed with six passing tests. A human publisher should review the final text before releasing it. The example is educational only.

title: pandas merge() Returned More Rows Than You Started With? Catch Duplicate Keys with validate=
description:
You left-joined 4 orders onto a customer table and got back 6 rows. Worse, the revenue column went from 520 to 830, and nobody noticed until the report reached a manager.

merge() did exactly what it was told. A left join keeps every left row, but if a key appears twice on the right, every matching left row is copied once per match. No error, no warning, just quietly inflated numbers.

Here is how to reproduce it, catch it automatically, and fix the three key problems that cause most "wrong row count" merges.

The 6-line reproduction 

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4],
                       "customer_id": [10, 11, 12, 10],
                       "amount": [250, 120, 90, 60]})
customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [10, 10, 11, 12],
                          "name": ["Asha", "Asha", "Ravi", "Meera"],
                          "city": ["Udaipur", "Jaipur", "Pune", "Delhi"]})

m = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")
print(len(orders), len(m), orders.amount.sum(), m.amount.sum())

On pandas 3.0 this prints:

4 6 520 830

Customer 10 has two rows (an old address and a new one), so orders 1 and 4 each come back twice:

   order_id  customer_id  amount   name     city
0         1           10     250   Asha  Udaipur
1         1           10     250   Asha   Jaipur
2         2           11     120   Ravi     Pune
3         3           12      90  Meera    Delhi
4         4           10      60   Asha  Udaipur
5         4           10      60   Asha   Jaipur

Step 1: Find the duplicate keys

Before blaming the join, look at the lookup table:

customers["customer_id"].value_counts().loc[lambda s: s > 1]
# customer_id
# 10    2

customers[customers.duplicated("customer_id", keep=False)]
#    customer_id  name     city
# 0           10  Asha  Udaipur
# 1           10  Asha   Jaipur

keep=False marks every copy, so you see all the conflicting rows side by side and can decide which one is correct.

Step 2: Make pandas refuse the bad merge

This is the part most tutorials skip. merge() has a validate= argument that checks the relationship you expect and raises if the data disagrees:

orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one")

MergeError: Merge keys are not unique in right dataset; not a many-to-one merge

The options are "one_to_one", "one_to_many", "many_to_one" and "many_to_many" (which checks nothing). Many orders per customer, one row per customer, is many_to_one. Put this on every merge in a pipeline that feeds a report: it turns a silent wrong number into a loud failure on the day the lookup table changes.

Step 3: Fix the data, not the symptom

Calling drop_duplicates() on the result hides the problem and can drop legitimate rows. Decide which lookup row wins, dedupe the right side, then merge with the check still on:

customers_latest = customers.drop_duplicates("customer_id", keep="last")

m = orders.merge(customers_latest, on="customer_id", how="left",
                 validate="many_to_one")
print(len(m), m.amount.sum())   # 4 520

If you have an updated_at column, sort by it first so keep="last" really means "most recent", rather than "whatever order the CSV happened to be in".

The opposite symptom: rows that should match don't

Sometimes the count is right but half the joined columns are NaN. Add indicator=True to see which rows actually matched:

orders = orders.assign(sku=["A1", "B2 ", "c3", "A1"])
prices = pd.DataFrame({"sku": ["A1", "B2", "C3"], "price": [5, 6, 7]})

m = orders.merge(prices, on="sku", how="left", indicator=True)
print(m["_merge"].value_counts())

_merge
left_only     2
both          2
right_only    0

left_only rows found no partner. Here it is a trailing space in "B2 " and lowercase "c3". Normalize both sides before joining:

for df in (orders, prices):
    df["sku"] = df["sku"].str.strip().str.upper()

After that every row is both.

Two more traps

Mismatched key types. If one side read IDs as numbers and the other as strings (common after read_excel or a JSON API), pandas 3.0 stops you:

ValueError: You are trying to merge on int64 and str columns for key 'customer_id'.

Convert explicitly with .astype(...) on one side. Don't just cast both to str, or 10 and "10.0" will never match.

NaN keys match each other. Unlike SQL, pandas treats missing keys as equal:

import numpy as np

a = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1.0, np.nan], "x": [1, 2]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"k": [np.nan, np.nan], "y": [3, 4]})
a.merge(b, on="k")
#     k  x  y
# 0 NaN  2  3
# 1 NaN  2  4

One missing key on the left just turned into two joined rows. Drop or fill null keys (df.dropna(subset=["k"])) before merging unless you really want them paired.

Quick checklist

  • Result has more rows than the left table after a left join? The right side has duplicate keys.
  • Find them with value_counts() or duplicated(..., keep=False).
  • Add validate="many_to_one" (or whatever relationship you expect) to every merge feeding a report.
  • Dedupe the lookup table deliberately, not the merged result.
  • Lots of NaN after the join? Use indicator=True, then strip and normalize case on string keys.
  • Check that key dtypes match, and drop null keys first.

If you want a refresher on how inner, left, right and outer joins differ (with diagrams and row counts for each), I wrote it up in pandas merge: inner, left, right and outer join examples. When your data starts life in spreadsheets, reading and writing Excel files with openpyxl covers the import side. And if a key column comes from an API, the free JSON formatter on Blogs World makes it easy to spot a stray string ID or trailing space before it reaches your join.
