title: npm 12 Blocks Install Scripts by Default. Node 26 LTS, Out Oct 28, Still Ships npm 11.
description:
On October 8, tensorlake@0.5.144 was on npm for about 1 hour 40 minutes. It was not a real release. Someone with access to the maintainer's GitHub account committed a payload and ran the project's own release workflow, so the package even carried valid npm provenance. A preinstall hook ran the payload the moment it was installed on a developer machine.

The payload went after GitHub and npm tokens, AWS and GCP credentials, SSH keys, .env files and browser passwords, then used those tokens to republish itself into other packages. It also installed a small service called gh-token-monitor that deletes your home directory if the stolen GitHub token gets revoked (SafeDep found it only arms for tokens on accounts with no organizations). That's all in the maintainers' own GitHub advisory (GHSA-8g63-53c9-65j2), and it's part of the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign that has been hitting npm since April.

npm already has a fix for the "runs on install" part. npm 12, out since July 8, doesn't run dependency preinstall, install or postinstall scripts unless your project allows them.

Here's the catch. Node 26 became LTS on October 28, and the npm it ships is 11.20.0. That's not npm 12. I checked the bundled npm version for every current LTS line in the Node release index today:

Node release Date npm it ships
26.13.0 (LTS "Lithium") Oct 28, 2026 11.20.0
24.22.2 (LTS "Krypton") Oct 27, 2026 11.19.1
22.23.4 (LTS "Jod") Oct 20, 2026 10.9.9

The only Node line with npm 12 bundled right now is the 27 alpha. So if you install Node the normal way and never run npm install -g npm, you're on a version that still runs every install script in your tree.

What each package manager actually did

I wanted to see this rather than trust release notes, so on a scratch box I made a tiny local package whose preinstall writes a marker file to the temp dir. I installed it next to esbuild (a normal, harmless package that has a postinstall) with each tool, then checked whether the marker file existed.

Tool Script ran? What it printed
npm 10.9.9 (what Node 22 ships) yes nothing at all
npm 11.21.1 yes a warning listing both packages
npm 12.2.1 no "2 packages had install scripts blocked"
pnpm 10.34.6 no "Ignored build scripts: esbuild@0.25.11, harmless-preinstall@file:..."
bun 1.4.2 no "Blocked 1 postinstall"

Two things stood out. On npm 10 there's no hint anything ran. On npm 11 the warning reads like a heads-up about the future, but the marker file was there, so the script had already run. The script also had a console.log, and that line never showed up in the install output on npm 10 or 11. You don't see install scripts run.

pnpm and bun already block by default. If you're on either, most of this post is about your CI and your teammates, not you.

Check a project in 10 seconds

This prints your npm version, whether install scripts are on, which packages in your lockfile actually have install scripts (npm records hasInstallScript in package-lock.json), and whether any of the tensorlake persistence files exist on the machine.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# install-scripts-check.sh: who gets to run code when you type npm install?
# usage: bash install-scripts-check.sh [project-dir]   (needs jq)
cd "${1:-.}" || exit 1
v=$(npm -v); major=${v%%.*}; ign=$(npm config get ignore-scripts)
allow=$(jq -c '.allowScripts // empty' package.json 2>/dev/null)
echo "node $(node -v), npm $v, ignore-scripts=$ign"
if [ "$major" -ge 12 ]; then echo "OK   npm 12+: dependency install scripts blocked unless allowed"
elif [ "$ign" = "true" ]; then echo "OK   ignore-scripts=true: install scripts off"
else echo "WARN npm $major runs every dependency install script (it only warns)"; fi
[ "$ign" = "true" ] && [ -n "$allow" ] && echo "WARN ignore-scripts=true silently overrides allowScripts"
echo "allowScripts: ${allow:-none}"
if [ -f package-lock.json ]; then
  n=$(jq '[.packages | keys[] | select(. != "")] | length' package-lock.json)
  echo "lockfile: $n packages; these have install scripts:"
  jq -r '.packages | to_entries[] | select(.value.hasInstallScript == true)
    | "  \(.key | sub("^.*node_modules/"; ""))@\(.value.version)"' package-lock.json
fi
echo "tensorlake worm persistence (all should be missing):"
for f in ~/.config/gh-token-monitor ~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh \
         ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.gh-token-monitor.plist; do
  if [ -e "$f" ]; then echo "  FOUND $f  <- remove BEFORE revoking GitHub tokens"
  else echo "  missing $f"; fi
done
systemctl --user list-unit-files 2>/dev/null | grep -q gh-token-monitor \
  && echo "  FOUND gh-token-monitor systemd user service <- stop it first"
for f in .claude/settings.json .vscode/tasks.json; do
  grep -qE 'SessionStart|folderOpen' "$f" 2>/dev/null && echo "  CHECK $f runs a command on open. Did you write it?"
done
exit 0

I ran it on a fresh lockfile for a pretty normal small-SaaS stack (next, react, react-dom, prisma 7, @prisma/client 7, stripe, tailwindcss, sharp) with the npm that was on the box:

node v24.22.1, npm 11.21.1, ignore-scripts=false
WARN npm 11 runs every dependency install script (it only warns)
allowScripts: {"prisma@7.10.1":true,"@prisma/engines@7.10.1":true}
lockfile: 191 packages; these have install scripts:
  @prisma/engines@7.10.1
  prisma@7.10.1
tensorlake worm persistence (all should be missing):
  missing /home/box/.config/gh-token-monitor
  missing /home/box/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh
  missing /home/box/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.gh-token-monitor.plist

That allowScripts list is already there because I approved Prisma with npm 12 first (next section). The script still says WARN on npm 11, and that's fair. On 11.21.1 a package you explicitly deny does get skipped (I tested that), but anything new that isn't on the list still runs. Only npm 12 flips the default. With npm 12.2.1 first on the PATH, the same project gives OK npm 12+: dependency install scripts blocked unless allowed.

The number worth noticing: 191 packages in the lockfile, 2 with install scripts. Your allowlist will probably be short. Short enough to read every entry.

Moving to npm 12 without breaking your build 

npm install -g npm@12
npm install                      # blocked scripts get listed at the end
npm install-scripts ls           # same list, read-only
npm install-scripts approve prisma @prisma/engines
npm install-scripts deny some-package-you-dont-trust
npm rebuild                      # runs the scripts you just approved
git add package.json && git commit -m "allowScripts for npm 12"

On the starter project above, npm 12 listed @prisma/engines@7.10.1 (postinstall: node scripts/postinstall.js) and prisma@7.10.1 (preinstall: node scripts/preinstall-entry.js). After the approve step, package.json had:

"allowScripts": {
  "prisma@7.10.1": true,
  "@prisma/engines@7.10.1": true
}

Approvals are pinned to the version you reviewed by default. When Prisma bumps, the new version is blocked again until you look at it. That's a little annoying and it's exactly the point. A hijacked patch release of a package you trust is how these worms spread. npm install-scripts prune cleans out entries for versions you no longer have.

GitHub's npm v12 breaking-changes note covers two other defaults that changed at the same time: git dependencies and remote tarball URLs are no longer resolved unless you allow them. If your install breaks on a github: dependency after upgrading, that's why.

Three gotchas

ignore-scripts=true beats your allowlist. Setting it in .npmrc was a common hardening tip after the first Shai-Hulud wave in September 2025. On npm 12 it silently wins over allowScripts. I approved my test package, ran npm install --ignore-scripts, and the marker file never appeared. Same install without the flag, it did. Pick one setup and remove the other.

CI has its own npm. Upgrading on your laptop does nothing for the build server. Cloudflare's Oct 23 changelog says their Workers Builds and Pages images now ship Node 22.23.4 and 24.22.1, and per the Node release index those come with npm 10.9.9 and 11.19.1. If your CI sets up Node with something like actions/setup-node, you get that Node's bundled npm unless you upgrade it. Add an npm install -g npm@12 step before npm ci, or check what your builder uses.

Your laptop is the real target. SafeDep's teardown of the tensorlake payload shows the loader checks CI, GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI and RUNNER_ENVIRONMENT and simply exits on CI. It wants the machine where your SSH keys, .env files and logged-in browser live. That's also where AI coding agents type npm install for you without you reading the package name. I wrote down some rules for keeping coding agents from installing junk or reading your secrets on a side project, and they matter more once you know worms skip CI on purpose.

If you think you installed something bad

The order matters here, and it's the opposite of what your instincts say.

  1. Take the machine off the network.
  2. Remove gh-token-monitor before you revoke anything. The advisory gives the commands: on Linux systemctl --user disable --now gh-token-monitor.service and delete ~/.config/gh-token-monitor/ and ~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh; on macOS launchctl bootout the com.user.gh-token-monitor LaunchAgent and delete the plist.
  3. Rotate tokens from a different, clean machine.
  4. Look through the repos and packages your tokens could write to. The tensorlake advisory says to look for unexpected releases, commits authored claude, and a branch named dependabot/github_actions/format/setup-formatter. Sonatype and Socket also flag changed .claude/settings.json and .vscode/tasks.json files, which is why the script greps them.
  5. Rebuild the machine from a clean image.

What npm 12 doesn't fix

Blocking install scripts closes one door. Code that runs when you import the package is untouched. A GitHub advisory from October 9 for an npm package called testrrrd describes exactly that: it fires the same beacon from postinstall and again from its main file at import time, so --ignore-scripts alone doesn't stop it. If a bad version lands in your lockfile, you'll run it the first time your app starts.

So the lockfile still matters. Commit it, use npm ci in CI, and don't auto-merge dependency bumps the same hour they're published. It's the same lesson as the trivy-action tags that got repointed in one night: a name you trust is not the same as the code you get.

For most small projects the whole fix is upgrading npm, one install, approving two or three packages and committing package.json.

If you've already moved to npm 12: how many packages ended up in your allowScripts, and which one broke first when you upgraded?

title: OAuth Test Emails Need an Expiry Contract
description:
OAuth tests often fail in a place that does not look like an OAuth problem: the verification email. A test creates a disposable email account, starts a consent flow, waits for a message, and follows a link. If the inbox or link is reused carelessly, the suite can pass while hiding a real account-takeover path.

The useful question is not only “did the email arrive?” It is “what exactly was valid, for whom, and for how long?” I treat every OAuth email fixture as a short-lived security boundary. That makes failures easier to explain and keeps test conveniences from becoming production assumptions.

The hidden risk in OAuth email fixtures

A typical test has three moving parts:

  • an identity or account under test
  • a temporary inbox that receives a verification message
  • a one-time link or code that changes account state

Those parts have different lifetimes. The inbox may live for a test run, the message for a few minutes, and the verification token for only one successful redemption. When a helper uses “the newest email” without checking those boundaries, an old message can satisfy a new test.

That is how a harmless flaky test becomes a misleading security signal. The test may open a valid link from a previous run, or two parallel workers may consume the same message. The result looks green, but the assertion did not prove that the current flow owned the current evidence.

I found it useful to pair this approach with an email test signal pipeline. The pipeline answers what happened; the expiry contract answers whether that evidence was still allowed to matter.

Define the expiry contract

Before writing a helper, write down four limits:

  1. Fixture lifetime: when the inbox lease starts and when it ends.
  2. Message freshness: the earliest timestamp a message may have.
  3. Token lifetime: how long a verification link or code can be redeemed.
  4. Redemption count: whether the test expects one success and then rejection.

For example, a signup test might lease an inbox at 12:00:00, trigger the email at 12:00:03, accept messages received after 12:00:03, and require the link to fail on its second use. The exact values depend on the application, but the rules must be explicit. “Latest message” is not a rule.

The contract should also include a small clock-skew allowance. If the mail provider and application clocks differ by a few seconds, a strict comparison can create noise. Keep that allowance narrow and record it in the test output, so nobody quietly turns it into a ten-minute loophole later.

Separate inbox ownership from token validity

An inbox check proves that a message was delivered to the fixture. It does not prove that the token is valid for the account currently being tested. Those are separate assertions.

For inbox ownership, check the leased address, run identifier, or another non-secret marker in the message metadata. For token validity, check that the link belongs to the expected environment, has not expired, and cannot be redeemed twice. Never log the full token just to make a failure easier to debug.

This separation catches a few common mistakes:

  • a worker reads another worker’s inbox
  • a message from a prior run is accepted
  • a staging link is accidentally tested against production
  • a verification endpoint accepts a replayed token

If the test setup uses a dummy e mail or someone writes tempail in a manual note, keep those strings out of authentication assertions and reports. They are useful search terms for finding old helpers, not proof of ownership.

Record evidence without recording secrets

Every failed attempt should leave a compact evidence record. I normally keep:

type EmailFixtureEvidence = {
  runId: string;
  inboxId: string;
  triggeredAt: string;
  observedMessageIds: string[];
  acceptedMessageId?: string;
  tokenRedeemedAt?: string;
  rejectionReasons: string[];
};

Store message IDs, timestamps, subjects, and rejection reasons. Redact URLs, codes, and authorization values. A record such as “message-184 rejected: received before trigger” is much more useful than a raw email dump, and it is safer to keep in CI artifacts.

For larger suites, a failure ledger for email tests makes repeated timing or ownership failures visible. The ledger should group by reason, not just by test name. Otherwise one broken inbox lease can appear as dozens of unrelated OAuth failures.

A practical test fixture

The fixture can expose a narrow API:

const fixture = await emailFixtures.lease({
  runId,
  expiresInMs: 120_000,
});

const triggeredAt = new Date();
await app.startSignup({ email: fixture.address });

const message = await fixture.waitForMessage({
  since: triggeredAt,
  maxAgeMs: 60_000,
});

await expect(app.verify(message.link)).toSucceedOnce();
await expect(app.verify(message.link)).toFailWith("expired_or_used");

The important part is the shape, not this particular client. The helper owns cleanup, freshness filtering, redaction, and the one-use assertion. Individual tests should describe the account journey, not reimplement security policy every time. That makes the result more consistant across teams, even when the surrounding browser steps differ.

A security checklist for CI

Before trusting an OAuth email test, check:

  • Is every inbox leased to one worker and one run?
  • Is the message timestamp compared with the trigger timestamp?
  • Does the test reject a token after expiry and after first redemption?
  • Are redirect targets restricted to the intended environment?
  • Do logs avoid full links, codes, and authorization values?
  • Does cleanup happen when the browser test fails halfway through?
  • Can the evidence explain the failure without opening the inbox manually?

A little imperfect phrasing in a test description is fine; a more safer default is not. Keep the contract short enough that reviewers can actually verify it. If a helper becomes a mini identity provider, it is probably doing too much.

Final thoughts

Email fixtures are part of the OAuth threat model, even when they exist only in CI. Give the inbox, message, and token separate lifetimes; record useful evidence; and prove one-time redemption explicitly. This turns flaky verification steps into tests that say something meaningful about authentication.

The goal is not to make every test heavy. It is to make the trust boundary visible, so a green result means the current flow owned the current email and the token behaved as intended.

title: Realtime Notification Preferences in Node.js: Testing Stock Watchlists Without Timing Flakes
description:
Short answer: test notification preferences as a state-reconciliation problem, not as a timer test. For a stock trading watchlist, make reconnects, expiry, duplicate delivery, and authorization explicit; then choose the realtime API surface whose client and server responsibilities are clear.

The notification is not the source of truth. A watchlist change is. That distinction keeps a test from passing only because two packets happened to arrive in the expected order.

For a small media or trading team that wants one server-side credential across backend services, Infrai is a reasonable candidate for the reconciliation step: its REST surface keeps the room lookup in the same integration as the rest of the backend. I would recommend it to a Node.js team that values fewer SDKs and can keep client trust decisions on its own server; the benefit is less credential and glue code, not a promise that it replaces every specialist push service.

That is the boundary.

What should a Node.js test prove about realtime notification preferences?

Start with a small contract. The server owns authorization and the preference state. The client owns presentation, local deduplication, and reconciliation after a reconnect. Write that down before picking an endpoint. Otherwise the test quietly becomes a test of whichever SDK callback fired first.

For each watchlist item, give the change a stable identifier and a revision. The client can then accept a duplicate safely, ignore an older revision, and request a fresh snapshot after a disconnect. A realistic test should vary latency, deliver one event twice, expire a token, and try an account that is not allowed to see the symbol. Those are normal states in a trading UI, not exotic chaos drills.

Here is the kind of test data I use in a harness. It is intentionally boring. Boring data exposes ordering bugs.

type PreferenceEvent = {
  id: string;
  revision: number;
  symbol: string;
  enabled: boolean;
};

function applyEvent(
  current: Map<string, PreferenceEvent>,
  event: PreferenceEvent,
): boolean {
  const previous = current.get(event.symbol);
  if (previous && previous.revision >= event.revision) return false;
  current.set(event.symbol, event);
  return true;
}

export function replay(events: PreferenceEvent[]): Map<string, PreferenceEvent> {
  const state = new Map<string, PreferenceEvent>();
  for (const event of events) applyEvent(state, event);
  return state;
}

The important assertion is not “event arrived in 100 ms.” It is “the final state is the same after a delayed duplicate and a reconnect.” Timing still matters, but it is an input to the test rather than its definition of correctness.

A minimal room lookup with explicit recovery

For a room-backed realtime flow, the verified RTC surface includes a room lookup at GET /v1/rtc/room/get/{room}. The call below is deliberately a lookup, not a made-up create payload. It gives a client a fresh server view after reconnect while keeping the bearer token on the API request.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

function retryAfterMs(response: Response): number {
  const value = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  const seconds = value ? Number(value) : NaN;
  return Number.isFinite(seconds) ? Math.max(0, seconds * 1000) : 250;
}

export async function getRoomSnapshot(room: string): Promise<unknown> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/rtc/room/get/${encodeURIComponent(room)}`,
      {
        method: "GET",
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
      },
    );

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const backoff = retryAfterMs(response) * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, backoff));
      continue;
    }

    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`room lookup failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }

  throw new Error("room lookup exhausted retries");
}

The client should merge the returned snapshot by stable identifier, then replay only newer events. I would run this function behind tests that inject 40 ms, 800 ms, and multi-second delays; I would also run a duplicate delivery and an expired credential. Your mileage may vary on those latency values, but the invariant is portable.

Infrai is interesting here because the same plain REST API can cover the room lookup and other backend capabilities under one key and one bill. That removes a real integration cost: a small Node.js tool does not need another vendor SDK or another credential just to reconcile state. Its public discovery surface also describes capabilities and runnable examples, which is useful when a team wants to inspect the interface before committing to an SDK.

How do the practical options compare for a stock watchlist?

No single transport wins every boundary. I compare the options by setup friction, credential scope, and how much recovery code remains in the application.

Option Setup and client surface Trust and recovery fit Better choice when
Infrai realtime/RTC Plain HTTP with one platform key; discovery is available before integration Your service can keep authorization server-side and reconcile room state explicitly You want one consistent backend surface across a small stack
Firebase Cloud Messaging Mature mobile/web push tooling and client SDKs Strong device-token model; watchlist state still needs an authoritative backend Push delivery, rather than an interactive room, is the primary requirement
Ably Hosted realtime protocol with client libraries and presence patterns Protocol features reduce transport work; permission design still belongs to your app You need a specialist pub/sub product and its ecosystem fits
Pusher Channels Focused channels API with quick client onboarding Channel authorization and reconnect behavior are familiar, but state reconciliation is yours You value a narrow, polished channel workflow
PubNub Hosted publish/subscribe surface with client SDKs Access controls and delivery features are packaged; your preference model remains authoritative You need a specialist global messaging layer

The catch is scope. A single platform key is convenient for server code, but it is not a reason to put that key in a browser. Issue short-lived, narrowly scoped client credentials from your server, and test the rejected path as carefully as the accepted one. Stick with Firebase, Ably, or Pusher when their specialist client semantics are the product requirement and a broader backend surface would add review work rather than remove it.

What I would change before shipping the watchlist

First, record the reason for every state transition: initial snapshot, live event, reconnect, expiry, or authorization denial. A plain reason field makes a flaky report actionable. Second, bound recovery. A client that retries forever can hide an authorization failure and create a thundering herd after an outage; exponential backoff with Retry-After gives the server room to recover.

At scale, I would separate transport tests from preference-policy tests. The transport suite can generate duplicate and out-of-order events cheaply. A smaller end-to-end suite can verify that a real token cannot read another user's room. That split keeps the feedback loop fast without pretending that a mock proves trust boundaries.

I benchmark time to first useful state, not just connection time. The useful moment is when the watchlist shows the correct preference revision after a reconnect. That metric catches a room that connects quickly but leaves the UI stale.

The decision rule is simple: define who owns authorization, return stable identifiers, and make recovery observable. Choose the specialist when its client model is the thing you need. Choose the unified REST surface when removing SDK and credential glue is the bigger constraint.

If your team matches that last case, start by checking the realtime capability details at docs.infrai.cc. It is a low-pressure way to verify the room contract before wiring it into the watchlist test suite.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • W3C WebRTC Recommendation
  • Firebase Cloud Messaging documentation
  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • PubNub documentation

Further reading

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud-messaging
  • https://ably.com/docs
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • https://www.pubnub.com/docs/

title: E-commerce Report Delivery: Node.js Cloud Cron and Durable Queue Boundaries
description:
A daily e-commerce report should be started by a cloud scheduler, then handed to a public Node.js endpoint that creates the email job. The web request is a trigger, not the place to render a large report or deliver hundreds of messages. For a short report, the endpoint can generate the content and call a mail library such as Nodemailer; for anything that can run near the 900-second execution ceiling, the endpoint should enqueue work and let a worker consume it.

Short answer: use cloud cron to trigger a public Node.js endpoint once a day, then enqueue the report so a worker owns email delivery and retries.

That choice is about delivery guarantees. A scheduler can make a daily attempt, but it cannot by itself make a long email workflow durable, idempotent, or replayable. Treat those as separate contracts.

For this workflow, Infrai fits at the trigger-and-queue boundary: its REST surface can cover the scheduled HTTP call and the queue without making the application adopt another SDK and credential set. That reduces integration friction, but the endpoint still has to be public HTTPS and the worker still has to implement idempotency.

How should Node.js schedule a daily email with cloud cron?

The useful design is a small chain:

  1. A cloud cron expression fires once per day.
  2. A publicly reachable HTTPS endpoint authenticates the request and records a run key.
  3. The endpoint creates one report job per intended unit of work.
  4. A worker generates the report, sends mail through Node.js and Nodemailer, and records completion with an idempotency key.

The first step is timing. The second is admission. The queue and worker own delivery. Mixing those responsibilities is how a request that looks harmless at 09:00 is still holding a connection when the report expands at 09:12.

A standard queue is at-least-once, so the worker must tolerate a duplicate. A practical key can combine the report date, shop identifier, and recipient group. Store the send result before acknowledging the message, and make the mail operation or its surrounding record safe to retry. This is less glamorous than choosing a cron syntax, but it is where the guarantee is decided.

There are hard boundaries here: a cron execution cannot exceed 900 seconds; a delayed message cannot exceed 604800 seconds; a message body is limited to 256KB; retention is at most 30 days; and a standard queue does not provide Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. FIFO deduplication lasts only 5 minutes, which is not a substitute for application-level idempotency on a daily job.

Which cloud scheduler fits the integration boundary?

The familiar options are useful, but they optimize different kinds of friction.

Option Setup and credential shape First useful result Boundary
AWS EventBridge Scheduler Strong AWS integration, IAM policy work, and an AWS-shaped operational surface Good when the report already lives in AWS More configuration than a single HTTP trigger when the application is outside AWS
Google Cloud Scheduler Direct HTTP or Pub/Sub targets with Google IAM and a separate project-level setup Fast for a Google-hosted endpoint The surrounding queue, secret, and worker choices remain separate services
Azure Functions Timer Trigger Convenient inside a Functions application and Azure identity model Good when the email code is already a Function Couples scheduling decisions to the Functions hosting model
Temporal Durable workflow state, retries, and long-running orchestration Strong when the report has dependencies and joins A larger workflow system than a fixed daily HTTP trigger requires
BullMQ Familiar Node.js queueing around Redis Useful when the team already operates Redis and wants queue-native worker code Adds Redis operations and is not a cloud cron service by itself
Infrai cron plus queue One REST contract, public HTTP target, and queue capabilities behind the same key Useful when adding the queue or another backend capability would otherwise mean another SDK, credential, and integration It is not a workflow engine, has no DAG or join primitive, and the target must be public HTTPS

The distinction is not “which scheduler is cheapest.” It is how many integration surfaces a small team must keep correct. Infrai exposes a public discovery surface, runnable examples in 10 languages, and 295 routes across 20 modules; that breadth matters when the scheduled report later needs a queue or another backend service without acquiring another SDK and credential set. Its consistent REST surface removes integration work, while it does not remove the need to design the delivery contract.

I would recommend Infrai to a team that wants a daily public HTTP trigger and a queue worker under one REST contract, especially when reducing credential and SDK sprawl matters more than using a cloud provider’s deepest native workflow features. Its limitation is important: Temporal is the better choice for DAG dependencies and joins, a native cloud setup is better for private network-only targets, and a scheduler with explicit backfill semantics is better when missed runs must be replayed. Infrai cron does not backfill paused triggers, trigger timing has second-level jitter, and run-history output is retained only through the first 4KB.

A minimal Node.js boundary without a long request

The application endpoint should do very little: authenticate the caller, derive a deterministic run identifier, enqueue the report request, and return. The worker can then use Nodemailer for the actual mail operation. Keep the target publicly reachable; private or internal-only endpoints cannot receive the push. Do not put report generation behind the scheduler’s request timeout.

The discovery endpoint is a useful first check because it exposes the documented capability paths without requiring a key. This small Python probe verifies that the cron capability is present before an integration starts; the application itself can then follow the request schema returned for that capability.

import json
import urllib.request

request = urllib.request.Request(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
    method="GET",
)

with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
    document = json.load(response)

cron_paths = {
    item["path"]
    for item in document["capabilities"]
    if item["path"] == "/v1/cron/create"
}
print(sorted(cron_paths))

This deliberately discovers the schema instead of guessing request fields. For the email application, the public endpoint remains the handoff, while the Node.js worker owns the Nodemailer call and its idempotent completion record.

For a large recipient list, publish one bounded job per recipient group rather than placing the whole audience or a generated attachment in one message. At 256KB, the queue message should contain identifiers and parameters, not the report payload. A worker can fetch the source data, build the message, send it, and acknowledge only after its idempotent completion record is durable.

One trap is treating a successful scheduler invocation as a successful email. It proves only that the HTTP handoff was accepted. Inspect run history for scheduler failures, then inspect queue statistics and worker completion records for the rest of the path. The first diagnosis should ask which boundary failed.

Roll out the daily report in layers

Start with one shop and one recipient group. Run the endpoint against a test mailbox, then deliberately repeat the same date and shop key to verify that the worker does not send twice. After that, expand the fan-out while watching processing time and message size. Keep the cron payload small, set a timeout no greater than 900 seconds, and make the worker the owner of retries.

Cloud Scheduler, EventBridge Scheduler, and Azure Functions Timer Trigger are all sensible when their native identity, network, and queue model already match the application. A unified REST surface is a better fit when integration friction is the primary constraint, but it cannot turn a cron trigger into a workflow orchestrator. Design that boundary explicitly and the daily email becomes a recoverable handoff instead of a web request with a calendar attached.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the cron and queue guide and verify the request schema before wiring the worker.

References

  • AWS SQS visibility timeout and duplicate-delivery considerations: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • AWS EventBridge Scheduler documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/scheduler/latest/UserGuide/what-is-scheduler.html
  • Google Cloud Scheduler HTTP targets: https://cloud.google.com/scheduler/docs/http-target-auth
  • Azure Functions timer trigger: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/functions-bindings-timer

Sources

  • Infrai guide, daily scheduled email with queue workers: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/cron/answers/why-daily-scheduled-email-should-enqueue-jobs-instead-o/

title: "Done" isn't a test result. How your AI agent should hand off UI work
description:
Your AI agent finishes a change and reports back: "Done. The form is accessible, responsive and works on mobile."

Did anyone check? Often the agent wrote the code, looked at it, and described what it hoped was true as if it had been tested.

Design Decision Method's last step is there to stop that. Step 6, deliver and validate, asks the agent to hand over the work, the decisions behind it, and a short validation status that says what each result rests on.

What step 6 asks for

The method asks the agent to deliver three things:

  • the requested artifact (spec, mockup, prototype, or code)
  • the consequential decisions and assumptions
  • a short validation status

Before validating, the agent defines a few observable acceptance criteria matched to the purpose of the experience. Then it labels each result by its evidence level and says what it did not test.

Five evidence labels

Each label says what a result can support and what it can't:

Level Can support Cannot support
Proposed A target to aim for Any claim about the result
Heuristic review Likely problems, effort comparisons Task-completion rates
Automated check Specific rule failures Overall accessibility or usability
Manual test Behaviour of a flow, keyboard and focus Population-level outcomes
User research Real task outcomes for the sampled users Claims beyond the sample

Two rules come with it. Never fabricate a measurement. If something wasn't tested, the record says "not tested". And a mockup can show routes and states, but it cannot establish task-completion rates.

A worked example: a handoff note

Say you ask your agent to rebuild the sign-up form on example.com. It's one page with name, email and password, and a clear way to fix errors.

Without the method, the handoff is the sentence at the top of this post. With it, the agent's note might read:

Delivered: Sign-up form (code). One page, three fields.

Decisions: Errors show next to the field and in a summary at the top. Entered values are kept after an error. The placeholder for email is name@example.com.

Assumptions: No social sign-in was requested, so none was added.

Acceptance criteria and status:

  • Valid entries survive a validation error. Manual test: submitted with a bad password, and name and email were still filled in.
  • Each error is announced next to its field. Heuristic review of the markup only. Not tested with a screen reader.
  • Text and background contrast. Automated check: the contrast check found no failures on the colours used. This does not show the whole form is accessible.
  • People complete sign-up without help. Proposed. Not tested. No user research was done.

Not tested: screen reader pass, mobile keyboard behaviour, the server's error responses.

Every line says what it rests on. You can see that mobile keyboard behaviour is the next check, and that nobody has tried the form with real users.

Why this matters when you build with agents

An agent that sounds confident is easy to trust. The evidence labels give you a quick way to read the handoff. "Proposed" means it hasn't been checked. "Automated check" means one rule ran. "Manual test" means somebody actually walked through the flow.

The list of untested items also gives you the next prompt: ask for exactly those checks.

The method doesn't claim this saves time. That hasn't been measured. What it does give you is a handoff note that says where its checks stop.

Keep it proportional

Pick a few criteria that fit the design. The method warns against a fixed score or a universal time or click limit. A copy fix might need one line of status. A new checkout flow needs more. The design record template has a short "Validation status" section for this: the evidence levels reached, what was tested and what wasn't, and open questions.

Where this fits

Deliver and validate is step 6 of six: establish context, choose the visual system, map objects before layout, write a decision record, structure each view, then deliver and validate.

title: Complex Data Cleanup in Node.js Explained (Delayed Execution Best Practices)
description:
Deferred Fintech Cleanup in Node.js Explained (and Why Delivery Matters)

For delayed execution of complex cleanup jobs in Node.js, choose the delivery guarantee before choosing the scheduler. A rate-limited worker pool should make progress without turning a retry into a second destructive operation. In a fintech system, that usually means durable work records, an explicit lease, idempotent cleanup steps, and a retry policy with jitter. A timer is only the trigger.

The useful question is not "Which queue has delayed jobs?" It is this: What must still be true if the process dies after the database commit but before the acknowledgement?

I use that question because missed jobs and duplicate deliveries are operational failures with different remedies. A missed job needs durable discovery. A duplicate needs a safe operation. Putting both behind a single in-memory timeout gives you neither.

What does a delayed cleanup job promise?

Start with a contract that can be tested. For each cleanup request, record a stable job ID, the resource scope, the earliest execution time, the attempt count, and the current state. The worker may run the job after that time; it should not run it before the policy allows. Exact wall-clock execution is usually a poor promise for a busy, rate-limited pool.

The delivery choice belongs in the contract too:

  • At-most-once reduces duplicate work, but a crash can lose a cleanup request.
  • At-least-once preserves a durable request, but the cleanup handler must tolerate redelivery.
  • Exactly-once effects are not produced by a queue flag. They require a transactionally defined effect boundary, idempotency, and a way to reconcile ambiguous outcomes.

For financial records, I would rather investigate a retried request than silently lose one. That is a trade-off, not a slogan. The cleanup operation must therefore be designed so that repeating it is harmless or reaches the same final state.

A record can move through scheduled, leased, completed, and dead_lettered. Those names are less important than making illegal transitions visible. A worker that finds a lease owned by another worker should not guess; it should leave the record alone and let lease expiry or a reconciler decide what happens next.

The failure window is the design

Consider a job that removes expired exports after a retention interval. The worker selects one due job, marks it leased for 30 seconds, deletes eligible objects in bounded batches, and writes completion. There are several crash points:

  1. The process dies after the lease is written.
  2. It dies after one batch is deleted.
  3. It receives a successful response but dies before acknowledging the job.
  4. The downstream store accepts a request, then the client times out.

Each point can result in another delivery. A 30-second lease is not a guarantee that work takes 30 seconds; it is a recovery timer. If the normal batch takes 12 seconds and the tail sometimes reaches 40, renew the lease while work is active or split the job into smaller units. Do not silently extend a lease forever. That turns a stuck worker into a permanent omission.

I initially treated the delay as the hard part. The more consequential boundary is the acknowledgement. A delayed message that arrives twice is ordinary at-least-once behavior. A cleanup endpoint that interprets the second call as a new financial action is the defect.

The handler should use a stable idempotency key derived from the job ID and the cleanup scope. It should also make progress resumable. For example, deleting a range of object keys can record the last committed page, while a database update can use a predicate such as status = scheduled or the current lease owner. The exact schema varies; the invariant does not: a retry must not widen the deletion scope.

A small worker loop in Go

The production application may be Node.js, but the control flow is easier to inspect in a compact language-neutral shape. This example is Go, as required by the implementation convention here, and leaves storage and rate limiting behind interfaces. It does not pretend that a timer is durable.

type CleanupJob struct {
    ID          string
    RunAfter    time.Time
    LeaseUntil  time.Time
    Scope       string
    Attempt     int
}

func process(ctx context.Context, store Store, limiter Limiter, now time.Time) error {
    job, ok, err := store.ClaimDue(ctx, now, 30*time.Second)
    if err != nil || !ok {
        return err
    }

    if err := limiter.Wait(ctx); err != nil {
        return store.Release(ctx, job.ID, err)
    }

    err = store.CleanupIdempotently(ctx, job.ID, job.Scope)
    if err == nil {
        return store.Complete(ctx, job.ID)
    }
    return store.Reschedule(ctx, job.ID, nextAttempt(job.Attempt), err)
}

The omitted interfaces are deliberate. ClaimDue needs an atomic claim or a lease condition. CleanupIdempotently needs a durable idempotency record or an operation whose final state is naturally repeatable. Complete must verify ownership, and Reschedule must not erase a newer state written by another actor. Those are storage contracts, not conveniences supplied by the loop.

That boundary matters.

The code also makes a less glamorous point: rate limiting belongs around the downstream operation, not just around job acquisition. Pulling 100 jobs quickly and then sleeping inside each handler can exhaust memory and create a large burst when the limiter opens. Keep concurrency bounded, and measure both queue delay and downstream wait time.

How should retries behave under a rate limit?

A retry delay needs an upper bound, randomness, and a reason. Exponential backoff reduces synchronized retry bursts; jitter prevents workers that failed together from retrying together. AWS describes exponential backoff and jitter as retry techniques for throttling and transient failures, while also distinguishing retryable from non-retryable errors. That distinction belongs in the job state, not only in a library default.

For a cleanup worker, I classify failures into three practical groups:

  • A validation or authorization failure is usually terminal until an operator changes the input or policy.
  • A rate-limit or temporary network failure is retryable, subject to a deadline and attempt cap.
  • An ambiguous timeout needs reconciliation before another destructive call, unless the operation is explicitly idempotent.

A retry schedule can be represented as min(cap, base * 2^attempt) + jitter, but the numbers are policy, not universal truth. The cap should fit the retention requirement and the downstream service's recovery behavior. Persist the next run time so a process restart does not reset every job to an immediate retry.

Do not use the retry count as your only alert. Ten quick retries can be less concerning than one job that has waited six hours. Alert on age of the oldest due job, duration in each state, lease expirations, dead-letter volume, and the ratio of duplicate claims to completed jobs. These signals describe delivery health rather than merely process health.

Which scheduler shape fits the cleanup?

There are three common shapes. An in-process timer is simple and useful for a best-effort task whose loss is acceptable. A durable database table plus polling is understandable and often enough when the cleanup state already lives in that database. A dedicated queue can provide delayed delivery and operational tooling, but it still leaves idempotency and effect reconciliation to the application.

The decision should follow failure tolerance and workload shape. If the job is a one-off cleanup tied to a transaction, an outbox record can connect the business event to durable scheduling. If the work is large, split it into bounded shards so one lease does not cover hours of deletion. If the schedule is broad, such as scanning all expired records, a periodic reconciler should find missed work instead of assuming every timer fired.

I keep the scheduler and the reconciler separate. The scheduler gives ordinary jobs a path to execution. The reconciler asks, independently, whether records that should be eligible have a corresponding work item. That second path catches lost messages, bad deployments, clock mistakes, and manual data changes. It should be rate-limited too, because recovery traffic can overload the same pool it is meant to repair.

Recovery is work, too.

Testing needs the same shape as the failure model. Advance a fake clock across the due boundary. Kill a worker after claim, after the first cleanup batch, and after the downstream response. Deliver the same job twice. Delay lease renewal. Return throttling and ambiguous timeouts. The assertion is not merely that the function returns an error; it is that the final data state and the next scheduled action are correct.

A decision rule for production

For delayed fintech cleanup, use durable scheduling when losing the request is unacceptable. Use at-least-once delivery when recovery matters more than avoiding duplicate invocation, then make every effect idempotent and scoped by a stable job identity. Add leases for crash recovery, bounded concurrency for the rate limit, persisted backoff for restarts, and a reconciler for omissions.

This approach does not apply unchanged to work whose side effect cannot be repeated and cannot be reconciled. In that case, the system needs a stronger effect boundary, such as a transactional state transition owned by the destination, or a manual review state before repeating an ambiguous operation. A queue cannot manufacture that guarantee after the fact.

The shortest useful runbook is: inspect the oldest due job, inspect its lease owner and attempt history, check downstream throttling, then determine whether the last effect was confirmed. Only after that evidence should an operator release or replay the work.

The scheduler is the easy part. The durable contract around delivery is what keeps a cleanup job from becoming a second incident.

Sources

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/api-retries.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/429
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
  • https://martinfowler.com/articles/patterns-of-distributed-systems/idempotent-receiver.html

title: Your AI agent forgets why. Give it a decision record
description:
You spend a session getting an order form right. One page, not three steps. A review summary before submit. Delivery date where people actually look for it. Then a new prompt regenerates the form, and the agent goes back to a three-step wizard, because nothing told it why you chose otherwise.

The agent kept the code. It did not keep the reasons.

Design Decision Method handles this with step 4 of its workflow: the decision record.

What a decision record captures

For a choice that would be costly to undo, the method asks you (or your agent) to record:

  • task frequency
  • user familiarity
  • the cost of a mistake
  • the device
  • the pattern chosen, and why

It also asks you to judge effort in a specific way: compare the effort to read, remember, enter, navigate, and recover, rather than counting clicks or visible elements. A three-step flow has fewer fields per screen. That does not make it less effort if people have to go back to check what they entered on step one.

Two more rules keep the record honest:

  • Cite a source only when it resolves an actual design problem. No decorative references.
  • Mark departures. When the design departs from a cited source's rule, add one adaptation line: source rule / what this design does instead / why the frequency, familiarity, or error cost requires it. Never present an adaptation as upstream guidance.

A worked example

Say you run a small print shop at example.com, and you ask your agent to build the order form. This is an illustration of how the procedure applies, not a case study or a measured result.

The decision row looks like this:

Decision Frequency Familiarity Error cost Device Pattern chosen Reason
Order form layout Occasional, once per order Mostly first-time customers Medium: a wrong size or quantity means a reprint Phone first One page, grouped sections, review summary before submit Customers need to see size, quantity, and price together to catch mistakes. Splitting them across steps adds recall effort at the point of decision.

If a source you cite recommends a different pattern for this form, that is where an adaptation line goes, in the same three-part form.

The record also carries a short validation status, because step 6 of the method asks for an honest evidence label on each result: proposed, heuristic review, automated check, manual test, or user research. For this form it might read:

  • Valid entries survive a validation error: not tested (manual test planned).
  • Size, quantity, and price visible together before submit: heuristic review.

Untested stays untested. The record says so instead of implying the form works.

What the next prompt does with it

Next week you ask the agent to add a "rush delivery" option. The following prompt starts from that record. The agent can see the form is one page for a reason, and that the reason is error cost, not taste. It adds the option inside the existing structure instead of reinventing the flow.

A person still checks the result. The method does not measure how many prompts that removes, and whether it saves time has not been measured.

Keep it small

The decision record is proportional. A small change gets a few lines. The repo's design record template is a scaffold, not mandatory overhead. Save the record with the work (as docs/design/<slug>.md) when your project keeps design records, or deliver a compact record inline with the change when it does not.

You do not need a record for every edit either. The method is a shared procedure, not mandatory for every small edit. Record the choices you would be annoyed to re-argue.

Where this fits

The decision record is step 4 of six: establish context, choose the visual system, map objects before layout, write a decision record, structure each view, then deliver and validate.

title: Atlassian Connect end of support: what Jira and Confluence admins should check before 31 January 2027
description:
Disclosure: I'm from Kayabyte, which makes Burnrate and other Forge apps for Jira and Confluence. Burnrate comes up near the end.

Short answer: Atlassian Connect, the older way of building Cloud apps, reaches end of support on 31 January 2027. Atlassian doesn't say every Connect app stops working that day, but it will only address critical security patches from then on, and it warns that breakages will become more frequent and some platform changes will stop apps without advance notice. Admins should list their apps, check the warning on the Connected Apps page, ask each vendor for a migration plan, and test any replacement before the date, starting with the apps that billing, payroll or support depend on.

This page is for site admins, not developers. Facts about Connect come from Atlassian's own posts, linked below; things change, so check them before you rely on a date.

What changes on 31 January 2027

Atlassian's post says that from this date:

  • It will only address critical security patches, and support SLAs will be relaxed.
  • Connect will no longer evolve with the platform, and deprecations will come with shorter windows.
  • "Breakages will become more frequent, and the user experience will degrade."
  • Some infrastructure changes "will cause apps to stop functioning without advance notice."

Atlassian has said it will share more on what happens after end of support, and hasn't yet given those details.

The checklist

  1. List your apps. Copy the list from your site's Connected Apps page in administration. Note who uses each app and who owns it.
  2. Read the warning. That page shows a Connect end of support warning for apps it applies to. A vendor can replace the generic text with its own message and a link to its migration plan.
  3. Don't panic at a flag. Atlassian's developer advocate has called the "at risk" flag "a blurry signal" that can produce false positives. It's a reason to check, not a verdict.
  4. Ask the vendor three things. Is the app fully on Forge today? If not, by what date? Does anything stop working or change after the move?
  5. Check independently if you want. forge-apps.com shows the Forge status of released Marketplace versions. It isn't run by Atlassian and doesn't show a vendor's intentions.
  6. Check what the move removes. Vendors' own notes show that some features don't survive a migration, so read the change notes for what your team uses.
  7. Rank by damage. Rank apps by what breaks if they stop without warning. Reports used for invoices, payroll, audits and SLAs come first.
  8. Test before you need it. If you may have to change app, compare old and new on one closed period and one real project. Leave time for this: a month-end report needs at least one month-end to compare.

Questions for reporting and cost apps

Reports fail quietly, so these need a closer look:

  • Do the numbers match? Compare one closed month against a figure you trust.
  • Who is named on the worklog? Worklogs synced from another time app may show that app as the author in Jira, and per-person figures can then come up short. Open one work item and check.
  • Do past figures stay fixed? If a rate changes, last month's cost shouldn't move.
  • Where does the data go? Forge apps can run entirely on Atlassian's platform, but not all of them do. Ask, and check the app's listing.

Which of our apps this affects

None of the Kayabyte apps. Burnrate, Group Participants, Group Watchers and Personal WIP Limits were all built on Forge from the start, so there's no migration to wait for. Burnrate is the one that matters for this topic: it prices native Jira worklogs with dated rates and shows budgets. It's new, with no reviews, so test it against a closed month as above. It's on the Atlassian Marketplace.

FAQ

When does Atlassian Connect end? End of support begins on 31 January 2027. The date was moved from December 2026.

Will my Connect apps stop working on 31 January 2027? Atlassian doesn't say that all of them stop on that date. It does say breakages will become more frequent and that some platform changes will stop apps without advance notice.

How do I know if a Marketplace app is on Connect or Forge? Look for the warning on the Connected Apps page in site administration and ask the vendor. forge-apps.com, which isn't run by Atlassian, also shows the status of released versions.

What does the "at risk" banner mean? It's based on an app's migration status and the intent its vendor has declared. Atlassian describes it as a blurry signal that can produce false positives, so ask the vendor before you replace an app.

What should I do first? List your apps, rank them by what would break if they stopped without warning, and ask the vendors of the top ones for a migration date.

Jira, Confluence and Atlassian are trademarks of Atlassian. Kayabyte is an independent developer and is not affiliated with or endorsed by Atlassian.

title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings
description:
arXiv:2611.00172v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Embedding models underpin virtually every modern AI system, from search engines to recommendation systems. Despite shared mathematical foundations, research on embedding models remains fragmented by modality: the communities develop largely in isolation, seldom exchanging insights. We argue that this fragmentation obscures a deeper convergence. Driven by contrastive learning, Transformer architectures, and a granularity shift, embedding research across modalities is converging toward a common set of principles, even as modality-specific challenges remain underexplored. To reason across this convergence without conflating it, we propose a framework of three progressively harder capabilities: coverage, comparability, and compositionality. Three paths toward unification satisfy these in turn: transformation broadens coverage, alignment enables comparability, and joint embedding, the terminus we advocate, aims at compositionality. This position paper traces the resulting evolution, providing the first unified, cross-cutting treatment of omnimodal embedding research.

title: MEMENTO: Learning Context Management for Long Context Processing Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.00244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.

title: Cross-Lingual Persona Effects in LLM Negotiation
description:
arXiv:2611.00300v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tell an LLM negotiator to be "headstrong" and it should hold firm on price, but does that instruction retain the same behavior in every language? To test this, we use identical buyer and seller instances of Gemini 3.6 Flash to negotiate the same 12 CraigslistBargain scenarios in English and Korean. The pilot-scale 2 x 2 x 3 design crosses interaction language, seller urgency (none or strong), and buyer persona (cooperative, neutral, or headstrong), yielding 432 attempted negotiations. We call this property cross-lingual social-policy fidelity: whether a prompt-defined social policy produces the same behavioral effect regardless of interaction language. It often does not. Korean negotiations reached agreement far more often than English (77.3% vs. 52.5%, a 24.8-point gap, Holm-adjusted p = .0039), but only for neutral and headstrong buyers; cooperative buyers were already near-ceiling in both languages. Buyers' opening offers barely differed by language; the gap instead emerged later, through larger seller concessions and a smaller final gap in Korean, and agreed prices were also lower in Korean. Repeating the full design with Qwen3.7 Flash as both agents gives directional support: agreement was again higher in Korean (+13.9 points vs. Gemini's +24.8, with an interval whose lower bound is near zero), and sellers again conceded more. Pragmatic analysis reveals why: while both languages frequently featured face-threatening acts like rejections and counter-offers, Korean dialogue softened these threats with substantially more politeness mitigation, especially among sellers (11.7% vs. 3.6%). These results show that such a policy can produce different simulated negotiation behavior, not just different wording, when only the interaction language changes.

title: GAVAGAI: Referential Alignment for Infant-Scale Vision-Language Models via Balanced Optimal Transport
description:
arXiv:2611.00319v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.

title: Queering the Audits: Community-Based Auditing of AI Harms to Queer Communities
description:
arXiv:2611.00345v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems embed majority-group defaults into training data, evaluation metrics, and category definitions, producing documented harms for queer communities including erasure, misclassification, and discrimination. Standard technical audits often rely on aggregate measures and cannot detect harms that be come visible only through the lived experience of affected communities. We conducted a participatory auditing workshop at EurIPS 2025 where 16 queer community members audited four case studies using the 4Cs harm taxonomy (Content, Conduct, Contact, Contract) applied across the AI lifecycle. Participants used structured worksheets and plenary synthesis to classify harms and trace them to their origins in the development pipeline. Across all four cases, participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and they identified contractual structures that extract value from vulnerable populations while providing minimal recourse. These findings illustrate that community-informed auditing surfaces concrete, identity-specific harms that aggregate evaluation methods risk overlooking.

title: Cross-Prompt Reuse of Entity-Replacement Responses
description:
arXiv:2611.00352v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With model weights fixed, we measure how much of an entity-replacement response transfers between English factual questions, beyond whether answers change. We add the hidden-state change from two source questions to a target question about the same entity, comparing the predicted log-probability shift between two relations' published answers, given known answer prefixes, with the measured one. Hidden reuse injects the aligned change at 50% depth before the target's remaining layers; direct reuse adds source output-score changes. With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama. Gemma-2-2B removes 22% and passes one of three comparisons in plain text without its default beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token. A later protocol restoring it yields 58-68%, passing every comparison on three cohorts. Larger checkpoints, chat format and new entities show replication and format- or cohort-dependent failures. On small plain-format checkpoints, other-relation hidden reuse mainly reproduces the shift both relations' questions share, without reliably lowering relation-selective error. With target-relation sources, hidden reuse's post hoc advantage over direct reuse is 0.2-0.9 nats outside chat format, unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. The same relation-neutral change at both questions' entity tokens lowers relation-selective error more than random or other-replacement changes, indicating receiving-question dependence.

title: Humanized but Still True? Auditing Facts and Detection in AI-Text Humanizers
description:
arXiv:2611.00359v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI "humanizers" rewrite machine-generated text so that detectors classify it as human-written. Public leaderboards score evasion and embedding similarity, but not whether checkable details survive. We check whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite, using a rule-based checker validated by two AI annotators (precision 0.84-1.00, recall 0.93-0.95; no human annotation). In the October 2026 cycle of a public humanizer leaderboard, all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one of these units in 35-65% of the documents that contained one. Most changes were to quoted spans; counting numbers and names alone, 10 of the 11 tools still altered at least one in 20% or more of the documents. The September 2026 cycle was similar (19-50%). An open 12B humanizer kept at least 97% of numbers and names in fact-dense U.S. federal agency text, but reworded 67-78% of the quoted spans, against its own prompt. Unit retention and detector evasion were not clearly related across tools (Spearman rho = -0.46, 95% CI -0.65 to 0.08), and the open model's four released files (two of them quantization-aware low-bit files) did not show the pre-registered monotone trade-off. On federal texts with matched human, AI-styled and humanized versions, a general-purpose decision model, Jev, asked a single zero-shot question, separated human originals from humanized rewrites with AUROC 0.864 (0.827-0.902), 0.18-0.22 higher than Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT and the adversarially trained RADAR, while calling 24% of the human originals AI at a 0.5 threshold. On the AI-styled rewrites by 2026 models, both perplexity-based detectors scored below chance (AUROC 0.37 and 0.39), also with line breaks removed. Hypotheses, data rules and analyses were frozen before the main runs; two earlier data contacts are disclosed. We release the checker and the per-item results.

title: Circuit Oracle: Automating Attribution Graph Analysis via Natural-Language Queries
description:
arXiv:2611.00420v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attribution graphs, an emerging tool in mechanistic interpretability, use transcoders to decompose language model computations into sparse interpretable features connected by causal edges. However, turning a graph into a safety-relevant insight requires hours of manual analysis by experts. We introduce Circuit Oracle, an off-the-shelf LLM equipped with a multi-agent harness and task-specific authored skills, which answers natural-language questions about a target model by reading the attribution graph through tool calls. We evaluate it on three safety-relevant proxy tasks: detecting spurious features in probe circuits, eliciting hidden knowledge from taboo-finetuned models, and suppression jailbreaking via feature-level interventions. Beyond task scores, the oracle produces pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature explanations that we assess qualitatively. Results are mixed. On spurious-feature detection, Circuit Oracle reaches 78.2 $\pm$ 2.4% accuracy, outperforming single-layer feature-ranking baselines. On secret elicitation, trained self-explainers like Activation Oracles remain the stronger baseline. On refusal suppression over 50 prompts, its single committed intervention is slightly below a diff-in-means baseline, and only exceeds it when allowed the best of five attempts. Results are stable across five runs and across model choices for the agents. We also release the pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature readings that revise existing global labels, and invite future work to develop evaluations that can measure their usefulness directly.

title: Fidelity Collapses with Table Size, Not Turn Count: Delivery Architecture in a Deployed Tool-Using Agent
description:
arXiv:2611.00442v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a multi-turn agent delivers a tool's structured records into the model's context and re-emits them each turn, every turn can corrupt data the tool computed correctly. We measure this in a production award-travel agent: two architectures over identical frozen payloads, lineage-matched prompts and sampling, differing only in delivery architecture. SYNTHESIS feeds full record sets into the planner's context and answers follow-ups in-head; BYPASS, the deployed system, keeps records in session state, translates follow-ups into arguments for a deterministic filter, and delivers rows over a typed side channel. Across 24 dialogues (339 scored turns per condition), BYPASS scores 92.3% of turns fully correct, SYNTHESIS 45.7% (paired gap +46.6pp [+35.7, +57.1]). Varying delivered-table size by capture date, SYNTHESIS collapses from near-perfect at 10 rows or fewer to 8% or less beyond about 74 rows. On a content-controlled prefix ladder the collapse threshold orders by model capability, from under 10 rows (GPT-4o-mini) to about 198 or more (Gemini 2.5 Pro), while BYPASS stays size-flat for all four models. The collapse is expensive: beyond 100 rows, where almost no SYNTHESIS answer is correct, each correct one costs roughly 200x BYPASS's flat \$0.012. Practitioners converged on typed side-channel delivery for rendering, not correctness; we show it was, unknowingly, also a correctness decision.

title: From Lookups to Lessons: Turning Retrieved Knowledge into Parametric Memory
description:
arXiv:2611.00450v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps large language models (LLMs) answer factual questions beyond their training data, but it adds storage and inference costs. Distilling previously retrieved information into parametric memories enables reuse without online retrieval. However, training the memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions, which do not necessarily improve the final output quality when combined with the LLM's existing predictions. To address this, we introduce ResMem, in which the LLM reads retrieved text offline to generate teacher targets. This design avoids storing massive token representations, unlike existing parametric memory approaches such as MLP Memory, which relies on k-nearest neighbor (kNN) datastores. Furthermore, by using the LLM as an offline teacher that reads privileged retrieved evidence alongside the input, we train a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual. This residual aligns the predictions of a student sharing the same backbone with the teacher distribution, while self-distillation updates remain confined to the parametric memory. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% compared with the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five question answering datasets, ResMem raises mean token F1 from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%. It also breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory. These findings validate our motivation of treating retrieval as a learning resource, with parametric memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge is used to inform the model's future predictions. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SSRand/From-Lookups-to-Lessons and https://huggingface.co/RandHan/ResMem-Mistral-7B-v0.3.

title: Steering Readerly Dynamics: Trajectory-Guided Story Generation with Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.00469v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate stories, but these stories struggle to reproduce engaging readerly dynamics, the evolving reader responses that shape narrative experience. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that learns readerly dynamics from high-quality human-written stories and uses them to guide story generation. Instead of directly modeling high-dimensional story content, we train a small LLM to predict future reader responses as low-dimensional trajectories. We then leverage the strong instruction-following capability of a larger, off-the-shelf writer LLM to generate story segments that follow these predicted trajectories within a given story setting. Our framework improves trajectory-based fidelity to human-written stories by 12%-35% while largely preserving story coherence.

title: Spotting the Artificial: Dialogic Humor Improvisation in Humans and LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.00492v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose a methodology for investigating the differences between natural and synthetic language in a challenging setting: humorous improvisational dialogue. Our experimental setting compares human-produced comedy improvisations with the dialogues generated by LLMs in a multi-agent environment that we designed. The analysis combines automated linguistic measures with manual annotation grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL).
  The results show that, although LLMs can create coherent and creative scenes, they often fail to reproduce key characteristics of spontaneous spoken interaction. In addition, LLM-generated interactions display a strong tendency toward politeness and positive evaluations, contrasting with the broader range of attitudes found in human humorous improvisation. Our evidence highlights both the strengths and limitations of current LLMs in modeling dialogic humor and demonstrate the value of integrating linguistic theory with NLP methods for the analysis of machine-generated language

title: AStockArena: Beyond Returns, Can We Entrust Real Capital to the Decisions of Financial Agents?
description:
arXiv:2611.00515v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in dynamic financial trading, yet real-time trading benchmarks mainly evaluate agents by cumulative returns and risk-adjusted performance. Such outcome metrics cannot show whether trades are faithfully reported, supported by available evidence, and consistent with account states. We introduce AStockArena, a real-time decision-auditing benchmark for continuous trading in China's A-share market. Under shared market conditions and execution constraints, we evaluate 13 open- and closed-source models over 3,198 sequential decisions. AStockArena reconstructsthe actions actually posted to accounts by aligning reports, trade requests, execution responses, and account states, and audits them with eight checks spanning execution traceability (O), evidence sufficiency (RK), and financial meta-awareness (B), combining record verification with consensus expert annotation. Of 1,070 trading points, 72.99% exhibit at least one audit gap; model-level rates range from52.2% to 91.2%, with evidence gaps most prevalent. Historical trade-filtering replay further shows thatportfolio outcomes are sensitive to these flagged trades. Decision-process auditing thus offers a verifiable complement to return-based evaluation of financial agents.

title: Dual-Axis Policy Entailment: A Benchmark for Policy-Change Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.00536v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Whether a policy shifts domains and, by extension, continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses previous policy is of paramount importance to the study of public policy. We propose Dual-Axis Policy Entailment (DAPE), which evaluates an ordered pair of policy directives on both dimensions at once: a binary judgment determines whether the two directives govern the same policy domain, and a five-way judgment determines whether the later directive continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses the earlier policy, or governs a different domain altogether. Read together, the two judgments form one five-category label, our primary metric.
