title: Planning a Corporate Website: Structure, Features, and Content
description:
A company website has to serve more than one visitor. A prospective customer may need to understand a service, an existing client may be looking for support, a partner may want a contact, and a job seeker may need current openings. A navigation menu is useful only when it helps those people complete their tasks.

This guide explains how to plan the pages, functions and ownership behind a corporate website. It uses a fictional B2B supplier as an example; it does not prescribe a fixed set of pages for every business.

Start with visitor journeys

List the site's business goals and the visitor's questions separately. A company may want quote requests, but a buyer might first need to know whether the service fits their equipment, location and timing. A form alone cannot answer those questions.

Visitor Typical question Useful destination
Prospective customer What does the company offer, and how do I get an estimate? Relevant product or service page and a clear contact route
Existing customer Where can I get help or find documentation? Support information, instructions or the responsible team
Partner Who handles cooperation? A partnership page or specific contact
Job seeker Are there suitable roles, and how do I apply? Current openings and an application method

Interview sales and support staff, review recurring questions and use existing site data where you have access. Choose a few priority actions to test. Do not add a portal or a complex catalog just because another company has one: every feature needs accurate data, an owner and maintenance.

Decide which pages deserve their own place

A small company may need only a handful of pages. A larger organization may have several business lines, support routes, locations and document collections. Create a separate page when it answers a distinct question and has enough reliable content to do so.

Home page

Explain what the company does, for whom and where visitors can learn more. Link to the main services or product groups and provide a clear way to reach the right team. Replace broad claims with concrete, verified descriptions.

For example, a fictional equipment supplier could describe the types of equipment it handles, the regions it serves and how a business can request an assessment. It should not promise a response time that its team cannot meet.

Services and products

Give each distinct service enough room to explain its purpose, process, limitations and next step. If a quote depends on several factors, say which information is needed for an estimate instead of inventing a fixed price.

For a product catalog, define who maintains specifications, documents and availability. Test search and filters only if visitors have enough products and attributes to make those features useful. Confirm product claims and technical documents with the people responsible for them.

Company and experience

Describe the organization's work and relevant expertise. A case study should explain the problem, the work performed and a result that can be supported. Obtain permission before publishing a customer's name, images or figures. If a project cannot be named, a carefully labeled description of the process may be more useful than a fabricated testimonial.

Contact, support and careers

Make it clear which channel reaches sales, support or another department. Include current contact details and working hours when relevant. A careers section is helpful when someone owns the process of updating vacancies and handling applications; an empty, abandoned page does little for applicants.

Add news, resources, frequently asked questions or documents when they support a real task and can be maintained. Requirements for particular disclosures vary by organization and jurisdiction; confirm them with the responsible specialist.

An example sitemap

Imagine a fictional company that supplies and services equipment for businesses. A first version might include:

Section Purpose Next step
Home Explain the main offerings and audience Choose equipment or service
Equipment Show categories, verified specifications and documents Ask about fit or request a proposal
Service Explain diagnosis, maintenance and limitations Contact the service team
Projects Share approved examples of completed work Explore a relevant offering
About Explain the company's profile and experience Find partnership information
Contact Separate sales, service and general inquiries Select the right channel

If support receives repeated questions, add useful instructions or a support form. If the company has no active hiring process, a careers page can wait. Test the proposed map with people who represent the audiences, and check whether internal department names make sense to outsiders.

Plan forms as operational processes

A request form is not finished when a visitor clicks “send.” Map what happens next: where the message goes, who owns the queue, what the visitor sees on success or failure, and how the team handles an outage.

Ask only for information needed to respond, such as a name, contact and description of the request. Offer an alternative contact method. With the owner's permission, submit a test inquiry and verify that it reaches the right person; handle test data according to the team's process.

Validate input on the server, limit unwanted submissions and avoid writing secrets or unnecessary personal data into open logs. Have the responsible specialist review the data-handling text and process for the applicable context.

Treat integrations as dependencies

A CRM, accounting service or email integration can save manual work, but it adds another failure path. Test the whole journey: submission, receipt, assignment, error handling and safe recovery without accidental duplicates. Confirm the actual capabilities and configuration of the products in use instead of assuming any two systems connect automatically.

For an early launch with a small volume of inquiries, a documented manual process may be more reliable than an untested integration. Add automation when the workflow and its owner are clear.

Assign ownership to content

For each important page, record its audience, purpose, content owner, source of facts and review date. Separate drafting, subject-matter review and publishing. A specification or support contact that has become outdated can frustrate customers even when the design looks polished.

Gather inputs from the people who know the service: common questions, real limitations, approved documents and permitted photographs. Keep a way for staff to report outdated information and a process for removing or revising it promptly. Publish news only if the team can maintain it.

Check navigation and accessibility

Use labels your visitors understand rather than internal department names. Ask a new user to find a service, contact the appropriate team and return to the section they came from. On a larger site, a sensible hierarchy, breadcrumbs and search may help; they should reflect the actual content structure.

Test representative pages on a phone and a desktop. Check text readability, keyboard operation, form labels, visible errors and text alternatives for meaningful images. Tables and menus should remain usable on small screens. These tests improve the experience, but one test or a sitemap alone does not guarantee search indexing or rankings.

A practical launch sequence

  1. Define audiences, priority tasks and the measures the team can observe.
  2. Give every proposed page a purpose, audience and content owner.
  3. Map each form and integration from input through failure handling.
  4. Verify facts, media permissions, contacts and planned translations.
  5. Ask representative users to complete key journeys on different devices.
  6. Check access, backups, links, forms, test-environment restrictions and a plan for fixing issues.
  7. Record who owns the domain, infrastructure and ongoing page reviews.

A corporate site is a service that needs care after launch. A smaller map with accurate content and clear owners is easier to maintain and extend as the organization grows.

title: AWS SysOps Is Now CloudOps Engineer: SOA-C03 Explained
description:
AWS Certified SysOps Administrator – Associate now has a new name: AWS Certified CloudOps Engineer – Associate. The exam code moved from SOA-C02 to SOA-C03. Here is what changed, what stayed the same, how the exam works today and how it leads on to DevOps Engineer – Professional, all taken from AWS’s official pages and exam guides.

What happened to SysOps Administrator

AWS renamed the certification as part of the SOA-C03 exam update. AWS says the new name reflects the evolving nature of cloud operations and a shift in industry terminology. The key dates were:

  • 9 September 2025: registration for SOA-C03 opened, along with the new exam guide.
  • 29 September 2025: the last day to take SOA-C02.
  • 30 September 2025: the first day to take SOA-C03.

The new name only applies to people who pass SOA-C03. It is not changed retroactively. If you already hold SysOps Administrator – Associate, you do not need to take the new exam. Your certification stays valid for 3 years from the date you earned it, and you can keep showing its badge until it expires. If you later pass SOA-C03 as well, you get a separate CloudOps Engineer badge.

What changed in the content

AWS’s announcement names three main shifts. Containers are now in scope. There is more emphasis on multi-account and multi-Region architectures. And there is more on automation and infrastructure as code. AWS also says no task statements were removed, but the outline is more detailed and some tasks were reorganised.

The exam guide’s comparison page shows how the domains moved:

SOA-C02 domain SOA-C02 SOA-C03
Monitoring, Logging, and Remediation (now Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization) 20% 22%
Reliability and Business Continuity 16% 22%
Deployment, Provisioning, and Automation 18% 22%
Security and Compliance 16% 16%
Networking and Content Delivery 18% 18%
Cost and Performance Optimization 12% merged into Domain 1

The comparison page also lists the specific changes:

  • Moved: SOA-C02 Tasks 6.1 and 6.2 (cost and performance) now sit in Task 1.3. VPNs moved from Task 4.2 to Task 5.1.
  • Added: the CloudWatch agent for EC2 instances, Amazon ECS clusters and Amazon EKS clusters; stacks with CloudFormation and the AWS CDK; enforcing compliance requirements such as Region and service selection; and CloudWatch network monitoring services.
  • Removed: configuring S3 static website hosting.

The June 2026 exam guide update

AWS published version 1.1 of the SOA-C03 exam guide on 1 June 2026. It changed the wording or examples of ten skills. It also added five services to the in-scope list: Amazon Bedrock, AWS DevOps Agent, AWS Health Dashboard, Kiro and AWS Security Agent. The revision history lists no change to the domains or their weights. If your study notes date from before June 2026, check the in-scope services list again. The revision history now also lists a version 1.2, published on 29 October 2026, so check the revisions page for any later changes.

Exam labs

The SOA-C02 exam guide originally included exam labs: tasks performed in the AWS Management Console or AWS CLI. AWS removed them from 28 March 2023 “until further notice”. After that, SOA-C02 was 50 scored and 15 unscored multiple-choice and multiple-response questions in 130 minutes.

The SOA-C03 exam guide lists only two question types, multiple choice and multiple response. It does not list exam labs. So if you remember SysOps as the exam with labs, that no longer matches the current guide.

SOA-C03 at a glance

Detail SOA-C03
Level Associate
Questions 65: 50 scored and 15 unscored
Time 130 minutes
Question types Multiple choice and multiple response
Passing score 720 on a scaled score of 100–1,000
Cost 150 USD
Delivery Pearson VUE test centre or online proctored
Languages English, Japanese, Korean and Simplified Chinese
Valid for 3 years

AWS will retire the Korean and Simplified Chinese versions of SOA-C03 after 19 November 2026. English and Japanese continue.

Unscored questions are not identified on the exam. Unanswered questions are marked wrong and there is no penalty for guessing. The exam uses a compensatory scoring model, so you need to pass the exam as a whole, not each section.

The exam guide describes a target candidate with 1 year of experience with deployment, management, troubleshooting, networking and security on AWS. It also asks for at least 1 year in a related operations role, such as system administrator. If you have no IT work experience, AWS suggests earning Cloud Practitioner first.

The five domains

Domain Weight
Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization 22%
Reliability and Business Continuity 22%
Deployment, Provisioning, and Automation 22%
Security and Compliance 16%
Networking and Content Delivery 18%

In short: CloudWatch, CloudTrail, EventBridge and Systems Manager for monitoring and remediation; scaling, health checks, Multi-AZ, AWS Backup and disaster recovery for reliability; CloudFormation, the AWS CDK, StackSets and event-driven automation for deployment; IAM, Organizations, AWS Config, KMS and GuardDuty for security; and VPCs, Route 53, CloudFront and flow logs for networking.

The path to DevOps Engineer – Professional

AWS’s exam page names DevOps Engineer – Professional (DOP-C02) and Security – Specialty as certifications that people go on to earn after CloudOps Engineer. DOP-C02 is a bigger exam:

Detail SOA-C03 DOP-C02
Level Associate Professional
Questions 65 (50 scored) 75 (65 scored)
Time 130 minutes 180 minutes
Passing score 720 750
Cost 150 USD 300 USD
Target experience 1 year on AWS 2 or more years on AWS

DOP-C02 has six domains: SDLC Automation (22%), Configuration Management and IaC (17%), Resilient Cloud Solutions (15%), Monitoring and Logging (15%), Incident and Event Response (14%), and Security and Compliance (17%). Its target candidate also needs experience with the software development lifecycle and with programming or scripting.

The link between the two matters for recertification. Earning DOP-C02 automatically recertifies CloudOps Engineer – Associate. It also works for older SysOps Administrator – Associate holders, who can recertify by upgrading to DevOps Engineer – Professional. People who hold both DevOps Engineer – Professional and SysOps Administrator – Associate can keep both current by passing the latest DOP-C02 exam. AWS also gives you a 50% discount voucher for your next exam once you earn a certification.

Our suggestions

This is our advice, not AWS’s. It is based on the official content above.

  • Studying from SOA-C02 material: start with the comparison page. Put extra time into containers with the CloudWatch agent, the AWS CDK, multi-account tools such as StackSets and AWS RAM, and CloudWatch network monitoring. Skip S3 static website hosting.
  • Planning your time: three domains carry 22% each, so 66% of the exam is monitoring, reliability and deployment. Give them most of your study hours.
  • Thinking about DOP-C02 next: the overlap is strongest in monitoring, IaC, resilience and security. The biggest new area is CI/CD. SOA-C03 lists designing CI/CD pipelines as out of scope, while SDLC Automation is the largest DOP-C02 domain.
  • Holding SysOps Administrator already: you do not have to sit SOA-C03. If DevOps Engineer – Professional is your goal anyway, passing it before your SysOps certification expires also recertifies it.

To check your readiness, ExamCrest has free SOA-C03 practice questions you can try first.

Confirm the latest details on AWS’s CloudOps Engineer – Associate page, the DevOps Engineer – Professional page and the recertification page before you book.

I run ExamCrest, where this post first appeared. Try free SOA-C03 practice questions: https://examcrest.com/exam/aws-soa-c03/free-questions?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=soa-c03-blog-copy

title: What is CLS in Core Web Vitals? How to stop your page jumping
description:
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) is a Core Web Vitals metric that measures how much visible content unexpectedly shifts around on a screen while a page loads. If you have ever tried to tap a button on your phone only to have a banner load at the last millisecond and cause you to tap an ad instead, you have experienced a poor CLS score firsthand.

Google treats visual stability as a key indicator of user experience. Pages that jump around irritate visitors, increase bounce rates, and lead to accidental clicks that frustrate potential customers.

Google measures CLS on a scale starting at zero, calculated by multiplying how far unstable elements move by the percentage of the screen they affect. A good CLS score is 0.1 or lower. A score between 0.1 and 0.25 needs improvement, and anything above 0.25 is considered poor. In my client work, keeping this number under 0.1 is essential for passing Google's real-user page experience assessments, as outlined in my guide on Core Web Vitals explained.

Why web pages shift while loading

Browsers build web pages incrementally. When someone requests your URL, the browser starts reading the HTML document from top to bottom, rendering text and basic structural elements immediately before all media files and external scripts finish downloading.

When an image, script, or custom font arrives a fraction of a second later, the browser must adjust the layout to fit that new asset. If your code did not tell the browser how much room to reserve ahead of time, existing text and buttons get pushed downward or sideways.

Layout shifts do not just happen during the initial page load. Any delayed action—such as an automated newsletter pop-up, an accordion expanding without smooth transitions, or a cookie consent banner loading late—contributes to your overall CLS score if it moves visible elements without direct user interaction.

The three most common causes of high CLS

In almost every website audit I perform, high layout shift scores come down to three specific technical oversights. Fixing these issues usually resolves the majority of page stability problems immediately.

  • Images, videos, and iframes without dimensions: When media tags lack explicit width and height attributes in the HTML, the browser allocates zero vertical pixels until the file downloads, suddenly shoving down everything beneath it when the image renders.
  • Dynamically injected banners and ads: Third-party scripts often insert cookie notices, chat widgets, marketing notification bars, or ads at the very top of the page after the initial layout has rendered.
  • Custom web fonts: When custom web fonts load slowly, the browser displays a temporary fallback font. If the custom font has different letter widths or line heights than the fallback, the entire text block reflows and shifts once the font arrives.

How to find which elements are shifting

Before changing your code, you need to identify exactly which elements are moving. You can start by running your page through Google PageSpeed Insights or using a free website speed test to see your current laboratory and field metrics.

Under the Diagnostics section in PageSpeed Insights, locate the audit titled 'Avoid large layout shifts'. Expanding this section reveals the exact HTML elements responsible for the highest shift scores, alongside screenshots showing the page before and after the shift occurred.

For a more granular view, open Chrome DevTools on your computer, navigate to the Performance tab, and record a page reload. DevTools creates an 'Experience' row that flags every individual layout shift with a red bar, listing the exact element and shift contribution when clicked.

How to fix CLS and keep your layout stable

Once you know which elements are causing the movement, the technical fixes are straightforward to implement in production code.

Always define explicit width and height attributes on your image and video elements. Modern browsers use these attributes to calculate the aspect ratio automatically, reserving the exact box space before the image file even downloads. If you build with modern frameworks like Next.js, the built-in Image component handles this automatically by requiring dimensions or an explicit layout fill strategy.

For dynamic elements like cookie banners or promotional headers, reserve space in your CSS using min-height or skeleton loaders. By reserving the height upfront, the container simply fills in when the script executes, preventing the main navigation and hero copy from dropping down.

To solve font shifting, use modern CSS font-display properties like 'optional' or adjust fallback font metrics to match your custom font dimensions. If you are struggling to resolve shifting across complex templates, bringing in a targeted speed and Core Web Vitals fix helps isolate script conflicts and stabilizes critical rendering paths.

Practical takeaways for a stable website

Eliminating layout shifts requires adopting consistent layout habits during development and marketing updates. Keeping these simple rules in mind protects your user experience and keeps your Core Web Vitals in the green.

  • Aim for a CLS score under 0.1 across both mobile and desktop visitors.
  • Never add an image, video, or iframe without explicit dimensions or an aspect-ratio rule in CSS.
  • Reserve vertical container space for third-party scripts, cookie notices, and marketing banners.
  • Preload key web fonts and align fallback font metrics to prevent text reflows.
  • Test your pages on throttled mobile connections before launching new components.

Want help with this? See my Speed & Core Web Vitals fix service, or send me your site for a free review.

title: Systems Thinking: Why the Best Technology Disappears Into the Background
description:
You do not think about the electrical grid. You plug in a device, and it works. You do not think about the water treatment system. You turn on a tap, and the water is clean. You do not think about the GPS satellite network. You enter a destination, and you are guided there.

These systems — electricity distribution, water treatment, satellite positioning — are extraordinarily complex. They represent decades of engineering, millions of components, and the coordinated effort of thousands of institutions. They also share one defining characteristic: they are invisible.

The invisibility is not accidental. It is the achievement.

What Invisibility Means

A system becomes invisible when it reliably does what it is supposed to do, every time, without requiring the user to understand how it works or manage its complexity. The electrical grid is invisible because when you plug something in, you do not need to think about generation, transmission, distribution, or voltage regulation. The system handles all of that. You experience only the outcome: a working device.

This kind of invisibility requires solving a specific set of engineering problems that are distinct from the problems of making a system functional.

Reliability is the first requirement. A system that works ninety percent of the time cannot become invisible. Every failure brings the system into consciousness — the user becomes aware of it in the moment it fails to do what they expected. A power outage makes people acutely aware of the electrical grid. A contamination event makes people acutely aware of the water treatment system. Reliability is what allows a system to fade into the background of daily life.

Simplicity of interface is the second requirement. A system that requires user management and attention cannot become invisible. If using the electrical grid required setting voltage parameters and managing load, nobody would be unaware of it. The interface — the plug socket, the switch — is so simple that the act of using it requires almost no conscious effort.

Appropriate scope is the third requirement. Systems become invisible when they do exactly what they are supposed to do and nothing else. A system that periodically asks users to make decisions they did not expect to make, or that generates outputs they did not ask for, keeps itself in consciousness.

Why Technology Products Fail at Invisibility

Most technology products are designed to be noticed. This is partly a function of the market dynamics of technology — differentiation requires visibility, adoption requires awareness, growth requires attention. But it is also a function of a design culture that conflates complexity with value.

A product with many features is visible because navigating the features requires ongoing attention. A product with a complex interface is visible because using it requires conscious effort. A product that frequently asks for user input is visible because it keeps inserting itself into the user's awareness.

This is fine for products where the value is in the complexity — professional tools, creative platforms, analytical software where the user's engagement with the complexity is part of the value. It is a serious problem for systems that are supposed to improve the background conditions of work rather than become work in themselves.

An agricultural diagnostic tool that requires a farmer to navigate multiple menus, enter contextual information, and interpret probabilistic outputs is not a background system. It is another thing the farmer has to manage, in addition to managing their farm. The tool's complexity competes with the farm for attention, and the farm usually wins.

Designing for Invisibility

Designing a system for invisibility requires a specific inversion of the usual technology design question.

The usual question is: what can this system do? The answer to this question tends to expand over time — more features, more capabilities, more surface area.

The question for invisibility is: what does the user need to do, and how can the system do everything except that? The answer to this question tends to contract over time — fewer interactions, simpler interfaces, more of the complexity absorbed by the system rather than delegated to the user.

ARCORA is designed around this inversion. The farmer needs to identify what is wrong with their crop and know what to do about it. Everything else — the image analysis, the disease classification, the treatment protocol lookup, the localisation into the appropriate language — is absorbed by the system. The farmer's interaction is two steps: take a photo, read the protocol. The complexity is real; the interface is not.

This is not simple to build. Absorbing complexity into a system, rather than delegating it to the user, requires that the system be genuinely capable of handling that complexity — which means higher accuracy requirements, more comprehensive training data, more thorough testing. The invisible system is harder to build than the visible one.

But it is the right goal. A tool that a farmer uses without thinking about it is a tool that actually changes how they farm. A tool they have to think about using is a tool they use rarely and eventually stop using entirely.

The best technology disappears. Building the kind of technology that disappears is the work.

Originally published at truffaire.in.

title: How to Compare Two API Responses and Find Hidden Changes Faster
description:
You've just deployed a backend update.

All your API tests are passing, but a frontend developer reports that something has changed in the response.

Yesterday, the API returned one structure.

Today, it returns something slightly different.

The response is still valid JSON. The HTTP status is still 200. Nothing immediately looks broken.

So how do you identify exactly what changed?

Let's explore a practical workflow for comparing API responses, debugging unexpected differences, and deciding which changes actually matter.

1. A realistic API regression scenario

Imagine you're testing an e-commerce API.

Before a deployment, the endpoint returned:

{
  "orderId": "ORD-1042",
  "customer": {
    "id": 101,
    "name": "Alex"
  },
  "payment": {
    "status": "completed",
    "amount": 2499
  },
  "delivery": {
    "status": "processing",
    "estimatedDays": 3
  }
}

After the deployment, the same endpoint returns:

{
  "orderId": "ORD-1042",
  "customer": {
    "id": 101,
    "name": "Alex"
  },
  "payment": {
    "status": "completed",
    "amount": 2499
  },
  "delivery": {
    "status": "pending",
    "estimatedDays": 5
  }
}

At first glance, both responses look nearly identical.

But two values changed:

delivery.status

Before: processing
After:  pending

And:

delivery.estimatedDays

Before: 3
After:  5

Are these changes defects?

Not necessarily.

They might be intentional business-rule changes.

But they deserve investigation.

A difference tells us what changed. It does not automatically tell us whether the change is wrong.

That distinction matters in API testing.

2. Why manually comparing responses becomes difficult

Comparing small JSON objects is straightforward.

But real API responses can contain:

  • Hundreds of properties.
  • Deeply nested objects.
  • Arrays containing multiple records.
  • Optional fields.
  • Dynamic timestamps.
  • Generated identifiers.
  • Different whitespace and formatting.
  • Values that change on every request.

When you compare two responses by scrolling between files, it's easy to overlook a small difference.

For example, changing:

"retryCount": 3

to:

"retryCount": 30

may be important even though only one digit changed.

A text comparison can make these differences visible.

However, we should first understand what kind of comparison we need.

3. Text comparison vs structural JSON comparison

There are two different approaches.

Text comparison

A text comparison looks for differences between characters, words, or lines.

For example:

Old:
"status": "processing"

New:
"status": "pending"

It highlights the changed text.

This is useful for:

  • Configuration reviews.
  • API response inspection.
  • Log comparisons.
  • Documentation changes.
  • Reviewing generated output.

Structural JSON comparison

A structural comparison understands JSON objects, arrays, keys, and values.

For example:

{
  "name": "Alex",
  "age": 28
}

And:

{
  "age": 28,
  "name": "Alex"
}

These have different text ordering.

But their parsed object properties have equivalent values.

A plain text comparison may report differences.

A structural comparison can treat the objects as equivalent.

Neither approach is universally better. Choose based on the problem you're investigating.

For the rest of this tutorial, we'll use both techniques.

4. Start by making the responses readable

Suppose your API responses are compressed into one line:

{"orderId":"ORD-1042","status":"processing","amount":2499}

And:

{"orderId":"ORD-1042","status":"pending","amount":2499}

For larger responses, comparing single-line JSON is inconvenient.

A simple improvement is to format both responses before comparing them.

In JavaScript:

const oldResponse = {
  orderId: "ORD-1042",
  status: "processing",
  amount: 2499
};

const newResponse = {
  orderId: "ORD-1042",
  status: "pending",
  amount: 2499
};

const oldText = JSON.stringify(
  oldResponse,
  null,
  2
);

const newText = JSON.stringify(
  newResponse,
  null,
  2
);

console.log(oldText);
console.log(newText);

Formatting creates readable indentation.

It also makes line-by-line differences easier to identify.

But formatting alone does not normalize property order or remove dynamic values.

Those concerns require separate handling.

5. Compare the responses using a browser tool

If your immediate goal is to inspect two safe, non-sensitive text samples, you don't necessarily need to write a temporary comparison script.

I maintain ToolZenHub, a collection of practical browser-based utilities.

Its Text Diff / Compare tool is available here:

https://toolzenhub.in/tools/text-diff/

Let's use our earlier API example.

Step 1: Prepare the original response

Copy the JSON response from before the deployment.

If you're comparing JSON, format the response first.

The JSON Formatter & Validator at ToolZenHub can help with this, but any suitable formatter is fine.

Step 2: Prepare the changed response

Copy the response from after the deployment.

Keep both versions formatted consistently.

Step 3: Open Text Diff / Compare

Paste the original response into the Original field.

Paste the newer response into the Changed field.

Step 4: Compare

Select Compare.

The tool identifies added, removed, and changed lines.

For similar lines that have been edited, it highlights changed words within those lines.

For our example, the important differences are:

-    "status": "processing",
-    "estimatedDays": 3
+    "status": "pending",
+    "estimatedDays": 5

This representation immediately shows which values changed.

Step 5: Decide what the differences mean

Don't stop after finding a changed line.

Ask:

  • Was the change expected?
  • Does it match an approved requirement?
  • Does it violate the API contract?
  • Will existing clients handle it?
  • Does an automated test need updating?
  • Is the test data stable?

Text comparison helps identify the change.

Engineering judgment determines its significance.

6. Whitespace can create unnecessary noise

Consider these two JavaScript snippets:

const total = 100;

And:

const   total = 100;

A text comparison normally identifies a difference.

But the difference may not matter to your investigation.

Similarly, configuration files may contain differences caused only by indentation.

ToolZenHub's Text Diff / Compare includes an option called:

Ignore whitespace-only changes

When enabled, it treats runs of spaces and tabs as equivalent and ignores certain surrounding whitespace differences.

This can help reduce noise.

However, be careful.

Whitespace is meaningful in some formats.

Examples include:

  • Python indentation.
  • Markdown formatting.
  • YAML structure.
  • Whitespace-sensitive test fixtures.
  • String values in certain contexts.

Do not ignore whitespace automatically when it could affect behavior.

Also note that a general text-diff option is not a full parser for those languages.

7. Understanding unified diffs

Many developer tools use a format called a unified diff.

You'll encounter it in:

  • Git patches.
  • Pull requests.
  • Code reviews.
  • Build pipelines.
  • Test reports.

A basic example looks like this:

--- old-response.json
+++ new-response.json
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
 {
   "orderId": "ORD-1042",
-  "status": "processing",
+  "status": "pending",
   "amount": 2499
 }

The symbols have specific meanings.

Symbol Meaning
--- Original file heading
+++ New file heading
@@ Location of the changed section
- Removed line
+ Added line
Space Unchanged context line

Once you understand this format, many Git and CI debugging outputs become easier to read.

ToolZenHub's Text Diff / Compare also provides a Copy diff action that produces a standard unified diff.

This can be convenient when sharing an example in a bug report or technical discussion.

Before sharing, ensure that the copied diff contains no sensitive information.

8. How to compare JSON objects programmatically

Manual inspection is useful during investigation.

But automated tests often need a repeatable comparison.

For simple JSON-compatible data, you can create a structural equality function.

Here's an illustrative implementation:

function deepEqual(a, b) {
  if (Object.is(a, b)) {
    return true;
  }

  if (
    a === null ||
    b === null ||
    typeof a !== "object" ||
    typeof b !== "object"
  ) {
    return false;
  }

  if (Array.isArray(a) !== Array.isArray(b)) {
    return false;
  }

  if (Array.isArray(a)) {
    return (
      a.length === b.length &&
      a.every((value, index) =>
        deepEqual(value, b[index])
      )
    );
  }

  const keysA = Object.keys(a);
  const keysB = Object.keys(b);

  if (keysA.length !== keysB.length) {
    return false;
  }

  return keysA.every((key) =>
    Object.hasOwn(b, key) &&
    deepEqual(a[key], b[key])
  );
}

const before = {
  name: "Alex",
  age: 28
};

const after = {
  age: 28,
  name: "Alex"
};

console.log(deepEqual(before, after));
// true

This function:

  • Compares primitive values.
  • Recursively compares arrays.
  • Compares object keys regardless of their order.
  • Requires array elements to remain in order.

It is intended for ordinary JSON-compatible values parsed into JavaScript objects.

It is not a general-purpose equality function for arbitrary JavaScript objects such as Maps, Sets, Dates, or objects with circular references.

It also does not report which property differs.

For production code, consider whether a well-tested assertion or comparison library is more appropriate.

9. Ignore dynamic fields deliberately

Some response fields change on every request.

For example:

{
  "requestId": "req-001",
  "generatedAt": "2026-11-04T10:00:00Z",
  "status": "success"
}

A second request might return:

{
  "requestId": "req-002",
  "generatedAt": "2026-11-04T10:00:01Z",
  "status": "success"
}

A strict comparison reports changes.

But these particular differences may be expected.

Instead of ignoring every mismatch, explicitly select the fields you intend to compare.

function extractStableFields(response) {
  return {
    status: response.status
  };
}

const before = {
  requestId: "req-001",
  generatedAt: "2026-11-04T10:00:00Z",
  status: "success"
};

const after = {
  requestId: "req-002",
  generatedAt: "2026-11-04T10:00:01Z",
  status: "success"
};

console.log(
  deepEqual(
    extractStableFields(before),
    extractStableFields(after)
  )
);
// true

This is an example of selecting fields for comparison.

It doesn't mean request identifiers or timestamps should never be tested.

Those fields may have their own important validation rules.

The goal is to avoid mixing unrelated assertions into one comparison.

10. API comparison with Playwright

Suppose you're validating an endpoint using Playwright.

You want to check that its important fields match an expected response.

A test could look like this:

const { test, expect } = require("@playwright/test");

test("order response matches expected fields", async ({
  request
}) => {
  const response = await request.get(
    "/api/orders/ORD-1042"
  );

  expect(response.ok()).toBeTruthy();

  const actual = await response.json();

  expect(actual).toMatchObject({
    orderId: "ORD-1042",
    payment: {
      status: "completed",
      amount: 2499
    }
  });
});

This example assumes your Playwright configuration has the correct API base URL and authentication, and that the sample endpoint exists.

toMatchObject() checks the specified properties and permits additional object properties.

This is useful when you want to verify an API contract without requiring every unrelated response field to match.

For stricter comparisons, you can use toEqual() when the complete object should match the expected structure and values.

Choosing the right assertion

Use a partial match when:

  • Additional response properties are acceptable.
  • You only care about specified fields.
  • The API contract allows compatible extensions.

Use a strict equality assertion when:

  • The entire response structure matters.
  • Unexpected properties should fail the test.
  • You have a deterministic expected object.

Avoid creating overly broad assertions merely to make tests pass.

Tests should reflect the intended behavior of the application.

11. A useful regression-testing workflow

Here's a practical process for investigating changed API responses.

Step 1: Capture known test data

Use a controlled test environment and known inputs.

Step 2: Record the response before the change

Keep the original response for comparison.

Step 3: Deploy or enable the updated behavior

Make sure the environment and test data remain comparable.

Step 4: Capture the new response

Use the same request conditions where possible.

Step 5: Format and compare

A text diff provides a quick visual summary of changes.

Step 6: Separate expected from unexpected changes

Classify differences using the requirements and API contract.

Step 7: Add or update automated assertions

Convert important findings into repeatable checks.

Step 8: Record evidence

Keep relevant sanitized examples and test results.

This workflow is useful for backend releases, migration testing, integration testing, and investigating regressions.

12. Limitations of a browser-based text diff

A text-diff tool is useful, but it is not a complete API regression-testing system.

For example, it does not automatically determine:

  • Whether a field violates an API schema.
  • Whether a changed response is correct.
  • Whether two arrays are semantically equivalent.
  • Whether a change breaks downstream consumers.
  • Whether a difference is expected under particular business rules.

ToolZenHub's Text Diff / Compare is explicitly a line-based comparison tool.

It displays differences and can highlight changed words within similar adjacent lines.

It doesn't claim to perform structural JSON validation.

The tool also has stated input limits of 300,000 characters and 20,000 lines per side.

For very large datasets, automated comparison scripts or specialized diff tools may be a better choice.

The ToolZenHub tool runs its comparisons in the browser without uploading the compared text to the website.

Even so, only use data that you're authorized to handle in that environment.

13. Quick debugging checklist

When two API responses differ, ask:

  1. Are both responses valid JSON?
  2. Have both been formatted consistently?
  3. Is the difference caused only by whitespace?
  4. Have property order or array order changed?
  5. Are dynamic fields creating noise?
  6. Which values changed?
  7. Were those changes expected?
  8. Does the API contract still hold?
  9. Are downstream clients affected?
  10. Can automated tests catch similar problems next time?

Final thoughts

A passing HTTP status doesn't prove that an API response is unchanged.

And a detected difference doesn't automatically prove that something is broken.

Effective API regression testing requires both:

Visibility into what changed, and an understanding of what those changes mean.

Use text comparison to quickly identify differences.

Use structural validation and automated assertions to verify the actual contract.

When you're investigating two response samples and want a quick side-by-side comparison, you can try the Text Diff / Compare tool I maintain at ToolZenHub:

https://toolzenhub.in/tools/text-diff/

It can help remove repetitive manual inspection, particularly when you're comparing configuration files, test outputs, and API response samples.

The real goal is to spend less time searching for changed lines and more time understanding whether those changes matter.

References

  • Playwright assertions
  • MDN: JSON.stringify()
  • Git documentation: Diff format

Disclosure: I maintain ToolZenHub, the website referenced in this article. This tutorial was prepared using AI assistance and should be reviewed before publication.

title: Build parametric 3D CAD parts from Claude Code with SolidCraft MCP
description:
If you have tried to get an AI agent to make a real, editable 3D part, you have probably hit the same wall: it writes an STL or a pile of OpenSCAD, and the moment you want to change one dimension you start over. A parametric CAD tool with a feature timeline fixes that, and SolidCraft is one that ships with its own MCP server.

tangency-labs/solidcraft is an open-source parametric 3D CAD application written in pure Rust. Per the README you sketch, constrain and build solids on a parametric feature timeline, change a dimension and watch the model rebuild, and run it on desktop, in the browser, or let AI agents model through the built-in MCP server. This post walks through the setup for Claude Code and what to expect.

What SolidCraft can do today

The README calls it "early but usable for simple parts" and backs that with a number: 75 of 76 public reference parts match their analytic or FreeCAD-computed volume, area, centre of mass and bounding box. The one miss is a tracked bug.

The feature list is already broad:

  • Sketches and constraints: lines, arcs, splines and text, solved by its own constraint solver, with parameter-driven dimensions.
  • Features: extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, fillet, chamfer, shell, draft, holes, threads, patterns, mirror, split and combine, all on an editable timeline.
  • Parameters and configurations with unit-aware expressions.
  • Assemblies with joints, motion studies, interference checks and mass properties.
  • Sheet metal with flanges, hems, fold and unfold, and flat patterns.
  • Files: STEP, IGES, 3MF, STL, OBJ and glTF in and out where supported, plus URDF export and its own .sc designs.

The important line for agent users is the last one in that list: the desktop app, browser app, headless CLI and MCP server all run the same commands. Whatever the agent does, you can open and edit by hand.

Step 1: install SolidCraft

Pick the build for your machine from the README:

  • Windows: the MSI installer from the latest release. The Windows downloads are not signed yet, so SmartScreen asks you to choose More info, then Run anyway.
  • macOS: the disk image (Apple silicon and Intel), signed and notarized.
  • Linux: the AppImage, or the Snap: 
sudo snap install solidcraft
  • Browser: solidcraft.io/app, no install. Good for a first look, but the MCP server needs the CLI.

If you prefer to build from source with Rust:

cargo run --release -p solidcraft -- --sample      # desktop app with a sample part
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- commands  # the command registry

Step 2: add the MCP server to Claude Code

solidcraft-cli mcp is a Model Context Protocol server. One line registers it with Claude Code:

claude mcp add solidcraft -- solidcraft-cli mcp

Two modes are worth knowing. Run headless, the server keeps its own design session. Started with --connect, it drives the running desktop app so you can watch every feature appear on the timeline. For a first session, the connected mode is far easier to trust.

On older Windows installers the CLI is not on PATH. The README says to give the full path instead, which by default is C:\Program Files\SolidCraft\solidcraft-cli.exe.

Step 3: ask for a part with real parameters

The README's own demo is a good template for a prompt: a Raspberry Pi 4 case built from an empty design, with a sketch dimensioned from the board's parameters, extrude, fillet and shell, M2.5 standoffs patterned on the 58 by 49 mm hole rectangle, port cut-outs, vent slots and engraved text. Then the case height goes from 24 to 32 mm in Parameters and everything rebuilds.

So ask for parameters, not just a shape:

Create a box enclosure 90 x 60 mm with a height parameter of 30 mm,
2 mm walls (shell), 1 mm fillets on the outer edges, and four M3 standoffs
patterned on a 70 x 40 mm rectangle. Name every dimension as a parameter.

When it is done, change height in the Parameters panel yourself. If the model rebuilds cleanly, the agent built it the right way. Export STEP for a machinist or STL or 3MF for a printer.

Step 4: script it when you need repeatability

A SolidCraft script is a JSON list of the same commands the UI runs. You can run one headless and write a file:

cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- run examples/bracket.json --out bracket.step

This is handy once the agent has produced a part you like: keep the command list in the repo and regenerate the STEP in CI instead of trusting a binary file.

What people are building with it

The builds we track on the SolidCraft page show where it fits:

  • A skeptical CAD user designed and delivered a custom part for a paying client with no crash, citing the editable feature timeline, constrained sketches and clean STEP and STL exports.
  • One user hit a "wire not closed" error on a simple sketch in FreeCAD, redid it in SolidCraft and had it working in two minutes.
  • A hobbyist replicated a Telecaster body from PDFs with SolidCraft connected to desktop ChatGPT, then had it add bindings and a kill switch. The first run missed the wire holes between the pickup pockets, so check the model.
  • Another builder made a bot that models in SolidCraft and used it to design printable armor that snaps onto 6-inch poseable figures.

Related tools

If you want text-to-CAD as a skill set for agents rather than a full CAD app, text-to-cad generates 3D CAD models from text and runs related manufacturing and drawing workflows locally. For organic shapes, scenes and renders instead of engineering parts, MCP for Blender connects Blender to an LLM the same way.

Caveats

  • The project describes itself as early. Use it for simple parts first and check volumes and dimensions before you send anything to a shop.
  • Agents still miss details, as the guitar body example shows. The parametric timeline makes fixes cheap, but you are the reviewer.
  • This walkthrough follows the README and has not been run end to end by us.

Source repo: tangency-labs/solidcraft. License: MIT or Apache-2.0.

title: How I Extended a Refaster Rule in Picnic's error-prone-support (and Recovered a PR GitHub Broke)
description:
This is post 4 in my open source series. After Zalando Logbook and the Adyen Java library, this one is about Picnic's error-prone-support, and it has a twist: the PR I opened got stuck in a broken state on GitHub, and I had to recreate it.

What is error-prone-support?

error-prone-support is an open source project from Picnic. It extends Google's Error Prone with extra bug checks and Refaster rules. A Refaster rule says "this code pattern should be rewritten like this", and it can fix it automatically across a codebase.

What I worked on

The project already had a rule called RequireNonNullExpression. I extended it to cover this pattern:

// Before: Optional.of() throws a NullPointerException if value is null,
// so the Optional can never be empty. The orElse() part is dead code.
String result = Optional.of(value).orElse(fallback);

// After: says exactly what the code really does
String result = requireNonNull(value);

The idea is simple. Optional.of(x) can never be empty, so wrapping and then calling orElse only hides what is happening. The rewritten version is shorter and honest about the null check.

It closed issue #436.

The twist: GitHub broke my PR

My first PR, #2264, got into a strange state after an accidental close. The page showed "Merge status cannot be loaded", and the Reopen button was disabled.

I contacted GitHub Support. They confirmed it is a known problem with no manual fix. The only way out was to create a new PR from the same branch.

So I opened #2275 with the exact same commits, plus the Javadoc wording a maintainer had suggested, and linked it back to the original. The review carried on from there.

What the review taught me

  • Do not duplicate what already exists. One maintainer pointed out that an existing check, OptionalOfRedundantMethod, already does something similar. I looked into the source and explained the difference in intent: its fix assumes the value might be null, while this rule targets values that are provably non-null. In the end, the cross-reference comment was dropped.
  • Test your assumptions, don't just argue them. I assumed Refaster rules chain together on one input. The maintainer explained that the tests do a single pass and users are expected to apply rules until nothing changes. I ran the full test suite (78 tests, 0 failures) to confirm my expected output was correct as it was.
  • Small style rules matter. The reviewers asked me to use @code instead of @link in Javadoc when a link would pull in a new dependency or import. It is a tiny change, but it follows how the project keeps its code clean.
  • Patience is part of the job. The review went slowly because of holidays and busy schedules. A maintainer even said they had not forgotten the PR. Waiting politely and staying responsive worked better than pushing.

The PR was approved and merged by the maintainers.

What I would tell someone starting out

  1. If GitHub or CI breaks your PR, don't panic. Recreate it from the same branch and link to the original.
  2. When a reviewer questions your approach, check the source and run a test before you answer. Answers backed by evidence end discussions faster.
  3. Learn the project's conventions (comments, Javadoc style, test layout) by reading existing code before you write yours.
  4. Thank reviewers. They are spending their time on your work.

Proof of my work

Everything here is public, so you can check it yourself:

  • PicnicSupermarket/error-prone-support #2275: the extended RequireNonNullExpression rule (merged)
  • The original PR #2264 and issue #436
