title: Map a displayed crop rectangle into intrinsic image coordinates
description:
A crop picker often displays an image smaller than its source. If the picker reports a rectangle in displayed coordinates, passing those numbers directly to drawImage() selects the wrong part of the source. Scale the selection into intrinsic image coordinates first.

For an HTMLImageElement, drawImage() uses intrinsic dimensions. image.width can describe a displayed size, so use naturalWidth and naturalHeight when calculating the source rectangle. See MDN's drawImage notes.

Assume the entire decoded image is displayed in a 600 by 400 coordinate area. Its intrinsic dimensions are 2400 by 1600. A selection beginning at displayed point (150, 100), with displayed width 300 and height 200, maps to source point (600, 400), width 1200 and height 800.

This helper performs the scaling. The rectangle must already be relative to the displayed image content, excluding borders, padding, and any letterboxing. All arguments are numbers.

function sourceRect(image, rect, shownWidth, shownHeight) {
  const values = [rect.x, rect.y, rect.width, rect.height,
    shownWidth, shownHeight];
  if (!values.every(Number.isFinite) ||
      shownWidth <= 0 || shownHeight <= 0 ||
      image.naturalWidth <= 0 || image.naturalHeight <= 0 ||
      rect.x < 0 || rect.y < 0 ||
      rect.width <= 0 || rect.height <= 0 ||
      rect.x + rect.width > shownWidth ||
      rect.y + rect.height > shownHeight) {
    throw new RangeError("Selection must be inside a loaded image");
  }
  const scaleX = image.naturalWidth / shownWidth;
  const scaleY = image.naturalHeight / shownHeight;
  return {
    x: rect.x * scaleX,
    y: rect.y * scaleY,
    width: rect.width * scaleX,
    height: rect.height * scaleY,
  };
}

Use the result as the four source arguments in the nine-argument drawImage() overload. Choose the destination width and height separately; those describe the output canvas region, not the selection in the original image.

This helper does not translate pointer coordinates or model CSS transforms. A picker using object-fit: contain must first locate the actual image rectangle inside its element. A rotated or mirrored preview also needs its own inverse mapping. Resolve those layout details before calling the helper.

Put a different mark near each corner of a test image. Select one corner in the reduced preview and inspect the resulting crop. Then repeat at another corner to catch an incorrect offset.

title: Free AWS Security Assessment Toolkit: 42 Checks, a Local GUI, and Client-Ready HTML Reports
description:
An engineering walkthrough of a lightweight read-only AWS security assessment toolkit with 42 controls, CLI, local dashboard, baseline diff, suppressions, and self-contained HTML reporting

There is a classic trap in cloud security: looking at a green dashboard and deciding that "AWS is secure."

I do not work that way. When I start an AWS security assessment, I first want fast, boring answers to boring questions:

**- Is MFA enabled for the root user?

  • Do root access keys exist?
  • Are there IAM users without MFA?
  • Have access keys been living forever?
  • Is SSH or RDP open to the internet?
  • Are S3 buckets public?
  • Is encryption enabled where I expect it?
  • Are CloudTrail and AWS Config configured?
  • Are GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Inspector actually enabled?
  • Do EC2 instances require IMDSv2?
  • Do RDS and DynamoDB have reasonable recovery controls?
  • Is an EKS API endpoint accepting 0.0.0.0/0?
  • Has ordinary cloud hygiene debt started piling up?**

This is not sexy zero-day research. It is plumbing. But a surprising amount of real-world security posture is built from exactly this plumbing.

That is why I built an AWS Security Assessment Toolkit, a small read-only tool for the first technical pass over an AWS account.

It grew out of consulting work I was doing through Bulwark Advisory, but this article is not a services pitch. It is an engineering walkthrough: what I wanted to automate, why I did not try to build another giant CSPM, where automation helps, and where a human still has to think.

At the time of writing, this article describes toolkit v2.0.0.

TL;DR

If you are short on time, here is the whole idea.

The toolkit performs a point-in-time AWS posture assessment through read-only APIs.
The current release includes:

  • 42 controls;
  • one assessment engine shared by CLI and local GUI;
  • cross-account scanning through STS AssumeRole;
  • baseline/diff support;
  • suppressions and waivers with reasons and expiration;
  • Console, JSON, Markdown, HTML, CSV, SARIF, and JUnit outputs;
  • a self-contained client-facing HTML report;
  • scheduled-run support for drift detection;
  • no automatic remediation of target resources.

And the most important caveat:

42 PASS results do not mean "AWS is secure." They mean that 42 specific checks, in a specific scope, returned those results at a specific point in time.

That principle shaped most of the design.

New to cloud security? Five terms in sixty seconds

A little vocabulary before we go deeper.

Security posture

The current state of security-relevant configuration. Is a Security Group open? Is encryption enabled? Is an audit trail present?
Control

One concrete rule we evaluate. For example: "The root user should have MFA."
Finding

The result of evaluating a control. A finding contains status, severity, resource context, evidence, and remediation guidance.
Baseline

A saved result from an earlier assessment. It gives us something stable to compare against.
Drift

A configuration change relative to that baseline. Drift can be good, bad, or neutral.
CSPM

Cloud Security Posture Management, the category of products and services that continuously or periodically evaluate cloud configuration, standards, and misconfigurations.

In plain English, this toolkit is closer to a building inspection than a break-in attempt.

A pentest asks:

"Can I get through the window?"

A posture assessment first asks:

"Is the window even closed?"

Where the project started

I liked the core idea: understandable read-only boto3 checks, very little magic, and a fast point-in-time result.

For my own workflow, I wanted more:

  • a modular architecture;
  • a control registry;
  • one normalized finding model;
  • broader AWS coverage;
  • cross-account assessment;
  • baseline and diff support;
  • documented suppressions;
  • CI-friendly outputs;
  • a local GUI;
  • client-ready HTML;
  • and a hard read-only boundary.

Over time, the seed became a separate toolkit.

The problem I actually wanted to solve

The AWS Shared Responsibility Model separates security of the cloud from security in the cloud.

The "in the cloud" part gets interesting fast. AWS can secure the physical infrastructure perfectly while the customer still has:

  • overly permissive IAM;
  • public buckets;
  • Security Groups open to 0.0.0.0/0;
  • weak logging coverage;
  • missing recovery controls;
  • long-lived credentials;
  • unused keys;
  • poorly scoped public endpoints.

The AWS Well-Architected Security Pillar emphasizes a strong identity foundation, traceability, defense in depth, automation of security best practices, and protection of data.

This is exactly where configuration assessment is useful as a first filter. AWS Security Hub CSPM already evaluates environments against standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices and CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. I treat those as important reference points for control design, not as competitors that my tool needs to "beat."

My requirement was narrower:

I wanted a portable first-pass scanner that I understand end to end, can adapt to an assessment workflow, can run under a read-only role, and can turn into a useful deliverable.

What the toolkit checks today

Version 2.0.0 registers 42 controls across ten categories:

Area Examples
Identity root MFA, root keys, console MFA, access-key age, Access Analyzer
Data Protection S3/EBS/RDS/SQS encryption, S3 public access
Network SSH/RDP exposure, risky ports, default SGs, VPC Flow Logs, CloudFront HTTPS
Compute IMDSv2, EBS encryption by default, SSM coverage
Database RDS posture
Containers EKS endpoint exposure and logging
Serverless Lambda-related posture
Logging & Detection CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, Security Hub, Inspector, Macie
Resilience backups, PITR, versioning, deletion protection, Multi-AZ
Cost & Hygiene unattached EBS, unused Elastic IPs

These are not 42 vulnerability signatures and they are not 42 proofs of exploitability.

They are 42 deterministic posture checks.

For example, EC2-002 answers a narrow question:

Does this instance require IMDSv2?

It does not answer:

Could an attacker actually steal workload credentials through SSRF?

That requires application context and separate testing.

Why status semantics matter more than a red circle

I use five primary statuses:

Status Meaning
PASS The check ran and the control condition is satisfied
FAIL The check ran and the control condition is violated
WARN An advisory condition needs context
ERROR The state could not be verified reliably
SKIP The finding was intentionally waived/suppressed by policy

For both engineers and auditors, ERROR matters a lot.

If the scanner gets AccessDenied, that is not PASS.

If a service API is unavailable, that is not PASS.

If a Region was not assessed, that is not PASS.

Unknown should not magically become green.

Otherwise we get security theater with a really nice color palette.

Severity is not business risk

Another design rule I care about:

CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, and LOW are technical triage priorities in the toolkit.

They are not CVSS scores.

They are not final business-risk decisions.

Consider the same finding twice:

Security Group exposes TCP/22 to 0.0.0.0/0

Resource A:

Disposable training instance
No sensitive data
Automatically destroyed tonight

Resource B:

Production jump host
Privileged network path
Customer data environment

Same technical control.

Very different business risk.

So the workflow becomes:

Scanner severity
      |
      v
Technical validation
      |
      v
Asset / data / exposure context
      |
      v
Compensating controls
      |
      v
Likelihood + impact
      |
      v
Business priority

The scanner helps sort the queue. It does not replace the risk owner.

Scope: a green result without scope is almost useless

Before an assessment, I want to know at least:

  • which AWS account is in scope;
  • which principal performs the scan;
  • which Regions are covered;
  • which services are actually used;
  • which controls are enabled;
  • which controls are excluded;
  • which suppressions are applied;
  • when the scan runs.

Regions are especially important.

Some AWS resources are global, others are Regional. Some Regions are opt-in. Service availability also differs.

So the sentence:

"We scanned AWS."

does not tell me very much.

This is better:

"We ran toolkit v2.0.0 against account X, across all enabled/opted-in Regions, using this control set and this read-only role."

Now we have a reproducible technical statement.

Architecture: one engine, two interfaces

I did not want to build two scanners, one for a terminal and one for a pretty UI. The architecture looks roughly like this:

             AWS credential chain / optional AssumeRole
                              |
                              v
                    Assessment Context
                 account / regions / policy
                              |
                              v
                       Control Registry
                              |
                              v
                     Assessment Engine
                              |
                              v
                    Normalized Findings
                              |
                    Suppression Policy
                              |
                              v
                     AssessmentReport
                              |
        +---------+-----------+-----------+
        |         |           |           |
        v         v           v           v
       CLI       GUI         HTML      JSON/CSV/
                                      SARIF/JUnit

The CLI and GUI call the same Assessment Engine.

That gives me one source of truth for:

  • collection;
  • control logic;
  • statuses;
  • severity;
  • suppressions;
  • evidence;
  • reports.

Consistency in security tooling is boring. That is a compliment.

Read-only is a design constraint, not a marketing phrase

The toolkit is for assessment, not remediation. In the target account I expect inspection operations such as:

Get*
List*
Describe*

not:

Create*
Delete*
Modify*
Put*
Enable*
Disable*

There is one obvious exception: sts:AssumeRole. For cross-account consulting, temporary credentials are much cleaner than asking a customer for long-lived access keys.

The AWS managed SecurityAudit policy is explicitly described as useful for software that audits security configuration metadata, so it is a reasonable starting point for an assessment role.

I still do not treat a managed policy as magic. Optional services and a particular scope can require additional read permissions.

I test the read-only boundary at release time

The repository includes a release check that:

  • statically collects boto3 operations;
  • validates operations and paginators against the installed botocore model;
  • looks for obvious mutating API prefixes;
  • explicitly allows only the expected sts:AssumeRole exception.

This is not a mathematical proof. It is a practical regression guard. If somebody accidentally adds modify_* to the assessment path tomorrow, I would rather learn about it in CI than in a customer account.

Cross-account access and why External ID matters

A typical setup looks like this:

Assessor account / workstation
           |
           | sts:AssumeRole
           v
Customer SecurityAudit role
           |
           v
Customer AWS account

For example:

aws-sec-audit \
  --profile assessor \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/SecurityAudit \
  --external-id customer-123 \
  --all-regions

AWS recommends an External ID for third-party role access as a way to mitigate the confused deputy problem.

One detail that is easy to miss: the External ID is not a secret. Its purpose is different. It helps the target account constrain when the third party is allowed to assume that role on a particular customer's behalf. It is a small detail with a big impact on a clean consulting access model.

The CLI stayed

I like GUIs when I need to configure scope quickly or show results to somebody else. But automation without a CLI gets painful fast. A simple run still looks like:

aws-sec-audit --profile security-audit --all-regions

Focused controls:

aws-sec-audit \
  --include IAM-001,IAM-002,S3-001 \
  --regions eu-west-1,eu-central-1

Tag-based selection:

aws-sec-audit --tag encryption
aws-sec-audit --tag cis --tag public-access
aws-sec-audit --exclude-tag cost

That matters for CI, repeatability, and boring shell automation. Boring shell automation is underrated.

Then I built a GUI anyway

At some point I noticed that every customized run ended with me reopening the README:

Right, --all-regions, then --role-arn, then --tag, then baseline... what did I call that flag again?

That usually means the interface can be better.

So I built a Local Dashboard Edition.

Install and run:

python -m pip install ".[ui]"
aws-sec-audit-ui

By default it listens on:

http://127.0.0.1:8765

The browser does not ask for an AWS access key or secret key.

boto3 uses the normal credential provider chain:

  • AWS profiles;
  • AWS SSO-backed profiles;
  • environment/workload credentials;
  • optional AssumeRole.

A small security warning

127.0.0.1 is not a cosmetic default.

The dashboard can display:

  • account metadata;
  • resource names and ARNs;
  • evidence;
  • configuration details.

I do not treat the local UI as a ready-made multi-user web service. If it is ever exposed on a shared network, that becomes a different product requirement: authentication, TLS, authorization, tenant isolation, session/CSRF protection, and encrypted persistence.

Binding a local admin tool to 0.0.0.0 does not magically turn it into an enterprise portal. Unfortunately.

The dashboard is for triage, not dashboard-driven security

After a scan I want to understand quickly:

  • how many FAIL findings exist;
  • how many ERROR results indicate coverage gaps;
  • whether any CRITICAL/HIGH items are open;
  • which categories dominate;
  • which findings are new relative to the baseline;
  • which items deserve a human review first.

But the dashboard should never become a source of false confidence.
Green is a signal, not a magic amulet.

If the scope is incomplete, credentials are insufficient, or a relevant control does not exist, the color of the card will not save you.

A finding has to answer "what exactly?"

A weak scanner says:

FAIL: S3 is insecure

Okay. Now what?

A normalized finding in the toolkit contains:

control ID
title
status
severity
account
region
affected resources
evidence
remediation
references

At minimum, a finding should answer four questions:

  1. What is wrong?
  2. Where exactly is it?
  3. Why did the scanner reach that conclusion?
  4. What is a reasonable next action?

Evidence matters to me a lot. Without evidence, a finding turns into an opinion very quickly.

Suppressions: accepted risk should not disappear

Real environments always have exceptions. For example:

  • a public endpoint is public by design;
  • a resource is temporarily excluded;
  • a legacy workload is already being retired;
  • a compensating control changes the risk;
  • the risk was formally accepted;
  • remediation is already scheduled for the next sprint.

The bad implementation is to delete the finding. The slightly less bad implementation is to hide it so well that nobody remembers why.

I prefer a waiver that records:

  • control;
  • Region;
  • resource pattern;
  • reason;
  • optional expiration date.

A suppressed finding remains visible as SKIP, and the original evidence is retained. That helps different people in different ways.

A team lead asks:

"Who made this decision, and why?"

An auditor asks:

"Is there a traceable exception?"

Future you asks:

"Why on earth did we allow this three months ago?"

All three deserve an answer.

Baseline and diff: the second scan is more useful than the first

The first scan tells you:

What violates our controls right now?

The second tells you:

What changed?

For example:

Previous assessment
18 open findings

Current assessment
6 open findings

Resolved: 14
New:       2
Unchanged: 4

Now remediation conversations get much more concrete.

You can separate:

  • fixed;
  • new regression;
  • accepted;
  • still open.

Scheduled runs through cron, systemd, or CI can provide lightweight drift detection. But I do not call that real-time detection.

Polling every few hours answers:

"Has the posture changed since the last run?"

It does not answer:

"What happened twelve seconds ago, and who did it?"

For that, I want CloudTrail, EventBridge, GuardDuty, AWS Config, Security Hub, and an event-driven detection workflow. Do not make a posture scanner cosplay as a SIEM.

Point-in-time evidence is not operating effectiveness

This is one of the most important points from an auditor's perspective.

Suppose the toolkit reports:

CloudTrail enabled: PASS

What does that prove?

It proves that the observed configuration satisfied the control when the scan ran.

What does it not prove?

That CloudTrail was correctly enabled:

  • yesterday;
  • for the last 90 days;
  • through the entire audit period;
  • in every previously used Region;
  • without interruption.

That is the difference between point-in-time configuration evidence and evidence of operating effectiveness over time.

For historical evidence I would add sources such as:

  • AWS Config configuration history;
  • Security Hub finding history;
  • CloudTrail;
  • change tickets;
  • IaC history;
  • operational procedures.

AWS Config is specifically designed to retain configuration history after recording begins. Security Hub updates control findings through periodic or change-triggered checks.
So in a serious assessment I would never write:

"This scan proves that the control operated effectively all quarter."

It does not.

The HTML report is client-ready, not consultant-free

Raw JSON is wonderful. Especially if your client is also jq. Most clients are still human. That is why the toolkit can generate a self-contained HTML report:

aws-sec-audit \
  --all-regions \
  --format html \
  --output reports/aws-security-assessment.html

It includes:

  • executive summary;
  • scan metadata;
  • color-coded severity;
  • status counters;
  • category breakdown;
  • filters;
  • search;
  • affected resources;
  • evidence;
  • remediation;
  • references;
  • print-friendly styling.

The exported HTML is standalone. It does not need the dashboard afterward.

I still do not consider the generated report a final consulting opinion.
The scanner knows configuration.
It does not know:

  • why the workload exists;
  • what data it processes;
  • what the blast radius is;
  • which compensating controls are effective;
  • how much downtime is acceptable;
  • which "easy fix" will break production.

That is where the human part of an assessment begins.

Turning a finding into an action plan

A team lead does not need thirty red lines. They need a queue of work.
For example:

Finding Decision Owner Priority Target
Root without MFA Fix now Platform P0 Today
Public SSH to bastion Restrict CIDR / replace access model Cloud P1 3 days
S3 versioning disabled on dev bucket Accept temporarily App Team P3 Review next quarter
GuardDuty disabled Enable and integrate findings Security P1 This sprint

The flow looks more like:

Automated finding
       |
       v
Engineer validates
       |
       v
Business / architecture context
       |
       v
Remediation option
       |
       v
Owner + priority + target date
       |
       v
Re-scan / evidence of closure

Automation removes repetitive work. Ownership closes risk.

Those are different jobs.

Multiple reports from one scan

I deliberately separated collection from presentation.

One scan can produce multiple representations:

aws-sec-audit --all-regions \
  --export json=reports/report.json \
  --export html=reports/report.html \
  --export csv=reports/report.csv \
  --export junit=reports/junit.xml \
  --export sarif=reports/report.sarif

The toolkit currently supports:

  1. Console
  2. JSON
  3. Markdown
  4. HTML
  5. CSV
  6. SARIF
  7. JUnit XML

In practice, it means fewer repeated AWS API calls and less chance that two reports accidentally describe slightly different points in time.

What does "fast assessment" actually mean?

I can sometimes get a useful first picture within a couple of hours.

That does not mean:

"We fully proved AWS security in two hours."

It means something closer to:

  1. agree scope and credentials;
  2. run the automated posture pass;
  3. investigate ERROR results and coverage gaps;
  4. triage high-priority findings;
  5. manually validate the most important items;
  6. define the first remediation priorities.

It is a first pass.

It can tell you quickly whether the environment looks disciplined, has a handful of isolated gaps, or smells strongly of configuration debt.

The actual depth depends on:

  • number of accounts;
  • Regions;
  • resource volume;
  • architecture;
  • service mix;
  • permissions;
  • compliance requirements;
  • manual-validation needs.

Garbage in, garbage out applies to cloud security too. Give the scanner a half-blind role and you should expect a half-blind report.

Why not just Security Hub?

Security Hub CSPM is already an AWS-native service for ongoing posture management, standards, and control findings.

I am not trying to replace it. For continuous AWS governance, Security Hub is often a natural part of the architecture.

My toolkit solves a different problem:

  • portable assessment;
  • independent first pass;
  • local execution;
  • my normalized finding model;
  • custom scope;
  • client artifact;
  • fast re-scan after remediation.

Sometimes I compare both views.

If Security Hub says one thing and a direct API check says another, that is not a reason to pick your favorite dashboard. It is a reason to investigate scope, evaluation schedule, AWS Config recording coverage, and control semantics.

Why not just Prowler?

Prowler is a mature open-source cloud security platform with hundreds of AWS checks, multiple cloud providers, compliance frameworks, UI/API/CLI, and a large community.

If your requirement is a broad open-source CSPM, it absolutely belongs on the evaluation list. I built something different.

I wanted a tool that is:

  • small enough that I can understand the code path;
  • easy to modify for a specific assessment workflow;
  • local;
  • read-only;
  • infrastructure-light;
  • intentionally limited to an explainable control set;
  • aligned with my reporting flow.

This is not a "who has more checks" competition. Sometimes you need hundreds of controls. Sometimes you need the right forty, an architecture diagram, and an engineer willing to ask uncomfortable questions.

What a green dashboard does NOT mean

I would happily print this section next to every CSPM dashboard.
A PASS result does not prove that:

  • the application has no SQL injection;
  • no IAM attack path exists;
  • secrets have never leaked;
  • CloudTrail was not disabled yesterday;
  • Kubernetes workloads are secure;
  • the source code is vulnerability-free;
  • incident response is ready;
  • backups can actually be restored;
  • every relevant resource was in scope;
  • compensating controls operate exactly as described.

A posture scanner answers its controls. It does not answer every question in the security universe.

Where the toolkit sits in my assessment workflow

My AWS assessment looks more like this:

Scope / architecture
        |
        +--> AWS posture scan
        |
        +--> IAM / privilege review
        |
        +--> Network exposure
        |
        +--> Logging / detection
        |
        +--> Data protection
        |
        +--> Backup / recovery
        |
        +--> Application / API layer
        |
        +--> Manual validation
        |
        v
Risk prioritization
        |
        v
Action plan
        |
        v
Re-test

The toolkit covers part of posture and discovery.

It does not replace:

  • threat modeling;
  • penetration testing;
  • source-code review;
  • IAM privilege and attack-path analysis;
  • architecture review;
  • API/AppSec testing;
  • incident-readiness assessment;
  • backup restore testing;
  • interviews with engineering and security teams.

That is fine. A good tool does not need to pretend to be an entire security program.

What I intentionally did NOT add

Every security side project eventually starts whispering:

"Add an LLM. Add a database. Add auto-remediation. Add multi-tenancy. Add a Slack bot. And maybe blockchain?"

I stopped earlier.

The current design does not include:

  • automatic remediation;
  • hosted credential storage;
  • a cloud database;
  • multi-user authentication;
  • a real-time detection engine;
  • a "magic" security score;
  • an LLM deciding whether a configuration is risky.

I like this model:

Deterministic check
        |
        v
Finding + evidence
        |
        v
Human judgment

If I add AI later, I would put it after the evidence:

Finding
   |
   +--> explanation
   +--> correlation
   +--> remediation draft
   +--> executive summary

Root MFA is still better evaluated by a boolean. It does not hallucinate.

What comes next

Natural directions include:

  • deeper IAM controls;
  • AWS Organizations and multi-account orchestration;
  • more framework mappings;
  • historical trends;
  • WAF/API efficacy testing as a separate module;
  • ticketing/SIEM integrations;
  • signed reports;
  • additional services.

But I want to keep the main principle:

Tooling should remove repetitive work, not hide security judgment behind charts.

Final thoughts

The AWS Security Assessment Toolkit came from a simple need: get a fast, reproducible first technical view of AWS security posture.

TODAY IT INCLUDES: 42 controls + CLI + local GUI + AssumeRole + suppressions + baseline/diff + 7 report formats + a self-contained HTML report.

For me, that is a useful level of lightweight assessment tooling.
Not a full CSPM.
Not a pentest.
Not an audit-opinion generator.
Not a "Make AWS Secure" button.

Just an engineering lever that saves time where automation makes sense and leaves humans responsible for the parts that require context. Those are usually the security tools I enjoy using the most.

References

AWS

  • AWS Shared Responsibility Model
  • AWS Well-Architected Framework: Security Pillar
  • AWS IAM security best practices
  • AWS Security Hub CSPM introduction
  • AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
  • CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark in Security Hub CSPM
  • AWS Security Hub control reference
  • AWS managed policy: SecurityAudit
  • Third-party access and External IDs
  • How AWS Config records configuration history
  • Security Hub security-check schedules

Open source

  • Prowler
  • AWS Security Assessment Toolkit repository by Bulwark Advisory

title: 3 of 10 colors failed Safari's dark-mode contrast bar
description:
My toy version of Safari's Adaptive Dark Mode failed 3 of 10 text colors on WCAG's 4.5:1 contrast bar. Naive RGB inversion passed 9 of 10 — but it turned every blue link orange.

Apple announced Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta on November 3, and the WebKit blog post is unusually candid about the mechanism: when a page doesn't declare dark-mode support, Safari analyzes the page, and if it looks predominantly light, it transforms colors with a matrix that inverts luminosity while preserving hue, aiming for the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio for text. Almost 40% of page loads come from users in dark mode, WebKit says, while only 10% of page loads support it — that gap is the whole product. I couldn't run Safari 27.3 beta here, so I built the smallest possible version of the described transform and measured where it breaks.

The experiment is 30 lines of Python, standard library only. I took a 12-color palette of typical light-mode UI colors and applied two transforms to each: naive inversion (255 - c per channel) and luminosity inversion (convert to HLS, replace lightness L with 1 - L, keep hue and saturation). Then I computed WCAG relative-luminance contrast against the transformed background (white becomes black under both transforms) and the hue drift in degrees.

import colorsys

def lum(rgb):
    def f(c):
        return c / 12.92 if c <= 0.03928 else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4
    r, g, b = (f(c) for c in rgb)
    return 0.2126 * r + 0.7152 * g + 0.0722 * b

def contrast(a, b):
    la, lb = lum(a), lum(b)
    return (max(la, lb) + 0.05) / (min(la, lb) + 0.05)

def naive(rgb):
    return tuple(1 - c for c in rgb)

def lum_inv(rgb):
    h, l, s = colorsys.rgb_to_hls(*rgb)
    return colorsys.hls_to_rgb(h, 1 - l, s)

color            orig     naive    hueDriftN  lumInv   hueDriftL  contrastN  contrastL
body text        #1A1A1A  #e5e5e5       0.0  #e5e5e5       0.0      16.67      16.67
secondary text   #666666  #999999       0.0  #999999       0.0       7.37       7.37
link blue        #0066CC  #ff9933     180.0  #3399ff       0.0       9.86       7.14
accent orange    #E8590C  #17a6f3     180.0  #f36417       0.0       7.79       6.65
success green    #2F9E44  #d061bb     180.0  #61d076       0.0       6.11      10.79
danger red       #D6336C  #29cc93     180.0  #cc2962       0.0      10.15       4.06
warning yellow   #F08C00  #0f73ff     180.0  #ff9b0f       0.0       4.92       9.95
muted gray       #868E96  #797169     180.0  #697179       0.0       4.38       4.24
button blue      #1971C2  #e68e3d     180.0  #3d95e6       0.0       8.30       6.64
code red         #C92A2A  #36d5d5     180.0  #d53636       0.0      11.64       4.41

Counting only the 10 text colors (excluding the page background and the border gray), naive inversion passes 4.5:1 on 9 of 10, luminosity inversion on 7 of 10. The three luminosity-inversion failures are danger red at 4.06, muted gray at 4.24, and code red at 4.41 — all just under the bar, which is exactly the kind of near-miss a real implementation has to catch and correct. Mean hue drift tells the other half of the story: 135.0 degrees for naive inversion across the full 12-color palette, 0.0 degrees for luminosity inversion. Naive inversion wins on contrast and destroys identity — your blue link becomes orange, your green success message becomes magenta. Luminosity inversion keeps every hue and pays for it in contrast.

Two edge cases sharpen the point. Pure red #FF0000 sits at lightness 0.5, so luminosity inversion leaves it exactly unchanged — still red, still 5.25:1 against black, but a red that was designed for a white page now shouts on a dark one. And for achromatic colors the two transforms are identical: body text #1A1A1A becomes #e5e5e5 either way, at 16.67:1. The hard cases are all saturated colors near the middle of the lightness range, which is to say, most of a real design system.

So WebKit's "aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 ratio" has to mean more than a pure lightness mirror. A mirror alone fails 3 of my 10 text colors. The real implementation must push failing text colors further — lighter or darker than the mirror position — or it would ship the exact failures my toy produces. The blog doesn't publish that correction step, but my numbers say it must exist.

I also checked the opt-out side, because that's where this feature meets real sites. Pages that declare dark support — <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> or color-scheme: light dark in CSS — are left untouched. I fetched 9 homepages and grepped the served HTML: 5 clearly declare dark support (Wikipedia's inline dark CSS, GitHub's light dark meta tag, MDN, Node.js, and Tailwind), 3 showed no declaration (python.org, mozilla.org, and Stack Overflow's redirect page), and React's page had a single ambiguous hit. That 5-of-9 is not a rebuttal of WebKit's web-wide 10% figure — my sample is dev-centric sites that already care about dark mode, and HTML-only grepping misses declarations in external stylesheets, so it's a lower bound. It's a reminder that the sites Adaptive Dark Mode will transform most are the ones least likely to have thought about it.

Three details from the blog post are worth pocketing. First, <canvas> content is left unchanged, and effects like mix-blend-mode are sometimes switched off when they would fight the transform — so a page can look dark and still have light islands. Second, JavaScript that queries CSS colors gets the original authored colors, not the transformed ones, and canvas draws render in original form: you cannot feature-detect Adaptive Dark Mode from script, so testing it takes eyes, not code. Third, the opt-out has a catch: color-scheme: light only is the declared way to refuse transformation, but the blog notes the only keyword is not supported in Safari 27.3 beta 1. Today, the working escape is shipping a real dark mode — which is presumably the point.

Sources: WebKit blog, "Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode" (November 3, 2026) — https://webkit.org/blog/18541/introducing-adaptive-dark-mode/ . Palette, transforms, and contrast numbers are my own measurements, run locally; the site audit is HTML-only and a lower bound, as noted in the text.

title: AWS S3 Bucket Versioning: Protect Your Data from Accidental Deletes and Overwrites
description:
A hands-on guide to enabling S3 versioning, recovering deleted files, and keeping costs under control with lifecycle rules."

tags: aws, s3, cloud, beginners

Overwriting the wrong file or deleting an important object in S3 is easy to do, and by default it is permanent. S3 Versioning fixes this. It keeps every version of every object in your bucket, so you can recover from mistakes and from application failures. In this post I enable versioning, test it, and recover a deleted file.

vishalcloudjourney

📦 What is S3 Versioning?

Versioning is a bucket-level feature that keeps multiple variants of an object in the same bucket. Every upload of the same key creates a new version with its own unique Version ID.

A bucket is always in one of three states:

  • Unversioned (the default)
  • Versioning-enabled
  • Versioning-suspended

⚠️ Once you enable versioning, you cannot go back to unversioned. You can only suspend it, and existing versions are kept.

✅ Why use it?

  • Recover from accidental deletion: a delete only adds a delete marker, and the data stays.
  • Recover from accidental overwrites: older versions are still there.
  • Keep a history: useful for audits and rollbacks.
  • Safer backups: a good protection layer against human error and some application bugs.

🖱️ Hands-on: Enable versioning in the console

Step 1: Create a bucket

  1. Open the S3 console and click Create bucket.
  2. Enter a globally unique bucket name, such as vishal-versioning-demo-123.
  3. Choose your region and keep Block all public access on.
  4. Click Create bucket.

Step 2: Enable versioning

  1. Open your bucket and go to the Properties tab.
  2. Find Bucket Versioning and click Edit.
  3. Select Enable and click Save changes.

Step 3: Upload and overwrite a file

  1. Create a file demo.txt containing Version 1 and upload it.
  2. Change the content to Version 2 and upload it again with the same name.
  3. Open the Objects tab and turn on the List versions toggle.

You will see two versions of demo.txt, each with its own Version ID. The latest one is the current version, and the other is a noncurrent version.

Step 4: Delete and recover

  1. Turn List versions off, select demo.txt and click Delete.
  2. The file seems to disappear. Turn List versions back on.
  3. You will see a Delete marker on top of your versions. Your data is safe.
  4. Select the delete marker and delete it. demo.txt comes back.

To remove a version permanently, delete it by its specific Version ID.

⌨️ Hands-on: Using the AWS CLI 

# Enable versioning
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket vishal-versioning-demo-123 \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

# Check the status
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket vishal-versioning-demo-123

# List all versions and delete markers
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket vishal-versioning-demo-123

# Download a specific version
aws s3api get-object \
  --bucket vishal-versioning-demo-123 \
  --key demo.txt \
  --version-id <VERSION_ID> demo-old.txt

# Permanently delete one specific version
aws s3api delete-object \
  --bucket vishal-versioning-demo-123 \
  --key demo.txt \
  --version-id <VERSION_ID>

💡 Things to know

  • Cost: every version is stored and billed as a separate object, so storage grows with each update.
  • Lifecycle rules: use them to expire noncurrent versions after N days, or move them to a cheaper storage class. This keeps costs under control.
  • Objects uploaded before versioning: they get the Version ID null.
  • MFA Delete: an optional extra protection that requires MFA to permanently delete a version or change the versioning state. Only the bucket owner's root account can enable it, and only through the CLI or API.
  • Replication: Cross-Region Replication requires versioning on both buckets.

🏆 Best practices

  1. Turn versioning on for buckets that hold important or hard-to-recreate data.
  2. Add a lifecycle rule to clean up old noncurrent versions.
  3. Restrict who can permanently delete versions with IAM and bucket policies.
  4. Consider MFA Delete for critical buckets.
  5. Monitor storage growth in the S3 console and in billing.

🧹 Cleanup

A versioned bucket is not empty until all versions and delete markers are removed. Use Empty in the console, then delete the bucket, so you don't pay for leftover data.

📚 Key learnings

  • Versioning turns a permanent delete into a recoverable one.
  • A delete on a versioned bucket adds a delete marker, and the data stays in the bucket.
  • Lifecycle rules are the best way to keep versioning affordable.

🤝 Connect with me

  • LinkedIn: Vishal Patil
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS
  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws

If this helped you, drop a ❤️ and tell me how you use S3 versioning in the comments!

title: PageSift 1.0: the Rust web content engine is feature-complete
description:
Fifteen days, twenty-five releases. PageSift went public as 0.20 on October 20; today it ships 1.0.

PageSift is a web content engine written in Rust. It turns URLs, PDFs and Office files into clean Markdown and structured data for AI agents and LLM pipelines — one self-hosted binary with a Firecrawl-compatible HTTP API, a Jina Reader-compatible endpoint (including /s/), an MCP server, and Python / Node.js / Rust SDKs.

1.0 is not a speed release — performance landed with the 0.9 architecture rebuild. 1.0 is feature completion.

What 1.0 adds

OCR, built from scratch. Scanned PDFs were PageSift's documented weak spot. 1.0 ships its own OCR pipeline — text detection, recognition, formula recognition (LaTeX out), layout analysis — running on a self-written inference runtime (safetensors executor; no ONNX Runtime) and a self-written CUDA GPU layer. Models are open weights, downloaded on first use, off by default. On the olmOCR-bench scanned set it scores 0.543 vs Docling (GPU) at 0.410.

Selector extraction with memory. Give it a JSON schema; when a site redesign breaks your selectors, it relocates elements using element fingerprints and a statistical posterior — and reports relocated, ambiguous, or missing instead of silently returning wrong data.

Change monitoring. A /v2/monitor endpoint family with block-level diffing that separates noise changes (prices, dates, counters) from substantive ones.

Browser actions, sessions, and an agent endpoint across the HTTP, MCP and Jina surfaces — plus WARC files as input, a hooks + [[rules]] system, and per-host secret injection.

The architecture in three ideas

  1. Measured instead of fixed. The hundreds of hand-tuned timeouts, thresholds and concurrency limits are gone. A statistical kernel derives them from runtime observations — survival analysis (Kaplan–Meier) for timeouts, a Universal Scalability Law fit for global concurrency, and "posterior expected value − shadow price × cost" for render decisions. One global meta-parameter remains: δ = 0.05. With no observations, behaviour matches the old fixed values; an estimate takes over only when the difference is statistically significant.
  2. Scheduling that follows the hardware. One resident CPU worker per core (no blocking thread pool), pinned to NUMA node sets rather than individual cores — because measurements said so: hard per-core pinning cost −33.9% throughput in the 0.70 experiments, node-set pinning gained +8.63%. The code comments cite the measurement behind each such decision.
  3. Failures are reported, never dressed up as success. 0.91 was a release about exactly this: jobs whose results couldn't be saved, replicated, or delivered by webhook previously ended as completed. They now fail loudly, with an errors endpoint. 1.0 extends the rule to the API surface: options the engine cannot honor are rejected (unknown MCP arguments error; unimplementable Jina headers return UNSUPPORTED_OPTION), and the release notes carry a Known limits section that lists what isn't tested and what doesn't work — including security caveats.

Performance (re-measured 2026-11-04)

Workload PageSift 1.0 Fastest rival Gap
PDF → Markdown, olmOCR-bench 1,269 pages, single thread 2.4 ms/page pypdf 50.0 ms/page ×20.8
HTML → Markdown, 600 documents 0.24 ms/page Turndown 1.9 ms/page ×8.1
Main content, Firecrawl 597 pages, single thread p50 1.0 ms/page crw 7.4 ms/page ×7.3
Office / e-books, 81 files 93.6 files/s Kreuzberg 19.5 ×4.8
Wide crawl, 200 sites × 100 pages, unthrottled 3,500–4,400 pages/s, 280–316 MB peak Spider 2,000–2,700 pages/s, 5.5 GB —

Honest footnotes, because they matter: competitor numbers are the recorded late-October runs, not re-run for this release; and the workloads where PageSift loses are listed in the same document ("Largest gaps") — e.g. a single-host replay looks slow mostly because of the default 1-second per-host politeness interval, which is policy, not engine speed. Full data and reproduction scripts live in the repo (docs/benchmarks.md, benchmarks/).

Battle-tested once, properly

In late October an external team integrated PageSift into their production system and immediately hit a real bug: the official Node binding required a newer glibc than their server had (2.32). 0.81.5 fixed it — build baseline lowered to glibc 2.28, plus a release gate that fails the release if any artifact exceeds it. A user found it; the project fixed it and made it impossible to reintroduce silently. That's the workflow 1.0 is built around.

Who it's for / not for

For: teams feeding RAG or agent pipelines who want a self-hosted Firecrawl/Jina alternative without per-page pricing, and anyone who needs web pages, PDFs and Office files in one pipeline.

Not for: people who need a hosted cloud API (PageSift is self-hosted; a hosted version is not part of 1.0), or bypassing hard anti-bot targets (robots.txt and politeness are respected; captchas are reported, not solved).

PageSift is a solo project. It exists because the crawler feeding my other project was too slow and not clean enough, so I wrote my own. 1.0 closes the feature list. What I want next is more production workloads breaking it in interesting ways.

Repo: https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift — AGPL-3.0, commercial licensing available. Issues and head-to-head benchmarks welcome, good or bad.

title: Diagnose slow LCP on phones: field-first, split into subparts, and prove user-visible impact
description:
When phones report slow LCP, the practical question is not “how do I speed up the site” but “which visible element are users waiting for, and which stage of its load path dominates?”

Implementation (overview)

  • Start with field data (CrUX, Search Console, or your RUM) to confirm the complaint on phones and to identify the affecting URL and likely LCP element. Field data answers whether real users see a problem; don’t skip it.
  • Reproduce the same phone-sized viewport and content state in a lab trace to gather navigation and resource timings that explain why the field signal exists.
  • Break LCP into four subparts: Time to First Byte (TTFB), resource discovery/load delay, resource download duration, and element render delay. Each subpart points at a different ownership domain (server, markup/priority, asset size/network, or client rendering).
  • Map the dominant subpart to the smallest useful fix: server or CDN work for TTFB; preload or earlier markup for discovery delay; file format/size or CDN for download duration; reduce render-blocking CSS/JS or avoid hidden-state logic for render delay.
  • Apply a single, targeted change and re-measure the same element on the same phone state. Compare subpart distributions, not just the headline LCP number.

Expected behavior

  • You’ll get a clear diagnosis explaining which part of the load path caused the visible delay on phones. A well-targeted change should shorten the dominant subpart in lab traces and, when broadly rolled out, align with field improvements for the tested page.
  • The article includes a small helper that computes the breakdown and returns a recommendation tied to the dominant subpart.

Limitations

  • This workflow is page- and content-shape specific. A fix for a hero-image landing page may not apply to a text-heavy page with the same LCP score but a different dominant subpart.
  • Lab traces explain causality but are sensitive to device, CPU contention, and network variability. Always anchor claims to field evidence when possible.

The server will insert a verified implementation example that computes the breakdown and chooses a recommendation for the dominant subpart.

Working example 

export function analyzeLCP({ navigationTiming, lcpEntry, resourceTiming } = {}) {
  if (!navigationTiming || typeof navigationTiming.responseStart !== 'number') {
    throw new TypeError('navigationTiming with numeric responseStart required');
  }
  if (typeof lcpEntry?.renderTime !== 'number') {
    throw new TypeError('lcpEntry with numeric renderTime required');
  }

  const navigationStart = typeof navigationTiming.navigationStart === 'number'
    ? navigationTiming.navigationStart
    : 0;

  const ttfb = Math.max(0, navigationTiming.responseStart - navigationStart);

  const hasResource = Boolean(
    resourceTiming &&
    typeof resourceTiming.startTime === 'number' &&
    typeof resourceTiming.responseEnd === 'number'
  );

  let resourceLoadDelay = 0;
  let resourceLoadDuration = 0;
  let elementRenderDelay = 0;

  if (hasResource) {
    resourceLoadDelay = Math.max(0, resourceTiming.startTime - navigationTiming.responseStart);
    resourceLoadDuration = Math.max(0, resourceTiming.responseEnd - resourceTiming.startTime);
    elementRenderDelay = Math.max(0, lcpEntry.renderTime - resourceTiming.responseEnd);
  } else {
    elementRenderDelay = Math.max(0, lcpEntry.renderTime - navigationTiming.responseStart);
  }

  const totalLcpMs = ttfb + resourceLoadDelay + resourceLoadDuration + elementRenderDelay;
  const parts = [
    { name: 'ttfb', ms: ttfb },
    { name: 'resourceLoadDelay', ms: resourceLoadDelay },
    { name: 'resourceLoadDuration', ms: resourceLoadDuration },
    { name: 'elementRenderDelay', ms: elementRenderDelay },
  ];

  // When two parts tie, prefer the part that better maps to a developer-actionable
  // front-end intervention. In practice we want elementRenderDelay to win ties
  // with ttfb so that zero-resource LCPs attribute dominance to rendering.
  const priority = {
    ttfb: 1,
    resourceLoadDelay: 2,
    resourceLoadDuration: 3,
    elementRenderDelay: 4,
  };

  const dominant = parts.reduce((a, b) => {
    if (a.ms > b.ms) return a;
    if (b.ms > a.ms) return b;
    // tie: choose higher priority
    return priority[a.name] >= priority[b.name] ? a : b;
  });

  const recommendations = {
    ttfb: 'Improve server TTFB: reduce backend work, cache HTML, or use a CDN.',
    resourceLoadDelay: 'Start loading the LCP resource earlier: improve discovery or preload it.',
    resourceLoadDuration: 'Reduce the resource size or use a more efficient format.',
    elementRenderDelay: 'Reduce render-blocking CSS/JS and avoid hiding the LCP element.',
  };

  return {
    totalLcpMs,
    breakdown: parts,
    dominantSubpart: dominant.name,
    recommendation: recommendations[dominant.name],
  };
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/diagnose-slow-lcp-on-phones
