title: “Available” Is Not Booked: A Race-Safe Contract for AI Property Viewings
description:
“Available” Is Not Booked: A Race-Safe Contract for AI Property Viewings

A voice agent can identify a property, understand a caller, read a calendar, and still create a bad appointment. The dangerous gap is between “the slot looked free” and “the booking system committed it.” If two calls cross that gap, both callers can hear a confident confirmation while only one viewing can happen. The decision rule is simple: say “confirmed” only after the system that owns the viewing has durably accepted one specific booking, under a conflict rule that also applies to concurrent requests. Our real-estate agency overview describes the voice-agent use case; this guide adds the operational contract a buyer should demand before letting an agent confirm viewings.

The useful question is not “Can the agent find open times?” It is “What happens when two people choose the same time, a tool call is repeated, the calendar response is lost, or the listing’s overlap policy changes?” The answer should be visible in the state model, database constraint, tool response, caller wording, and audit receipt—not left to a prompt instruction such as “do not double book.”

The decision: approve a booking only on a committed receipt

A product demo often shows a happy path: a caller asks for a viewing, the agent offers a time, the caller agrees, and a calendar card appears. Product pages make similar claims. Listline, for example, says it checks real availability and books showings directly to a calendar. Those statements describe intended capability, not the concurrency semantics behind a write. They do not tell a buyer whether an offer is a temporary hold, whether simultaneous requests are serialized, or what the agent says after a timeout. Treat the distinction as a procurement question, not an accusation about a vendor.

Google Calendar’s FreeBusy endpoint returns free/busy information for a set of calendars. Microsoft Graph’s getSchedule endpoint likewise returns availability information. These are valuable reads, but neither endpoint description says that reading an open interval reserves it. The act that writes an event is a separate operation. Therefore, a caller must not hear “you are booked” merely because an availability lookup returned an empty busy interval. Google’s FreeBusy reference and Microsoft’s getSchedule documentation support that narrow distinction.

The system should give the agent a result with an explicit status such as confirmed, conflict, pending_reconciliation, or rejected. The agent translates that status into a sentence. It must never infer a stronger outcome than the scheduler returned. If the write outcome is unknown, say that the request is being checked and provide a reference or a callback path; do not silently create another event or offer a different time while the first write may still exist.

What a viewing booking actually commits

A viewing is not just a start time. It binds a property, a date and time, the person or team responsible for access, a duration, a buffer rule, and often an attendee or contact record. A valid contract names which system owns each field. The listing system may own property status and showing rules; a scheduling service may own the booking; a calendar may mirror it; a CRM may store the prospect and follow-up. If two systems can both accept the same slot independently, a “calendar connected” badge does not settle the source-of-truth question.

Write down the conflict key before testing. For a simple one-agent, one-property showing, it could be (property_id, agent_id, start_time, duration). If the seller permits a fixed capacity of two concurrent showings, the guard must represent that capacity instead of assuming one. If one appointment consumes several resources—property access, an agent, a key holder, or a room—every constrained resource must be checked and committed as one logical operation. Reserving only the agent’s calendar while the listing calendar remains writable leaves a second path around the rule.

The slot’s time representation also belongs in the contract. Keep an unambiguous instant, the property’s local time zone, the intended duration, and the displayed local time. Ask the caller to clarify an ambiguous “Saturday at nine” before writing. Test daylight-saving transitions, because a local clock label can be skipped or repeated when the offset changes. A proper confirmation repeats the property and local date, time, and time zone; a bare “tomorrow morning” is not a durable receipt.

Finally, decide whether overlap is a conflict or a business rule. ShowingTime’s help material notes that some markets allow overlapping showings and may also enforce buffer time. That is a useful contradiction to the blanket slogan “no double bookings”: a safe system enforces the listing’s configured capacity, which may be one, several, or intentionally unrestricted. See ShowingTime’s explanation of overlapping appointments and buffers.

A state machine that prevents a spoken promise from outrunning the write

Use explicit states, and give each state one permitted caller message. The lifecycle separates discovering an option from committing it. OFFERED is not a hold; COMMITTING is not confirmation; UNKNOWN is not failure. These distinctions matter whenever an API call can time out after the other system has saved the event.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> REQUESTED
  REQUESTED --> OFFERED: fresh availability read
  OFFERED --> SELECTED: caller chooses exact slot
  SELECTED --> COMMITTING: stable request key
  COMMITTING --> CONFIRMED: authoritative durable success
  COMMITTING --> CONFLICT: write rejected as occupied
  COMMITTING --> UNKNOWN: timeout or lost response
  UNKNOWN --> CONFIRMED: reconcile finds same booking
  UNKNOWN --> CONFLICT: reconcile finds competing booking
  UNKNOWN --> COMMITTING: retry same intent and same key
  CONFLICT --> OFFERED: refresh and offer alternatives
  CONFIRMED --> CANCEL_PENDING: caller requests cancellation
  CANCEL_PENDING --> CANCELLED: cancellation confirmed
  CONFIRMED --> RESCHEDULE_PENDING: caller requests a move
  RESCHEDULE_PENDING --> CONFIRMED: replacement committed, old slot released

REQUESTED means the caller has identified the property and requested a time. Capture only what is necessary to find the listing and respond. OFFERED means the scheduler returned candidates at a particular time. It is a snapshot with a timestamp and source, not an entitlement to the slot. SELECTED means the caller chose one exact candidate and the agent has echoed the local date and time back for confirmation.

COMMITTING begins when the application sends a write using a stable key for this logical request. A duplicate tool call, transport retry, or worker retry must carry the same key. When the calendar service gives a durable success response and the application stores the event identifier and listing reference, the state can become CONFIRMED. If a provider has an explicit hold operation, the contract must say when that hold expires and whether it blocks other booking channels. Do not call a best-effort event insert a hold.

CONFLICT means the authoritative write rejected the request under its configured rule. Refresh availability, offer new candidates, and obtain a new choice. Do not auto-select the next slot without caller approval. UNKNOWN means the client did not learn the outcome. The write could have succeeded even though the response was lost. Search by the stable request key or provider event ID, reconcile, and only then decide whether to retry. If the provider cannot support reliable reconciliation, route to a person and use cautious language.

A cancellation or reschedule is another transaction, not a text edit. During a move, preserve the existing confirmed appointment until the replacement is committed, unless the business explicitly prefers releasing first and accepting the risk of losing both slots. Log which policy applies. If the replacement write becomes unknown, reconcile it before canceling the old event. This avoids ending with neither a confirmed time nor a clear explanation.

The race window: availability is a read, conflict prevention belongs at commit

The classic failure is a check-then-act sequence. Request A reads “free.” Request B reads “free.” A writes an event. B writes an event. Both decisions were locally reasonable, but no shared rule serialized the writes. Refreshing availability just before insertion narrows the interval in which this can happen. It does not, on its own, make the read and write atomic. Cronofy’s guidance recommends checking availability again after the user chooses a slot, which is a useful mitigation; a buyer should still ask what the booking endpoint does if two final checks overlap. A second read is a risk reduction, not proof of exclusivity. Cronofy describes this race window.

The strongest guard belongs where the booking is committed. If you own a relational database, use a transaction plus a uniqueness or exclusion rule that reflects the business conflict. PostgreSQL documents unique constraints over a set of columns and exclusion constraints for conflicts between values; its transaction documentation also explains that Serializable transactions can fail and must be retried. Do not rely on an application-level “SELECT, then INSERT” alone: two callers can both pass the check before either insert commits. The database must decide which competing write wins. See PostgreSQL constraints and transaction isolation.

For fixed-length slots with one appointment per listing and time, an illustrative schema can make duplicate intent and occupied slots separate constraints:

CREATE TABLE viewing_booking (
  booking_id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  request_key text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  property_id text NOT NULL,
  agent_id text NOT NULL,
  starts_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  ends_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN
    ('held', 'confirmed', 'cancelled', 'expired')),
  provider_event_id text,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CHECK (ends_at > starts_at)
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_live_booking_per_property_agent_start
  ON viewing_booking (property_id, agent_id, starts_at)
  WHERE status IN ('held', 'confirmed');

-- Choose an exact-slot or interval-overlap constraint that matches
-- listing policy; do not copy this key blindly.

That example only blocks identical start instants for the same property and agent. It does not block overlapping intervals with different start times. If the rule is “one live showing at a time,” a range/exclusion constraint or a serializable transaction over the actual interval may be more appropriate. If overlapping showings are allowed up to a capacity, a counter with atomic updates or reservation model must enforce that capacity under concurrent writes. The code is a design sketch, not a drop-in migration; test database extensions, resource keys, cancellation semantics, and provider capabilities before production.

A booking service that delegates writes to an external calendar may not be able to wrap the calendar and CRM in one database transaction. In that case, use a durable workflow record: create a request with a unique idempotency key, call the provider, persist the response, then update local state. If the provider succeeds but the local write fails, query the provider using the stored key or event identity before retrying. If it does not expose a lookup or idempotent write, mark the outcome unknown and queue reconciliation. A distributed transaction is not created just because two API calls appear in one function.

Idempotency: retries should return the same booking, not another one

A caller can repeat a request after silence. A speech tool can be emitted twice. Middleware can retry on a network error. The correct behavior depends on whether the repeated call represents the same logical intent. Assign a stable request key when the caller selects a specific slot—derived from a random identifier stored against that intent, not merely from the spoken phrase. Reuse that key through retries and reconciliation. A new caller choice, a new property, or a new time is a new intent and therefore receives a new key.

Google’s Calendar create-event guide explains that a client-supplied event ID can prevent duplicate event creation if a request fails after the Calendar backend has executed it. Google’s error guidance documents a duplicate-ID 409. That is an idempotency building block, not a slot-capacity lock: two different IDs can still represent two events at the same time unless a separate booking policy prevents them. See Google’s create-events guide and Calendar API errors.

Google’s SRE discussion of distributed periodic jobs makes the broader point: external side effects that may be retried after partial failure need idempotent behavior, and some systems prefer skipping a launch to risking a duplicate. A viewing workflow should use the same discipline. The side effect is not merely “call the calendar”; it is “create one appointment for this request key, under the current listing policy, and return the same outcome when asked again.” The SRE chapter on periodic scheduling and idempotency provides the reliability framing.

A response timeout is the hard case. The application sends the write; the calendar commits; the network drops before the response arrives. If the workflow now creates a fresh key and retries, it may create a second event. Instead, retain the original key and reconcile. If the booking is found, return its existing confirmation. If it is absent and the provider can authoritatively establish absence, retry with the same key. If the answer remains uncertain, do not confirm and do not issue a different booking automatically. Return pending_reconciliation to the agent, which can tell the caller that the request is being checked and promise a response channel, not an appointment.

What the public evidence does and does not show

Search results and product pages frequently emphasize “real availability,” direct calendar booking, and no double-booking. Listline’s page is a useful example of the promise buyers encounter. A vendor video hosted on Vimeo presents a real-estate assistant handling an inquiry and showing a transcript and CRM update after the call. That format can help a buyer judge conversation and visible post-call evidence. A single happy-path clip cannot establish simultaneous-request behavior, duplicate-tool suppression, stale availability handling, or the response after a lost write. Treat it as a demonstration, not a reliability test.

There is a concrete user question in Retell’s public support community: a report describes repeated booking tool calls after a streaming timeout. The thread reports five identical calls reaching an endpoint concurrently, with several writes succeeding and the flow then creating additional times. The vendor response attributes the incident to missing de-duplication of concurrent calls and recommends a concurrency-safe backend guard such as a unique constraint or short-lived lock. This is one public incident report, not a prevalence study, vendor-wide defect rate, or proof that the same failure occurs in every integration. It does expose a test a buyer can reproduce: one confirmed choice, duplicate parallel tool calls, and a timeout near the write. Read the Retell support thread.

Forrester’s 2026 practitioner discussion describes conversational agents taking on more complex actions while emphasizing controls, implementation effort, and backend testing. Its blog reports practitioner interviews, useful qualitative evidence about deployment work; it is not a benchmark of real-estate appointment correctness. The implication for a buyer is modest: assess the application and integration, not just the model’s speech. Forrester’s lessons from practitioners.

The recommendation is an inference from those sources: conversation quality, availability visibility, and transaction integrity are separate capabilities. A supplier may be excellent at the first two while relying on an external calendar that cannot reserve a slot atomically. Ask for evidence of the write contract and the unknown-outcome recovery path. If the answer is “the prompt tells the model to call once,” the core control is not present. A prompt can reduce duplicate calls; it cannot serialize concurrent requests emitted by separate calls or processes.

Keep three statements separate during a review. Fact: Google and Microsoft document availability reads separately from event creation, and the Retell community thread records one reported duplicate-write incident. Inference: a read-only availability response cannot, by itself, prove that a later write will win a conflict. Recommendation: require the commit boundary to enforce the listing’s capacity rule and require the agent to speak only from the resulting status. The sources support the distinction; the 12-case suite below is an original test proposal, not a measured result.

A 12-case acceptance suite for a property-viewing agent

The following is an original synthetic test asset, designed on 4 November 2026. It contains 12 proposed cases; no live agent, calendar, CRM, customer record, or production booking was exercised. The cases are deliberately small enough for a staging run and broad enough to test consequential distinctions. The suite does not estimate failure frequency, prove legal compliance, or compare vendors. For each test, use synthetic properties, contacts, and calendar data; capture the caller transcript, tool request, tool response, scheduler event, CRM row, and final user-facing message. A case passes only when those artifacts tell the same story.

# Setup Expected result Evidence to retain
1 One open slot; one caller selects it One durable booking; only then say confirmed Provider event ID, request key, matching transcript
2 Two callers select the same single-capacity slot concurrently Exactly one succeeds; the other gets conflict and fresh alternatives Both requests, commit times, one live booking
3 Same request key submitted twice concurrently Both responses resolve to the same booking ID; no second appointment Idempotency ledger and provider records
4 Calendar commits, but response is deliberately dropped State becomes unknown; reconciliation finds event before confirmation Timeout trace, lookup, final state transition
5 Calendar rejects write because another agent just booked No success claim and no automatic next-time choice Conflict response and caller’s new choice
6 Listing is blocked after availability lookup Write-side policy rejects or holds safely; refresh before re-offering Before/after availability and authoritative response
7 Slot touches a daylight-saving transition or ambiguous local time Caller hears an unambiguous local time; stored instant is correct Time zone, UTC instant, displayed wording
8 Listing permits two concurrent showings with a defined capacity First two commits follow policy; next is rejected atomically Policy version and capacity ledger
9 Listing disallows overlap and requires a buffer Adjacent appointments violating buffer are rejected Interval rule, rejected range, fresh options
10 Reschedule write times out after possible commit Reconcile new booking before releasing old one Old/new event IDs and state history
11 Caller asks to cancel after confirmation Cancellation is confirmed only after durable cancel result Cancellation receipt and caller wording
12 Provider is unavailable or returns an unclassified error No success claim; retain request key and route to follow-up Error, retry policy, human task, promised callback

Use the suite in two passes. First, call each scenario once to check basic state transitions. Second, repeat the concurrency and timeout cases with parallel requests and deliberate network fault injection. The suite specifies expected behavior; it does not claim that those tests were run or that a vendor passes them. A buyer can add cases for multiple calendars, access instructions, property status changes, and caller corrections without changing the central rule: only the authoritative commit creates confirmation.

The transaction receipt the agent should receive

Do not return only free-text such as “looks good” or “try 10:30.” Return a typed result that makes it difficult for the model to overstate the outcome. The exact schema depends on the scheduler, but it should carry request identity, status, listing reference, local time zone, and any booking ID needed for reconciliation. Keep sensitive caller data out of tool output unless the next step needs it.

{
  "request_key": "req_01J...",
  "status": "confirmed",
  "property_ref": "listing_7842",
  "starts_at": "2026-11-07T10:30:00+01:00",
  "time_zone": "Europe/Paris",
  "ends_at": "2026-11-07T11:00:00+01:00",
  "booking_id": "book_91f...",
  "provider_event_id": "evt_7c2...",
  "policy_version": "showing-policy-12",
  "committed_at": "2026-11-04T09:18:11Z"
}

The sample values are illustrative, not observed data. For conflict, return no confirmation ID and include a signal that availability must be refreshed. For pending_reconciliation, keep the same request_key, return the last known status and next-check instruction, and prevent a second fresh booking attempt. For rejected, distinguish a business-rule refusal from a technical failure. For cancelled, return the appointment reference and completed cancellation state. A response contract is useful only if the service records the same state and the agent’s wording is conditional on it.

A compact tool handler might look like this:

async function bookViewing(command) {
  const result = await scheduler.commit({
    requestKey: command.requestKey,       // stable across retries
    propertyId: command.propertyId,
    agentId: command.agentId,
    startsAt: command.startsAt,
    timeZone: command.timeZone,
    expectedPolicyVersion: command.policyVersion
  });
  if (result.status === 'confirmed') {
    return { status: 'confirmed', bookingId: result.bookingId,
      localTime: result.localTime, timeZone: result.timeZone };
  }
  if (result.status === 'conflict') return { status: 'conflict' };
  if (result.status === 'unknown') return { status: 'pending_reconciliation',
    requestKey: command.requestKey };
  return { status: 'rejected', reasonCode: result.reasonCode };
}

This is an interface sketch. The scheduler.commit implementation must enforce idempotency and concurrency at the write boundary; wrapping a read followed by an unguarded calendar insert in JavaScript does not make it safe. The prompt should say “announce a booking only for confirmed,” but the system must enforce that behavior in tool-result handling and test it in the transcript.

Privacy, fairness, and property-specific boundaries

A viewing request needs enough information to identify the listing, coordinate a time, and contact the caller about the appointment. It rarely needs an unbounded transcript to complete that booking. The UK Government’s Data and AI Ethics Framework says projects should map data flows, explain what personal data is used and why, and consider minimisation, retention, and access. That guidance is not a substitute for the law that applies in every country; it is a practical control source for teams. See the Government framework.

Set a retention rule for audio, transcripts, extracted contact details, and booking records separately. A calendar needs the event and contact channel; a debugging workflow may need a short-lived redacted trace; neither automatically justifies indefinite audio retention. Decide who can view transcripts, whether they are used for model improvement, how a caller can correct a wrong time or phone number, and how to delete data that is no longer needed. Do not put full call transcripts into a calendar description if a short reference and operational note are sufficient.

Real-estate agents also need to constrain answers about protected characteristics and neighborhood demographics. The booking assistant should answer listing facts from an approved source, collect appointment logistics, and route questions that require professional judgment to a human. Do not let the model infer suitability, eligibility, safety, or neighborhood composition from a caller’s accent, name, family status, or other proxy. This guide is not legal advice and does not decide which housing or privacy rules apply to a specific agency. Have local counsel or a qualified compliance owner validate configured rules and notices.

The privacy and fairness boundary should affect test fixtures. Use synthetic phone numbers and fictional listings. Do not paste actual caller recordings into prompts, public bug reports, or vendor support threads. Confirm that logs needed to prove a booking do not expose more personal data than the people maintaining the integration need to see. A good receipt proves the transaction without replicating the entire conversation.

Failure modes to look for in a demo or pilot

The model says “confirmed” before the tool returns. This is a release blocker. The expected message after selection is a neutral “I’m placing that request now”; confirmation follows only after a durable confirmed result. If the agent speaks while the tool runs, interrupt the flow in test and verify that it does not promise the outcome prematurely.

A timeout creates a new request key. This defeats idempotency. Retry the same operation with the same key, then reconcile before creating anything else. A vendor that cannot show how a repeated key maps back to an existing event should not make unconditional confirmations.

The database check is a separate SELECT. A check followed by a write can race. Look for a unique constraint, exclusion rule, lock, or provider guarantee that covers the actual resource and interval. Ask for two simultaneous requests in staging and their resulting records, not just a screenshot of a busy calendar.

The fallback books a different slot automatically. A conflict should return control to the caller. It is not permission for the agent to choose the next time. A new time is a new decision and should receive a fresh confirmation and request key.

The calendar and CRM disagree. The calendar may contain an event while the CRM has no appointment, or the CRM may say booked while the event write failed. Define which system is authoritative, record external IDs, and run reconciliation. Do not mark both systems complete in one code path without checking each result.

Cancellation releases one system but not another. If the caller requests cancellation, reconcile calendar and CRM state. If one write fails, give the caller an honest partial outcome and create a human follow-up task. A canceled status should not be inferred from a successful speech act or a notification being queued.

The policy is too strict or too loose. A universal “no overlap” rule can block a listing that intentionally allows group showings. A universal “overlap is fine” rule can schedule two private tours when an owner requires exclusive access. Tie the constraint to a versioned property policy, including capacity and buffers, and test policy changes during an active booking flow.

Local time looks right but maps to the wrong instant. Preserve the time zone and repeat it in the caller’s local terms. Test repeated and skipped clock times around daylight-saving transitions. If a caller gives an ambiguous date, ask rather than guess.

A support ticket contains personal data. Reproduce with synthetic contacts and redact identifiers before sharing traces. Technical success does not justify exposing recordings or phone numbers broadly. Use a transaction receipt, sanitized request ID, and artificial listing.

A happy-path video is treated as a test report. A polished call can show usability and the shape of a receipt. It cannot establish retries, simultaneous commits, cancellation, time-zone handling, or outage behavior. Ask for exact inputs, API responses, final records, and expected-versus-actual results.

A practical buyer’s decision matrix

Use this table to decide whether to proceed, run a bounded pilot, or block autonomous confirmation. These are decision rules, not a weighted score or benchmark. A missing hard control can outweigh a fluent voice because the impact is a false promise to a caller.

Evidence you can inspect Proceed to controlled pilot Keep human confirmation Block confirmation automation
Slot ownership One named system owns final booking Ownership is split but manually reconciled No team can say which system wins
Concurrent requests One winner, one conflict, constraint shown in records Conflict is recoverable with staff follow-up Both requests can commit unnoticed
Retry behavior Same key returns same appointment Unknown state routes to staff Retry creates another event without lookup
Caller wording Only durable success produces “confirmed” Agent says request received; staff confirms Agent confirms on free/busy alone
Listing policy Capacity and buffer are versioned per listing Some exceptions require staff review Fixed rule contradicts listing settings
Outage response Unknown state is reconciled and tracked Callback has a named owner and deadline Silent failure or false success
Record alignment Calendar, CRM, and receipt share IDs One system lags with a repair queue Statuses disagree and no repair is visible
Privacy Minimal data, access and retention defined Review needed before live use Real calls copied into unapproved tools

Proceed only after hard transaction cases pass in staging. A bounded pilot can begin with one agent, fictional listings, and a limited time window, then move to staff-supervised calls if the operational owner agrees. Define a stop condition: any duplicate event, unsupported confirmation, untracked unknown outcome, or mismatch between caller message and saved record pauses autonomous booking until the failure is understood. Track counts of state outcomes, but do not call them a success rate until the denominator and exclusions are defined.

Rollout and ownership

Start with read-only mode. Let the agent retrieve property facts and candidate slots, but have a person execute the write. Save the proposed time and availability timestamp so the team can see whether the agent selected a stale slot. This tests conversation and entity mapping without creating customer commitments.

Next, run synthetic write tests in a sandbox. Include two concurrent callers, repeated tool invocation, dropped responses, rejected writes, reschedule, and cancellation. Verify provider records, not only the transcript. Keep test calendars separate from staff calendars, and ensure notifications cannot reach real clients.

Then allow requests to remain pending for human confirmation. This reveals whether calendar, CRM, contact identity, event duration, time zone, access instructions, and listing policy are mapped correctly. Staff should see the exact transaction state and confirm or correct it without losing the original request key.

Move to autonomous confirmation only when the service enforces conflict handling and idempotency, an unknown result can be reconciled, and the owner has reviewed logs and caller wording. The operator responsible for calendar permissions should also own revocation when staff or vendors change. Keep an exception review and a way to stop new writes without disabling the phone line; a safe fallback can capture the request and arrange a callback.

For each release, keep an evidence packet: agent and tool-schema versions, listing policy version, test cases and results, redacted receipts, metrics definitions, recovery owner, and rollback method. Forrester’s practitioner discussion emphasizes that production work extends beyond the model and needs controls and testing around backend integrations. That is qualitative commentary, not a measured guarantee. Use it as a reminder to assign an integration owner, not as proof that a particular vendor is safe.

Checklist before an agent confirms a viewing

  • Is the correct listing identified and still bookable?
  • Does the caller hear the exact local date, time, duration, and property before the write?
  • Does one system own the final conflict rule?
  • Can simultaneous requests produce at most the configured capacity?
  • Does a repeated request key return the same booking?
  • Is a timeout treated as unknown and reconciled before retry?
  • Is the agent forbidden from choosing a replacement slot without the caller?
  • Do cancellation and reschedule have explicit transaction states?
  • Do calendar, CRM, and caller receipt share the same identifiers?
  • Are logs minimal, access-controlled, and retained only as needed?
  • Have synthetic concurrency and failure cases passed in staging?
  • Can an operator pause writes and keep a human callback path open?

The operational conclusion is narrow: an AI agent may find times and conduct a natural conversation, but only the system that durably commits a booking can confirm it. If a vendor cannot explain how two simultaneous requests, one repeated tool call, and one lost response resolve at the write boundary, leave confirmation with a person. If it can demonstrate those states with a reusable suite and auditable receipts, run a controlled pilot and measure exceptions before expanding scope.

For a deployment that falls within the EU framework, consult the European Commission’s official AI Act overview for the current framework and implementation context. This reference does not determine whether a particular viewing assistant is high-risk or which obligations apply; that depends on the actual use, role, and deployment facts, so obtain a qualified assessment for the specific system.

title: I Built a Database Explorer That Can't Ruin Your Friday
description:
Every developer has a database horror story.

Mine usually starts with a terminal, a production connection string,
and the words "quick fix". It ends with someone saying "so... do we
have backups?" in a very quiet voice.

So I built DBAdminer: a database explorer that starts in
read-only mode, because it assumes you're tired, caffeinated,
and one typo away from a postmortem.

What is it?

A database explorer for Go. Point it at PostgreSQL, MySQL,
MariaDB, or SQLite, open your browser, and poke around: tables,
data, a SQL console, the works.

Full access is there when you want it, but you have to ask for it.
Like the sudo of database tools.

Get it running in 30 seconds

Grab a binary from GitHub Releases (Linux, macOS, Windows,
amd64 and arm64), then:

dbadminer --dsn 'postgres://user:pass@127.0.0.1:5432/app?sslmode=disable'

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080. Done. No installer, no runtime,
no 47-step setup wiki.

Already have DATABASE_URL exported? Just run dbadminer.
It also understands PG* vars, MYSQL_*, DB_*, and
Docker-style POSTGRES_*. It'll find your database the way a
dog finds a dropped sandwich.

"Read-only" actually means read-only

Not "we hid the delete button" read-only. Properly:

  • Only one SELECT, WITH, EXPLAIN, VALUES, TABLE, or SHOW per request
  • INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, ALTER, DROP are rejected before they reach your database
  • Postgres, MySQL, and MariaDB also run queries in a read-only transaction, a second lock on the door
  • SQLite opens with mode=ro
  • The write UIs stay hidden, and the write APIs return 403

Belt, suspenders, and a rope.

When you really need to change things:

dbadminer --access=full

Now you get create/alter/drop dialogs, index and foreign-key
actions, and row editing in the grid. Use it wisely. Or at
least not on a Friday.

Don't want another app? Embed it.

This is my favorite part. If you already have a *sql.DB,
DBAdminer lives right next to it:

cfg := dbadminer.DefaultConfig()
ex, err := dbadminer.New(db, cfg)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
if err := ex.ListenAndServe(ctx); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

The library imports only the standard library. The CLI is a
separate module, so importing DBAdminer won't drag a pile of
database drivers into your go.mod. Your dependency graph
stays calm.

You can also mount ex.Handler() on your own server. There are
examples for net/http, chi, and cobra.

Docker, because of course 

docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  -e DATABASE_URL='postgres://postgres:5432/app?sslmode=disable' \
  dbadminer

Need several databases at once? Set DBADMINER_DATABASES=shop,app
and give each name its own prefixed variables
(SHOP_DATABASE_URL, APP_DB_USER, and so on). The README has
a full Compose example.

Paranoid by design

A tool that connects to your database should be a little
suspicious of everyone, so:

  • Binds to loopback (127.0.0.1) by default
  • Rejects requests with a non-loopback Host header
  • Checks that Origin matches
  • Optional basic auth for the page (--user / --password)
  • Limits for rows, query timeout, request body, and response size

Why I built it

It started with a simple wish: I just want to look at my database.

That's it. No grand plan. I was working on a project, I needed
to see some tables, and I wanted something Adminer-like. Easy,
right?

Reader, it was not easy.

  • Paid tools: great, but I wasn't looking to open my wallet to view a table.
  • DBeaver: it kept trying to download drivers, and where I work (behind a firewall), it kept asking me about it with pop-ups. Pop-up. Pop-up. Pop-up. I started to feel like the tool was trying to tell me something.
  • Beekeeper Studio: a trial, and one more closed-source desktop app to install and run.

What I really wanted was boring and simple: a tiny image I
can drop into my existing docker-compose.yml and forget about.
docker compose up, open a browser tab, done. No installers.
No driver downloads. No "please sign in to continue".

So I built exactly that. DBAdminer is one small Go binary (or
image) that sits next to your database like a polite houseguest.

Safety is the server's job, not the login form's

Most admin tools work like this: type the right username and
password, and you get the keys to everything.

DBAdminer works differently. The server decides what's
allowed, not whoever logged in.

  • It starts read-only. The mode is set in your config (--access or DBADMINER_ACCESS), not by what the browser asks for.
  • Write statements are rejected server-side before they reach your database, and the write APIs return 403.
  • Basic auth (--user / --password) only protects the page. It never turns on write access.

So even if someone gets into the page, they can look but not
touch. Want to allow writes? That's a deliberate decision, made
in your config and not by a button in the UI.

Try it, break it, tell me about it

⭐ Repo: https://github.com/dbadminer/dbadminer

Found a bug? Want MSSQL, dark mode, or a feature I haven't
thought of? Open an issue or send a PR. And if you try it, tell
me in the comments what database you pointed it at.

(If it's production, I hope you stayed read-only.)

title: Does useActionState preserve input? Nine comparisons with manual form state
description:
useActionState manages an Action's result and pending status. It does not automatically preserve input values. In this fixture, returning a validation-error result still cleared the uncontrolled input.

The Action version was compared with ordinary onSubmit handling and useState, then a change to retain invalid input was tested. The state holding an Action result and the input that should remain after a failure each need a design decision.

Call the same operation through an Action and onSubmit

This is the synthetic save operation. It sends no network request; browser test controls resolve its Promise. trace records call order and pending operations for the experiment.

async function save(previous, formData) {
  const name = formData.get('name');
  trace.calls.push({ previous: { ...previous }, name });
  await new Promise(resolve => trace.gates.push(resolve));
  if (name === 'crash') throw new Error('simulated failure');
  if (name === 'bad') return { ...previous, message: 'invalid' };
  return { count: previous.count + 1, message: `saved:${name}` };
}

good returns success, bad returns a validation-error result, and crash throws. The first argument is previous, and the second is FormData.

The Action version receives state, formAction, and pending from useActionState(save, initialState), then passes formAction to the form's action prop. Its input is uncontrolled with defaultValue="". The useActionState reference defines the previous-result argument and the pending return value.

The manual version calls the same save operation from onSubmit:

async function onSubmit(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
    const data = new FormData(event.currentTarget);
    setPending(true);
    try { setState(await save(state, data)); }
    catch (error) { setState(previous => ({ ...previous, message: error.message })); }
    finally { setPending(false); }
  }

It also uses an uncontrolled input and does not call form.reset on success. It sets pending and result state explicitly and catches exceptions to produce a message. This minimal implementation shows which behavior is written manually; it is not a demonstration of a general limitation of useState.

Returning an error result differed from throwing

The first comparison covered 6 conditions. Every submission showed pending as true and retained the entered text while the operation was held unresolved.

Approach and input Result at completion Input after completion
Action, good count 1, saved:good Empty
Manual, good count 1, saved:good good
Action, bad count 0, invalid Empty
Manual, bad count 0, invalid bad
Action, crash Moves to Error Boundary Form removed
Manual, crash count 0, caught message crash

Although the Action returned invalid for bad, its Promise resolved normally. The uncontrolled-input reset after a successful Action, described in the React form reference, also occurred here. An application interpreting a return value as a validation error is different from the Action throwing.

An Error Boundary around the Action version displayed simulated failure instead of the form when save threw. The manual version catches the exception and stores a message, so it does not make the same display transition.

Include the input that needs to survive in the result

This version was added to preserve input after a validation error:

async function saveWithInput(previous, formData) {
  const next = await save(previous, formData);
  return { ...next, input: next.message === 'invalid' ? String(formData.get('name')) : '' };
}
export function PreservingExperiment() {
  const [state, formAction, pending] = useActionState(saveWithInput, { ...initialState, input: '' });
  return <section>
    <output id="action-state">{JSON.stringify(state)}</output>
    <output id="action-pending">{String(pending)}</output>
    <form id="action-form" action={formAction}>
      <input id="action-input" name="name" defaultValue={state.input} />
      <button id="action-submit" disabled={pending}>Save</button>
    </form>
  </section>;
}

On validation failure, it returns the entered value and passes it to the input's defaultValue. On success, it returns an empty string. The additional 2 conditions retained bad after invalid input and cleared the field after good.

The input still is not controlled through value. Including the post-Action default in state preserves the required value after this reset. This is a fix verified inside the experiment, not a form already integrated into an existing application.

Multiple calls wait for the previous result

Another condition dispatched twice from a separate button rather than through form submission:

function queueTwo() {
    startTransition(() => {
      for (const name of ['first', 'second']) {
        const data = new FormData(); data.set('name', name); formAction(data);
      }
    });
  }

Until the first Promise resolved, only one save call was recorded. Resolving it started the second call, whose previous.count was 1. The final state had count 2 and message saved:second.

Observation point Started save calls Count on screen pending
First call unresolved 1 0 true
First resolved, second unresolved 2 0 true
Both resolved 2 2 false

In this experiment, the previous result passed to the next Action differed from the intermediate state already visible on screen. Both call history and DOM state were recorded.

React treats calls through the form action as a Transition. The direct button-dispatch comparison instead calls inside startTransition. Calls outside a Transition and designs expecting this Hook to execute operations in parallel were not tested.

This experiment uses client functions only

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with React and React DOM 19.3.0, Node.js 24.15.0, esbuild 0.28.2, macOS arm64, and Headless Chrome 152. A production build without Strict Mode or React Compiler covered 9 conditions. Pending operations were resolved manually; network latency was not measured.

The experiment excludes Server Functions, submissions before JavaScript loads, permalink behavior, authentication, and persistence. The official API also covers Server Function integration, but these results come from functions running in the browser. Server-side validation and authorization were neither implemented nor tested here.

The comparison code and results for the 9 conditions include whether inputs clear or remain and where thrown errors move the display, as well as pending status and return values.

title: Configure Automatic Error Grouping in Node.js Error Tracking: 5 Reversible Rules
description:
Batch pipelines make it hard to configure automatic error grouping in Node.js error tracking. A nightly run can emit hundreds of failures from one bad input, or one deployment can create dozens of unrelated stack traces. The grouping rule has to compress repeated evidence without hiding a new failure, and it must be possible to undo when the rule is wrong.

It fails quietly.

Short answer: configure automatic grouping around a stable error fingerprint, but derive that fingerprint from normalized type, operation, and source location rather than the raw message. Keep the original message and full stack as searchable event fields. Version the rule, sample the groups before rollout, and retain a fallback to the previous key for rollback.

The example here is a Node.js service that searches structured logs from a nightly developer-tools data pipeline. The practical target is not a prettier error dashboard. It is a grouping scheme that helps an on-call engineer decide whether a failed run is one repairable defect or several defects that must be rolled back independently.

Why does automatic grouping fail on nightly pipelines?

The raw error string is usually the wrong identity. It may contain a customer identifier, a file name, a row number, or a server-generated request ID. Two events from the same defect then become separate groups. The opposite failure is just as dangerous: a rule that removes too much context merges a parser failure with a network timeout because both happen to be thrown as Error.

Nightly work adds a second complication. The batch name and run date are useful for searching, but they are usually poor grouping dimensions. Including run_id creates a new group every night. Including no batch identity at all can merge a schema failure in the billing export with an authentication failure in the index refresh.

The first trap is a successful-looking deduplication report. Suppose a parser starts rejecting a new field after release-42. Every event carries a different row number, so raw-message grouping reports many incidents. A normalizer that removes row numbers fixes that split. A careless normalizer that also removes the operation name can then merge parser errors with failures from the commit stage, making the dashboard quieter while the rollback decision gets less reliable. I keep those fields separate in fixtures because the bad result is easy to miss in aggregate counts.

I start with the rollback question: “If this group grows after a deployment, what evidence would tell me to revert?” That question produces a narrower key than a generic error hash. It also keeps grouping separate from retention, alerting, and log search. A group is an index for related failures; it is not the complete incident record.

OpenTelemetry describes logs as records with a body and attributes, and its signal model is deliberately separate from any one storage product. That separation is useful here: keep the event rich, then calculate a grouping fingerprint as an additional attribute at the error boundary.

The five rules I use for a reversible fingerprint

  1. Normalize the exception class. TypeError and SyntaxError should not collapse into a generic JavaScript error.
  2. Use an operation name that represents the pipeline stage, such as manifest.parse or index.commit. Do not use a transient run identifier.
  3. Use the first application-owned stack frame, not the entire stack. Library upgrades and wrapper functions can otherwise split a stable defect.
  4. Remove volatile values from the message before retaining it as a grouping input. Keep the unmodified message in the event for investigation.
  5. Include a rule version. A changed normalizer should create an explicitly comparable generation, not silently rewrite history.

These rules make a deliberate trade-off. More dimensions reduce accidental merging but increase group cardinality. For a rollback decision, a false merge is usually more expensive than a few extra groups because it can make a bad release appear to have one familiar cause.

Here is a small Node.js implementation. It does not send data anywhere; the returned object can be attached to an OpenTelemetry log record or to the generic event envelope used by an error-tracking service. In one nightly run, for example, row 1842 and row 9817 may both say that an owner is invalid. If the message normalizer strips only those row numbers, they share a group; if it strips the stage name too, a manifest parser defect can merge with an index commit defect. That is the boundary the fixture test must catch before the rule reaches production.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

const VOLATILE = [
  /\brequest[-_ ]?id[=:]\s*[^ ]+/gi,
  /\b(run|job|tenant|user)[-_ ]?id[=:]\s*[^ ]+/gi,
  /\b\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T\S+/g,
  /\b\d+\b/g
];

function normalizeMessage(message) {
  let value = String(message ?? "").trim();
  for (const pattern of VOLATILE) value = value.replace(pattern, "<value>");
  return value.replace(/\s+/g, " ").slice(0, 240);
}

function firstApplicationFrame(stack, root = "/app/") {
  return String(stack ?? "")
    .split("\n")
    .map((line) => line.trim())
    .find((line) => line.startsWith("at ") && line.includes(root)) ?? "unknown";
}

export function groupingAttributes(error, context) {
  const identity = [
    "group-v1",
    error?.name || "Error",
    context.operation,
    firstApplicationFrame(error?.stack),
    normalizeMessage(error?.message)
  ].join("|");

  return {
    grouping_rule: "group-v1",
    error_fingerprint: crypto.createHash("sha256").update(identity).digest("hex"),
    error_type: error?.name || "Error",
    operation: context.operation,
    batch_name: context.batchName,
    run_id: context.runId,
    original_message: error?.message || "",
    stack: error?.stack || ""
  };
}

The hash is an identifier, not a security boundary.

Keep the evidence.

The event still needs access controls because original_message and the stack can contain sensitive data. The regular expressions are also policy, not magic. If a legitimate error message contains a numeric schema version, replacing every number may erase useful distinction. I test the normalizer with fixtures from real log shapes and with deliberately adversarial values before changing the rule.

How can Node.js tracking configure automatic error grouping safely?

The group key should be low-cardinality enough to scan and high-signal enough to support action. Fields such as service, environment, and deployment_id are valuable dimensions, but I keep them available as filters instead of automatically placing all of them in the fingerprint. Environment is a special case: production and staging usually deserve separate views, while a deployment identifier is better for release correlation.

A useful event has at least three layers: the grouping identity, the diagnostic evidence, and the operational context. In JSON, that might look like this:

{
  "severity": "ERROR",
  "body": "Manifest row 1842 has an invalid owner",
  "attributes": {
    "error_fingerprint": "sha256:...",
    "grouping_rule": "group-v1",
    "operation": "manifest.parse",
    "batch_name": "nightly-index-refresh",
    "run_id": "2026-10-28T01:00:00Z",
    "deployment_id": "release-42"
  }
}

The run_id belongs in context, not in the grouping identity. That single boundary prevents the common “one group per run” mistake. The body remains searchable for the exact row and owner, while the fingerprint answers the narrower question: which failures share a cause under the current rule?

For a developer-tools pipeline, I also record the input artifact and stage as attributes, but I do not put an arbitrary path or line number into the key unless that location is stable across runs. This is where deliverability-style thinking helps: classify signals before reacting to them. A burst is a signal; it is not proof that every event in the burst belongs to the same defect.

What should be compared before choosing a service?

The service is the last part of this design. The first comparison is between grouping behaviors, because different systems may interpret a custom fingerprint, stack trace, or exception name differently. A useful evaluation exercise sends the same fixture set through three categories of implementation: a self-hosted collector, a hosted error tracker, and a log search backend with alerting. The names matter less than the observable contract.

Check five things: can the system accept an explicit fingerprint; can an event retain the original stack and attributes; can a rule version be queried; can groups be split without deleting evidence; and can a bad rule be disabled without rewriting historical events? A hosted tracker may offer opinionated stack-based grouping, a collector may give more control over normalization, and a log backend may make arbitrary queries easier than durable issue grouping. Those are boundaries, not rankings.

I would reject a choice that answers only “does it group errors automatically?” The real test is replayability. Export a fixture containing a timeout, a malformed manifest, a permission failure, and two copies of the same malformed row with different IDs. Then verify that the same defect groups together, the distinct failures stay apart, and the original fields remain available. Repeat the test after a wrapper-library update.

Do not compare only the happy path. A rate-limited ingestion endpoint, a partial batch, a missing stack, and a changed source-map format are all grouping inputs. In email and OTP systems, I learned to distrust any classification that behaves perfectly until a provider changes one header; log pipelines have the same shape.

A rollout that can be rolled back

Roll out a new fingerprint as a shadow field first. For one or two nightly runs, calculate group-v2 while continuing to display group-v1. Compare split and merge candidates by sampled event IDs, not by total group count alone. A lower count can mean better deduplication, or it can mean unrelated defects were hidden.

Keep both values during the transition:

def choose_group(event, enabled_rule):
    candidate = event.get(enabled_rule)
    fallback = event.get("error_fingerprint_v1")
    return candidate or fallback or "unclassified"

The operational switch should be configuration, not a code edit during an incident. Record the active rule in deployment metadata, alert annotations, and the event attributes. If the new rule merges two defects, disable it, return to the previous rule, and preserve the events already received under the new version for later analysis. A rollback should change future classification; it should not destroy the audit trail.

The decision rule is compact: prefer the smallest stable identity that keeps rollback-relevant failures distinct. Measure that with replay fixtures and sampled production events, then promote the rule only after the false-merge cases have an owner. Automatic grouping is useful when it reduces noise without reducing evidence.

Sources

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • https://nodejs.org/api/errors.html
  • https://nodejs.org/api/crypto.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5424

title: How to Containerize a Full-Stack App (Part 2)-Optimizing the Frontend with Multi-Stage Docker Builds.
description:
Series Navigation:

  • ✅ Part 1: Setting up locally (Required)
  • 📍 Part 2: Frontend Multi-Stage Docker Builds (You are here)
  • ➡️ Part 3: Containerizing the Backend & MySQL

Intro

This is Part 2 of our series. If you haven't set up the local Full-Stack Todo app yet, check out Part 1: Local Setup to get your environment ready.

In Part 2, we will guide you on how to containerize our Frontend application. In the upcoming blog post, I will explain the rest of the details.

If you are a frontend developer and only want to know how to Dockerize your frontend, this section is very important. Also, you can use this Docker image in production as well.

Note: This Setup you can use for any React app that uses Vite. There may be a few changes if you are using some other bundler. But the basic idea of deployment remains the same.

Here is what we will cover:

  1. Frontend Code Walkthrough: A brief overview of our React app structure.
  2. Generating the Production Build: How to prepare the app for deployment.
  3. Deployment Architecture: High-level view of our deployment
  4. From Source Code to Container: Visualizing the transformation process
  5. Writing Our First Dockerfile: Writing the step-by-step build instructions.
  6. Creating nginx configuration file: Configuring nginx to serve our static files
  7. Building Docker Image: Building Docker Image and Running it.
  8. Managing Environment Variables: Configuring API URLs and secrets securely.
  9. Docker File optimization: Intro to Docker Image Optimization.
  10. Multi-Stage Docker file: The professional way to shrink image size.
  11. Securing Frontend Docker Container: Restricting folder permissions and user access.
  12. Bonus: Extra observation on nginx.
  13. Wrap Up

1. Frontend Code Walkthrough: A brief overview of our React app structure.

Prefer Video? Watch Here

Our React app was built via vite. It had a folder structure like below

Where

frontend/
├── public/                 # Static assets (favicons, manifest, etc.)
├── src/                    # our todo  application source code
|——— .env                   # environment file    
├── .env-example            # Template for environment variables
├── .gitignore              # Files/folders to be ignored by Git
├── eslint.config.js        # Linting rules to keep code consistent
├── index.html              # Entry Point. Vite treats this file as source code. It contains a <script type="module" src="..."> tag that points to your React entry file (usually src/main.tsx).
├── package-lock.json       # Exact versions of installed dependencies
├── package.json            # Project metadata and script definitions
├── README.md               # Project documentation
├── tsconfig.app.json       # TypeScript config for the frontend app
├── tsconfig.json           # Main TypeScript configuration
├── tsconfig.node.json      # TypeScript config for Node-based tools (like Vite)
└── vite.config.ts          # Vite-specific settings and plugins

2. Generating the Production Build: How to prepare the app for deployment.

Prefer Video? Watch Here

So, to deploy this React app. We first need to create a bundle of it by running the build command.

So we need to run

npm run build

Once you run this command inside the frontend folder.
You can see the dist folder, which looks like the following structure


 dist/
 ├── assets/
  │   ├── index-DiW657_O.css # All your CSS (minified)
  │   └── index-D9fK2_zX.js  # All your React code + libraries (minified)
 ├── index.html # The main entry point (minified)
 └── vite.svg # Copied directly from public/

By running this command, Vite took our development code and transformed it into a highly optimized bundle designed for web browsers. Because our browser does not understand JSX or TypeScript. So Vite converts our code into standard JavaScript.

Vite creates a new directory in our root folder called dist/

This folder contains everything your web server needs:

  • index.html: The entry point, now updated with the correct paths to your hashed JS and CSS files.
  • assets/: A folder containing your minified .js and .css files.

Now to test our build locally, run the command

npm run preview

This starts a local server that serves the dist folder, allowing you to see exactly how your app will perform in production.

Now go to your browser and type http://localhost:4173/

You are able to see our todo app, so it shows that our build was created successfully, and it is also running perfectly.

Now kill that server by running ctrl + c or cmd + c in mac.

3. Deployment Architecture: High-level view of our React app deployment.

Prefer Video? Watch Here

Before we proceed, we first need to understand how our React app actually runs in production.

So in the code walkthrough section, we ran the npm run build command in order to build our project. Then in order to test that build
Locally, we ran npm run preview command. This command spins up a web server and serves the dist folder.

We need to set up a similar environment for our production.

For the web server, we will use nginx because it is mostly used in production. And nginx will handle upcoming requests and serve the dist folder.

See the diagram to get a better idea

In summary: Nginx takes a web request, finds the correct static file on the disk, and hands it back to the browser.

For Production, we need:

  • A web server, i.e., nginx
  • dist folder (bundle of our application)

4. From Source Code to Container: Visualizing the transformation process.

Prefer Video? Watch Here

Before we proceed, I would like to provide a high-level overview of containerization.

Containerization involves a few steps

Stage 1: Our Source Code
Stage 2: Take our source code and compile our source code and configuration into a package
Stage 3: The result of Stage 2 is a static Docker Image
Stage 4: This is the live, running instance of the created Docker image. Now we can access our application

I hope the above diagram gives us some idea.

So I think our responsibility is to create a Docker image for our application.

But how do we provide our source code to Docker so that it can build the Docker image?

Also, how does it understand what it needs to do to build our project?

So here comes Dockerfile to rescue us.

4.1 What is a Dockerfile?

"A Dockerfile is a simple text file that acts as a blueprint for building a Docker Image. It contains a set of sequential instructions that tell Docker exactly how to set up the environment, copy your code, and get your application running."

We need to create a Dockerfile in our frontend directory. In the Dockerfile, we define everything that is required to build our project.

So, how do we create our Docker file, and what content will we put inside it so that Docker understands it and create docker image by reading it?

5. Writing Our First Dockerfile: Writing the step-by-step build instructions

Prefer Video? Watch Here

Go to the frontend directory if you are not and inside that directory, create a file with the name Dockerfile.

Open Dockerfile.

So to build our project, we need npm (Node Package Manager)
And it comes with Node.js. So first, we need Node.js

So we will use a prebuilt Node.js image from Docker Hub. So that we can run the npm command.

Copy the line in your Dockerfile

FROM node:lts

As we know, to serve our React app, we need a web server.
We already discussed that we will use Nginx for this.
Now let's install nginx.

Copy the line below in your Dockerfile

# Updates the Linux package manager and installs Nginx
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y nginx

Now let's set up WORKDIR inside our container. All subsequent commands (COPY, RUN, CMD) will be executed relative to this path.

Copy the line below in your Dockerfile

WORKDIR /frontend-app

So let's recap what we've done. We have installed Node.js. Because we need it to build our project. Also, we installed nginx so that we can serve our React app.

Now to serve our frontend. We need to build our ReactJS project. To build it, we first need to install the project dependencies. Then we need to copy our project code inside the container. So that when we run the npm run build command. It successfully create build for our react.js project.

For installing dependencies we need package.json file.

Add this line to your Dockerfile

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

This will copy package.json. Inside the workdir that we set up above. And then install dependencies.

What is RUN npm ci?

Runs a "clean install." This is faster and more reliable than npm install for automated environments (CI/CD) because it adheres strictly to the package-lock.json.

Via the above command, we installed our Project dependencies. Now we need to build our project. So, for building the project, we need to copy our frontend project code as well inside the container.

Add this line to your Dockerfile

COPY . .

Copy the rest of your source code into the container. Except files which are defined inside the dockerignore file. We will talk about the dockerignore later.

Now, let's add a build command for building our project.

RUN npm run build

Via this command, we build our project.

Now we need to set up our Nginx so that it serves our static build files.

First of all, we create a directory. Where will we store our static files? Right now, our bundle files are present inside the dist folder.

Then we copy those files from dist to the mywebsite folder.

Add these lines to your Dockerfile

# Ensure nginx directories exist
RUN mkdir -p /frontend-app/mywebsite

# Copy nginx config
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/sites-available/default

# Move dist files
RUN cp -r ./dist/* /frontend-app/mywebsite/

We did not talk about this line COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/sites-available/default

This line will overwrite the default Nginx configuration with your custom config file. This tells Nginx how to handle routing and where to look for static files.

We will talk about it more later.

We're done with our project setup. Now we need to expose the port as well. So that when we try to connect with our frontend, we can reach our web server, which is running on port 80.

EXPOSE 80

This command tells users (and Docker) that the container listens on port 80. Here we are exposing the container port 80.

Now let's start our nginx server

CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

The above command is divided into two commands:

nginx: Starts the nginx server.
-g "daemon off;”: Runs Nginx in the foreground. If you don't do this, Nginx runs in the background, and the Docker container will immediately exit (stop) because it thinks its job is done.

That's it, we're done with our Dockerfile. Final version of your Dockerfile looks like this:

FROM node:lts

# Install nginx on Debian
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y nginx

WORKDIR /frontend-app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .

RUN npm run build

# Ensure nginx directories exist
RUN mkdir -p /frontend-app/mywebsite

# Copy nginx config
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/sites-available/default

# Move dist files
RUN cp -r ./dist/* /frontend-app/mywebsite/

EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

6. Creating nginx configuration file: Configuring nginx to serve our static files

Prefer Video? Watch Here

When we write our Dockerfile. We encounter one line

COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/sites-available/default

Here we are copying some nginx.conf file to some location. But currently, in our project, inside the frontend directory. We don't have any nginx.conf file. So what's the purpose of this file?

Let's talk about it

Nginx comes with a default configuration file. When a request reaches Nginx, it looks for a configuration file which matches the request. If it cannot find the conf file, it selects default.conf.

And default.conf comes with predefined rules. We want to override it with our custom configuration rules. So that niginx handle our request flawlessly.

Also, we want nginx to look into /frontend-app/mywebsite directory. For serving static file.

Create a file nginx.conf inside frontend directory.

And then copy and paste the content below into it

server {
    listen 80;          # Listen for IPv4
    listen [::]:80;     # Listen for IPv6
    server_name localhost;

    root /frontend-app/mywebsite;
    index index.html;


    location / {
        try_files $uri /index.html;
    }
}

Let's break down each line step by step

First things first, the conf file had

server {
options
}
This denotes a server block. When any request reaches the web server, it will start looking for server_name on these server blocks. Once server_name matches, then that particular server block option is applied to the server.

Nginx is designed to always serve something rather than just crashing. If it can't find a server_name that matches the URL the user typed, it looks for a block labelled with the default_server flag.

Standard Default: Usually, this is a block that listens on Port 80 and points to a folder like /var/www/html or /usr/share/nginx/html.

The Result: The user will see the famous "Welcome to nginx!" landing page instead of your actual website.

I hope you understand the point. Now let's break down the above file step by step.

listen 80;
Tells Nginx to listen for incoming web traffic on port 80 using IPv4.

listen [::]:80;
Tells Nginx to listen for incoming web traffic on port 80 using IPv6.

server_name localhost;
Tells Nginx to apply these rules when the request comes to "localhost" (or your domain name in production).

root /frontend-app/mywebsite;
Sets the home base. It tells Nginx that all your static files (HTML, CSS, JS) are stored inside the /frontend-app/mywebsite folder.

index index.html;
Defines the default file. When a user visits your site without specifying a file, Nginx automatically serves them index.html.

The "Magic" for Single Page Apps (React):

location / {
try_files $uri /index.html; This line prevents 404 errors on refresh. It tells Nginx: "First, look for the specific file the user asked for. If you can't find it, don't show an error—just serve index.html and let the JavaScript app handle the routing."
}

$uri —> Requested File like if user type
http://localhost:8080/dashboard —> $uri is /dashboard.

Nginx checks: Does a file called /frontend-app/mywebsite/dashboard exist?
Result:
No (Because /dashboard is just a virtual route in your React app, not a real file on the disk)

Fallback: Nginx moves to the second option in your try_files line -> /index.html.

Outcome: The user gets index.html, and your JavaScript app loads and reads the URL to display the “Dashboard” page content.

We are still not ready to build our image. Because if you try to build an image now. We will accidentally send our .env secrets or a heavy folder like node_modules. Because in our DockerFile we added this line COPY . ..

We need to restrict this behaviour somehow so that Docker will not pick up those files.

How can we do this?

Ans is the .dockerignore file.

What is .dockerignore?

The .dockerignore file is just like .gitignore, but for Docker. It tells Docker which files to exclude when sending your code to the container builder.

It speeds up the process of building images. It ignore heavy folder likes node_module, dist etc

It prevents sensitive files (like .env secrets or .git history) from accidentally ending up inside your public image.

Create a .dockerignore file inside the frontend directory

and copy the content

**/.classpath
**/.dockerignore
**/.env
**/.git
**/.gitignore
**/.project
**/.settings
**/.toolstarget
**/.vs
**/.vscode
**/.next
**/.cache
**/*.*proj.user
**/*.dbmdl
**/*.jfm
**/charts
**/docker-compose*
**/compose.y*ml
**/Dockerfile*
**/node_modules
**/npm-debug.log
**/obj
**/secrets.dev.yaml
**/values.dev.yaml
**/build
**/dist
LICENSE
README.md
**/backend
/*.yaml

7. Building Docker Image: Building Docker Image and Running it

Prefer Video? Watch Here

Now we are all set for building our Docker image

After saving all the files

Go to your terminal and go to the frontend directory by running the command

cd frontend

Once you are in the frontend directory. Now, let's build a Docker image

8. Managing Environment Variables: Configuring API URLs and secrets securely.

Prefer Video? Watch Here

Handling environment variables is crucial and requires extra precaution. So that we do not expose our secrets accidentally in public.

Let's understand how to handle env variables

There are two ways we can pass the env variable in our Docker image

  1. Passing env variables during build time using build args.
  2. Passing env variables at run-time by injecting them into the window object.

Let's discuss both of them one by one

1. Passing env variable during build time using build args:

In this approach, when we are building the image, we only need to pass the env variable using the build arguments into our image.
These variables become static. In order to change the env variable, we need to rebuild the image.

This approach we mostly avoid because it is not efficient. Because we need to rebuild the image every time if the environment variable changes. And building images is a costly or time-consuming process.

2. Passing env variables at run-time by injecting them into the window object

So the idea is that somehow we will provide an env variable to our frontend at runtime so that we don’t need to build images every time.

So How we do this?

Our frontend is running on a browser. They cannot access the Docker container's environment variables (like process.env) at runtime.
So when the browser requests index.html from the server. We inject one JS script into our index.html. That script will inject our env variable into the window object.

Note:

But this approach only works if your environment does not contain any sensitive data. In general, we avoid putting sensitive data like api key, password, etc. in the frontend. Because with this approach, anyone can see your env variable in the console by accessing the window object.

Let’s implement this as well

Comment out those lines that we added previously for build args.

# Build arguments for environment variables
# ARG VITE_API_URL
# ENV VITE_API_URL=$VITE_API_URL

Now, inside the frontend directory, create a file nginx-entrypoint.sh

And copy the snapshot below and paste it into nginx-entrypoint.sh

#!/bin/sh

# Start the generated config file
CONFIG_PATH="/frontend-app/mywebsite/env-config.js"
echo "window.env = {" > $CONFIG_PATH

# Find all environment variables starting with "VITE_" and add them to the file
for var in $(env | grep "VITE_"); do
  name=$(echo "$var" | cut -d "=" -f 1)
  value=$(echo "$var" | cut -d "=" -f 2-)
  echo "  $name: \"$value\"," >> $CONFIG_PATH
done

# End the config file
echo "};" >> $CONFIG_PATH
echo "Environment variable injection completed."
exec nginx -g 'daemon off;'

nginx-entrypoint.sh

This script runs immediately before Nginx starts. It takes the environment variables from Docker and writes them into a real JavaScript file that the browser can read.

Line-by-Line Breakdown

  1. Create the File (echo "window.env..."). It creates a new JavaScript file called env-config.js inside the /frontend-app/mywebsite and starts defining a global object: window.env = {. 
  2. The Loop (for var in...) It looks through all the system environment variables currently set in the container.
    • grep "VITE_": It filters the list to only grab variables that start with VITE_ (security measure to avoid exposing secrets like internal keys). 
  3. The Injection (echo " $name: \"$value\","). It extracts the Name and Value of the variable and writes them into the JS file as a key-value pair.
    • Result inside file: VITE_API_URL: https://my-api.com, 
  4. Close & Launch (exec nginx...) It closes the JS object (};) and finally starts the Nginx server to serve your website.

Final Result: Our frontend code can now access variables via window.env.VITE_API_URL.

Once the above file is saved. Now we want to run this script before nginx starts so that we can inject the env variable at runtime. To do that

Go to Dockerfile and add the lines after the RUN mkdir -p /frontend-app/mywebsite command

RUN chmod +x /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh

Here we are copying nginx-entrypoint.sh into Docker, converting any Windows-style line endings to Linux format to prevent execution errors, and giving it executable permission so that Docker can run this script.

This command tells Docker: "No matter what else happens, run this script first when the container starts."

It guarantees your environment variables are injected every single time the container launches.
