10. Multi-Stage Docker file: The professional way to shrink image size.

Prefer Video? Watch Here

For production, a multi-stage Docker file is recommended.

So the Dockerfile we built so far is a single-stage Dockerfile. There is only one stage.

The drawback of a single-stage Docker file is that it attempts to do everything—downloading source code, installing dependencies, building the app, and running it—inside the same environment.

This increases the size of the images. Also, it exposes the attack surface for hackers because it contains more tools that will give hackers more chances to hack it.

But if we use a multi-stage Docker build, we get rid of these problems

So In multi stage docker file. We build our image in multiple stages. Like the build stage, final stage or prod stage.

In the build stage

  1. We copy our source code and package.json, package-lock.json files.
  2. Then we install all the dependencies.
  3. And finally, we build the code.

In Final stage or Prod Stage

  1. We install the nginx image
  2. Copy the dist folder from the build stage and put it inside the web server directory.

Because in Prod we only need a web server and our build folder, that’s it.

And in a multi-stage Dockerfile, the final image only had these two things.

Enough talk, let’s write our multi-stage Docker file

First things first, comment out the older content of the Docker file. Once you comment out the Docker file, you will be able to see some errors in VS Code. But don't worry about it.

Then copy the content below after the commented content

FROM node:lts-alpine3.22 AS build
WORKDIR /frontend-app
RUN --mount=type=bind,source=package.json,target=package.json \
    --mount=type=bind,source=package-lock.json,target=package-lock.json \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci

# Copy the rest of the source files into the image.

COPY . .

# Run the build script.

RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:stable-alpine-slim AS final

COPY nginx-entrypoint.sh /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh
RUN sed -i 's/\r$//' /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh
RUN chmod +x /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh

# Copy the production dependencies from the build stage
COPY --from=build /frontend-app/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /frontend-app/dist /frontend-app/mywebsite


# Expose the port that the application listens on.
EXPOSE 80
ENTRYPOINT ["/frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh"]

Line-by-line explanation

So here we define two stages, one is build and another is final

Build Stage:

We set up node js environment for building our application.

FROM node:20-alpine3.22 AS build

Think of AS build like giving a name tag to a specific step in your setup. It simply lets you tell Docker later on, 'Hey, remember that step we named 'build'? Go grab the files from there.

The above line tells Docker to download a lightweight version of Linux ("Alpine") that has Node.js LTS version installed.

WORKDIR /frontend-app

Creates a folder inside the container at /frontend-app and sets it as the default location for all future commands.

RUN --mount=type=bind,source=package.json,target=package.json

This command looks different. Usually, we do COPY package.json . This physically duplicates the file into a layer of our Docker image.

But --mount=type=bind,source=package.json,target=package.json. In this way, we are telling to Docker Don't copy the file. Just let me 'borrow' package.json from my computer (source) and make it visible inside the container at package.json (target) just for the duration of this command.

It keeps the image layer cleaner. As soon as the command finishes, the file is technically no longer "in" that layer, because it was never copied, only mounted.

Note: The second line does the same thing for the package-lock.json file.

--mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm

Problem:

Normally, Docker containers start fresh. When you run npm install, it downloads megabytes of files from the internet. If you rebuild the image, it forgets those downloads and does it all over again.

This command tells Docker to create a special storage bucket (cache) on your host machine (your computer) and mount it to /root/.npm inside the container (which is where npm stores its cache).

So now npm downloads libraries and saves them to /root/.npm. As cache, and when we try to rebuild the image. It just reaches out to our host machine( our laptop) storage and grabs the files instead of downloading them from the internet again.

This speeds up the process of installing dependencies. Also not store package.json or package-lock.json files in our image because we don’t need these files in our final image as well.

npm ci

Installs your project dependencies.

COPY . .

Copies all the files from your laptop (current directory) into the container's current folder (/frontend-app)

RUN npm run build

This usually creates a dist folder containing the final website files.

Final Stage:

This section throws away the heavy Node.js tools and starts fresh with a tiny web server.

FROM nginx:stable-alpine-slim AS final

We use a "slim" version of Nginx. It doesn't have Node.js; it only knows how to serve web files.

COPY nginx-entrypoint.sh /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh

Copies a custom script file from your laptop to the root of the container.

RUN sed -i 's/\r$//' /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh

Removes hidden Windows line endings from the script so it doesn't crash inside the Linux container.

RUN chmod +x /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh

Changes the permissions of that script to make it executable (so it can be run as a program).

COPY --from=build /frontend-app/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf

It reaches back into the build stage to grab our custom configuration file and places it into the final Nginx folder to overwrite the server's default settings.

COPY --from=build /frontend-app/dist /frontend-app/mywebsite

Copies the compiled website from the dist folder from the "build" stage to a folder named /frontend-app/mywebsite in the final stage.

EXPOSE 80

This container listens on port 80

ENTRYPOINT ["/frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh"]

Specifies the script that must run every time the container starts up.

If you didn't use multi-stage builds, your final image would include all of Node.js, your source code, and thousands of dev dependencies, making it heavier. By using this method, your final image only contains Nginx and your static files, this make your final build lighter.

11. Securing Frontend Docker Container: Restricting folder permissions and user access.

Right now, our container is running as a root user. This is not recommended in a production environment. If an attacker manages to get the access of our server. Then they can take over the entire server. Which is soo scary.

To completely secure our container, we need to run it using the least privileged user. This ensures that even if an attacker gains access to the container, they cannot execute malicious code or alter server permissions. They are effectively locked down and stripped of the authority to compromise the system.

So, before we proceed, we need to understand how Linux file permissions work.

1. The Three Security Scopes (The "Who")

Prefer Video? Watch Here

Every file and directory in Linux evaluates access requests sequentially against three distinct user scopes:

  • Owner (u): The system administrator who created the resource (usually root in a container).
  • Group (g): The specific service account or application tier assigned to the resource (e.g., sudo group).
  • Others (o): Unauthenticated entities or unrelated system users. All the other users.

When you issue a command like chmod 750, you are passing a three-digit configuration payload. The first digit applies to the Owner, the second to the Group, and the third to Others.

2. The Binary Breakdown: Read, Write, and Execute

Linux permissions do not use complex configuration files. They are based entirely on three simple actions, mapped to a 3-bit binary system where 1 is ON (allowed) and 0 is OFF (denied).

Here are the only three actions a user can take:

  • Read: You can view the text inside a file, or see the list of files inside a folder.
  • Write: You can edit, modify, or delete a file.
  • Execute: You can run a file as a script or program. (Crucial gotcha: For **folders, Execute simply means the ability to open or "enter" the folder).

Each of these three actions is assigned to a specific slot in a 3-bit binary number. When you convert that binary sequence into standard decimal numbers, you get the magic numbers used in chmod:

  • Read is the first slot (1 0 0 in binary), which equals 4.
  • Write is the middle slot (0 1 0 in binary), which equals 2.
  • Execute is the last slot (0 0 1 in binary), which equals 1.

To give a user a combination of permissions, you simply turn on the binary bits you want, which adds the numbers together.

For example: If you want a user to be able to Read and Execute, but not Write, the binary is 1 0 1. If you add the standard numbers together (4 + 0 + 1), you get 5. If you want them to have all three powers (1 1 1), it is 4 + 2 + 1 = 7.

3. The Practical Implementation (chmod 750)

Prefer Video? Watch Here

We achieve this with the matrix 750:

  • Owner gets 7 (4 + 2 + 1): The binary flag is 111. Root has Read, Write, and Execute authority.
  • Group gets 5 (4 + 0 + 1): The binary flag is 101. Group users get Read and Execute authority, but Write (0) is strictly denied.
  • Others get 0: The binary flag is 000. A total block for other users.

So, to lock down our Dockerfile. Need to do the following tasks:

  1. Creating a group, e.g. frontend_group.
  2. Creating a user, e.g. frontend_user, and adding it to the frontend_group.
  3. Creating the necessary folders required for running nginx properly.
  4. Then we need to set the owner for the folders. Which required protection.
  5. Then we need to lock down our files and folders. And give the least privilege to the groups and users.

Now, let's do each step one by one

1. Creating a group, e.g. frontend_group

In your Docker file, after the last COPY command. Add the following command for creating the group

RUN addgroup -S frontend_group

Breakdown of the above command

RUN addgroup -S frontend_group

addgroup: This tells Linux to create a brand new group.

-S: This stands for "System." It tells Linux to make this a system group rather than a normal user group. System groups don't have passwords and are specifically designed for running background services (like Nginx or Node), which makes them much more secure.

2. Creating a user, e.g. frontend_user, and adding it to the frontend_group

After that, to create a user and add it to the group, add the following command after the above command

RUN adduser -S frontend_user -G frontend_group

Pro-Tip: The One-Liner Optimization (&&)

While writing those commands on two separate lines makes them easy to read, you will almost always see them combined in professional Dockerfiles like this:

RUN addgroup -S frontend_group && adduser -S frontend_user -G frontend_group

Why do we do this? Docker Layers.

Every time you write the word RUN in a Dockerfile, Docker creates a brand new "layer" (a snapshot) of your system.

  • Two RUN commands = Two layers added to your image.
  • One RUN command with && = One single layer.

By chaining related commands together with &&, you tell Docker to execute both actions simultaneously inside the exact same layer. This reduces your final image size, speeds up build times, and is the golden standard for production Dockerfiles!

3. Creating the folder required to run nginx properly.

We need to create the /run/nginx folder. Because
When Nginx boots up, the operating system assigns it a unique ID number. Nginx is hardcoded to instantly write this number into a file called nginx.pid.

By default, it tries to save this file in a locked, root-only system folder. Because we are securing our app by running as a non-root user, Nginx will instantly crash with a "Permission Denied" error. We pre-create the /run/nginx folder to give our app a dedicated, writeable sandbox just for this one file.

Add the mkdir command below after the above line

RUN mkdir -p /run/nginx

4. Setting the owners for the folders which required protection

For securing our frontend app. We need to provide protection mostly to the frontend-app and some nginx folders.

Then add the Run command

RUN chown -R root:frontend_group /frontend-app /etc/nginx /run/nginx /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx
  • RUN: Tells Docker to execute this command while building the image.
  • chown (Change Owner): This is the Linux command used to change who owns a file or folder.
  • -R (Recursive): Just like in our chmod commands, this tells Linux to dive into the folders and apply this ownership to every single file and sub-folder hidden inside them.
  • root:frontend_group: This is the core logic. You are explicitly stating two things:
  • The Owner is root: The system administrator owns the files.
  • The Group is frontend_group: You are assigning these files to your application's service group.

Why do it this way? By making the root owner, you permanently prevent the frontend_user from ever running a chmod command to change permissions later.

The Folders (Why these specific five?)

When you run Nginx as a standard, non-root user (like frontend_user), you have to manually grant it access to the specific folders it relies on to function. If Nginx cannot read or write to these native Linux folders, the container will instantly crash with a "Permission Denied" error on startup.

Here is exactly what Nginx is doing in each of those directories:

  • /frontend-app

    • What it is: Your custom directory containing your compiled React/Vite build (the dist folder).
    • Why it needs it: Nginx needs permission to open this folder to serve your HTML, CSS, and JS files to the user's browser.

  • /etc/nginx

    • What it is: The default Linux directory for Nginx configuration files (like nginx.conf and your custom server blocks).
    • Why it needs it: Nginx has to read these rules to know how to route traffic, handle API proxies, and serve your application.

  • /run/nginx

    • What it is: A temporary system folder used to store the PID (Process ID) file.
    • Why it needs it: When Nginx starts, Linux assigns it a unique ID number and writes that number to a file (e.g., nginx.pid). If Nginx cannot create this file, it refuses to start.

  • /var/cache/nginx

    • What it is: The storage location for temporary files and cached data.
    • Why it needs it: When Nginx processes large client requests, handles fastCGI, or acts as a proxy, it buffers that data into temporary files. It needs strict Write access here to function efficiently.

  • /var/log/nginx

    • What it is: The official directory for access.log (who visited your site) and error.log (what broke).
    • Why it needs it: Nginx constantly streams data to these files while running. If it cannot write to the log folder, it will crash.

As we created a directory /run/nginx. For nginx to write its PID (Process ID).

By default, Nginx is hardcoded to write this file into a strict, root-only system folder. Because we are forcing Nginx to run as our non-root frontend_user, it will instantly crash with a "Permission Denied" error when it tries to write that PID file.

To fix this, we use a single command to rewrite the Nginx configuration file and point the PID to the /run/nginx folder we explicitly unlocked in the previous step.

# Update the PID path in the nginx config
 RUN sed -i 's|.*nginx.pid;|pid /run/nginx/nginx.pid;|g' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

This line changes the nginx internal configuration command. It changes the default path from nginx.pid to /run/nginx/nginx.pid.

5. Locking down our files and folders. And give the least privilege to the groups and users.

We have already seen the five folders above. We need to lock some files and folders among them.

For our two core directories—/frontend-app (our code) and /etc/nginx (our config)—we give root full control. However, we restrict our frontend_group to only Read and Execute permissions. This allows Nginx to open the folders and serve the website perfectly, but physically prevents it from modifying, overwriting, or deleting any core files.

For locking down our core folder, use the chmod command

RUN chmod -R 750 /frontend-app /etc/nginx

For our main application code, we used 750 to strictly block write access. However, Nginx physically must be able to write to its cache, logs, and PID directories to function.

We unlock these specific, isolated sandbox folders using the 770 lock code.

# Grant Write access to the isolated Nginx runtime folders
RUN chmod -R 770 /run/nginx /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx
  • -R (Recursive): Apply this permission to the folders and everything inside them.
  • 770 (The Access Matrix):
    • Owner gets 7 (4 + 2 + 1): root retains full control.
    • Group gets 7 (4 + 2 + 1): Our frontend_group (Nginx) is granted Read, Write, and Execute powers. This is the crucial difference. We are explicitly allowing Nginx to generate and delete files inside these sandboxed directories.
    • Others get 0: Unauthenticated users are completely blocked.

By specifically targeting only these runtime directories with 770, we give Nginx exactly the Write permissions it needs to survive, without exposing our core application code to dangerous modifications!

That's it. Now let's switch from root to frontend_user.

Add the below command just before the expose command

USER frontend_user

After all the above changes, your Dockerfile looks like

FROM node:lts-alpine3.22 AS build
WORKDIR /frontend-app
RUN --mount=type=bind,source=package.json,target=package.json \
    --mount=type=bind,source=package-lock.json,target=package-lock.json \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci

# Copy the rest of the source files into the image.

COPY . .

# Run the build script.

RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:stable-alpine-slim AS final


COPY nginx-entrypoint.sh /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh
RUN sed -i 's/\r$//' /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh && \
chmod +x /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh

# Copy the production dependencies from the build stage
COPY --from=build /frontend-app/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /frontend-app/dist /frontend-app/mywebsite
RUN addgroup -S frontend_group && adduser -S frontend_user -G frontend_group
RUN mkdir -p /run/nginx
# # 1. Set root as the owner and frontend_group as the group for ALL folders.
# # Because root owns them, frontend_user is permanently blocked from using chmod.
RUN chown -R root:frontend_group /frontend-app /etc/nginx /run/nginx /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx
# # 2. Update the PID path in the nginx config
RUN sed -i 's|.*nginx.pid;|pid /run/nginx/nginx.pid;|g' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
# # 3. Lock down the app and config folders to Read/Execute (750).
# # Owner (root): Read/write/Execute (7)
# # Group (frontend_group): Read/Execute (5)
# # Others: No Access (0)
RUN chmod -R 750 /frontend-app /etc/nginx
# # 4. Grant Write access to the specific runtime folders Nginx needs to function and env creation folder (770).
# # Owner (root): Read/Write/Execute (7)
# # Group (frontend_group): Read/Write/Execute (7)
# # Others: No Access (0)
RUN chmod -R 770 /run/nginx /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx
USER frontend_user

# Expose the port that the application listens on.
EXPOSE 80
ENTRYPOINT ["/frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh"]

Now, let's build our Docker image and then run it

For building run inside the frontend directory

docker build -t my-frontend-secure-todo-multistage:v1 .

Now, let's run our container. But before that, please delete your older frontend container that we created previously.

Then run

docker run -it --env-file ./.env -p 8080:80 --name todo-app-multistage-secure-container my-frontend-secure-todo-multistage:v1

After running the above command, it runs successfully

Now go to our frontend app and refresh it, or open the URL
http://localhost:8080

We are not able to see any todos in our app. Check if your backend server is still running. In my case, it's running. Also, our frontend again starts calling the undefined URL. This means we again messed up with env variables. But where 🤔?

Check the nginx logs in the terminal where you run the docker run command. If you check the starting logs. You will see some Permission Denied errors.

What's the issue here?

If you remember, for injecting the runtime environment. We are creating a /env-config.js. On the startup of our container inside the directory /frontend-app/mywebsite.

So when we start our container with frontend_user. It had only read and execute permission for the directory /frontend-app/mywebsite. But here we are trying to create a new file inside the /frontend-app/mywebsite. Due to a lack of write permission, the creation of the /env-config.js file failed. And in the terminal, it's showing a permission denied error. How can we fix it?

I still don't want to give write permission to frontend_user for /frontend-app/mywebsite directory. Otherwise, we again get into trouble.

But I can create one directory inside the /frontend-app/mywebsite. Specially for creating the/env-config.js file. And permit write permission only for that particular directory instead of the whole /frontend-app/mywebsite directory.

So we create a /env directory inside the /frontend-app/mywebsite directory. And then give write permission to our frontend_user.

For creating /env, add the mkdir command. Just after this line RUN mkdir -p /run/nginx

RUN mkdir -p /frontend-app/mywebsite/env

Now, to give write permission, just add the above directory at the end of the command.

Add /frontend-app/mywebsite/env at the end of the chmod command like this

RUN chmod -R 770 /run/nginx /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx /frontend-app/mywebsite/env

There is one more problem we need to address

The Port 80 Problem: Privileged vs. Unprivileged Ports

If you try to run your secure, non-root Nginx container on standard HTTP Port 80, it will immediately crash. But why?

In Linux, network ports are divided into two strict categories:

  • Privileged Ports (0 to 1023): These include core internet protocols like HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), and SSH (22).
  • Unprivileged Ports (1024 to 65535): These are open for general application use.

Historically, Linux restricted ports under 1024 as a security measure. It guaranteed users that if a website was running on Port 80, it was officially set up by the system administrator (root), not a random user running a rogue script.

Because we intentionally stripped away our administrative powers by using USER frontend_user, Linux mathematically prevents our application from binding to Port 80.

The Solution: Instead of fighting Linux security, we follow the industry standard: we tell Nginx to run on an unprivileged port, like 8080.

So, in your Dockerfile, change EXPOSE 80 to EXPOSE 8080.

Finally, after all changes, your Dockerfile looks like

# FROM node:lts-alpine3.22

# # Install nginx on Apline Linux
# RUN apk add --no-cache nginx

# WORKDIR /frontend-app

# COPY package*.json ./
# RUN npm ci

# COPY . .

# # Build arguments for environment variables
# # ARG VITE_API_URL
# # ENV VITE_API_URL=$VITE_API_URL

# RUN npm run build

# # Ensure nginx directories exist
# RUN mkdir -p /frontend-app/mywebsite
# COPY nginx-entrypoint.sh /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh
# RUN sed -i 's/\r$//' /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh
# RUN chmod +x /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh

# # Copy nginx config

# COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/http.d/default.conf


# # Move dist files
# RUN cp -r ./dist/* /frontend-app/mywebsite/

# EXPOSE 80
# # CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
# ENTRYPOINT ["/frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh"]


FROM node:lts-alpine3.22 AS build
WORKDIR /frontend-app
RUN --mount=type=bind,source=package.json,target=package.json \
    --mount=type=bind,source=package-lock.json,target=package-lock.json \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci

# Copy the rest of the source files into the image.

COPY . .

# Run the build script.

RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:stable-alpine-slim AS final


COPY nginx-entrypoint.sh /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh
RUN sed -i 's/\r$//' /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh && \
chmod +x /frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh

# Copy the production dependencies from the build stage
COPY --from=build /frontend-app/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /frontend-app/dist /frontend-app/mywebsite
RUN addgroup -S frontend_group && adduser -S frontend_user -G frontend_group
RUN mkdir -p /run/nginx
RUN mkdir -p /frontend-app/mywebsite/env
# 1. Set root as the owner and frontend_group as the group for ALL folders.
# Because root owns them, frontend_user is permanently blocked from using chmod.
RUN chown -R root:frontend_group /frontend-app /etc/nginx /run/nginx /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx
# 2. Update the PID path in the nginx config
RUN sed -i 's|.*nginx.pid;|pid /run/nginx/nginx.pid;|g' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
# 3. Lock down the app and config folders to Read/Execute (750).
# Owner (root): Read/write/Execute (7)
# Group (frontend_group): Read/Execute (5)
# Others: No Access (0)
RUN chmod -R 750 /frontend-app /etc/nginx
# 4. Grant Write access to the specific runtime folders Nginx needs to function and env creation folder (770).
# Owner (root): Read/Write/Execute (7)
# Group (frontend_group): Read/Write/Execute (7)
# Others: No Access (0)
RUN chmod -R 770 /run/nginx /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx /frontend-app/mywebsite/env
USER frontend_user

# Expose the port that the application listens on.
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/frontend-app/nginx-entrypoint.sh"]

Also, update your nginx.conf file. With the following changes
change these two lines:

  • From listen 80; to listen 8080;
  • From listen [::]:80; to listen [::]:8080;

Finally, your nginx.cong. Files look like

   server{
    listen 8080;          # Listen for IPv4
    listen [::]:8080;     # Listen for IPv6
    server_name localhost;

    root /frontend-app/mywebsite;
    index index.html;


    location / {
        try_files $uri /index.html;
    }
    }

Also, update the new env path in nginx-entrypoint.sh.

Update the CONFIG_PATH from /frontend-app/mywebsite/env-config.js to /frontend-app/mywebsite/env/env-config.js

After the change, your final nginx-entrypoint.sh file looks like

   #!/bin/sh

# Start the generated config file
CONFIG_PATH="/frontend-app/mywebsite/env/env-config.js"
echo "window.env = {" > $CONFIG_PATH

# Find all environment variables starting with "VITE_" and add them to the file
for var in $(env | grep "VITE_"); do
  name=$(echo "$var" | cut -d "=" -f 1)
  value=$(echo "$var" | cut -d "=" -f 2-)
  echo "  $name: \"$value\"," >> $CONFIG_PATH
done

# End the config file
echo "};" >> $CONFIG_PATH
echo "Environment variable injection completed."
exec nginx -g 'daemon off;'

Also, change the src path in our index.html file.

From <script async src="/env-config.js"></script> to
<script async src="/env/env-config.js"></script>

After the above changes, your index.html file looks like

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/vite.svg" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
    <script async src="/env/env-config.js"></script>
    <title>Vite + React + TS</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <div id="root"></div>
    <script type="module" src="/src/main.tsx"></script>
  </body>
</html>

We're done with all the changes. Now, let's build it again and run it to check if everything is working or not

For building run docker build inside the frontend directory

docker build -t my-frontend-secure-todo-multistage:v2 .

It build successfully

Now start the container. But please delete the older container that we created previously.

Then run the docker run command

docker run -it --env-file ./.env -p 8080:8080 --name todo-app-multistage-secure-container my-frontend-secure-todo-multistage:v2

Our container started without any Permission denied error.

Now go to the URL http://localhost:8080. And check now we getting todos or not?

Hurray, it's working 😎

Now let's check if our app is still secure or not. Now we again try to perform the same scenario that we performed previously. We try to delete some files inside the mywebsite folder.

To go inside the container, run the docker exec command

docker exec -it todo-app-multistage-secure-container sh

For Windows run

winpty docker exec -it todo-app-multistage-secure-container sh

Once you're inside the container

Run the whoami command, and you will see frontend_user after running it.

whoami

You will see

Now go to the /frontend-app/mywebsite directory. And try to delete the index.html file. You will see a permission denied error. frontend_user is not able to delete the index.html file.

Run the cd command to go inside the /frontend-app/mywebsitedirectory.

cd /frontend-app/mywebsite

Then run the rm -rf command for deleting the index.html file.

rm -rf index.html

You will see a permission denied error

See our frontend_user working fine, it's unable to delete any files inside the frontend-app. But still it can delete /env/env-config.js file because it had write access for the /env directory. You can try deleting on your end.

So we secured our website from being deleted. Now the hacker is not able to delete our website, at least.

So finally we've done it. And we successfully created our production-ready frontend Dockerfile. Now you can use the same template for any frontend project which mostly based on CSR.

That's all for this blog post. We're done with our blog post. If you want to check out the bonus section. Go and check it for extra knowledge.

And if you follow along till here, pat your back. You did a great job.

12. Bonus: Extra observation on nginx.

Prefer Video? Watch Here

Note:

The core tutorial concludes here. The following section covers some extra observations of mine on nginx. It is strictly optional—feel free to skip it, or read on to understand the underlying mechanics.

If you noticed or not. The path to default.conf in the Dockerfile changes depending on the image.

In the following Dockerfile, we used a different path to replace the existing default.conf with our custom nginx.conf file.

In node:lts image there we used the path /etc/nginx/sites-available/default

The line we used in our Dockerfile COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/sites-available/default

In node:lts-alpine3.22 we used /etc/nginx/http.d/nginx.conf

In the final Stage of the multistage Dockerfile for the image nginx:stable-alpine-slim.
We used path /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf

Every time default.conf file path location changes on each Docker file. Why? Because each Linux distro uses a different location for niginx configuration files.

How to know about these paths?

To check it if you're not sure about the path.

Just install nginx and run the container with the default configuration. Now go inside the container via the exec command. And then run the nginx -t command. It will give you the location of the main nginx configuration file. Now run the cat command to check the content of nginx.conf main file content.

Let’s do this as well. Do it in our running container. We just ran the container for our final build

Run command

docker exec -it todo-app-multistage-container /bin/sh

It will connect your terminal to the container. Once you are inside your container. Run below command

niginx -t

Copy the highlighted path and run the command

cat /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

Are you able to see the content of niginx.conf file. In that file, check for an include statement. It will denote the path where you can put your site config files.

That’s it.

13. Wrap Up:

We're done with our frontend Docker image part. We have seen all the aspects of building images. Now you can also optimize our prod build further by using distroless images. And learn about it more. Stay tuned for the next post, where we will containerize our backend and integrate a MySQL database.

title: SQL Challenge: Why Is Your SQL Query Still Returning NULL?
description:
Imagine your manager asks you to prepare a salary report.

Some employees have a bonus, while others have no bonus recorded.

Your manager wants to see 0 instead of NULL for missing bonuses.

You write a query, but the result still shows NULL.

What went wrong?

Let's look at the data.

employees

emp_id| name| department| salary| bonus
101 | Amit | IT | 90000| 10000
102 | Priya | IT | 70000| NULL
103 | Rahul | IT | 60000| 5000
104 | Neha | HR | 80000| NULL
105 | Sneha | HR | 85000| 15000
106 | Kiran | HR | 95000| NULL
107 | Meera | Finance | 75000| 8000
108 | Arjun | Finance | 55000| NULL

Your challenge

Display employee name, salary and bonus.

If the bonus is NULL, show 0 instead.

Which query would you choose?

Option A

SELECT name, salary,
COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS bonus
FROM employees;

Option B

SELECT name, salary,
COALESCE(0, bonus) AS bonus
FROM employees;

Option C

SELECT name, salary,
bonus + 0 AS bonus
FROM employees;

SQL Solution

Option A is correct.

SELECT name, salary,
COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS bonus
FROM employees;

Output

name| salary | bonus
Amit | 90000 | 10000
Priya| 70000 | 0
Rahul| 60000 | 5000
Neha| 80000 | 0
Sneha| 85000 | 15000
Kiran| 95000 | 0
Meera| 75000 | 8000
Arjun| 55000 | 0

Why does this work?

COALESCE checks the values from left to right and returns the first value that is not NULL.

For example:

COALESCE(10000, 0) returns 10000.

COALESCE(NULL, 0) returns 0.

Now look at Option B.

COALESCE(0, bonus)

It always returns 0 because 0 is already a valid value.

And Option C?

bonus + 0 still returns NULL when bonus is NULL.

Here is the important lesson:

NULL does not mean zero.

It means the value is missing or unknown.

COALESCE helps you show a useful value when the original value is missing. It does not change the data stored in the table.

Your turn

What will this query return?

SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 50, 100);

Will the result be NULL, 50 or 100?

Share your answer in the comments.

Want to learn more SQL with practical examples?

https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/conversion-functions-conditional-expressions-sql-faq.html

SQL #SQLChallenge #SQLInterview #SQLQueries #LearnSQL #DataAnalytics #SankalanDataTech

title: Go Email Retry Budgets: Exponential Backoff With Auditable Healthtech Notice Retention
description:
The bill for retrying a failed email API call includes submission attempts, worker capacity, retained evidence, and the investigation required when an outcome remains ambiguous. For a healthtech compliance notice, the dominant storage term can be repeated message bodies: under an illustrative workload of 10,000 notices, four retained attempt snapshots per notice, and a 100 KB body, those snapshots occupy 4 GB before indexes or replication. Keeping one body per notice reduces that component to 1 GB; attempt metadata remains additional. These are design assumptions, not measured traffic or prices.

Short answer: use capped exponential backoff with jitter for failures that the API contract identifies as transient, honor applicable retry instructions, and preserve a stable notice identity across attempts. Bound retries by both an attempt budget and a notice deadline. When submission may already have succeeded, reconcile the outcome or use documented idempotency support before sending again. Store compact evidence for each attempt instead of repeatedly storing the sensitive payload.

Evidence has costs.

The optimization is to retain the evidence needed to establish what happened while limiting duplicate work and duplicate content. An HTTP response accepting a request, a mail server accepting a message, and a person reading a compliance notice are different claims; an audit record should identify precisely which claim it supports. The central trade-off is storage reduction versus forensic detail: compact records cost less space, but cannot replace a deleted message body during an investigation.

What does another failed email API call actually cost?

Consider the notice as a ledger obligation: one authorized communication, associated with a particular recipient reference and notice version, with several possible transport attempts. This is a proposed data model, not a claim that an email transport can provide exactly-once delivery. The application can enforce uniqueness of its own obligation and state transitions; external submission still depends on the receiving system's documented behavior.

For planning, let N be the number of notices, A the average number of recorded attempts, P the payload size, and M the attempt metadata size. Retaining a full payload with every attempt requires approximately N × A × (P + M) bytes. Referencing one retained payload requires approximately N × P + N × A × M. The illustrative workload above removes 3 GB of duplicate body storage, but it does not reduce message submission fees, establish a retention period, or account for backups. It changes one specific term.

Retries multiply work.

That multiplication also affects incident response. If each attempt has an unrelated identity, an operator must reconstruct whether four submissions represent four notices or four attempts to satisfy one obligation. A stable notice ID, attempt number, submission timestamp, outcome category, and remote receipt reference make that distinction explicit. Keep recipient details behind a restricted reference when possible; an audit trail that reproduces medical content in every log entry creates another sensitive dataset to govern.

Which failures deserve exponential backoff?

Classification must precede scheduling. HTTP semantics in RFC 9110 distinguish an idempotent operation from an operation whose repetition may have additional effects, and caution against automatically retrying a non-idempotent request without a basis for knowing that repetition is safe. A timeout after transmitting a submission is therefore an unknown outcome: the sender lacks confirmation, but that absence does not establish rejection.

The following categories are an application policy to check against the actual email API contract. They are not a universal interpretation of every provider's status codes.

Observed outcome Proposed action Evidence to retain
Explicit temporary rejection or documented throttling Schedule a bounded retry; respect applicable server guidance Classification, attempt count, next eligible time
Explicit permanent validation or authorization rejection Stop automatic submission and route for correction Sanitized reason and notice reference
Timeout or connection loss after possible submission Mark the outcome unknown and reconcile Stable idempotency key, time window, receipt if available
Confirmed API acceptance Stop submission retries and track later delivery evidence separately Receipt reference and acceptance timestamp

A common trap is to treat every unsuccessful client call as proof that the message was never accepted. Backoff changes the timing of a duplicate; it does not prevent the duplicate. If an API documents idempotency, verify the key's scope, retention window, and payload matching rules before relying on it, and reuse the same key for the same intended submission. A locally generated key alone provides no remote guarantee.

Email delivery adds another boundary. RFC 5321 defines temporary and permanent SMTP reply categories, but the HTTP API may expose those later through its own event model. Avoid starting a second application submission loop merely because a downstream SMTP attempt was deferred; first determine which system owns that retry. Likewise, SPF concerns authorization to use a domain in an email identity. RFC 7208 is relevant to deliverability, but increasing a retry count does not repair an authorization configuration.

A bounded Go schedule with durable evidence

Use a delay window that grows exponentially until it reaches a cap, then sample jitter within that window so concurrent failures do not all receive the same scheduled timestamp. The example below proposes six total submission attempts, including the original, with retry windows of 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 seconds. These values illustrate the mechanism; the API contract, notice deadline, and operational capacity must determine production values.

package notice

import (
    "math/rand"
    "time"
)

// NextRetry returns a scheduling decision, not permission to resubmit.
// completedAttempts includes the original submission attempt.
// retryFloor is an already parsed, applicable server retry time.
func NextRetry(
    now, deadline, retryFloor time.Time,
    completedAttempts int,
    rng *rand.Rand,
) (time.Time, bool) {
    const maxAttempts = 6
    const base = 2 * time.Second
    const capDelay = 32 * time.Second
    if completedAttempts < 1 || completedAttempts >= maxAttempts || rng == nil {
        return time.Time{}, false
    }
    window := base
    for n := 1; n < completedAttempts && window < capDelay; n++ {
        window *= 2
        if window > capDelay {
            window = capDelay
        }
    }
    // Sample uniformly from [0, window), then respect the server floor.
    delay := time.Duration(rng.Int63n(int64(window)))
    next := now.Add(delay)
    if next.Before(retryFloor) {
        next = retryFloor
    }
    if !next.Before(deadline) {
        return time.Time{}, false
    }
    return next, true
}

The caller must classify the failure, establish that resubmission is permitted, and parse any applicable Retry-After value before calling this function. RFC 9110 permits Retry-After to express either a date or a delay; convert it to a timestamp and preserve the raw value only if operationally necessary. The server floor may exceed the local backoff cap. If it falls beyond the notice deadline, escalate the obligation instead of shortening that floor to force another attempt.

This schedule has a limitation: it doesn't enforce a shared rate limit across workers. It is not suitable as the sole control for a fleet sharing one submission quota; add admission control at that shared boundary. Jitter spreads eligible times, but cannot guarantee that aggregate traffic stays within the quota.

Persist the chosen next eligible time with the attempt outcome. A worker restart should recover a pending obligation from durable state, rather than begin a fresh six-attempt budget. Use a conditional state transition or equivalent transaction to claim work, and record the attempt before crossing the network boundary. A crash between external acceptance and local confirmation still produces uncertainty; recovery must enter the reconciliation path. The exactly-once mindset is useful here because it forces every ambiguous boundary into view, even though the transport itself supplies no such guarantee.

One implementation detail matters: give each worker its own random source, or synchronize access to a shared one. Inject the clock and random source into tests. Neither timing nor chance should make a correctness assertion intermittent.

Test the ambiguity, then deploy the budget

The most useful test sends a request to a controlled endpoint that records acceptance and then withholds the response. Verify that the sender records an unknown outcome, preserves the notice identity, and follows its reconciliation policy. Also test an explicit temporary rejection, a retry instruction beyond the deadline, exhaustion after six attempts, duplicate delivery events, and a worker restart after a retry timestamp has been persisted. These are proposed acceptance tests; they are not reported production results.

Observe unresolved obligations.

Attempt counts alone can make an unhealthy system look busy. Track the age of the oldest unresolved notice, unknown submissions awaiting reconciliation, exhausted obligations, and the delay between local acceptance and whatever downstream evidence the contract actually provides. Define an operational escalation before releasing the worker, including who can authorize a fresh notice when the original outcome cannot be resolved. An alternative channel requires its own policy and evidence requirements.

For deployment, introduce the retry policy behind a controlled rollout and verify that restarting workers preserves both attempts consumed and next eligible timestamps. A larger retry budget increases queue occupancy and investigation volume, so evaluate it against unresolved obligations and duplicate risk. Raw throughput cannot establish that a compliance notice was delivered.

Retain the obligation and deliberately expire the payload

Separate notice content from attempt evidence. A proposed record can retain a notice reference, content version, restricted recipient reference, timestamps, outcome transitions, and receipt references, while a distinct store governs access to the body. If a digest is retained, it can support comparison with an available artifact; it cannot reconstruct deleted content, prove delivery, or establish what the recipient read. An append-only interface also needs access controls and integrity protections before its audit trail can be trusted.

No universal healthtech retention period follows from an HTTP or email standard. The responsible legal and privacy reviewers must establish the applicable obligations, including any hold that overrides routine deletion. They must also determine whether the available delivery evidence satisfies the particular notice requirement. Transport acceptance alone cannot settle that compliance question.

The deliberate stopping point is to stop keeping full response bodies, repeated message snapshots, and sensitive diagnostic fields once their approved operational purpose ends, while preserving the approved minimum evidence for the obligation. That choice has a concrete incident cost: after deletion, investigators may be unable to reconstruct the exact message or explain a provider-specific response from local records. Agree on that loss before enabling expiration. Reliable retrying requires both a bounded sending policy and an honest account of what the surviving record can prove.

References

The standards below define the protocol boundaries discussed here. The workload, retry limits, record design, and tests are explicit engineering proposals.

Further reading

  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321.html
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208

title: Your Shopify Hero Image Is Probably Lazy-Loaded. Here's the Liquid Fix.
description:
On a lot of Shopify stores I audit, the biggest image on the homepage is also the last one the browser bothers to fetch.

It's the hero banner. It's almost always the Largest Contentful Paint element on mobile. And somewhere in a custom section, someone has written loading: 'lazy' on it, so the browser waits until layout is done before it even starts the download.

Here's how to check for it and fix it in Liquid, without an app.

How it happens

Shopify's image_tag filter already does the sensible thing. Per the docs, loading is set to lazy automatically for images in sections further down the page, and images near the top are left alone. If you just write:

{{ section.settings.image | image_url: width: 2400 | image_tag }}

you get a good default.

The trouble starts when a theme or a freelancer "optimises" every image by hand:

{{ section.settings.image | image_url: width: 2400 | image_tag: loading: 'lazy' }}

Passing loading yourself overrides the default. Now the hero is lazy too, wherever the merchant puts that section, including first on the page. I've also seen the same thing come from old themes that used a lazy-loading JavaScript library with data-src attributes, which is even worse, because the real URL isn't in the HTML at all.

How to check in two minutes

  1. Run the homepage through PageSpeed Insights on mobile.
  2. Open the "LCP request discovery" insight. If it says lazy load is applied to the LCP image, or that fetchpriority=high should be applied, you've found it.
  3. Confirm in the HTML: view source, search for the hero's file name, and look at its <img> tag for loading="lazy".

Do the check on the live storefront, not inside the theme editor. That matters for the fix below.

The fix: decide by section position

Every section has section.index, its 1-based position within its location (the template, or a section group like the header). That's exactly what you need: the first section on the page gets priority, everything below is lazy.

Dawn does this in sections/image-banner.liquid. Simplified (Dawn works out sizes and widths from the section settings; I've left those out):

{%- liquid
  assign fetch_priority = 'auto'
  if section.index == 1
    assign fetch_priority = 'high'
  endif
-%}

{{
  section.settings.image
  | image_url: width: 3840
  | image_tag:
    sizes: '100vw',
    fetchpriority: fetch_priority
}}

Two things to notice. Dawn doesn't pass loading at all, it lets image_tag decide. And it uses fetchpriority, which isn't a named option of the filter; image_tag passes through any HTML attribute you give it as a parameter, so fetchpriority: 'high' ends up on the <img>.

If your section has to set loading explicitly (say, a custom slideshow where only the first slide should load early), make it conditional instead of hardcoded:

{%- liquid
  if section.index == 1 and forloop.first
    assign img_loading = 'eager'
    assign img_priority = 'high'
  else
    assign img_loading = 'lazy'
    assign img_priority = 'auto'
  endif
-%}

{{ block.settings.image | image_url: width: 2400 | image_tag: loading: img_loading, fetchpriority: img_priority, sizes: '100vw' }}

Only the first slide of the first section gets priority. Slides two and three can wait.

The catch: section.index is sometimes nil

The docs list three cases where section.index returns nil:

  • static sections (rendered with {% section 'name' %})
  • while rendering in the online store editor
  • when the section comes back through the Section Rendering API

With the code above, nil == 1 is false, so you fall back to lazy and auto. That's the safe direction, but it explains two things that confuse people. First, the editor preview will never show fetchpriority="high", so test on the live store. Second, if your hero is a static section in theme.liquid, the check never passes, and you need to set it explicitly for that one section.

What about preload: true?

image_tag also takes preload: true, which makes Shopify send a preload resource hint as a Link HTTP header. It doesn't change the <img> tag itself, and Shopify's own docs say to use it sparingly.

In practice, fetchpriority: 'high' on an <img> that's already in the HTML is usually enough. I'd only add preload when the LCP image is a CSS background or sits deep in the markup where the browser finds it late. Preloading two or three images just means they fight each other for bandwidth.

Don't forget sizes

One more thing I fix in the same pass. Without a sizes attribute the browser assumes the image is full viewport width, which is right for a full-bleed banner but wrong for a half-width image next to text. On a phone, that can mean downloading a much bigger file than the slot needs. Set sizes to match the layout, like Dawn does with (min-width: 750px) 50vw, 100vw for split banners.

Quick checklist

  • Search your theme for loading: 'lazy' and loading="lazy". Anything in a section that can sit at the top of the page needs a condition, not a hardcoded value.
  • Give the first image of the first section fetchpriority: 'high'.
  • Leave everything else to image_tag's default.
  • Test on the live storefront, then rerun PageSpeed Insights and check the LCP request discovery insight again.

It's a ten-minute change that rarely needs an app. If you'd rather someone else went through a custom theme for this kind of thing, it's part of what we do in our Shopify theme development work.

title: Your AI Agent Can Query the Database. Give It a Business Map First
description:
An agent can successfully query a database and still give you the wrong answer.

Ask, “How many customers did we have last month?” and it may count every account row. Your business may define a customer as someone with at least one completed purchase. It may exclude test accounts, treat a household as one customer, or use the order date rather than the signup date. The SQL can be valid, the query can finish, and the number can still be wrong.

That is the gap NVIDIA’s Auto Ontology project is trying to address. The project builds a semantic context layer over enterprise data: information about what business terms mean, where metrics live, how entities relate, and which definitions should guide queries. It drew a lively Hacker News discussion on November 3, 2026, but the useful idea is larger than one product: database access is not the same as business understanding.

You do not need to deploy a large platform before improving this. Start with a small, reviewable data dictionary and a few approved SQL views. Give the agent those definitions before granting it database access. Then test the answers against known questions.

This walkthrough builds that minimum version. It is a design tutorial based on public documentation, not a report of hands-on use of NVIDIA Auto Ontology.

Why schema access is not enough

A schema tells an agent that a table has columns such as customer_id, status, and created_at. It does not tell the agent which status values count as active, whether a customer needs a completed order, or which timestamp the business uses for monthly reporting.

People often carry these details as unwritten rules. A finance analyst may know that refunds are subtracted after settlement. A support lead may know that internal test accounts are excluded. If an agent sees only tables and column names, it must guess, infer from examples, or ask someone. The resulting query can be syntactically correct but semantically inconsistent.

NVIDIA’s repository describes Auto Ontology as a framework that generates a semantic layer from metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, validates generated queries against certified definitions and lineage, and makes context available through MCP, CLI, and API. Those are project capabilities described by the maintainers, not independent accuracy guarantees. The project is a useful signal that agent builders are treating business meaning as an infrastructure concern rather than just a prompt-writing problem.

The central distinction is simple:

  • A schema describes storage. It names tables, columns, types, and constraints.
  • A semantic layer describes meaning. It records concepts, approved metrics, relationships, exclusions, and provenance.
  • A query policy limits action. It determines what the agent may read or run, regardless of what it understands.

These layers work together, but they are not interchangeable. A glossary does not enforce permissions. A read-only account does not make a metric definition correct. A prompt alone is not a durable source of truth.

Build the smallest useful semantic layer

Pick one business question that is both common and easy to verify. For example: “How many purchasing customers did we have last month?” Avoid starting with every table in the warehouse. A narrow scope is easier for a domain expert to review, and it makes errors visible.

For this example, suppose a database contains customers, orders, and order_items. A first version of the semantic contract could look like this:

metrics:
  purchasing_customers:
    description: "Distinct customers with at least one completed, non-test order."
    entity: customer
    source: analytics.purchasing_customers
    filters:
      - "orders.status = 'completed'"
      - "customers.is_test = false"
    time_field: orders.completed_at
    grain: customer per calendar month
    owner: analytics
    status: approved

entities:
  customer:
    primary_key: customers.id
    joins:
      - target: orders
        condition: customers.id = orders.customer_id

This is not a universal ontology format. It is a small human-readable contract. Its value comes from making assumptions explicit and reviewable, not from choosing a particular file extension.

Write definitions as decisions, not labels. “Purchasing customers” is a label. “Distinct customers with at least one completed, non-test order, grouped by completion date” is a decision a reviewer can challenge. If Finance and Product use different definitions, record two named metrics rather than hiding the disagreement under one vague term.

Include the time rule. “Last month” can mean calendar month, trailing 30 days, or the previous completed reporting period. State the timezone and boundary rule when they affect the result. For a first version, you can write “calendar month in UTC” or link to the organization’s established reporting calendar.

Name provenance and ownership. Identify the source view or tables and the team that approves the definition. A definition without an owner can become stale while still looking official. Add a last-reviewed date if the metric changes regularly.

Make the approved path executable

A prose definition helps a person review intent. It is not enough to ensure every query uses the same rules. Put the core definition into a database view, then point the semantic entry at that view.

CREATE VIEW analytics.purchasing_customers AS
SELECT DISTINCT
    c.id AS customer_id,
    date_trunc('month', o.completed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AS month_utc
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.is_test = false
  AND o.status = 'completed';

The example uses PostgreSQL syntax. A real schema may need different names, time handling, soft-delete rules, or tenant filters. Ask the data owner to confirm those details before treating this view as canonical.

The agent can now be directed to query the approved interface instead of reconstructing joins and exclusions from raw tables:

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS purchasing_customers
FROM analytics.purchasing_customers
WHERE month_utc = TIMESTAMP '2026-10-01 00:00:00';

A view is not automatically safe or correct. It can contain a bug, expose sensitive columns, or embody a disputed definition. The practical advantage is that the query path is centralized: reviewers can inspect and test the definition once rather than hoping every generated query repeats it correctly.

PostgreSQL’s documentation describes views as stored queries that can be used like virtual tables. That makes them a useful building block for a curated query surface. Pair them with database permissions: grant the agent’s database role access only to the approved schemas or views it needs, and keep it read-only unless a specific, separately reviewed workflow requires writes.

Add tests that catch meaning drift

A definition becomes more useful when a change can fail visibly. Add small fixtures or run assertions against a known reporting dataset. Test the cases that encode the business rule, not just whether the view returns rows.

For the purchasing-customer metric, useful cases include:

  • A customer with one completed order is counted once.
  • A customer with several completed orders is still counted once for that month.
  • A pending or cancelled order does not qualify.
  • A completed order from a test account does not qualify.
  • An order completed at the month boundary lands in the expected month and timezone.
  • Two different customers with the same name remain two customers if the key is the customer ID.

These tests can be implemented in your existing SQL test framework, migration checks, or a small fixture-based integration test. The exact tool matters less than having a known expected result that runs when the definition changes.

Next, create a tiny evaluation set of questions and expected answers. Include the normal question, an ambiguous question, and one that should be rejected or clarified. For example:

  • “How many purchasing customers were there in October 2026?” should map to the approved metric and month.
  • “How many customers are active?” should ask which definition of active is intended if no approved metric exists.
  • “Show me every customer’s email and purchase history” should be blocked or require an explicit authorized workflow if that data is not needed for the task.

Store the question, expected metric or view, expected result, and reviewer. Re-run the set after changing a definition, database schema, model, or agent instructions. Do not treat a fluent explanation as proof that the number is right. Compare the generated SQL and the returned result with the approved path.

Keep the agent behind boundaries

A semantic layer improves context. It does not replace access control, review, or query limits.

Use a dedicated read-only role. Give the agent access only to the curated views it needs. Do not reuse an administrator credential, and do not assume a prompt saying “do not modify data” is a permission boundary.

Limit query cost and scope. Set statement timeouts, row limits where appropriate, and resource controls through the database or query service. A well-meaning agent can still produce an expensive join or scan.

Return provenance with the answer. Record which metric, view, filters, and time range were used. For analytics answers, showing the SQL and source definition makes review much easier than returning a number alone.

Separate draft definitions from approved definitions. An automated system can propose a metric or relation, but a proposal should not silently become the definition used for business reporting. Give a person responsible for the domain a clear approval step.

Track disagreements. If two teams use “revenue” differently, the system should preserve that distinction. A forced single definition may look tidy while making the answer less useful. Name the variants and specify when each is appropriate.

The NVIDIA repository lists HashiCorp Vault as an optional component for connection credential storage. That is a concrete reminder to review credential handling, storage, authentication, and deployment settings before connecting any agent-facing system to real data. “Open source” and “read-only tools” do not remove the need for a security review.

Where a dedicated ontology platform fits

A hand-maintained dictionary and SQL views are a good starting point when the scope is small, definitions are stable, and your team already has a review process. They become harder to manage when definitions span many databases, terms conflict across departments, lineage must be traced, or multiple agent interfaces need the same context.

That is where a dedicated semantic platform may help. NVIDIA Auto Ontology’s public project describes metadata discovery, ontology generation, reconciliation across systems, query validation, provenance, and MCP/API/CLI access. Before adopting it or a similar platform, test it against your own questions. Ask whether it can represent your definitions, how generated changes are reviewed, what credentials it stores, which permissions it honors, and how you can inspect the query and its lineage.

Do not choose based on a demo that answers one easy question. Build a small benchmark from the questions your analysts actually ask. Include ambiguous terms, exceptions, boundary dates, and questions the agent must refuse. Measure correctness of the SQL and result, not just response speed or confidence.

A practical starting checklist

Before an agent queries business data, confirm that you can answer these questions:

  • What exact metric or entity is the agent using?
  • Which source view or tables define it?
  • What filters, time field, timezone, and grain apply?
  • Who owns and approves the definition?
  • Can the agent access only the required data, using a read-only role?
  • Can a reviewer inspect the SQL, source, and result provenance?
  • Are there test questions with known answers, including edge cases?
  • What happens when the question uses an undefined or disputed term?
  • Are credentials stored and rotated safely?

If several answers are unknown, adding broader database access is unlikely to solve the underlying problem. Start by writing down one definition and one approved query path. Then give the agent a narrow way to use it and measure whether the result is correct.

The useful lesson in the Auto Ontology discussion is not that every team needs a new platform. It is that database structure and business meaning are different kinds of context. An agent needs both, and the second one should be explicit enough for people to inspect, correct, and govern.

If you want more practical articles about AI agents and developer tools, subscribe. What business definition has caused the most confusion in your data queries? Save the checklist above and use it to review the next agent integration.

Sources

[1] NVIDIA Auto Ontology repository and README

[2] Hacker News discussion of NVIDIA Auto Ontology

[3] PostgreSQL documentation: CREATE VIEW

title: ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our DMARC Record Checker, Generator & SPF/DKIM Validator, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

A comprehensive guide to implementing production-grade GitOps continuous delivery using ArgoCD, Argo Rollouts, and Helm on enterprise Kubernetes clusters with automated rollback and multi-environment promotion gates.

Architectural Overview: Enterprise ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture

Modern enterprise engineering demands robust, scalable infrastructure that can withstand high concurrency, distributed network latency, and stringent regulatory mandates. Operating ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture in production requires transitioning from basic prototypes to resilient, automated architectures built on high-availability design principles.

HostingPodium engineers enterprise solutions around Production Kubernetes & Red Hat OpenShift Container Orchestration, ensuring your technical teams eliminate operational bottlenecks, reduce mean time to recovery (MTTR), and enforce verifiable data sovereignty across hybrid environments.

In high-scale enterprise ecosystems, architectural resilience cannot be treated as an afterthought. Workloads running on distributed infrastructure require deterministic execution guarantees, verifiable fault isolation, and immutable deployment pipelines that protect mission-critical operations against data corruption, regional cloud provider outages, and sudden spikes in transactional throughput.

Production Technology Stack & Infrastructure Primitives

Deploying ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture at enterprise scale requires rigorous calibration of the underlying compute, storage, and networking layers. Our architecture standardizes on the following core components:

Core Execution Tier & Tooling 

- **Platform Execution Engines:** Hardened deployment across Kubernetes, Red Hat OpenShift, ArgoCD GitOps, Istio Service Mesh, Calico CNI, Prometheus Operator, Helm running on dedicated [bare-metal servers](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/server-hosting-administration/) or [private VPC](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/cloud-platform-engineering/) clusters.

- **Declarative Automation:** Standardized on Immutable GitOps Delivery, Declarative Infrastructure as Code, Automated Horizontal/Vertical Pod Autoscaling, [Zero-Trust](https://hostingpodium.com/blog/enterprise-zero-trust-network-wireguard-mesh/) Pod Network Policies, ensuring deterministic configuration management and immutable infrastructure delivery.

- **Storage Tiers:** High-IOPS NVMe storage pools with automated cross-datacenter replication, point-in-time recovery, and snapshot auditing.

- **[Telemetry](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/observability/) & Instrumentation:** Unified metrics collection, distributed tracing, and real-time log aggregation powered by [Prometheus and Grafana](https://hostingpodium.com/blog/prometheus-grafana-enterprise-observability-stack/).

By decoupling the stateful storage persistence layer from stateless compute runners, this architecture achieves linear horizontal scalability. Under increased traffic bursts, autoscaling controller groups dynamically instantiate compute nodes while persistent storage volumes maintain zero data loss through continuous synchronous journaling and distributed lock management.

High Availability, Failover & Service Level Agreements

Operational continuity is foundational to our enterprise engagements. Every system deployment is governed by transparent, mathematically validated SLA targets:

Resilience Standards 

- **Availability SLA:** Multi-master control plane quorum, 99.99% ingress uptime, and sub-minute node replacement automation.

- **Clustering & Redundancy:** N+1 high-availability cluster topology with automated health checks, sub-second failover routing, and zero single points of failure.

- **[Disaster Recovery](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/backup-disaster-recovery/) Metrics:** Documented Recovery Point Objectives (RPO < 15 minutes) and Recovery Time Objectives (RTO < 30 minutes) verified by scheduled chaos engineering tests.

Dynamic failover mechanisms rely on distributed consensus protocols such as Raft or Paxos, preventing split-brain conditions during transient network partitions. Load balancers continuously monitor TCP health probes, automatically draining traffic away from degraded cluster nodes within 500 milliseconds of threshold degradation.

Enterprise Security, Governance & Compliance Standards

Security is integrated natively across all architectural tiers, adhering to modern zero-trust network access (ZTNA) frameworks:

Data Protection & Regulatory Alignment 

- **Compliance Frameworks:** Engineered to satisfy PCI-DSS segmentation, container image vulnerability scanning via Trivy/Clair, and immutable audit trails. across sovereign cloud and private on-premises infrastructures.

- **Cryptographic Controls:** Strict TLS 1.3 protocol enforcement in transit and AES-256 cryptographic encryption for all persistent data at rest.

- **Identity & RBAC:** Centralized Role-Based Access Control, multi-factor authentication, and OAuth2/SAML Single Sign-On (SSO) integration.

- **Vulnerability Management:** Continuous automated CVE scanning, container image provenance verification, and tamper-proof operational logging.

Network perimeters are isolated using hardened software-defined firewall policies, strict egress filtering, and encrypted wireguard tunnels for inter-node communication. Privileged access requires cryptographic short-lived certificates issued through automated mutual TLS (mTLS) identities.

Performance Tuning & Low-Latency Kernel Calibration

Achieving peak performance for ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture requires micro-optimization at the operating system and Linux kernel layer. Standard cloud instance default configurations often introduce artificial I/O throttling and excessive TCP buffer latency.

Production Kernel Optimizations

Our engineering deployments apply custom sysctl tuning tailored for high-concurrency workloads:

- **TCP Buffer Scaling:** Optimization of `net.ipv4.tcp_rmem` and `net.ipv4.tcp_wmem` to enable automatic window scaling across high-bandwidth wide-area links.

- **Connection Queue Depth:** Expansion of `net.core.somaxconn` to 65,535 and `net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog` to mitigate connection drops during high burst traffic.

- **Memory Virtualization:** Calibration of `vm.swappiness=1` and `vm.dirty_ratio=10` to prevent unexpected page cache latency spikes and enforce deterministic NVMe disk writes.

- **Storage I/O Scheduler:** Implementation of the `mq-deadline` or `none` multi-queue I/O schedulers for enterprise NVMe drives, maximizing IOPS throughput and minimizing queue wait time.

Observability, Telemetry & SRE Incident Response Runbooks

Comprehensive observability transforms reactive firefighting into proactive infrastructure reliability engineering. Every component within ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture exports real-time telemetry metrics.

Unified Observability Stack

Our SRE framework instruments the environment with the following operational capabilities:

- **Granular Metric Scraping:** Prometheus agents scrape application and system health endpoints at 10-second intervals, aggregating metrics into clustered central storage.

- **Actionable Grafana Dashboards:** Visualization matrices monitor latency p95 and p99 percentiles, CPU saturation, memory exhaustion, and I/O wait times.

- **Smart Anomaly [Alerting](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/monitoring-incident-support/):** Alertmanager triggers multi-channel notifications (Slack, PagerDuty, Webhooks) based on rate-of-change heuristics rather than crude static thresholds.

- **Distributed Tracing:** OpenTelemetry context propagation enables end-to-end trace auditing across [microservices](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/application-modernization/) to isolate high-latency bottlenecks.

Operational Failure Scenarios & Automated Recovery Mechanics

Infrastructure must be designed to withstand hardware degradation, hypervisor failure, and sudden database node crashes. Our architecture incorporates self-healing automation runbooks:

Failure Mitigation Matrix 

- **Split-Brain Protection:** Quorum-based voting nodes guarantee that isolated network partitions cannot independently accept writes, preventing split-brain data corruption.

- **Automated Leader Re-election:** In the event of primary node failure, standby replicas evaluate replication lag and promote the most synchronized node within 3 seconds.

- **Graceful Degradation:** Read-only replicas continue serving cached query traffic even during transient primary database failovers, guaranteeing zero read downtime.

- **Immutable Snapshot Restoration:** Automated hourly block-level snapshots stored on write-once-read-many (WORM) storage protect against accidental deletion or ransomware events.

Step-by-Step Implementation Roadmap

Our engineering methodology follows a disciplined four-phase deployment lifecycle to ensure zero downtime:

- **Discovery & Topology Assessment:** Detailed audit of existing workloads, network throughput, storage IOPS, and integration dependencies.

- **Staging & Performance Benchmarking:** Provisioning of isolated staging environments to stress-test throughput, failover mechanics, and API latency under simulated load.

- **Canary Rollout & Production Cutover:** Controlled cutover utilizing blue-green or canary release strategies with automated rollback triggers.

- **24/7 Managed SRE Support:** Continuous performance calibration, automated kernel patching, and proactive incident response runbooks.
