title: How to read PostgreSQL EXPLAIN output
description:
TL;DR

  • Read the plan tree from leaves to root; cost, rows, and width are estimates, not measurements.
  • Start with plain EXPLAIN when execution consequences are unknown. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and adds observed time, rows, and loops.
  • Before diagnosing a row-count mismatch, check for early stops and loops. A substantial mismatch in a node that ran to completion warrants investigation.
  • One plan does not prove a cause: check statistics, parameters, and representative conditions. Rollback does not undo nextval sequence advances or resource consumption.

What does a PostgreSQL EXPLAIN plan show?

A PostgreSQL EXPLAIN plan shows the planner's chosen strategy as a tree of nodes, each representing one retrieval or processing step, along with estimated cost, row count, and row width for every node.

Scans sit at the leaves. Joins, sorts, and aggregates appear above them. In text output, the final result is at the top, indented -> lines mark child nodes, and Filter and Index Cond describe nodes rather than forming new ones. Follow rows from leaves to root, but execution order depends on the algorithm: a nested loop rescans its inner child for each outer row, while a hash join builds before probing.

Start with a plan that has just one node. The documented sequential scan of the regression-test table tenk1 in PostgreSQL 18 produces:

Seq Scan on tenk1 (cost=0.00..445.00 rows=10000 width=244)

Four fields appear: 0.00 startup cost, 445.00 total cost, 10,000 estimated rows, and 244 bytes average row width. These figures come from the documented PostgreSQL regression-test database example. They weren't measured in a separate run.

Run EXPLAIN (without ANALYZE) to inspect the tree and fields without executing the statement's planned operations.

What do cost, rows, and width actually mean?

Cost, rows, and width are the planner's predictions based on statistics and configurable cost parameters. They aren't measurements of elapsed time, actual I/O, or observed result size.

The two cost values use a configurable scale, with parameters including seq_page_cost (default 1.0) and random_page_cost (default 4.0). An upper node's cost includes its children's costs, so summing a branch double-counts modeled work. Costs compare modeled work under consistent assumptions. They're neither milliseconds nor portable benchmarks across servers, datasets, or PostgreSQL versions.

Row and width estimates depend on sampled statistics. The planner uses pg_class page and row counts and pg_statistic selectivity information. ANALYZE gathers these by sampling, so estimates remain approximate even after fresh analysis.

To move from predictions to observations, compare rows= with actual rows in an analyzed plan to find where estimates first diverge. Check completion and loops before concluding the estimate is wrong.

What does EXPLAIN ANALYZE add, and what should you watch out for?

EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and reports actual time (startup and total, in milliseconds), actual rows, and loops alongside the original estimates.

When a node runs more than once (such as the inner side of a nested loop), the reported time and rows are per-execution averages. Multiply these averages by loops to estimate accumulated node time and rows, not the statement's elapsed time.

In the documented LIMIT 2 query against tenk1, the child Index Scan estimates 10 rows if run to completion, but the parent Limit stops after obtaining 2:

Limit (cost=0.29..14.33 rows=2 width=244) (actual time=0.051..0.071 rows=2.00 loops=1)

-> Index Scan using tenk1_unique2 on tenk1 (cost=0.29..70.50 rows=10 width=244) (actual time=0.051..0.070 rows=2.00 loops=1)

(Filter conditions and summary lines omitted from the documented excerpt.)

PostgreSQL explicitly says this isn't an estimation error. Before diagnosing a row-count mismatch, check whether a parent node such as Limit stopped the child early.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE performs INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE with ordinary side effects. The documentation recommends wrapping in a transaction and rolling back, but sequence values from nextval aren't reclaimed after rollback, and resource consumption persists. Use plain EXPLAIN first when execution consequences are unknown.

When does a row-count mismatch actually matter?

A substantial mismatch in a node that ran to completion warrants investigation, but one plan can't establish whether the mismatch changed the plan choice or caused the slow query.

Correlated predicates, skewed distributions, and insufficient distinct-value estimates can produce genuine errors that fresh ANALYZE alone may not fix.

A distinct-value estimate isn't itself an EXPLAIN node-row count. GoCardless reported (engineering blog, last edited September 2022) that PostgreSQL estimated approximately 25,000 distinct payout_id values, while the team's approximate data counts implied almost 3.5 million. The author reports that the distinct-value estimate became stable after the team raised a statistics target to 5,000. Server version, hardware, and hosting aren't established in the account. Check what the statistics represent. The value 5,000 isn't a universal target.

When investigating a mismatch in a node that ran to completion:

  1. Establish execution context: exact SQL, parameters, and PostgreSQL version.
  2. Find where estimated and actual rows first diverge.
  3. Inspect pg_stats for the relevant columns (most_common_vals, histogram_bounds, n_distinct).
  4. Test a targeted remedy and verify under representative conditions.

What are the limits of one EXPLAIN plan?

One plan shows what PostgreSQL chose and, with ANALYZE, what happened during that single execution. It doesn't establish why the plan was slow or that a fix generalizes.

A literal query investigated manually can produce a different plan from a prepared statement's generic plan. EXPLAIN EXECUTE can show the prepared statement's plan. PostgreSQL also warns against extrapolating small-dataset results to substantially different situations.

Treat the plan as a diagnostic starting point. Combine it with statistics inspection, representative data, and (for intermittent problems) auto_explain logging under controlled overhead.

Frequently asked questions about reading PostgreSQL EXPLAIN plans

Are EXPLAIN cost units milliseconds?

No. Costs use a configurable scale. EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports actual time in milliseconds. Don't treat cost comparisons across servers, datasets, or versions as timing measurements.

Does EXPLAIN ANALYZE change my data?

It executes the statement, so INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE can change data, and even SELECT can have side effects when it calls functions such as nextval. Rolling back a transaction doesn't reclaim nextval sequence advances or resource consumption. Use plain EXPLAIN when execution consequences are unknown.

Should I run ANALYZE whenever estimated rows differ from actual rows?

Not automatically. Check for early stops and loops first. If a node that ran to completion still shows a substantial mismatch, inspect relevant pg_stats. Fresh ANALYZE updates sampled statistics but may not resolve the mismatch.

title: Not Every Slow Query Needs a New Index
description:
What a SQL review taught me about assumptions, AI-written queries, and common-sense tuning

A development team asked me to review the SQL behind a change-data publishing job before they moved it from once a day to once an hour. In QA, one full run took 10 to 12 minutes. After the review, the same run took under 30 seconds. In production, most of its queries now finish in under a millisecond.

Almost none of that came from adding indexes. It came from reading the queries, asking what the job actually needed, and checking each assumption against real data. This post walks through what we found, in the order we found it, and what I would tell any team (or any AI assistant) writing SQL against a busy production database.

The short version:

  • You don't always need to tune the database. Often you need to understand the use case and explain how the database behaves.
  • Functions on indexed columns and "this column might be null" assumptions are the most common silent performance killers.
  • What is harmless in QA can be dangerous in production, because the data is shaped differently.
  • An index can make a query slower. Measure after every change.

The setup

The job polls a PostgreSQL read replica for rows that changed since its last run and publishes them as events. It is a classic checkpoint pattern:

  1. Read a ceiling: the newest change timestamp in the source tables.
  2. Count the rows changed between the last checkpoint and that ceiling.
  3. Page through them with keyset pagination, 500 rows at a time.
  4. Store the ceiling as the next checkpoint.

I'll use a generic schema for the examples:

Table Rows (largest) What it holds
accounts ~1M Users, organizations and partners, with an account_type column
contracts ~1,100 Partner contracts, keyed by the owning account
memberships ~650k Which accounts belong to which organization, with a membership_type
org_members ~9M Account-to-location assignments
locations ~hundreds of k Organization addresses

Every table has created_at and updated_at. The source system also maintains updated_at_num, a numeric YYYYMMDDHHMISS copy of updated_at, and that column is indexed on every table. Keep that last detail in mind.

Lesson 1: A function on an indexed column throws the index away

Every change-window filter in the job looked like this:

WHERE COALESCE(a.updated_at, a.created_at) >  :checkpoint
  AND COALESCE(a.updated_at, a.created_at) <= :snapshot

The intent is reasonable: if a row was never updated, fall back to its creation time. But PostgreSQL can only use a B-tree index when the predicate matches the indexed expression. Wrap the column in COALESCE, and the index on updated_at (or updated_at_num) is no longer a candidate. Every window query became a sequential scan of the whole table.

The COALESCE also encoded an assumption: that updated_at can be null. So before changing anything, we checked:

SELECT count(*) FROM accounts WHERE updated_at IS NULL;      -- 0
SELECT count(*) FROM accounts WHERE updated_at_num IS NULL;  -- 0

Zero on every table. The source system sets both timestamps when a row is created, so the fallback could never fire. The fix was to drop the function and filter on the indexed column directly:

WHERE a.updated_at_num >  :checkpoint
  AND a.updated_at_num <= :snapshot

That one change turned every window query into an index range scan.

Two things to take from it:

  • Don't defend against a condition until you've checked whether it exists. A one-line count(*) settled a question the code had been paying for on every run.
  • If you really do need the fallback, write it so it can use an index. Either (updated_at > x AND updated_at <= y) OR (updated_at IS NULL AND created_at > x AND created_at <= y), or an expression index on exactly COALESCE(updated_at, created_at).

Lesson 2: What is fine in QA can bite in production

The COALESCE wasn't the only defensive habit. One query filtered on TRIM(a.account_type) = 'STAFF'. In QA that is harmless: small tables, fast scans, correct results. In production it does two quiet things:

  • It stops any index on account_type from being used.
  • It hints that some values might be padded with spaces. If that were true, every other query that compares account_type without TRIM would silently miss those rows.

Again, the answer was in the data:

SELECT count(*) FROM accounts WHERE account_type <> TRIM(account_type);  -- 0

No padded values, so the TRIM came out, and the queries became consistent with each other.

I want to be clear about where this comes from. The developers I work with write good SQL. But we are now in an era where a lot of SQL is drafted by AI assistants, and they are very good at producing queries that return the right answer. They are much less good at knowing your data. A model will happily add COALESCE, TRIM, LOWER or DISTINCT "just in case", because in the abstract each one is safer. On a 10,000-row QA table you'll never notice. On a 10-million-row production table, each one can turn an index lookup into a full scan.

The result being correct does not mean the assumptions behind it are. Before a query ships, check it against the data's real shape: null counts, value distributions, duplicates, and how skewed the busiest keys are. Or ask a database engineer to review it. It never hurts.

Lesson 3: Carry every filter you know into the subquery

The partner-count query looked like this:

SELECT count(*)
FROM contracts c
JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = c.account_id
WHERE c.org_id = :org
  AND a.updated_at_num > :checkpoint AND a.updated_at_num <= :snapshot
  AND c.account_id IN (
        SELECT DISTINCT m.parent_account_id
        FROM memberships m
        WHERE m.membership_type = 'PRIMARY'
          AND m.is_deleted = false
          AND (m.end_date IS NULL OR m.end_date >= :as_of));

The outer query was narrowed to one organization and a one-hour window: 59 candidate rows. The subquery wasn't narrowed at all. PostgreSQL read 1.77 million membership rows, built a distinct list of 831 IDs, then matched that list against the 59 candidates. That was 31,395 buffers and 83 ms to return a count of zero.

Two changes fixed it:

  AND EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM memberships m
        WHERE m.parent_account_id = c.account_id   -- correlate to the outer row
          AND m.org_id = :org                      -- the filter the outer query already had
          AND m.membership_type = 'PRIMARY'
          AND m.is_deleted = false
          AND (m.end_date IS NULL OR m.end_date >= :as_of));
IN (SELECT DISTINCT …) Correlated EXISTS with filters
Execution time 83 ms 0.8 ms
Buffers 31,395 181
Memberships access Parallel sequential scan Index lookup per candidate

A note on IN versus EXISTS: PostgreSQL already turns IN (subquery) into a semi-join, so the two often plan the same way. The DISTINCT adds nothing, since a semi-join never returns a row twice, and it can push the planner toward building the full list first. Switching to EXISTS helps. The bigger win is adding the filter. If the outer query is limited to something you also know about the subquery's rows, say so in the subquery too. Don't rely on the planner to infer it.

Lesson 4: Ask what a query is for before you tune it

The slowest query in the job didn't return any data. It computed the run's ceiling:

SELECT max(ts) FROM (
    SELECT max(updated_at_num) AS ts FROM accounts WHERE account_type IN (...)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT to_char(max(password_changed_at), 'YYYYMMDDHH24MISS')::numeric FROM accounts WHERE account_type IN (...)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT max(updated_at_num) FROM org_members
    UNION ALL
    SELECT max(s.updated_at_num)
    FROM staff_links s JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = s.account_id AND a.account_type = 'STAFF'
) x;

It took 853 ms and about 1 million buffers to return one number. The plan showed three different behaviours:

Branch How PostgreSQL ran it Cost
max(updated_at_num) on one table Backward index scan, stops at the first row 0.2 ms
max(password_changed_at) Sequential scan; the column has no index ~590 ms
max(...) over a join Full join of every staff account, then aggregate ~270 ms

PostgreSQL has a neat shortcut here. As the CREATE AGGREGATE documentation explains, a MIN- or MAX-like aggregate can be answered from an index, because SELECT max(col) FROM tab is equivalent to SELECT col FROM tab ORDER BY col DESC LIMIT 1. The planner walks the index backward and takes the first non-null value. It also works on partitioned tables and UNION ALL views, by merging each child's index. It does not work through a join. The planner source (planagg.c) limits the shortcut to queries that reference exactly one table, so the join branch had to build the whole join just to find its largest value.

That is where understanding the use case matters more than tuning. This value is an upper bound for the next change window. It doesn't have to be the exact newest staff row; it only has to be at least as high. Dropping the join and taking max(updated_at_num) over all of staff_links gives a bound that is never lower, and costs a single index probe. The join filter still applies in the query that reads the window.

The same review turned up a second easy win. The ceiling was global, but the job ran it once per scope, inside a loop, so it returned the same value several times per run. Computing it once per run cost nothing to change.

The password_changed_at branch I left alone. More on that in Lesson 6.

Lesson 5: A test that returns zero rows proves nothing

My first round of EXPLAIN ANALYZE used a one-hour window, the job's steady state. Most queries looked great: under a millisecond. Then I noticed how often the plans said (never executed). In that hour, no organization had changed, so every join after the first step was skipped. The plan was cheap because there was no work, not because the work was cheap.

Widening the window to 30 days told a different story. One query that ran in 0.7 ms on the hourly window chose a completely different plan:

  • It started from the membership table instead of the changed rows.
  • It read every one of the 15,368 primary memberships, then probed accounts for each.
  • It found 31 changed rows, after 72,522 buffers.

The cause was a row estimate. The planner expected 188 primary memberships and got 15,368, about 80 times more. With 188, starting from memberships looks cheap. A likely reason is how PostgreSQL combines filters: by default it multiplies each condition's selectivity as if they were independent, so correlated filters (type, deleted flag, end date) can be badly underestimated. Check that statistics are fresh with ANALYZE first. If the columns really are correlated, CREATE STATISTICS can tell the planner how they relate.

So I now test every change-data query with three windows:

Window What it tells you
Normal (one hour) Steady-state cost
Wide (30 days) What happens after an outage or a missed run
Full history The very first run, when the checkpoint is empty

The first run is easy to forget. Here it was fine: page one of the full-history query took about 20 ms, because the planner could stop as soon as it had 500 rows. But you only know that by running it.

Lesson 6: "Good enough" is a valid result. Index only what doesn't scale

After the rewrites, I had a list of index candidates that would have made every remaining query near-instant: one on password_changed_at, a partial index for a rare account type, and a few more. Before building any of them, I added up what an hourly run actually cost without them:

Part of the run Cost
Ceiling queries, once per run ~1.5–1.8 s
Change-window queries, per scope ~1.2 s for the largest
Whole run ~6–7 s, every buffer from cache

The slowest single statement was under a second, far from any timeout. Every index you add costs writes, storage and maintenance forever, and here the database was a replication target that would pay for each one on every write. So most of the candidates were dropped. That is a fine outcome. Not every slow-looking query needs an index; sometimes it needs nothing.

One query was different, because its cost multiplied. It loaded full account details in chunks of 100 IDs, and each chunk joined org_members on account_id, a column with no index. Every chunk scanned a 9-million-row table: about 0.7 s.

Scenario Accounts to load Chunks Time
Hourly ~50 1 ~0.7 s
30-day catch-up ~20,000 ~200 ~2.5 min
First run ~870,000 ~8,700 ~1.7 hours

That is the test I use now: don't ask whether a query is slow, ask whether its cost grows with the data or the backlog. Fixed costs can usually be tolerated. Costs that multiply need an index. We added exactly one: org_members (account_id).

Lesson 7: A new index can make a query slower

The new index worked exactly as planned: the org_members step went from scanning 5.4 million rows to reading 2,217 buffers. Then I looked at the total for the chunk query. It had gone from 723 ms to 26.9 seconds.

Before the index After the index
org_members Parallel sequential scan, 174k buffers Index scan, 2,217 buffers
memberships One scan of the 15k primary rows, hashed 7,191 index probes, each discarding ~14,000 rows
Total 723 ms, 243k buffers 26,872 ms, 22.7M buffers

With org_members suddenly cheap, the planner switched to a nested loop and probed memberships once per organization row through an index on org_id. That index holds every membership in the organization, one per member account. The accounts in this chunk belonged to very large organizations, so each probe walked about 14,000 entries to find the one primary membership it needed.

The planner expected roughly one row per probe. When it knows a value in advance, PostgreSQL can look it up in its most-common-values statistics. Here each probe's value came from the outer row at run time, so the planner estimated an average number of rows per organization. The handful of very large organizations didn't fit that average, and re-running ANALYZE doesn't change how the estimate is made.

The fix was another index, but a very small one: a partial index containing only the rows the query asks for.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY memberships_primary_org_idx
    ON memberships (org_id) INCLUDE (parent_account_id, end_date)
    WHERE membership_type = 'PRIMARY' AND is_deleted = false;

It holds about 15,000 rows instead of 650,000, so it is small and cheap to maintain, and each probe now lands directly on the row it needs. PostgreSQL uses a partial index only when it can prove, at planning time, that the query's WHERE clause implies the index predicate. The docs point out that a bind parameter such as membership_type = $1 can't prove that. Because this query uses membership_type = 'PRIMARY' AND is_deleted = false as literal values, the planner can match the partial index without any code change.

The lesson isn't "avoid indexes". It's that an index changes the plan around it, not just the step it targets. Re-run the full EXPLAIN ANALYZE after every index, and read the total, not just the line you were fixing.

Building the indexes online

Both indexes went in with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so writes kept flowing. A few things I check every time:

1. Look for old transactions first. Per the CREATE INDEX docs, a concurrent build waits before each table scan for transactions that have modified the table, and after the second scan for any transaction holding a snapshot older than that scan. My pre-check found 65 sessions from a replication tool sitting idle in transaction for 28 days. Before cancelling anything, check whether they actually matter:

SELECT count(*) AS sessions,
       count(backend_xmin) AS holding_snapshot,
       count(backend_xid)  AS holding_xid
FROM   pg_stat_activity
WHERE  state = 'idle in transaction'
  AND  now() - xact_start > interval '1 day';

Ours held no snapshot, no transaction ID and no locks on the target tables, so they couldn't block the build or hold back vacuum. That's a cleanup item, not a blocker.

2. Run with autocommit on. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block, and some SQL clients wrap scripts in one.

3. Decide on lock_timeout deliberately. It lets a build fail fast instead of queueing behind a long transaction, but a build that fails partway leaves an invalid index behind. I left it unset and watched the progress view instead.

4. Check for invalid indexes afterwards. CREATE INDEX ... IF NOT EXISTS sees an invalid leftover's name and skips it with only a NOTICE. Drop it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY and build again, or rebuild it with REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;

5. Build smallest to largest, and watch replication lag during the big ones.

A review checklist

This is what I now run through for any SQL headed to a large production table, whether a person or an AI wrote it.

Predicates

  • No functions wrapped around indexed columns in WHERE or JOIN (COALESCE, TRIM, LOWER, casts, date math).
  • Every "defensive" expression is backed by a data check: null counts, padded values, duplicate keys.
  • Filters the outer query knows are repeated inside subqueries and on every joined table.
  • IN (SELECT DISTINCT ...) replaced with a correlated EXISTS, or at least the DISTINCT dropped.
  • Partial-index conditions written as literals, not bind parameters, so the planner can match them.

Purpose

  • For each query, what is it for? A ceiling, a count or a page may not need the precision it was written with.
  • Values that don't change within a run are computed once per run, not inside a loop.
  • Keyset pagination sorts on a unique key, or ends with a unique tie-breaker.

Evidence

  • EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on production-sized data, for normal, wide and first-run windows.
  • No (never executed) hiding the parts you care about.
  • Estimated versus actual rows compared; a gap of 10x or more is worth chasing.
  • Costs that multiply (per chunk, per page, per backlog hour) indexed; fixed costs judged against the schedule.
  • The full plan re-run after every new index.

Closing: tuning is mostly a conversation

Looking back, the biggest gains came from questions, not configuration:

  • "Can this column actually be null?" No, so the COALESCE went, and the existing index started working.
  • "What is this MAX used for?" An upper bound, so it didn't need the expensive join.
  • "Does this cost grow with the backlog?" Only in one place, so we added one index instead of six.

None of that needed database expertise the developers couldn't learn. It needed someone to explain how the planner reads a predicate, why a function hides an index, and why QA data isn't evidence for production. Once that was clear, the developer rewrote the queries himself, and the run time in QA went from 30–50 minutes to under 30 seconds.

Some tuning really is just common sense and basic troubleshooting: read the plan, check the data, and ask what the query is for. If your team writes SQL, especially with an AI assistant drafting it, get a database engineer to look at it before it meets production data. It never hurts, and sometimes it saves you an hour-long first run, or a 27-second query you didn't know you had.

References

  • CREATE AGGREGATE: how MIN/MAX-like aggregates use an index
  • planagg.c: the MIN/MAX optimization and its single-table restriction
  • Indexes on Expressions
  • Partial Indexes
  • Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes
  • Row Estimation Examples: MCV lists, averages and combining conditions
  • Statistics Used by the Planner: including extended statistics
  • Using EXPLAIN
  • CREATE INDEX: Building Indexes Concurrently

title: Three commits ahead of its own version number
description:
What is a git tag for, if nobody can install the tag?

I mean that as a real question. A Claude Code plugin marketplace has no registry... there's no publish step, no proxy, and no immutable artefact sitting somewhere with a checksum. The version lives in a .claude-plugin/plugin.json inside a git repository, and everyone installs from main.

The tag is decoration, and worse than that it can be wrong

I went looking for a tool to do this and couldn't find one, which surprised me more than it probably should have.

The nearest fit was cocogitto, and it's a perfectly good tool doing a job it wasn't really shaped for. Even in its monorepo mode (I looked at 7.0.0) it wants a tag per package and owns the changelogs, and I had one repository holding eight independently-versioned plugins, eight manifests with a version inside each, and no tag anyone could install.

So the versions were internal to the plugins, the tags were vanity, and nothing was keeping the two in agreement. That's fine for a while... until the vanity becomes inaccurate, and then you have a number people are trusting for no good reason.

The gap a release MR leans on

The release-merge-request pattern is a good one and I've written about it working well. Features land on main. A bot keeps a release MR open with the version bump and the changelog in it. When you want to cut a release you merge that MR, and the tag and the artefact go out together.

It works because there's a gap. Between a feature merging and the release MR merging, main runs ahead of the last published version, and that's pretty much harmless, since hardly anyone consumes main. They consume the registry, and the registry still has the old version on it, correctly labelled.

Take the registry away and that gap becomes a window with people standing in it. Anyone installing while three features have merged and the release MR has not gets those three features, in code that announces itself as the version before them. I'd call that wrong rather than stale, since it'll tell you, in its own manifest, something about itself that isn't true.

When main is the distribution channel, the gap has nowhere to hide. So the version has to move in the same commit as the change, or it lies.

Three ways to make that happen, and two of them can't work

Once you accept "same commit", it stops being a policy question. Something has to work the version out and get it into the commit, and there are only really three candidates.

The obvious one is a pre-commit hook. I disliked the look of it straight away and couldn't say why (usually a sign I've noticed something I haven't put into words yet). The bump is derived from the conventional-commit type, and at pre-commit time the commit doesn't exist. The hook can't tell whether it's looking at a fix or a feat, since the message hasn't been written yet.

Right, so let CI write it. This one fails for a much better reason, one I was slow to find. A push made with a job token creates no pipeline. That's true on GitLab, it's equally true of GitHub's GITHUB_TOKEN, and both do it for a good reason: otherwise CI would trigger itself round and round forever.

So a bump written by CI lands as a new head commit that no pipeline will validate, and the merge request then sits there blocking on its own must-pass rule, waiting patiently for a run that can never be scheduled (two perfectly reasonable features, and between them they'd built me a deadlock).

That leaves the boring option: the job only reads. It works out what the version should be, holds it against what the manifests say, and fails with the thing that's wrong and the command that fixes it. You run skillup apply, commit the result, and the pipeline that checks that commit is an ordinary one off an ordinary push.

I wanted one of the first two, obviously. They don't interrupt anyone. The option that actually survives contact makes a person stop and type a command, and I've mostly stopped resenting it.

What it cost in places that aren't code

A gate's only a gate if you can't walk round it, so this reached out into the repository settings: branch protection on main, merge requests mandatory, and fork contributions unsupported (for now), because a fork pipeline can't be trusted to have run the check.

That last one's a real cost. It's a public marketplace that a stranger can't currently contribute to without me changing something first.

That's the trade I made to stop the version numbers lying. It may not survive the first person who wants to send me a plugin.

Two details that cost an afternoon each

No shelling out. skillup talks to git through the estate's own repository library rather than os/exec. The temptation to shell out is strongest on small tools, which is when the reasoning gets skipped: this one isn't important enough to earn an exception to a security rule.

Clone depth. The gate sets GIT_DEPTH: "0", and the comment above it is the useful part. skillup reads each manifest's whole history to work out what's changed since its last bump, and it needs no tags at all to do that. Under the default shallow clone it doesn't error.

It gives you a confidently wrong answer instead. In a job whose one purpose is deciding whether a version number is telling the truth!

Somebody else will hit this next

What I keep coming back to is that I had to build it at all.

Plugin marketplaces, agent skill libraries, dotfiles repos, anything installed by pointing a tool at a git branch: I suspect they all have this problem in one form or another. Most of release engineering assumes a registry sitting between you and your consumers, and take it away and the tooling has very little to say. Eighteen hundred lines of Go, for a job that a registry would have done for free.

And skillup's own releases, incidentally, go out through a release merge request. Tagged, versioned, published, the pattern working as it should, because skillup has somewhere to be published to. The eight plugins it looks after don't. That's the difference between the two, and it was the better part of two weeks before I saw it clearly enough to build for it.

Originally published at phpboyscout.uk on 4 November 2026.

title: Sam Altman's Hardware Gaslighting: Why Local Inference Terrifies Cloud AI Monopolies
description:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stirred up significant controversy across the developer and local AI community when he remarked:

"Running inference on local hardware is a terrible allocation of scarce resources. Compute should be concentrated in massive hyperscale data centers where efficiency is maximized."

Let's call this what it actually is: Hardware Gaslighting.

The Economic Threat of Local Silicon

Why does the CEO of the world's most heavily funded AI startup care whether an engineer runs a model on their own MacBook Pro or RTX 4090?

Because software sovereignty destroys subscription monopoly rents.

When an engineer or enterprise runs a quantized 8B or 70B open-weights model locally:

  1. Recurring API Revenue Becomes $0: No monthly token invoice, no rate limit throttling, no credit card lock-in.
  2. Data Privacy is Absolute: Zero proprietary source code or customer logs leave the perimeter.
  3. Silicon Belongs to the Builder: A one-time capital expense for a 128GB Unified Memory Mac Studio or local multi-GPU rig amortizes to zero within months.

The Silicon Valley playbook has always relied on the "You will own nothing and be happy" cloud rentier model. When developers started running production-grade inference on commodity hardware, the panic began.

The Hypocrisy of the "Efficiency" Argument

The argument that centralized 5-gigawatt data centers in the desert are "environmentally more efficient" than running a model on idle edge silicon is computationally absurd.

  • Per-Token Network Latency: Transmitting prompt contexts across transatlantic fiber lines burns gigawatt-hours of networking infrastructure.
  • Cooling Overhead (PUE Penalty): Cooling hundreds of thousands of GPUs in concentrated hyperscale centers requires massive industrial chilling plants.
  • Idle Capacity: Millions of personal laptops, workstations, and local servers sit with billions of unused TOPS of compute every single second.

Claiming that putting a 70B model on your local machine is "wasteful" is equivalent to an airline telling you that owning a bicycle is an inefficient allocation of transportation assets.

Software Sovereignty Is Non-Negotiable

The future of engineering doesn't belong to developers waiting in line for API rate limits to reset. It belongs to builders who own their compute, run their own weights, and refuse to pay rent on their own intelligence.

Don't surrender your silicon.

Originally published on Kürşat Yılmaz Technical Blog

title: Color Name Tool: Find the Closest CSS Name for Any Hex Code
description:
Every designer has lived this moment: a client sends a screenshot, a brand guideline lists a hex code with nothing else, and someone asks "so what color is that, exactly?" The honest answer is that most hex codes have no exact name at all. There are roughly 16.7 million displayable colors and only 148 CSS named colors. A good color name tool bridges that gap — it takes your hex code, measures the distance to every named color, and hands you the closest match in plain English.

Why Color Names Exist at All

Computers speak in numbers. #3b7ddd is unambiguous; "a medium blue with a hint of gray" is not. Named colors exist because humans need handles. CSS standardized 140 color names in the 1990s — rebeccapurple joined later as a tribute — and designers have used them in conversation ever since: "make the button tomato," "use forestgreen for success."

Names compress information. Saying "this heading is darkslategray" tells a developer exactly what to type and tells a designer the intended mood. The catch is coverage: 148 names for 16.7 million colors means almost every color from a brand palette or a photograph has no exact name. That is where nearest-match identification earns its keep.

How Color Matching Actually Works

The Color Name Identifier compares your color against the full CSS named-color list using two different yardsticks, because "closest" depends on how you measure.

RGB Distance: Fast but Crude

The simplest approach treats a color as a point in three-dimensional space — red, green, blue — and computes the straight-line distance. Firebrick and your hex code might sit 40 units apart; crimson sits 90. Sort by distance, and the nearest name wins. This is cheap to calculate and usually lands in the right neighborhood, which is why it works well as a first pass.

LAB Distance: Closer to Human Perception

RGB distance has a flaw: it disagrees with your eyes. A shift of 30 units in green looks far more dramatic than 30 units in blue, and two colors close in RGB can read as totally different hues. The CIE LAB color space was designed to fix exactly this — distances in LAB correspond to perceived difference. Serious matching ranks candidates in LAB so that "closest" means closest to what a human would pick, not what arithmetic picks. The tool shows you the ranking either way, so you can judge whether the top match is a confident hit or a near-miss that deserves a second look.

Using a Color Name Tool Step by Step

The workflow is deliberately short. Paste your hex code into the input — the leading hash is optional. The tool immediately returns the closest named color, its hex value, its RGB breakdown, and how far it sits from your original color. If the distance is small, you have found your name; if it is large, the ranked list below shows the runners-up, and one of them usually fits better.

Watch the distance number, not just the name. A gap under 20 units is effectively the same color to most screens. A gap over 80 means the named palette simply does not contain what you are holding, and the honest answer is "unmatched" — the ranking still tells you which named color family it belongs to.

From Screenshot to Name: Picking the Color First

Often the color lives in an image, not a stylesheet. A competitor's landing page, a product photo, a mood board — you cannot paste a picture into a hex field. The Image Color Picker closes that loop: load the image, click the exact pixel you care about, and read off the hex code. Once you have the code, feed it to the name identifier and the full pipeline from picture to vocabulary is done in under a minute.

Converting Formats Along the Way

Names are only one dialect of color. Design tools speak hex, CSS increasingly speaks HSL, image editors speak RGB, and print shops want CMYK approximations. The Color Converter moves between all of these instantly, so once the name identifier tells you a color is close to steelblue, you can express steelblue in whatever format the next step demands.

And when one color is not enough — say the identifier points you at steelblue and you need a matching accent pair — the Color Palette Generator builds coordinated sets around any starting hue, using the same colorimetric logic that makes the match believable in the first place.

Who Actually Uses This

Frontend developers use it to replace magic hex codes with readable named colors in prototypes. Brand designers use it to check whether a new brand color collides with an overused name. Content writers use it to describe UI colors accurately in documentation — "the toolbar uses darkslategray" reads better than "the toolbar uses a dark gray, kind of bluish." Accessibility auditors use it as a sanity check before running the full contrast math: if your text color is dimgray on a whitesmoke background, the names alone warn you.

Why Run It in the Browser

A color is not a secret, but your design work is your business. The identifier runs entirely client-side: the hex goes in, the ranking comes out, and nothing touches a server. No account, no upload, no analytics on your palette. That matters when you are checking unreleased brand colors on a machine you do not fully control — an airport laptop, a shared studio machine, anywhere.

The Takeaway

Color names are a compression layer between human language and machine numbers, and 148 names will never cover 16.7 million colors. The practical move is nearest-match: measure distance in a perceptual space, pick the closest name, and read the distance to know how confident to be. Paste the hex, check the gap, and if the color lives in an image, grab it first with a picker. The whole question "what color is this" deserves a thirty-second answer, and now it has one.

title: Hermetic CI/CD Pipeline Design for Game Studios
description:
• Why hermetic builds end the 'works on my machine' firefight
  • Essential components that make a pipeline truly hermetic
  • Practical patterns for hermetic CI/CD with Jenkins, Docker, and GitLab
  • How to cut build time: caching, distributed compilation, and artifact caching
  • Practical playbook: step-by-step implementation checklist

Hermetic CI/CD is the engineering move that converts random, environment-driven failures into repeatable, auditable processes: containerize the build environment, pin the toolchain by digest or lockfile, and treat every input as an explicit, versioned dependency. Making builds hermetic removes the single largest source of wasted time in shipping playable game builds.

Your nightly CI fails intermittently, console certification rejections arrive at random times, and QA validation drags because the build on CI is not the same as the one you run locally. Those are the symptoms of environment drift: SDK and compiler mismatches, asset import differences, non-deterministic build flags, and implicit network dependencies that change over time. The outcome is repeated firefighting: chasing which machine, which SDK, or which environment variable changed since "it worked yesterday".

Why hermetic builds end the 'works on my machine' firefight

A hermetic build treats a build as a function: defined inputs → deterministic process → reproducible outputs. When you make the inputs explicit (base image, SDK bundle, exact tool versions, lockfiles, asset manifests) you make the build verifiable and repeatable. That’s the practical goal behind the broader reproducible builds movement: guarantee that a given source and declared environment produce the same binaries and artifacts every time.

A contrarian, practical insight: hermeticity is not only about security or compliance — it’s about velocity. The upfront cost to lock and automate toolchains buys back hours per week across QA, artists, and engineers by eliminating debugging time spent investigating environment causes. The ROI scales with team size: the more people and platforms, the faster the payoff.

Important: Hermetic does not mean “slowly rigid.” It means declarative and versioned. Keep the runtime flexible, but the build inputs immutable.

: Reproducible Builds — definition and rationale. See Sources.

Essential components that make a pipeline truly hermetic

Every hermetic pipeline contains the same building blocks. Treat this as a checklist you enforce by automation and code:

  • Immutable base images and digest pinning — use image digests (sha256) not floating tags in FROM lines so the base is identical across runs. FROM myregistry/game-builder@sha256:<digest> ensures the same OS + SDK bundle every run.
  • Declarative toolchain bundles — embed or vend the platform SDKs and compiler toolchains into the CI image (or into an immutable Nix/Bazel environment). For consoles where redistribution is restricted, store signed SDK archives in an internal artifact repo and fetch them by checksum.
  • Deterministic build steps and flags — ensure compiler flags, environment variables, and timestamps are reproducible (strip or fix timestamps, sort inputs, use deterministic linkers where possible). Record the canonical build command and environment in ci/ scripts and in your CI job.
  • Build isolation — run builds in ephemeral containers or pod-based agents to remove leftover state and cross-run contamination. Use ephemeral workspaces so absolute paths are consistent across builders.
  • Content-addressed outputs and provenance — publish artifacts by content-hash (or signed versioned artifacts), store an SBOM or manifest containing checksums of inputs, and record the exact image digest, git SHA, and build commands used to produce the artifact. This becomes your audit trail.

Use the container build features that are designed for hermetic builds: pin images by digest and enable BuildKit cache mounts to keep dependency retrieval deterministic and fast. --mount=type=cache keeps package caches between builds without baking them into the image layers, which preserves reproducibility while improving network efficiency.

Example minimal Dockerfile pattern (use BuildKit syntax and pinned base):

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.4
FROM ubuntu@sha256:... AS toolchain
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt,sharing=locked \
    apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential clang=1:XX-YY

FROM ubuntu@sha256:... AS builder
COPY --from=toolchain /usr /usr
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY . /workspace
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r ci/requirements.txt
RUN ./ci/build.sh

# produce a minimal runtime image or export artifacts

Caveat: always record the digest after build (e.g., docker buildx imagetools inspect) and keep that digest in your release metadata.

Practical patterns for hermetic CI/CD with Jenkins, Docker, and GitLab

This section gives battle-tested patterns you can drop into existing pipelines. Every snippet below assumes your build image is already built and pinned (game-builder@sha256:...).

Jenkins (Declarative Docker agent)

  • Use the docker agent or a Kubernetes pod template so each build runs in a pinned image. This avoids controller drift and lets you run the same container locally for reproduction. Example Jenkinsfile: 
pipeline {
  agent {
    docker {
      image 'registry.internal/game-builder@sha256:abcdef123456...'
      args  '--shm-size=1g'
    }
  }
  stages {
    stage('Checkout') { steps { checkout scm } }
    stage('Build') { steps { sh './ci/build.sh' } }
    stage('Archive') { steps { archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'build/artifacts/**', fingerprint: true } }
  }
}

The Jenkins declarative docker agent is a straightforward path to containerized builds for legacy Jenkins farms.

Kubernetes-based ephemeral agents (preferred at scale)

  • Use the Jenkins Kubernetes plugin to spin ephemeral pods where each pod’s container references an immutable image digest. This eliminates agent drift and keeps the controller light. podTemplate (YAML) lets you declare the exact container spec in the pipeline.

GitLab CI with pinned images and caches

  • For gitlab-runner with Docker executor, declare image: by digest, use cache: for intermediate caches, and publish artifacts: on success so downstream stages or QA can consume deterministic builds: 
image: registry.internal/game-builder@sha256:abcdef123456

stages:
  - build
  - test
  - publish

build:
  stage: build
  script:
    - ./ci/build.sh
  cache:
    key: ${CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG}
    paths: [.cache/]
  artifacts:
    paths: [build/artifacts/]
    expire_in: 7d

GitLab’s Docker executor runs builds in isolated containers and GitLab’s Dependency Proxy lets you cache upstream docker blobs to avoid external rate-limit failures.

Secrets, code signing and platform SDKs

  • Keep signing keys and restricted SDKs in an HSM or secret store (Vault / cloud KMS). Use short-lived credentials in CI via the runner/controller credentials mechanism; never bake SDK credentials into images. For console SDKs that cannot be redistributed, CI should retrieve signed SDK archives from an internal artifact repo and verify checksums before install.

Automation patterns you should adopt:

  • Make every build reproducible by script: ci/build.sh should accept --clean and --read-only-network modes.
  • Keep Dockerfile, build scripts, and lockfiles in the same repo as the code that uses them — treat the environment as code.

: Jenkins Pipeline examples for docker agent.

: Jenkins Kubernetes plugin and podTemplate ephemeral agents.

: GitLab Runner Docker executor docs.

: GitLab Dependency Proxy and caching features.

How to cut build time: caching, distributed compilation, and artifact caching

Hermetic builds and speed are not mutually exclusive. You can have both reproducibility and fast iteration by separating the immutable build environment from how you accelerate the build.

  • Compiler-level caching — For C/C++ builds (e.g., Unreal), use ccache, sccache, or engine-aware object caches. sccache supports remote S3/GCS backends and can serve cached object files across CI jobs and developer machines; set SCCACHE_BUCKET and related env vars during CI to share cache storage.
  • Distributed compilation — Use solutions that parallelize or distribute object compilation across a cluster (Incredibuild, FASTBuild, or distributed distcc setups). These tools let you maintain a hermetic toolchain while sharding CPU-bound work across many machines.
  • Remote build caches / action caches — Build systems like Bazel use a content-addressed remote cache (CAS) and action cache; when the action key matches, the output gets reused across machines and CI, providing hermeticity + speed. Use a remote cache server (or bazel-remote) with authentication to give CI exclusive write or read/write policies.
  • Asset import caches — For Unity teams, the Unity Accelerator (local cache server) stores imported assets so editors and CI instances don’t reimport the same FBX/PNG repeatedly; this dramatically reduces asset pipeline time. For Unreal, DDC (Derived Data Cache) and shared shader caches serve a similar role.
  • Dependency proxies and artifact repositories — Mirror and cache external dependencies locally (GitLab Dependency Proxy, Artifactory, Nexus). A local pull-through cache guarantees the same upstream blob is used, prevents outages, and reduces build-network jitter.

Example sccache snippet for CI (environment variables):

export SCCACHE_BUCKET=game-studio-sccache
export SCCACHE_REGION=us-west-2
export SCCACHE_S3_KEY_PREFIX=unreal
export RUSTC_WRAPPER=$(which sccache)
# For C/C++ wrappers, configure CC/CXX to use sccache as wrapper where supported.

sccache has multiple storage backends (S3, R2, Redis) which you can pick based on cost and latency.

When to use which acceleration:

  • Small teams: start with sccache/ccache + artifact repo + dependency proxy.
  • Medium-to-large studios: add distributed compilation (FASTBuild/Incredibuild) and shared DDC/Accelerator for assets.
  • If you use Bazel or similar action-based build systems, configure a remote cache (HTTP/gRPC) and restrict write access to CI workers to avoid cache poisoning.

Practical playbook: step-by-step implementation checklist

Treat this as your rollout plan. Each step ships value and keeps the build green.

  1. Audit and record current environment (2–3 days)
    • Lock git SHA for engine / submodules. Run gcc --version, clang --version, python --version. Produce a short env/ manifest of all tool versions and paths.
  2. Build a pinned base image (1 week)
    • Create a game-builder image that contains compilers, SDK installers, asset importers. Publish with a tag and capture the resulting digest: docker buildx build --push -t registry/internal/game-builder:1.2.3 . then docker inspect to get @sha256:.... Use that digest in CI.
  3. Make local reproducible build script (1 week)
    • Add ci/build.sh that runs the build using --read-only-network and emits an artifact-manifest.json (git_sha, image_digest, build_command, input_checksums).
  4. Convert CI jobs to use pinned images (2–4 days)
    • Update Jenkinsfile and .gitlab-ci.yml to use image: registry/internal/game-builder@sha256:.... Use cache and artifacts to save intermediate results.
  5. Add caching and distributed compilation (2–4 weeks, iterative)
    • Add sccache or ccache. Configure remote backend (S3 or internal object storage). Pilot FASTBuild or Incredibuild on a subset of targets to measure speedups.
  6. Add a dependency proxy and artifact repo (1 week)
    • Stand up GitLab Dependency Proxy, Nexus, or Artifactory and configure CI to prefer those endpoints.
  7. Automate tests in CI (1–2 weeks per engine)
    • Unity: run -runTests with Test Framework in batchmode and publish results as JUnit XML.
    • Unreal: use AutomationTool / Gauntlet to run functional and performance tests as part of CI and publish results artifact.
  8. Instrument and monitor CI (2 weeks)
    • Expose Jenkins/CI metrics to Prometheus or an OpenTelemetry pipeline; track build durations, success rates, cache hit rates, test flakiness. Create Grafana dashboards and alerts for sustained regressions (e.g., build success < 95% for 24h).
  9. Implement release gating and staged rollouts (ongoing)
    • Publish signed, versioned artifacts to a staging repo. Promote artifacts through channels (internal QA → external alpha → production) and use feature flags for progressive delivery (runtime toggles allow safe rollout).
  10. Enforce and educate (ongoing)
    • Make hermetic image build/rebuilds part of PR review. Provide a developer-quickstart.md showing how to run the container locally for reproducing CI builds.
  11. Measure and iterate (always)
    • Track build success rate, mean build time, cache hit ratio, and time-to-recover. Use these to prioritize further automation (more caching, indexed artifact directories, parallelized stages).
  12. Archive and attest
    • For each release, archive artifact-manifest.json, store the image digest, and sign the artifact. Store SBOMs and checksums in your release database for audits.

Runbook snippets (examples):

  • Get digest after pushing: 
docker buildx build --push -t registry.internal/game-builder:1.2.3 .
docker pull registry.internal/game-builder:1.2.3
docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' registry.internal/game-builder:1.2.3
# store the returned repo@sha256:...
  • Quick cache hit check for sccache: 
sccache --show-stats

Automated tests are not optional for hermetic flows. Unity’s Test Framework supports -runTests in batchmode and produces NUnit-compatible results; integrate this into your CI so each commit validates both code and asset import behavior. Unreal’s Automation tooling (AutomationTool / Gauntlet / RunUAT) supports running functional and performance suites in CI and reporting structured results.

Prometheus + OpenTelemetry are practical ways to monitor the build farm and CI controller. Instrument build duration, queue depth, cache hit ratios, and test flakiness; wire alerts to Slack or PagerDuty for sustained regressions so they get addressed before blocking production.

Sources:
Reproducible Builds - Explains the concept of reproducible and hermetic builds and why declaring inputs and deterministic builds matter.

Image digests | Docker Docs - How to pin images by digest and why digest pinning ensures immutable base images.

BuildKit | Docker Docs - BuildKit features such as cache mounts (--mount=type=cache) and reproducible build best-practices.

Creating your first Pipeline | Jenkins - Examples showing agent { docker { image ... } } and declarative pipeline patterns.

Kubernetes plugin | Jenkins plugin - Running ephemeral Jenkins agents in Kubernetes pods via podTemplate for agent isolation and reproducibility.

Docker executor | GitLab Runner Docs - How GitLab Runner runs jobs in isolated Docker containers and configuration for caches and images.

Dependency Proxy | GitLab Docs - GitLab's pull-through cache for container images and caching logic for manifests/blobs.

sccache (Mozilla) - GitHub - sccache features, backends (S3/R2/Redis), and configuration options for shared compilation caching.

FASTBuild - High-Performance Build System - FastBuild features for distributed, cached, high-performance builds used by many studios.

Unity Accelerator | Unity Manual - Unity's local cache server to speed up asset imports and reduce editor/CI re-import time.

Unity Test Framework — Command line arguments | Unity Docs - Running Unity automated tests in batch mode and CI-friendly flags.

Unreal Engine 5.1 Release Notes / Automation details - Notes and automation tooling references for UE Automation, Gauntlet, and test runners.

Remote Caching - Bazel Documentation - How Bazel uses action keys and a content-addressed remote cache to provide reproducible cached outputs.

Sonatype Nexus Repository - Artifact repository best-practices for hosting and proxying build artifacts and container images.

Incredibuild Supported Tools - Incredibuild support matrix and how it accelerates compilation and build tasks across large C++ codebases.

OpenTelemetry | Jenkins plugin - Observability and tracing integration for Jenkins, enabling metrics and traces to Prometheus/OpenTelemetry backends.

Prometheus — Overview | Prometheus Docs - Prometheus concepts and guidance for scraping and alerting for CI/CD targets.

Make the build environment a first-class artifact: version it, pin it, and monitor it — the engineering time you invest now becomes consistent velocity for the entire studio.

    color: #635bff;
