title: OpenPDF in Java: Encryption Setup, CSS Support, Footers
description:
Give OpenPDF's HTML module a two-column grid ledger whose total an inline script writes, and the PDF comes back with Hosting120.00Support80.00 on one line, a bold Total, and no figure after it. That run used 3.0.5, released on 22 May 2026 by the LibrePDF project, whose library began as a fork of iText 4.2.0. The ledger leads this post and five more problems follow, each one run against those jars or traced to the source that documents it.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

What Happens to Flexbox, Grid and Script in openpdf-html?

They are ignored. The core library's HTMLWorker parser has been deprecated since 2.1.0, and the openpdf-html module built for HTML is a Flying Saucer fork from June 2025 whose README says Flying Saucer set out to render XHTML with CSS 2.1 in plain Java, simpler than a browser engine. That README still marks HTML5 as in progress and lists JavaScript as a roadmap item. In the 3.0.5 jar, the CSSName property table holds 127 names, display, float and border-collapse among them, with none for flexbox, grid or gap.

import org.openpdf.pdf.ITextRenderer;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;

public class FlexGridScript {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // A flex row, a two-column grid and a script that writes the total, as a browser template would have them.
        String html = "<html><head><style>"
                + ".row { display: flex; gap: 16px; }"
                + ".card { flex: 1; border: 1px solid #999; padding: 8px; }"
                + ".ledger { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 3fr 1fr; }"
                + "</style></head><body>"
                + "<div class='row'><div class='card'>North</div><div class='card'>South</div>"
                + "<div class='card' id='east'></div></div>"
                + "<div class='ledger'><span>Hosting</span><span>120.00</span>"
                + "<span>Support</span><span>80.00</span><b>Total</b><b id='sum'></b></div>"
                + "<script>document.getElementById('east').textContent = 'East';"
                + "document.getElementById('sum').textContent = (120 + 80).toFixed(2);</script>"
                + "</body></html>";

        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("flex-grid-script.pdf")) {
            ITextRenderer renderer = new ITextRenderer();
            renderer.setDocumentFromString(html);
            renderer.layout();
            renderer.createPDF(out);
        }
    }
}

Opened in a viewer, the 1,233-byte page shows two boxes stacked down the left edge, North over South, with their text starting at x = 48.8 and their borders spanning the full text width, so the flex row never formed. Below them sits an empty bordered strip where East belonged, since no script ran, and the ledger reads as the single line quoted at the top. Browser-built templates and script-drawn charts end up the same way. The module's layout model stays CSS 2.1, so columns come from tables or floats and every total is computed in Java first.

Why Does Encryption Throw NoClassDefFoundError?

Because Bouncy Castle is optional in the POM and required at run time. The 3.0.5 core pulls in exactly one runtime library, Brotli4j at version 1.23.0, and leaves bcprov-jdk18on to the application as optional. The class below reads an existing two-page statement, sets AES-128 encryption on a PdfStamper and stamps every page.

import org.openpdf.text.Element;
import org.openpdf.text.Font;
import org.openpdf.text.FontFactory;
import org.openpdf.text.Phrase;
import org.openpdf.text.Rectangle;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.ColumnText;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfContentByte;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfGState;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfReader;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfStamper;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfWriter;

import java.awt.Color;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;

public class StampAndEncrypt {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        PdfReader reader = new PdfReader("statement-table.pdf");
        PdfStamper stamper = new PdfStamper(reader, new FileOutputStream("statement-copy.pdf"));

        // The user password opens the file, and the owner password lifts the permission flags.
        stamper.setEncryption("view-2026".getBytes(), "owner-2026".getBytes(),
                PdfWriter.ALLOW_PRINTING, PdfWriter.ENCRYPTION_AES_128);

        Font font = FontFactory.getFont(FontFactory.HELVETICA_BOLD, 60, Font.NORMAL, new Color(200, 0, 0));
        PdfGState translucent = new PdfGState();
        translucent.setFillOpacity(0.25f);

        // getOverContent draws above the existing page, so the stamp lands on top of the table.
        for (int page = 1; page <= reader.getNumberOfPages(); page++) {
            Rectangle size = reader.getPageSize(page);
            PdfContentByte over = stamper.getOverContent(page);
            over.saveState();
            over.setGState(translucent);
            ColumnText.showTextAligned(over, Element.ALIGN_CENTER, new Phrase("COPY", font),
                    size.getWidth() / 2, size.getHeight() / 2, 45);
            over.restoreState();
        }
        stamper.close();
        reader.close();
    }
}

On the declared dependencies alone, setEncryption threw NoClassDefFoundError for a Bouncy Castle ASN.1 class, ASN1OctetString on some runs and ASN1Encodable on others, from inside the PdfEncryption constructor, and a 0-byte statement-copy.pdf was left on disk. With bcprov-jdk18on 1.84 added, the same class produced a copy of about 4.5 KB, encrypted at revision 4 with the AESV2 filter, opening with view-2026, with a translucent COPY across both pages. Because the error only appears when the code path runs, a test suite that never encrypts will not catch it. The fix is an explicit Maven dependency on Bouncy Castle, and the next section explains why 1.84 is not the version to pick.

Which Advisories Touch an OpenPDF Build?

A query to OSV on 3 November 2026 found no record for either OpenPDF artifact at version 3.0.5, the core or the HTML module. The records that do come up sit one step away.

  • CVE-2026-8763 scores 9.1 Critical under CVSS 3.1 (NIST): A Name Constraints bypass in Bouncy Castle 1.84, the version the OpenPDF 3.0.5 build declares.
  • CVE-2026-13506 scores 7.5 High under CVSS 3.1 (NIST): Forcing a lazy ASN.1 sequence resets the nesting-depth guard, again in 1.84. Both records are fixed in bcprov-jdk18on 1.85, released on 12 July 2026, and the master branch of OpenPDF still pins 1.84 on 3 November 2026. Bouncy Castle's October records, such as CVE-2026-18036, also list 1.85 and are fixed in 1.86.
  • CVE-2017-9096 scores 8.8 High under CVSS 3.0 (NIST): XML external entities in iText before 5.5.12, and GHSA-86p9-x5pw-94qx widens it to the com.lowagie:itext artifact up to 4.2.2, whose 4.2.0 tag is where OpenPDF started. The com.github.librepdf coordinates are not listed, and the 3.0.5 XmlParser disables external entities.

The rest of the exposure comes from intended behavior. OpenPDF's security policy calls the library neither sandboxed nor hardened, and the project leaves every check on HTML, fonts, image locations and paths to whoever calls it, naming local file access, server-side request forgery and path traversal among the cases it does not block. In a test run, an <img> whose src was a file: URI pulled a PNG off the local disk into the PDF. Because the project asks that no CVEs be filed for such behavior, an advisory scan will not list it, and the remedy it gives is jsoup sanitizing, whitelisted src and href values and generation inside a container or sandbox. Licensing is MPL-2.0 OR LGPL-2.1+ for the core and the LGPL 2.1 or later for openpdf-html.

Who Is Affected by the Java 21 Floor?

Any team whose services run on Java 17 or below. The README sets Java 21 as the minimum for the 2.1.x line and later, and javac from JDK 17 stops on the first OpenPDF import of a 3.0.5 example.

error: cannot access Document
  bad class file: openpdf-3.0.5.jar(/org/openpdf/text/Document.class)
    class file has wrong version 65.0, should be 61.0

The Java 17 option is the 2.0.x branch, last released as 2.0.5 on 26 May 2025, which is older than openpdf-html itself (first shipped as 2.1.0 in June 2025) and than the move to the org.openpdf packages in 3.0.

How Much Layout Code Does a Simple Invoice Need?

Every placed element is a coordinate in points from the bottom-left corner of the page. A one-page US Letter invoice with a logo, a right-aligned title and a rule under the letterhead takes the class below.

import org.openpdf.text.Document;
import org.openpdf.text.Element;
import org.openpdf.text.Font;
import org.openpdf.text.Image;
import org.openpdf.text.PageSize;
import org.openpdf.text.Paragraph;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.BaseFont;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfContentByte;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfWriter;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;

public class InvoiceLayout {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // US Letter is 612 x 792 points, and the 120-point top margin leaves room for the letterhead.
        Document document = new Document(PageSize.LETTER, 36, 36, 120, 36);
        PdfWriter writer = PdfWriter.getInstance(document, new FileOutputStream("invoice-layout.pdf"));
        document.open();

        BaseFont sans = BaseFont.createFont("fonts/LiberationSans-Regular.ttf", BaseFont.IDENTITY_H, BaseFont.EMBEDDED);
        BaseFont sansBold = BaseFont.createFont("fonts/LiberationSans-Bold.ttf", BaseFont.IDENTITY_H, BaseFont.EMBEDDED);

        // Absolute positions count from the bottom-left corner, so y = 792 is the top edge.
        Image logo = Image.getInstance("img/logo.png");
        logo.scaleToFit(150, 60);
        logo.setAbsolutePosition(36, 792 - 36 - logo.getScaledHeight());
        document.add(logo);

        PdfContentByte canvas = writer.getDirectContent();
        canvas.beginText();
        canvas.setFontAndSize(sansBold, 20);
        canvas.showTextAligned(Element.ALIGN_RIGHT, "Invoice 4471", 576, 730, 0);
        canvas.endText();
        canvas.setLineWidth(0.75f);
        canvas.moveTo(36, 684);
        canvas.lineTo(576, 684);
        canvas.stroke();

        // Flowing elements start at the top margin and wrap between the side margins.
        Font body = new Font(sans, 11);
        document.add(new Paragraph("Bill to: Ève Lefèvre, Rue du Rhône 12, Genève", body));
        document.add(new Paragraph("Consulting, October 2026: CHF 3,200.00", body));
        document.close();
    }
}

The run produced a 25,786-byte Letter page with the logo scaled to 150 by 60 points at y = 696, Invoice 4471 ending at x = 576 and the rule at y = 684. Each of those numbers was chosen by hand, so a switch to A4, a taller logo or a new margin means recalculating them. Developers coming from HTML and CSS templates feel this most.

Why Does a Page X of Y Footer Take an Event Class?

OpenPDF's HeaderFooter class can print the current page number but not the total, so a footer reading Page 2 of 3 takes a PdfPageEventHelper, a PdfTemplate placed empty on each page and a write in onCloseDocument, once the total is known. In the test run, getPageNumber() returned 4 inside onCloseDocument for a three-page file, so the count written into the template has to subtract one. The three pages then shared a single 30 by 12 point form object for the total, and each read Page 1 of 3 through Page 3 of 3. Any report with running footers needs this class or the library's other route, stamping the numbers afterwards through PdfStamper when the total is already fixed.

Moving the Ledger to IronPDF for Java

For teams that would rather keep that ledger in HTML, IronPDF for Java is a commercial option that renders with Chromium, through an engine it downloads on first run or takes from a platform ironpdf-engine artifact. Our 2026.11.3 run of the first section's page laid the three cards out side by side, kept the ledger in two columns and printed the script's 200.00. It is added from Maven Central as one dependency, com.ironsoftware:ironpdf, that runs on Java 8 and later, and the 2026 line there has reached 2026.11.3, published on 3 November.

With IronPDF for Java, page numbers become a TextHeaderFooter passed to addTextFooter with Page {page} of {total-pages}, and a SecurityOptions object sets the user and owner passwords before saveAs writes the file. Markup from users still needs sanitizing before any renderer sees it.

To run your own templates through IronPDF for Java, there is a free trial.

Five Checks Before Shipping OpenPDF

OpenPDF 3.0.5 needs Java 21, an explicit and current Bouncy Castle, sanitized input, CSS 2.1 templates and hand-placed layout, and IronPDF for Java answers the HTML rendering, layout and Java-version items with a Chromium renderer on Java 8 and later.

OpenPDF, Flying Saucer, iText and Bouncy Castle are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with any of them, and the facts above are drawn from their public repositories, Maven Central records and advisory databases.

Drafted with AI. OpenPDF code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team against com.github.librepdf:openpdf 3.0.5 and com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3 on 3 November 2026.

title: Using Flying Saucer 10.7.0: Grid, @font-face and Java 21
description:
A dashboard template with a two-column CSS grid and a net total that a script writes after load prints as one column with no total when Flying Saucer renders it. The renderer ships for Java as org.xhtmlrenderer:flying-saucer-pdf, and 10.7.0, released 24 October 2026, is its current version. We ran into that grid while testing the library for this post, so it comes first, and later sections draw on more 10.7.0 runs, the R8 user's guide, the code and what NVD, GHSA and OSV record.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

What Does Flying Saucer Do With CSS Grid and a Script-Written Total?

It lays the grid items out as ordinary blocks and drops the script. The engine targets CSS 2.1, extended with its own -fs- print properties and some later CSS. A set in the code, CSSName.UNSUPPORTED_CSS3_PROPERTIES, names 52 CSS3 properties that layout passes over, grid and flexbox among them, and the R8 user's guide says script tags are ignored.

import org.xhtmlrenderer.pdf.ITextRenderer;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;

public class GridScriptCards {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // A two-column grid with a total that a script writes after load, as many dashboards do.
        String xhtml = "<html><head><style>"
                + ".grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 16px; }"
                + ".tile { padding: 10px; border: 1px solid #999; }"
                + "</style></head><body>"
                + "<div class='grid'><div class='tile'>Orders 412</div><div class='tile'>Returns 9</div></div>"
                + "<p id='total'></p>"
                + "<script>document.getElementById('total').textContent = 'Net orders 403';</script>"
                + "</body></html>";

        ITextRenderer renderer = new ITextRenderer();
        renderer.setDocumentFromString(xhtml);
        renderer.layout();
        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("grid-script-cards.pdf")) {
            renderer.createPDF(out);
        }
    }
}

grid-script-cards.pdf is a single US Letter page with Orders 412 above Returns 9 at the same left margin, and the text layer has no Net orders 403. During the run the Html5Support logger printed one warning naming display: grid, grid-template-columns and gap as unsupported, then the PDF was written as normal. That warning, first logged in 10.2.0, is the only sign of the problem. Any template a front-end team designs in a browser is affected, and the routes around it are a float and table layout or the project's separate Chrome module, covered below.

Does @font-face Embed the Font in the PDF?

Not with the CSS a browser accepts. A plain @font-face rule resolves the font for layout, but the PDF only names it, so the reader's viewer has to supply the face.

import org.xhtmlrenderer.pdf.ITextRenderer;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class FontFaceCss {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // The same @font-face rule a browser would use, with the TTF resolved against the base URL.
        String xhtml = "<html><head><style>"
                + "@font-face { font-family: 'Brand'; src: url('georgia.ttf'); }"
                + "h1 { font-family: 'Brand'; }"
                + "</style></head><body><h1>Quarterly summary</h1></body></html>";

        ITextRenderer renderer = new ITextRenderer();
        renderer.setDocumentFromString(xhtml, Path.of("fonts").toUri().toString());
        renderer.layout();
        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("font-face.pdf")) {
            renderer.createPDF(out);
        }
    }
}

The heading in font-face.pdf references a TrueType font called Georgia with no font file in its descriptor, so on a machine without Georgia the viewer substitutes another face. Adding the vendor property -fs-pdf-font-embed: embed to the rule, which the user's guide documents, produced an embedded Georgia subset in a second run. Brand fonts depend on embedding. So does the PDF/A archive format, an ISO preservation standard whose rule 6.2.11.4.1 requires all fonts embedded, and it has a second font catch. With a font registered as BaseFont.IDENTITY_H and PDF/A-3b requested, veraPDF 1.30.3 failed the output on the CIDSet rule 6.2.11.4.2, while BaseFont.CP1252 passed for Western European text.

Can CMS HTML Go Straight Into setDocumentFromString?

No. The parser is XML, and the user's guide says most HTML found in the wild can't be rendered and should go through TagSoup, JTidy or a similar cleaner first.

import org.xhtmlrenderer.pdf.ITextRenderer;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;

public class RawCmsFragment {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // Valid HTML5 as a browser reads it, with an unclosed <p> and <li> and a bare <br>.
        String html = "<h1>Release notes</h1>"
                + "<p>Version 3.2 ships today.<br>Highlights:"
                + "<ul><li>Faster search<li>New export menu</ul>";

        ITextRenderer renderer = new ITextRenderer();
        // The XML parser rejects the string here, before layout starts.
        renderer.setDocumentFromString(html);
        renderer.layout();
        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("release-notes.pdf")) {
            renderer.createPDF(out);
        }
    }
}

The run stopped in setDocumentFromString with XRRuntimeException wrapping a SAX error at line 1, column 24, saying the markup following the root element must be well-formed, and no file was written. Parsing with jsoup and passing its W3CDom result to setDocument rendered this fragment in a test run, and it adds a dependency and a step to every render.

Which Advisories Show Up in a Dependency Scan?

Mostly history rather than the current release, with one recent batch in a dependency.

  • Builds through 9.3.2: A default flying-saucer-pdf build resolves com.lowagie:itext 2.1.7, and GitHub's GHSA-86p9-x5pw-94qx flags that artifact for CVE-2017-9096 at every version up to 4.2.2, with no fixed version.
  • CVE-2017-9096 scores 8.8 High under CVSS 3.0 (NIST): An XXE weakness in iText's XML parsing, which NIST also scores 6.8 on CVSS 2 and NVD doesn't tag as disputed.
  • OpenPDF from 9.4.0: It took over the PDF layer at that release, which came out at the end of December 2023.
  • XXE changes with no CVE: Two hardening changes, one to XMLResource in 9.12.1 (June 2025) and one to DocumentBuilderFactory in 10.4.0 (July 2026), shipped with no CVE identifier, which leaves scanners blind to builds that lack them.
  • Advisories on the current tree: Neither OSV nor GHSA lists any advisory for a Flying Saucer artifact, and OSV, queried for the libraries 10.7.0 pulls in on 3 November 2026, had nothing for them either. The exception is Apache's Batik page, which names seven medium-rated CVEs in 1.19, the version 10.7.0 pulls in, and everything older, all patched by the 1.20 release of 20 October 2026.

Teams still on 9.3.2 or earlier carry the iText finding. Moving to 10.4.0 or later picks up the iText and XXE changes, while the Batik fixes need a release that moves off 1.19, and none had reached Maven Central on 3 November 2026.

What Changes With the Chrome Module and the Java 21 Floor?

The Chrome module trades the CSS gap for a browser to manage, and the 10.x line needs a recent JVM.

The module, flying-saucer-chrome-pdf, first shipped with 10.3.0 in June 2026 and hands each page to chrome-headless-shell. Unless told otherwise it asks Google's chrome-for-testing feed for the current Stable build and refreshes that answer daily, so the browser doing the printing changes underneath the application, and on 3 November 2026 that answer was build 156.0.8078.80. Calling setChromeVersion pins it. Two more details in the 10.7.0 source matter in production. The print call fires on Page.loadEventFired with no dedicated delay setting in ChromiumPdfOptions (a desktop Chrome run needed addExtraArg("--virtual-time-budget=5000") in one-shot mode to print a late script's text), and on Linux arm64 the platform check throws even though the chrome-for-testing JSON offers linux-arm64 downloads for Stable. The exception suggests setBinaryPath, yet the check runs before that path is read, and a test with os.name Linux and os.arch aarch64 still threw with a path supplied.

Java is the other constraint. Since 10.0.0 in September 2025, every 10.x jar targets Java 21 (class file 65), and compiling against 10.7.0 with the JDK 17 javac failed with a wrong-version error in the test run. Java 17 projects are held to 9.x, where 9.13.4 is the newest build. Separately, the parent POM leaves slf4j-api to the application as a provided dependency, and without it constructing the first renderer threw NoClassDefFoundError.

Where Does IronPDF for Java Fit These Checks?

If the trade-offs above don't fit a project, IronPDF for Java is a commercial library that prints HTML through Chromium. On 2026.11.3, our run of the grid above put Orders 412 and Returns 9 in two columns and printed Net orders 403 from the script. Scripts run by default, since ChromePdfRenderOptions starts with setEnableJavaScript on, a WaitFor can pause the capture for a fixed delay, network idle or a named element, raw CMS HTML needs no jsoup pass, and PDF/A-3b output is one saveAsPdfA call.

The library itself is com.ironsoftware:ironpdf on Maven Central, built as Java 8 bytecode, with eleven 2026 builds by 3 November 2026, numbered by month, the newest published that day. The engine it bundles or downloads is pinned by each IronPDF release, so a Chromium update arrives only as an IronPDF version bump. A free trial is available for testing it against your own templates.

Summing Up the Flying Saucer Checklist

Grid and script missing from the PDF, unembedded @font-face fonts, an XML-only parser, a Chrome module that follows the Stable channel and a Java 21 floor are the checks this post ran on Flying Saucer 10.7.0, and the iText 2.1.7 dependency behind CVE-2017-9096 belongs to pre-9.4.0 builds. For pages built for a browser, IronPDF for Java renders them in Chromium from a single dependency, and our HTML file example shows the call.

Flying Saucer, OpenPDF, iText, Apache Batik, Georgia, Chrome and veraPDF are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with any of them, and the details above come from each project's source, documentation, release notes and the NVD, GHSA and OSV databases.

Drafted with AI. Flying Saucer code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team on 3 November 2026, with IronPDF APIs checked against com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3.

title: JasperReports 7.1.1 PDFs: Fonts, Extra JARs and PDF/UA Tags
description:
An HTML timesheet sent through a JasperReports text field came out as nine plain lines of 10-point Helvetica down the left margin. That run used JasperReports Library 7.1.1 (Maven Central, 1 November 2026, GNU LGPL v3), the Java engine that compiles JRXML band designs, fills them and writes PDF among other outputs. What follows is a checklist of what tripped up a Java 17 build on its way to a PDF, with every item reproduced in a run or traced to the changelog and the advisory databases.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

What an HTML Timesheet Looks Like in a JasperReports Text Field

HTML enters only as the content of a text element flagged markup="html", where a Swing JEditorPane parses it, per the markup sample in the vendor's docs. The test template is one such field, fed a timesheet the way a web app would serve it, <style> block and all.

import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JREmptyDataSource;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JRException;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperCompileManager;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperExportManager;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperFillManager;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperPrint;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class TimesheetMarkupReport {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws JRException {
        // A stylesheet rule, a CSS grid and a table, as a web app would serve the timesheet.
        String html = "<style>.over { color: #c00; font-weight: bold }</style>"
                + "<h2>Timesheet, week 42</h2>"
                + "<div style='display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr'><div>A. Novak</div><div>R. Osei</div></div>"
                + "<table border='1'><tr><th>Engineer</th><th>Hours</th></tr>"
                + "<tr><td>A. Novak</td><td>38.5</td></tr>"
                + "<tr><td>R. Osei</td><td class='over'>44.0</td></tr></table>";

        Map<String, Object> parameters = new HashMap<>();
        parameters.put("Html", html);

        // html-markup.jrxml holds one text field with markup="html" that prints the Html parameter.
        JasperPrint print = JasperFillManager.fillReport(
                JasperCompileManager.compileReport("html-markup.jrxml"), parameters, new JREmptyDataSource());
        JasperExportManager.exportReportToPdfFile(print, "timesheet-markup.pdf");
    }
}

Read with pypdf, the content stream of the 1,147-byte timesheet-markup.pdf holds nine text runs at x = 40, each about 12.58 points below the last and all in 10-point Helvetica, so the h2 is the size of a table cell. A. Novak and R. Osei, meant to sit side by side in the grid, follow each other down the page. Engineer, Hours and the four cell values do the same with no border drawn around them, and 44.0 prints in black because the .over class never took effect. There is not a single rectangle or line operator on the page.

Script never runs here, and the 7.0.2 release deleted the old Chrome add-on for JavaScript visualizations. For HTML-first teams, the vendor's route is a rebuild of each layout in Jaspersoft Studio.

Fonts That Stop a Report at Fill Time

Point a style at a family the JVM has never seen, such as fontName="Report Serif", and JasperFillManager throws JRFontNotFoundException before any page exists. The trace passes through TextMeasurer, since line breaking needs real glyph widths. According to the exception's Javadoc, refusing to guess is deliberate, because a stand-in font shifts the metrics and may clip text.

Leaving the font unset has a cost too. An invoice template that marks its title bold="true" and names no font exported a file with one font, Helvetica, and drew that title in the regular weight. The recommended route for bold faces and custom families is a font extension, registered in a properties file at the classpath root, though a pdfFontName attribute on each element also printed bold in a test run.

net.sf.jasperreports.extension.registry.factory.simple.font.families=net.sf.jasperreports.engine.fonts.SimpleFontExtensionsRegistryFactory
net.sf.jasperreports.extension.simple.font.families.reportserif=fonts/reportserif/fonts.xml

Add a fonts.xml mapping the family to DejaVu Serif regular and bold, and the export embeds both as subsets. A house typeface means maintaining that bundle alongside the templates.

Encryption, PDF Export and the Extra JARs They Need

Since 7.0.0 the PDF writer lives in jasperreports-pdf, and leaving it out produced a JRRuntimeException naming that artifact. The writer runs on 1.3.43.jaspersoft.2, a Jaspersoft fork of OpenPDF hosted in a Jaspersoft repository and absent from Central, so a Central-only mirror cannot resolve it as declared. Since 7.0.8 the writer also accepts stock OpenPDF 1.3.43 from Central in its place, and a swapped-in run exported both timesheet reports with one warning that link annotation tagging for PDF/UA was off. Its OpenPDF 3 sibling from 7.1.0, jasperreports-openpdf, pulls in a Jaspersoft build of OpenPDF 3.0.5 compiled for Java 21, and that build raised UnsupportedClassVersionError on Java 17.

Encryption brings in one more JAR, as this export of a compiled timesheet.jasper with two passwords shows.

import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JRException;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperFillManager;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperPrint;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.data.JRMapCollectionDataSource;
import net.sf.jasperreports.export.SimpleExporterInput;
import net.sf.jasperreports.export.SimpleOutputStreamExporterOutput;
import net.sf.jasperreports.pdf.JRPdfExporter;
import net.sf.jasperreports.pdf.SimplePdfExporterConfiguration;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class EncryptedTimesheet {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws JRException {
        Map<String, Object> parameters = new HashMap<>();
        parameters.put("Week", "week 43");

        // Map rows need no bean class, and each key matches a field in the template.
        List<Map<String, ?>> rows = List.of(
                Map.of("project", "Billing API", "engineer", "A. Novak", "hours", 30.0),
                Map.of("project", "Data platform", "engineer", "R. Osei", "hours", 38.5));

        JasperPrint print = JasperFillManager.fillReport(
                "timesheet.jasper", parameters, new JRMapCollectionDataSource(rows));

        JRPdfExporter exporter = new JRPdfExporter();
        exporter.setExporterInput(new SimpleExporterInput(print));
        exporter.setExporterOutput(new SimpleOutputStreamExporterOutput("timesheet-week-43.pdf"));

        // A user password to open the file, an owner password to change it, and printing as the one permission.
        SimplePdfExporterConfiguration config = new SimplePdfExporterConfiguration();
        config.setEncrypted(true);
        config.set128BitKey(true);
        config.setUserPassword("week43");
        config.setOwnerPassword("payroll-admin");
        config.setAllowedPermissionsHint("PRINTING");
        exporter.setConfiguration(config);

        exporter.exportReport();
    }
}

Run with only the JasperReports JARs, exportReport threw NoClassDefFoundError naming an org.bouncycastle.asn1 class (ASN1OctetString or ASN1Encodable, varying between runs) and left a 0-byte timesheet-week-43.pdf behind. Bouncy Castle does not arrive with the PDF extension, and the vendor's PdfEncrypt sample adds bcprov-jdk18on itself. With version 1.86 added at runtime, the result needed week43 to open, used 128-bit RC4 (V 2, R 3), and allowed printing and nothing else. That matches the usual password-protection split of an open password and a change password.

Advisories That Still Apply to 6.x and Early 7.x

The table lists the records in NVD, CVE.org, OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database on 3 November 2026 for the library and for the Jackson version its last 6.x release declares.

Advisory Score and scorer Affected Fixed in
CVE-2025-10492, deserialization 9.8 NIST (CVSS 3.1), 8.7 Jaspersoft (CVSS 4.0) Library 7.0.3 and earlier 7.0.4
CVE-2026-6009, deserialization 8.7 Jaspersoft (CVSS 4.0), NVD analysis pending Library 7.0.6 and earlier 7.0.7
4 jackson-core advisories 3 high and 1 moderate (GitHub) Jackson 2.17.1, declared by 6.21.5 Jackson 2.22.3, and 7.1.1 uses 2.22.4
12 jackson-databind advisories 5 high and 7 moderate (GitHub) Jackson 2.17.1, declared by 6.21.5 Jackson 2.22.3, and 7.1.1 uses 2.22.4
CVE-2026-110879, jackson-databind type validator bypass 9.8 HeroDevs (CVSS 3.1), NVD analysis pending Jackson 2.10.0 to before 2.18.12, which covers 2.17.1 2.18.12, 2.21.8 and 2.22.4
CVE-2026-68498, jackson-core memory exhaustion 7.5 HeroDevs (CVSS 3.1), NVD analysis deferred Jackson 2.16.0 to before 2.18.10, which covers 2.17.1 2.18.10, 2.21.6 and 2.22.2

Both library records describe Java deserialization with a path to remote code execution, and neither is marked disputed. Of the Jackson entries, CVE-2026-91776 is one of the high ones, about jackson-databind keeping every unknown raw type ID. OSV holds CVE-2026-110879 and CVE-2026-68498 with no affected package attached, so a query for Jackson 2.17.1 does not return them, and their ranges come from CVE.org. The last 6.x release, 6.21.5, dates from 4 July 2025, before either library fix, and no later 6.x release is on Maven Central. A 7.1.1 build with the PDF extension and Bouncy Castle came back with zero OSV matches across its 34 JARs, and the move there runs through the template change below.

Version 7 Template Conversion and the PDF/UA Tagging Change

Version 7 swapped the Commons Digester parsers for Jackson XML, and its changelog says the 7.x library on its own cannot open .jrxml or .jrtx files saved by 6.x or earlier. Jaspersoft Studio 7 or newer converts them. Every .jasper file needs a fresh compile, imports change where packages moved into separate JARs, and the 3D pie, bar and stacked bar charts come out flat because the 7.1.1 chart theme hands each 3D type to its flat chart method. Since 7.0.6, jasperreports-maven-plugin can run the update and compile steps inside a build.

Accessibility work meets an edition line in the same changelog. Release 7.0.8 put PDF tagging behind a PdfTagger interface and moved its newest, fullest implementation into the JasperReports Library Professional extensions, and tagging is what PDF/UA and PDF/A files rely on.

Where an HTML Renderer Fits

Markup that loses its layout, fonts to package, extra JARs, a Jaspersoft repository, 6.x advisories and an edition line for tagging add up to a long list, and IronPDF for Java shortens it whenever the source is an HTML page.

Our timesheet string went to PdfDocument.renderHtmlAsPdf untouched on 2026.11.3, and the grid split the two names into columns while the .over rule printed 44.0 in bold red. The renderHtmlAsPdf example shows the call. For the password step, getSecurity().setPassword and setOwnerPassword do the work, and the ironpdf POM declares no Bouncy Castle dependency to add. Tagged output comes from convertToPdfUA and convertToPdfA in that one com.ironsoftware:ironpdf dependency, which has eleven 2026 builds on Maven Central, 2026.1.3 through 2026.11.3.

What This Means for HTML Reports on JasperReports

For reports that start as HTML pages, IronPDF is where we would begin, since the timesheet above needed no JRXML rewrite. A free trial key is enough to run your own page through it.

Did the version 7 template conversion or the font setup take your team longer?

JasperReports and Jaspersoft are trademarks of their owner, we have no affiliation with Actian or the Jaspersoft business, and the details above draw on the project's changelog, POMs and samples, NVD, CVE.org, OSV, Maven Central and our own runs.

Drafted with AI. JasperReports code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team against net.sf.jasperreports:jasperreports 7.1.1 on 3 November 2026, with the IronPDF details checked against the com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3 API.

title: Why Go Interfaces Are Different: A Deep Dive for OO Developers
description:
If you are transitioning to Go from object-oriented heavyweights like Java, C#, or C++, you will quickly notice that Go feels different. There are no classes, no inheritance hierarchies, and no implements keyword. Yet, Go is deeply polymorphic.

The secret lies in Go interfaces. They are arguably the most powerful and defining feature of the language. But because they don't behave like interfaces in traditional object-oriented programming (OOP), they often trip up newcomers.

In this article, we will explore Go vs Java interfaces, dig into the Go interface architecture to see how they work under the hood, and demonstrate how Go's unique design fundamentally changes the way you write and test software.

The Paradigm Shift: Go vs Java Interfaces

In languages like Java or C#, interfaces are explicit. A class must explicitly declare that it implements an interface.

Here is how you might define and implement an interface in Java:

// Java Explicit Interface
public interface DataWriter {
    void write(String data);
}

// The class MUST declare "implements DataWriter"
public class ConsoleWriter implements DataWriter {
    @Override
    public void write(String data) {
        System.out.println(data);
    }
}

This creates a rigid, top-down dependency. The ConsoleWriter must know about the DataWriter interface at compile time.

Go, on the other hand, uses implicit interfaces. A type implements an interface simply by implementing its methods. There is no implements keyword.

// Go Implicit Interface
type DataWriter interface {
    Write(data string)
}

// ConsoleWriter knows NOTHING about DataWriter
type ConsoleWriter struct{}

// It implicitly implements DataWriter by having this method
func (c ConsoleWriter) Write(data string) {
    fmt.Println(data)
}

Because of implicit interfaces in Go, the dependency graph is inverted. The consumer of the behavior defines the interface, not the producer. A package providing a ConsoleWriter doesn't need to know how other packages will use it. If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, Go treats it like a duck.

Go Interface Under the Hood

To truly master Go, you need to understand the Go interface under the hood. How does the runtime know a struct satisfies an interface if it was never explicitly declared?

In the Go runtime code (written in C and Go), an interface is not just a pointer to an object. It is a two-word data structure known as an iface (for interfaces with methods) or an eface (for the empty interface any / interface{}).

When you assign a concrete type to an interface variable, Go constructs an iface struct that contains two pointers:

  1. tab (Type Word): A pointer to an itab (interface table) which holds metadata about the concrete type and a list of function pointers (the virtual method table) that map the interface's methods to the concrete type's methods.
  2. data (Data Word): A pointer to the actual concrete value in memory. 
classDiagram
    class iface {
        *itab tab
        *void data
    }
    class itab {
        *interfacetype inter
        *_type _type
        uint32 hash
        [4]byte _
        [1]uintptr fun
    }
    class ConcreteValue {
        "Actual data (e.g., struct fields)"
    }

    iface --> itab : tab
    iface --> ConcreteValue : data

When you call a method on an interface, the Go runtime follows the tab pointer to find the correct function in the itab, and passes the data pointer to it as the receiver.

The magic of the Go interface architecture is that the itab is generated on the fly (and then cached) the first time a specific concrete type is assigned to a specific interface type. This dynamic generation is what makes implicit interfaces possible without sacrificing the performance of static typing.

The Power of Go Small Interfaces

Rob Pike, one of Go's creators, famously coined the proverb: "The bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction."

In Java or C++, it is common to see massive interfaces with a dozen methods (IUserService, IDatabaseManager). In Go, the standard library sets a different precedent: Go small interfaces.

The most famous interfaces in Go are just one method long:

type Reader interface {
    Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)
}

type Writer interface {
    Write(p []byte) (n int, err error)
}

Why is this so powerful? Because small interfaces are highly composable. If your function only needs to write data, it should accept an io.Writer, not a massive os.File or NetworkConnection struct.

By keeping interfaces small (1-3 methods), you maximize the number of types that can implicitly satisfy them, making your code vastly more reusable.

How Go Makes Testing Easier

The combination of implicit implementation and small interfaces revolutionizes Go unit testing interfaces.

In traditional OOP, if you want to mock a third-party class, that class must implement an interface provided by the third-party library. If they didn't provide one, you are stuck writing wrappers.

In Go, because interfaces are satisfied implicitly, you define the interface in your own testing package based strictly on the subset of methods you need.

Imagine you are using a massive third-party PaymentGateway struct with 50 methods, but your function only uses Charge().

// Third-party package (you can't change this)
package stripe

type PaymentGateway struct { /* ... */ }
func (p *PaymentGateway) Charge(amount float64) error { /* ... */ }
func (p *PaymentGateway) Refund(id string) error { /* ... */ }
// ... 48 more methods

To test your code, you don't need to mock all 50 methods. You define a tiny, local interface right where you need it:

// Your package
package billing

// 1. Define the interface locally
type Charger interface {
    Charge(amount float64) error
}

// 2. Depend on the interface, not the third-party struct
func ProcessOrder(c Charger, amount float64) error {
    return c.Charge(amount)
}

Now, the third-party stripe.PaymentGateway implicitly satisfies your local Charger interface, but in your test file, you can easily swap it out for a simple test double.

Fakes vs Mocks Go: A Pragmatic Approach

When writing test doubles for those interfaces, developers coming from other languages usually reach for Mocks (using tools like gomock or testify/mock). Mocks are dynamically generated objects that record how they were called and assert expectations (e.g., "Expect Charge() to be called exactly once with 50.00").

However, the Go community strongly leans towards fakes over mocks.

A Fake is a lightweight, working implementation of an interface built specifically for tests. It doesn't use reflection or assertion frameworks; it just uses plain Go logic.

Here is how you would write a fake for our Charger interface:

// billing_test.go
package billing

import "testing"

// Fake implementation
type FakeCharger struct {
    ChargedAmount float64
    ShouldFail    bool
}

func (f *FakeCharger) Charge(amount float64) error {
    if f.ShouldFail {
        return errors.New("insufficient funds")
    }
    f.ChargedAmount += amount
    return nil
}

func TestProcessOrder(t *testing.T) {
    // Arrange
    fake := &FakeCharger{}

    // Act
    err := ProcessOrder(fake, 50.00)

    // Assert
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("expected no error, got %v", err)
    }
    if fake.ChargedAmount != 50.00 {
        t.Errorf("expected 50.00 to be charged, got %v", fake.ChargedAmount)
    }
}

Why Fakes over Mocks in Go?

  1. Type Safety and Refactoring: Mocks often rely on string-based method names and interface{} arguments, which break silently during refactoring. Fakes are standard Go code—if the interface changes, the compiler catches the broken fake immediately.
  2. Readability: When comparing fakes vs mocks Go, fakes are much easier to read. You are just reading Go code, not deciphering a domain-specific mocking language.
  3. Statefulness: Fakes can easily maintain state (like an in-memory map replacing a database), allowing you to test complex state transitions that are notoriously difficult to set up with mock expectations.

Conclusion

Go interfaces are fundamentally different from what you might be used to in Java or C#. By removing the explicit implements keyword, Go encourages a bottom-up architecture where abstractions are discovered rather than designed upfront.

By understanding the two-word iface structure under the hood, embracing small single-method interfaces, and utilizing fakes for testing, you can write Go code that is highly decoupled, incredibly easy to test, and true to the idiomatic spirit of the language.

title: I Replaced Docker Desktop on Windows (It’s Faster, and It Doesn’t Need WSL)
description:
Here's a confession: I don't use WSL.

I don't open an Ubuntu shell. I don't run Linux tools on Windows.
The only reason WSL was on my laptop was Docker.

And yet it was the heaviest thing on my machine.

I'd stop every container. docker ps was empty.
vmmem was still sitting on 2 GB of my RAM.

I'd delete 5 GB of images to make room.
My disk got none of it back.

Bind-mounted projects were slow.
And Docker Desktop had a steady supply of small bugs:
the kind you fix by restarting it, then restarting it again.

None of it was a bug I could report and wait out.
Docker Desktop runs on WSL 2, and WSL 2 is a whole
general-purpose Linux VM. I was paying for all of it
to use one thing.

So I asked a dumb question:
what if the VM only had to run Docker?

The problem

If you run Linux containers on Windows, you know the drill:

  • vmmem keeps a gigabyte or two long after your containers stop
  • you delete images and the VHDX never shrinks
  • a project bind-mounted from C:\ is slow
  • at a company with 250+ people, Docker Desktop needs a paid plan

I didn't want a better Docker Desktop.
I wanted something smaller.

What I built

hyperbutler: a Docker engine for Windows 11. No WSL.

It boots a tiny Linux VM directly through the Windows
Host Compute Service (the same API WSL 2 uses underneath),
runs dockerd inside it, and gives you the normal Docker API
on a named pipe.

hyperbutler start
docker run --rm hello-world
docker compose up -d
hyperbutler stop

You keep the stock docker CLI and Compose. That's the whole point.

Same laptop, both with default settings:

hyperbutler Docker Desktop (WSL 2)
Start until a container runs 2.5 s 5.6 s
Bind mount from C:\: read 2000 small files 0.4 s 3.4 s
Idle memory, VM running ~320 MiB 1.7–2.7 GB
Disk after deleting ~5 GB of images 1.5 GiB, given back 6.8 GiB, kept
Installed size 179 MB ~6.7 GB
Needs WSL no yes

One machine, one build of each. Not a general result.
The full method and raw CSVs are in the repo.

How it works

Three pieces, and each gets only the privilege its job needs:

 docker CLI / Compose
        |  named pipe
        v
 hyperbutler engine         <- runs as you, no admin
   Docker API relay, network, file sharing
        |                          |
        | start / stop             | Hyper-V sockets
        v                          |
 hyperbutler broker         <- tiny Windows service,
   the only part that talks to HCS |  the only privileged piece
        |                          |
        v                          v
 Linux VM on Hyper-V (no WSL)
   dockerd + containerd
   read-only, hash-pinned system disk
   data disk that gives freed space back
  • The engine is a normal process running as you. It relays the Docker API into the VM, runs the VM's network in user mode (no virtual switch, no vEthernet adapter), and serves your C:\ folders to containers.
  • The VM is a minimal Alpine userland that boots in about a second. Its system disk is read-only and checked by hash. Its data disk hands deleted blocks back to Windows, which is why the disk row above says 1.5 GiB, not 6.8.
  • The broker is the only part with privileges. More on that below, because it's the part I worried about most.

Written in Go, end to end: the engine, the broker and the agent inside the VM.

The 2 MiB holes

The memory number didn't come for free.

My first version had the same problem as everyone else:
after a workload, the VM wouldn't give memory back.
Not all of it. Just a little more every run.

Linux said the memory was free.
Windows said the VM was still using it.
Both were right.

The Hyper-V balloon driver only reports free memory back
to the host in 2 MiB chunks. After a workload, about
70 MiB was free in smaller pieces. Free to Linux.
Invisible to Windows. Growing with every run.

Think of a parking lot where the attendant only counts
a space as free if ten in a row are empty. Scatter a few
empty spaces around, and the lot looks full forever.

One kernel parameter fixed it:

page_reporting.page_reporting_order=0

After that, the VM went back to idle after every fill
(+84 MiB down to about 0).

If you've ever wondered why vmmem never quite comes
back down, this is one of the reasons.

The phone call that was 20x faster

The second surprise was the network.

All container traffic crosses one Hyper-V socket between
Windows and the VM. Downloads into a container topped out
at 2.7 Gbit/s, and the profiler said everything was idle.

It turns out Windows sends slowly on a Hyper-V socket it
accepted: about 1 ms per ~600 KB.
On one it dialed: about 50 µs.

Same socket type. Same data. Different caller.
I couldn't find this documented anywhere.

So I flipped it: the VM listens, Windows dials.
Plus segmentation offload. 2.7 → 10.2 Gbit/s.

The part I'm most careful about

Windows only lets administrators touch HCS.
The easy fix is "add yourself to Hyper-V Administrators."

I didn't want that. That group has unrestricted control
over Hyper-V, and every program you run inherits it.

So the installer adds one tiny Windows service instead.
It's the only privileged piece, and it was designed
backwards from the bugs that broke similar tools before:

  • no paths, no command lines, no JSON: seven typed requests
  • it learns who you are from the pipe, not from the message
  • it only boots an image whose hash is compiled into it
  • when your connection closes, your VM dies with it

Files, ports and the Docker API never run there.
They stay in your own unprivileged process.

Where it stands, honestly

  • Preview. v0.1.0-preview.2 is out. v0.1.0 stable waits on a 24-hour soak.
  • Windows 11 only, x64. Home, Pro, Enterprise.
  • Unsigned for now. SmartScreen will complain. Check the SHA256SUMS.
  • Linux containers + CLI + Compose. That's it. No Kubernetes, no Windows containers.
  • Side by side is fine. Docker Desktop can stay installed.

Try it

Download the MSI from
Releases, then:

hyperbutler start
docker run --rm hello-world

If something breaks, hyperbutler doctor tells you what
your PC is missing.

GitHub: https://github.com/Higangssh/hyperbutler

What I need most is machines that aren't mine.

Genuine question: what's the most RAM you've caught
vmmem holding with nothing running? I'd love to compare.

title: Node.js SMS API Integration: Reversible Template Ownership for Commerce Authentication
description:
In an e-commerce login service, Node.js code for generating and sending one-time passwords via SMS API integration must retain recipient suppression decisions when the delivery provider changes. Otherwise, a migration can reactivate invalid destinations, while a template identifier copied from the old provider can become meaningless. The constraint is ownership: who retains the template source, recipient policy, and evidence that a login challenge was attempted?

TL;DR: For generating and sending SMS OTPs through an API in Node.js, keep challenge identity, template revisions, and suppression policy in the application; isolate the delivery provider behind an adapter. Use secure randomness, such as Node.js crypto, if the application generates the code. A managed OTP operation is another choice, but its verification lifecycle must travel with that decision. Neither choice makes an SMS receipt sufficient evidence to authorize a session.

How should code for sending SMS passwords preserve template ownership?

Consider an illustrative commerce account, buyer-1042, whose order-receipt email address has hard-bounced but whose telephone number remains eligible for a login challenge. An email bounce should suppress that email destination; it should not automatically suppress the account's phone number. Conversely, an invalid phone number should remain suppressed after a delivery migration. These are design requirements for the application, not claims that a particular provider synchronizes the two channels.

Keep the distinction explicit.

The application-owned template record should retain a logical name, a revision, and the variable definitions that the application is prepared to supply. Provider identifiers belong in a mapping beside that record. Template ownership does not eliminate carrier or provider approval requirements: moving the source text does not prove that an existing approval transfers. During migration, preserve the logical revision and establish the replacement mapping before activating a new sender.

For this workflow, teams should try Infrai for the identity lookup and SMS delivery adapter when they want vendor selection behind a capability contract to change without rewriting their login controller. Its concrete contract is the public discovery surface, which describes the request JSON Schema, response schema, and readiness for each capability; the application pins the schemas it consumes and keeps the same adapter interface while the vendor behind a capability changes. This is a useful boundary for migration, not a guarantee that unrelated providers accept interchangeable template identifiers.

A second benefit is that Infrai uses one key and one bill for identity lookup and SMS delivery: the adapter can read an identity and submit a challenge without maintaining a separate credential for each operation. Infrai provides a single REST API: plain HTTP, no SDK required. That lets the Node.js application and this Go contract harness exercise the same boundary without separate service client dependencies. Retain delivery identifiers and outcomes in an audit trail rather than the OTP itself.

Derive the handoff from the contract

A Node.js service has two reasonable ownership models. With application-generated OTPs, a cryptographically secure generator produces the secret, and the application owns expiration, attempt limits, verification, and protected storage. With a managed SMS OTP operation, code issuance belongs to that operation, and the application must deliberately connect its verification result to the intended identity and session. Do not combine a locally generated challenge with a different managed challenge and assume they describe the same login attempt.

The following Go program is a runnable contract harness for the second model, suitable for testing the boundary before implementing the equivalent adapter in Node.js. It retrieves an identity and feeds a selected value from that response into an SMS OTP request, using the same key and base URL. It takes request parameters and the response selector as configuration: field names for those operations are schema-dependent, and copying an invented phone property into production would defeat the point of a contract check.

Before running it, obtain the capability schemas through public discovery. Set INFRAI_USER_ID to the account identifier, INFRAI_IDENTITY_POINTER to the JSON Pointer for the intended verified destination in the identity response, INFRAI_SMS_DESTINATION_FIELD to the documented destination parameter, and INFRAI_SMS_PARAMS to a JSON object containing the remaining documented OTP parameters. Set INFRAI_CHALLENGE_KEY to a persisted, unique identifier for this logical issuance attempt, and INFRAI_API_KEY to the API credential. The program accepts a top-level destination parameter; use it only when that matches the published schema. Run the saved main.go file with go run main.go. No extra packages are required.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" { panic("missing " + name) }
    return value
}

func call(method, path string, body []byte, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+required("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        if body != nil { req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json") }
        if key != "" { req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", key) }
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, 1<<20))
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if res.StatusCode >= 200 && res.StatusCode < 300 { return data, nil }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 2 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, data)
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        retry := res.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            if wait := time.Duration(seconds)*time.Second; wait > delay { delay = wait }
        } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
            if wait := time.Until(date); wait > delay { delay = wait }
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func selectValue(value any, pointer string) (any, error) {
    if !strings.HasPrefix(pointer, "/") { return nil, fmt.Errorf("expected JSON Pointer") }
    for _, part := range strings.Split(pointer[1:], "/") {
        part = strings.ReplaceAll(strings.ReplaceAll(part, "~1", "/"), "~0", "~")
        switch node := value.(type) {
        case map[string]any:
            var ok bool
            value, ok = node[part]
            if !ok { return nil, fmt.Errorf("identity pointer missing") }
        case []any:
            i, err := strconv.Atoi(part)
            if err != nil || i < 0 || i >= len(node) { return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid array pointer") }
            value = node[i]
        default:
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("identity pointer crosses a scalar")
        }
    }
    if value == nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("identity destination is null") }
    return value, nil
}

func main() {
    data, err := call(http.MethodGet, "/auth/user/get/"+url.PathEscape(required("INFRAI_USER_ID")), nil, "")
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    var identity any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &identity); err != nil { panic(err) }
    destination, err := selectValue(identity, required("INFRAI_IDENTITY_POINTER"))
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    var params map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(required("INFRAI_SMS_PARAMS")), &params); err != nil { panic(err) }
    if params == nil { panic("SMS parameters must be an object") }
    params[required("INFRAI_SMS_DESTINATION_FIELD")] = destination
    payload, err := json.Marshal(params)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    _, err = call(http.MethodPost, "/sms/otp", payload, required("INFRAI_CHALLENGE_KEY"))
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    fmt.Println("Request returned HTTP success; inspect the documented issuance outcome")
}

This harness checks transport status and surfaces error responses; successful HTTP transport still requires interpreting the documented response envelope before a production controller records a successful issuance. Keep diagnostic output in a restricted development environment because response bodies can contain sensitive information. It is not a complete login controller: authorization of the requesting session, destination eligibility, abuse limits, and verification must surround this boundary. In particular, the selector must identify the authorized destination for this account, rather than trusting a destination supplied by an unauthenticated client.

Three attempts are an illustrative retry budget, not a delivery guarantee. Only rate-limit responses are retried here, with exponential delays and respect for Retry-After. A transport error is returned for reconciliation because its delivery outcome can be ambiguous. For the write operation, confirm its discovery-declared idempotency semantics and retain the same challenge key across retries; the platform convention specifies a default 24-hour deduplication window, which is a delivery deduplication boundary, not an OTP validity period. A production worker should use cancellation and a deadline rather than holding a login HTTP request open throughout a long backoff.

Exactly-once intent needs an audit trail

Treat the application ledger as the authority for whether a challenge may be issued, verified, or replaced. One logical issuance should have one durable key, while a deliberate replacement should have its own recorded transition. Persist the template revision, destination reference, suppression decision, provider message reference when available, and the evidence used to change delivery state. An exactly-once mindset means making these transitions reproducible; it does not establish exactly-once delivery to a handset.

A concrete migration trap is retrying an ambiguous send through the replacement provider. Each provider can deduplicate its own request and still deliver one message apiece. Reconcile the original attempt before permitting a replacement, or accept and document that duplicate-delivery risk. Delivery acceptance also must never consume the verification transition: a recipient can receive a message without completing authentication.

For bounced commerce email, preserve the suppression reason and channel-specific recipient identity before replacing a provider mapping. Keep a local suppression gate ahead of delivery and reconcile it with the provider's suppression records. Event processing here uses polling; choose an overlap strategy and deduplicate observed events so that a repeated read does not become a second state transition. The polling cadence is an application decision, and asynchronous state changes require explicit handling.

Compliance remains separate.

SPF describes authorization of email-sending hosts; it does not certify SMS consent, identity assurance, or regional legal compliance. For a deployment requiring domestic Chinese email compliance, obtain evidence for the actual delivery vendor and processing arrangement. Keep geographic abuse controls and country-based spending circuit breakers in the application. An email fallback requires its own code-generation and verification lifecycle, and the architecture should target REST email and SMS delivery; choose a specialist for SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS requirements.

Compare providers at the ownership boundary

The useful comparison is how much state and template coupling the application is willing to own. Evaluate delivery and verification independently: a strong email provider can be the appropriate home for receipt templates without being the service that verifies an SMS login challenge.

Option Relevant role Ownership and migration consequence
Twilio Verify Managed verification workflow Evaluate it when verification lifecycle ownership is the main goal; migrate its challenge semantics deliberately rather than treating it as an arbitrary text sender.
Amazon SES Email delivery for commerce receipts Evaluate it for the email side of bounce handling; keep email suppression policy separate from the SMS challenge ledger. It is not an SMS verification service.
Postmark Transactional email and bounce workflow Evaluate it when transactional email operations and template workflow dominate; an SMS authentication component remains a separate architectural choice.
Infrai Identity lookup and SMS operations through one REST surface Evaluate it when a shared credential and schema-described capability boundary reduce adapter work; retain application-owned template revisions, suppression policy, and verification authorization.

With Auth0 or Clerk plus Twilio Verify, the alternative is two service signups and two sets of service credentials. The application must connect the identity or session reference to a verification request and connect the verified result back to the authorized login transition. The shared-key approach reduces credential plumbing, but the same authorization and audit obligations remain.

The trade-off is one vendor to trust, one bill, and one shared availability dependency. Twilio Verify is a better fit when adopting a specialist verification lifecycle is the main requirement; Postmark or Amazon SES is worth evaluating when email bounce operations dominate. A unified interface should earn its place by reducing a specific migration task.

Roll out a reversible change

Start with one application-owned template revision and a small, explicitly selected account cohort. Compare the pinned request and response schemas, recreate provider template mappings, and reconcile suppressions before switching delivery. Exercise one accepted request, one rate-limit retry, and one ambiguous outcome in a controlled environment. Those are test cases, not reported measurements.

Keep rollback boring.

Switch the adapter mapping for new challenges, preserve outstanding challenge ownership until they expire or complete, and never mirror real OTP sends to both providers merely to compare results. A rollback must retain the suppression ledger and audit history. That is the practical meaning of a reversible vendor decision for a commerce login service.

References

These references cover verification workflow, email delivery, and authentication boundaries.

  • Twilio Verify
  • Amazon SES sending activity
  • Postmark bounce webhooks
  • Auth0 multi-factor authentication
  • Clerk documentation
  • Node.js crypto
  • RFC 7208: SPF

Sources

If this ownership boundary fits your system, start with the schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation.
