title: Parsing Run Times in a Calculator: mm:ss, Seconds, and the Ties That Cost Points
description:
Any calculator that scores a timed event has the same quiet problem: people type times in five different ways. One person types 14:30. Another types 870. A third types 14.30 and means fourteen minutes and thirty seconds. If your parser guesses wrong, the score is wrong, and the user usually cannot tell.

This post walks through a small, boring approach that has held up well for me when building fitness-test calculators: accept a few clearly defined formats, reject everything else with a helpful message, and compare times as whole seconds.

Decide what you accept, and write it down

Before writing code, list the formats you will accept. Mine are:

  • mm:ss such as 14:30 or 9:05
  • m:ss with a single-digit minute
  • h:mm:ss for very long events, such as 1:02:15
  • plain seconds such as 870, only when the field is labelled as seconds

Everything else is an error. That includes 14.30, 14,30, and 14m30s. It is tempting to be generous, but a decimal point in a time field is genuinely ambiguous, because it can mean 14.3 minutes or 14 minutes 30 seconds. When a wrong guess changes someone's score, asking again is the kinder choice.

A parser that returns seconds or an error 

// Returns total seconds, or null if the text is not a valid time.
export function parseTime(text) {
  const t = String(text).trim();

  // Plain seconds: digits only
  if (/^\d+$/.test(t)) return Number(t);

  // mm:ss or h:mm:ss
  const parts = t.split(":");
  if (parts.length < 2 || parts.length > 3) return null;
  if (!parts.every(p => /^\d+$/.test(p))) return null;

  const nums = parts.map(Number);
  const seconds = nums[nums.length - 1];
  const minutes = nums[nums.length - 2];
  const hours = nums.length === 3 ? nums[0] : 0;

  if (seconds > 59) return null;
  if (nums.length === 3 && minutes > 59) return null;

  return hours * 3600 + minutes * 60 + seconds;
}

Three details matter here.

Seconds above 59 are rejected. 14:75 is not "fifteen fifteen". It is a typo, and silently accepting it moves the score by a full minute.

Minutes are only capped when hours are present. 75:00 is a valid way to type a very slow walk, but 1:75:00 is not valid.

The function returns null, not zero. A zero would flow through the scoring code as a fantastic time. Returning null forces the caller to handle the failure.

Compare in integers, display in strings

Once everything is whole seconds, scoring becomes simple integer comparison against a table. This avoids a class of bugs where "9:05" < "10:00" is evaluated as a string comparison and returns the wrong answer, because "9" sorts after "1".

// Rows are sorted from fastest to slowest.
// maxSeconds is the slowest time that still earns the points.
export function scoreRun(seconds, table) {
  for (const row of table) {
    if (seconds <= row.maxSeconds) return row.points;
  }
  return 0;
}

Only convert back to mm:ss when you show a value to the user:

export function formatTime(totalSeconds) {
  const m = Math.floor(totalSeconds / 60);
  const s = totalSeconds % 60;
  return `${m}:${String(s).padStart(2, "0")}`;
}

Ties and boundaries

Scoring tables usually say something like "14:00 or faster". That means the boundary belongs to the better row. If the table's slowest time for 70 points is 14:00, then exactly 840 seconds should earn 70 points, and 841 seconds should earn the next row down.

I write boundary tests for every row, three of them each:

  1. One second faster than the boundary
  2. Exactly the boundary
  3. One second slower than the boundary 
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert";

test("boundary is inclusive", () => {
  const table = [
    { maxSeconds: 840, points: 70 },
    { maxSeconds: 900, points: 60 },
  ];
  assert.equal(scoreRun(839, table), 70);
  assert.equal(scoreRun(840, table), 70);
  assert.equal(scoreRun(841, table), 60);
});

The numbers above are illustrative. When you build a real calculator, copy the thresholds from the governing document for the test you are scoring, and cite that document on the page.

Be kind in the error messages

A good error message names the field, shows an example, and does not blame the user:

  • "Enter your run time as minutes and seconds, like 14:30."
  • "Seconds must be between 00 and 59."

I also keep the raw text in the field when validation fails. Clearing the input makes people retype everything, and they notice.

Input masks: use sparingly

Auto-inserting a colon as people type looks polished, but it breaks on mobile keyboards and with paste. If you add a mask, make sure pasting 14:30 and typing 1430 both work, and that backspace behaves. In my experience a plain text input with clear validation beats a clever mask.

Accessibility notes

  • Use a visible label, not placeholder text alone.
  • Set inputmode="numeric" only if you also accept the colon on that keyboard. Otherwise a numeric keypad can make mm:ss impossible to type on some phones.
  • Announce validation errors with aria-live="polite" so screen readers pick them up.

What I would test first

If you only have time for a few tests, write these:

  • parseTime("14:30") equals 870
  • parseTime("870") equals 870
  • parseTime("14:75") is null
  • parseTime("14.30") is null
  • parseTime("") is null
  • Every boundary in the table, three ways

I applied this approach in AFTPTCalc, a free set of military fitness test calculators I maintain: https://aftptcalc.com/ . The scoring tables there are kept as data and checked row by row against the published source documents.

Disclosure: I used an AI writing assistant to help draft and edit this post. The code and examples are my own and the numbers are illustrative.

title: Terraform State Locking, Drift Detection & Ephemeral Preview Environments
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our DMARC Record Checker, Generator & SPF/DKIM Validator, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

Master enterprise Terraform state locking with S3 and DynamoDB, automated infrastructure drift detection, OPA policy enforcement, and ephemeral CI preview environments.

Architectural Foundations of Remote State Management

Enterprise infrastructure automation requires deterministic state serialization. When scaling infrastructure-as-code across large engineering organizations, local state files fail to provide atomicity, leading to race conditions, state corruption, and silent overwrites. HostingPodium deploys a battle-tested pattern leveraging Amazon S3 for state persistence paired with native DynamoDB conditional writes for atomic state locking. This configuration guarantees that concurrent pipeline executions cannot mutate the state graph simultaneously.

To configure this resilient storage backend, initialization routines must enforce strict encryption, versioning, and state locking parameters. Below is the production-grade backend configuration utilized across our multi-region deployments:

terraform {
 backend "s3" {
 bucket = "hostingpodium-tf-state-prod"
 key = "core/networking/terraform.tfstate"
 region = "us-east-1"
 encrypt = true
 dynamodb_table = "hostingpodium-tf-locks"
 kms_key_id = "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/a1b2c3d4-e5f6"
 }
}

The underlying DynamoDB table requires a specific partition key definition. The Terraform client issues a PutItem API call utilizing conditional expressions to ensure the lock identifier (LockID) does not already exist. If a concurrent pipeline attempts an operation while the lock is active, the AWS SDK throws a TransactionConflictException, halting execution safely. Engineers must monitor lock acquisition timeouts and tune backoff intervals within their CI runners to prevent cascading pipeline failures during high-concurrency deployments.

State Serialization and Consistency Pitfalls

State locking prevents concurrent writes, but it does not resolve semantic divergence between the recorded state and actual cloud provider resources. Infrastructure drift occurs due to manual out-of-band modifications, cloud provider outages, or eventual consistency windows in REST APIs. Left unmitigated, drift invalidates the planning phase, introducing unpredictable apply behaviors and security posture degradation.

Automated Infrastructure Drift Detection Pipelines

Mitigating configuration drift requires proactive, scheduled detection mechanisms rather than reactive troubleshooting during deployment windows. At HostingPodium, we implement dedicated GitLab CI cron schedules that execute non-destructive planning cycles against production environments. These pipelines isolate discrepancies by parsing plan outputs and emitting structured telemetry to our observability stack.

The operational runbook for automated drift detection relies on executing terraform plan -detailed-exitcode. This command returns specific exit codes: 0 for empty diffs, 1 for operational errors, and 2 when non-empty changes are detected. By capturing exit code 2, our CI runners immediately dispatch alerts to PagerDuty and open high-priority tickets within Jira.

The following GitLab CI job snippet illustrates the drift detection pattern used in our platform engineering pipelines:

infrastructure_drift_detection:
 stage: validate
 image: hashicorp/terraform:1.7.5
 rules:
 - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"'
 script:
 - terraform init -input=false
 - terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -out=tfplan.binary
 allow_failure: true
 after_script:
 - |
 if [ $? -eq 2 ]; then
 echo "CRITICAL: Infrastructure drift detected in production state."
 curl -X POST -H 'Content-type: application/json' \
 --data '{"text":"Drift detected in production core network."}' \
 $SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL
 fi

Policy as Code Integration with OPA and TFSec

Executing dry-runs without policy guardrails exposes environments to misconfigurations, open security groups, and compliance violations. We enforce mandatory compliance checks before any human review or merge request approval occurs. This enforcement layer combines Open Policy Agent (OPA) and TFSec to evaluate the generated execution plan JSON.

Developers write declarative policies using Rego to govern resource constraints. For example, enforcing that all AWS S3 buckets mandate server-side encryption and block public access is validated locally and within the pipeline. If a plan violates these policies, the pipeline fails before reaching the apply stage.

The evaluation sequence proceeds as follows:

  • Terraform generates an execution plan binary.
  • The binary is converted to JSON via terraform show -json tfplan.binary > tfplan.json.
  • TFSec scans the JSON for known static analysis vulnerability signatures.
  • OPA evaluates the Rego policy bundle against the JSON state mutations.

Below is an example Rego policy enforcing explicit tagging standards across all compute instances:

package terraform.validation

default allow = false

allow {
 not missing_required_tags
}

missing_required_tags {
 resource := input.resource_changes[_]
 resource.type == "aws_instance"
 required := {"Environment", "Owner", "CostCenter"}
 provided := {tag | resource.change.after.tags[tag]}
 count(required - provided) > 0
}

Ephemeral Preview Environments in GitLab CI

Delivering rapid iteration cycles requires running isolated infrastructure instances per merge request. Ephemeral preview environments spin up dedicated subnets, container clusters, and databases on demand, allowing frontend and backend engineers to validate changes in a staging ecosystem before merging code to the main branch.

Implementing ephemeral preview environments introduces the challenge of dynamic resource naming and state key partitioning. Each merge request must utilize an isolated state file path to prevent collision. We derive the state key dynamically using the GitLab merge request IID.

The preview environment lifecycle is managed through pipeline lifecycle hooks:

Pipeline Stage Action Executed State Management Strategy
Merge Request Open terraform apply -auto-approve Dynamic Key: preview/mr-$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID/terraform.tfstate
Code Push / Update terraform apply -auto-approve Updates existing isolated state file
Merge Request Close terraform destroy -auto-approve Destroys resources and deletes remote state entry

To automate cleanup, merge request closure events trigger a teardown pipeline. This guarantees zero resource leakage and eliminates cloud spend accumulation from abandoned feature branches. The teardown job configuration utilizes environment variables to target the exact state key associated with the originating merge request.

Enterprise Security, Approvals, and Audit Compliance

Production deployments demand rigorous segregation of duties. Engineers write code and open merge requests, but automated CI pipelines require explicit manual approvals from senior systems architects before executing terraform apply against production environments.

GitLab CI provides protected environments and required approval rules that lock production deployment jobs. When a pipeline reaches the apply stage, it pauses execution and awaits human verification. The approver reviews the diff output, OPA policy evaluation reports, and TFSec scan summaries directly within the merge request interface.

Auditability is maintained by archiving all plan binary files and execution logs to immutable object storage with Object Lock enabled. This compliance trail satisfies SOC2 and ISO27001 requirements, mapping infrastructure changes directly to authenticated git commits and user identities.

By unifying remote state locking, automated drift detection, policy-as-code guardrails, and dynamic preview environments, platform engineering teams establish a scalable foundation for modern cloud operations. This architecture eliminates operational friction while enforcing strict reliability guarantees across all deployment targets.

Production Verification Checklist & Operational Runbook: Terraform State Locking, Drift Detection & Ephemeral Preview Environments in GitLab CI

Before promoting any Terraform State Locking, Drift Detection & Ephemeral Preview Environments in GitLab CI deployment into production traffic, senior platform and SRE teams validate deterministic failure handling, kernel resource ceilings, and observability telemetry across terraform s3 backend state locking, automated infrastructure drift detection, opa policy as code tfsec, gitlab ci plan apply approvals. Unlike lab prototypes, production clusters must survive upstream network partitions, sudden concurrency bursts, and rolling node maintenance without dropping in-flight client transactions.

Pre-Cutover Acceptance Gates

  • Synthetic Load & Tail-Latency Benchmarking: Execute sustained concurrency tests against staging endpoints for Terraform State Locking, Drift Detection & Ephemeral Preview Environments in GitLab CI, verifying that p95 and p99 response latencies remain within contractual SLO boundaries under 3x peak projected load.

  • Fault Injection & Chaos Verification: Simulate primary worker termination, AZ link degradation, and storage IOPS saturation to confirm automated failover and circuit-breaker recovery complete within sub-second thresholds.

  • Telemetry & Alert Routing Validation: Confirm Prometheus scrape targets, structured JSON log pipelines, and OpenTelemetry trace propagation emit actionable metrics for terraform-state-locking-drift-detection-gitlab-ci before live traffic cutover.

  • Immutable Rollback Readiness: Verify that declarative GitOps manifests, database migration snapshots, and previous container image digests can restore the prior production state in under 120 seconds.

# Production Readiness Verification Probe (terraform-state-locking-drift-detection-gitlab-ci)
systemctl is-active --quiet prometheus-node-exporter && echo "TELEMETRY_OK"
sysctl net.core.somaxconn net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse vm.swappiness
curl -fsSL -o /dev/null -w "http_code=%{http_code} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer}s
" http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz

By enforcing these pre-cutover verification gates alongside 99.99% network and compute uptime guaranteed by written SLA with 15-minute engineer response windows, engineering teams ensure Terraform State Locking, Drift Detection & Ephemeral Preview Environments in GitLab CI operates with predictable throughput, cryptographic isolation, and continuous audit compliance across ISO/IEC 27001 certified physical data centers, automated CIS benchmark compliance, and strict disaster recovery RPO < 15 min.

title: The Missing Feature Every AI Assistant Needs: Transparent Usage Indicators
description:
Overview:

This article examines why transparent usage indicators should be a fundamental part of modern AI assistants and digital services.

Keywords: Artificial intelligence (AI), AI assistants, user experience (UX), user interface (UI), usage limits, usage quotas, usage meters, usage indicators, usage tracking, rate limits, throttling, resource allocation, feature availability, usage transparency, product design, human-computer interaction (HCI), customer experience (CX), user expectations, digital trust, product usability, subscription services, and responsible AI design.

The Missing Feature Every AI Assistant Needs: Transparent Usage Indicators

Transparent usage indicators should be a standard part of every AI experience. Whether we're generating images, analyzing files, using advanced models, conducting research, or accessing other features, users deserve to know where they stand.

A little transparency goes a long way toward building trust in a product.

I think there are at least four things AI assistants need to do a much better job of:

  1. A visible usage meter: Show users how much of their available usage remains, rather than making them guess.

  2. Advance warnings: Notify users when they're approaching a usage limit, not just after they've exceeded it.

  3. A clear reset countdown: Tell users exactly when their usage will become available again, preferably before they run into a restriction.

  4. Feature-specific usage information: Clearly explain which limits apply to which features, so users understand what they can still do when one limit is reached.

AI tools should empower users, not leave them guessing about when their access might suddenly disappear.

Can you think of anything else that should be included? Let me know in the comments!

title: Testing accessibility in AG Grid: a grid-aware helper for Jest and Playwright
description:
Dense data grids are where accessibility problems like to hide. A table with thousands of rows, virtualized columns, inline buttons and color-coded values can look fine and still be hard to use with a keyboard or a screen reader.

General tools such as axe-core are great for checking a page. They are not built around grid-specific questions: Is the total row count exposed when rows are virtualized? Does the arrow key actually move focus one cell? Is a status shown only by a colored dot?

So I wrote a small helper, ag-grid-a11y-test, that adds grid-aware checks on top of the tools you already use. This post shows how to use it.

Status: early preview (alpha), not on npm yet. The code is public on GitHub and I am sharing it so people can try it and give feedback. The rules come from the ARIA grid pattern and AG Grid's commonly rendered markup. I have not yet validated them against every AG Grid version, so treat findings as prompts to investigate, not proof of conformance. Your feedback will decide what changes next.

What it checks

Structure (works in jsdom or a real browser):

  • The grid has a grid or treegrid role and an accessible name
  • aria-rowcount and aria-colcount are present and consistent with row and column indexes (important for virtualized grids)
  • Rows and cells have aria-rowindex and aria-colindex
  • Column headers have accessible names (this catches icon-only headers)
  • Sortable headers expose aria-sort

Patterns common in financial and data-heavy tables:

  • Icon-only buttons and checkboxes with no accessible name
  • Cells that show only an icon or colored element, with no text
  • Negative values shown by color alone (opt-in, you tell it your CSS class)
  • Abbreviated numbers like 1.2M (advisory)

Keyboard navigation (real browser, via Playwright):

  • Arrow keys move focus one cell and return to the start
  • Tab can eventually leave the grid (a warning if not, since a very large grid can cause false positives)

Each finding has a severity: error (very likely a real problem), warning (verify), or info (advisory).

Install

The package is not published to npm yet, so install it from the GitHub repo. Clone it and build a local package:

git clone https://github.com/Hitesh-Gharate/accessibility.git
cd accessibility
npm install
npm run build
npm pack   # creates ag-grid-a11y-test-0.1.0.tgz

Then install that file into your Angular project (adjust the path):

npm install --save-dev ../accessibility/ag-grid-a11y-test-0.1.0.tgz
# optional, for the axe-core adapter
npm install --save-dev axe-core

The examples below import from ag-grid-a11y-test, which is the package name inside that file.

Use it in an Angular unit test (Jest) 

import { TestBed } from '@angular/core/testing';
import { auditGrid, assertNoViolations, formatReport } from 'ag-grid-a11y-test';
import { PositionsGridComponent } from './positions-grid.component';

it('positions grid passes accessibility checks', async () => {
  const fixture = TestBed.createComponent(PositionsGridComponent);
  fixture.detectChanges();
  await fixture.whenStable();
  fixture.detectChanges();

  const result = auditGrid(fixture.nativeElement, {
    gridSelector: '.ag-root',
    negativeValueClasses: ['loss'], // your app's class for negative values (optional)
  });

  console.log(formatReport(result)); // everything, including warnings and info
  assertNoViolations(result);        // fails the test on errors only
});

jsdom has no layout engine, so AG Grid may not render rows unless virtualization is turned off in your test grid options. Check the AG Grid docs for the exact option names in your version.

A failing result reads like this (an example of the report format):

Grid accessibility audit: 1 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 info.
  [ERROR] grid-rowcount: The grid is missing a valid integer aria-rowcount (use -1 if the total is unknown).
      at div.ag-root
      help: Without it, virtualized grids do not tell assistive technology how many rows exist.

To be stricter, use assertNoViolations(result, { failOn: ['error', 'warning'] }). To silence a rule you have reviewed, use ignoreRules: ['abbreviated-number'].

Use it in a real browser (Playwright)

A real browser is the most reliable option, and it is the only way to test keyboard behavior.

import { test } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';
import { auditKeyboardNavigation, fromAxeResults, mergeResults, assertNoViolations } from 'ag-grid-a11y-test';

test('positions grid is accessible', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/positions');
  await page.waitForSelector('.ag-root [role=gridcell]');

  // 1. Structure and pattern checks, executed inside the page
  await page.addScriptTag({ path: require.resolve('ag-grid-a11y-test/browser') });
  const domResult = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const lib = (window as any).AgGridA11y;
    return lib.serialize(lib.auditGrid(document.body, { gridSelector: '.ag-root' }));
  });

  // 2. axe-core, scoped to the grid
  const axe = fromAxeResults(await new AxeBuilder({ page }).include('.ag-root').analyze());

  // 3. Keyboard navigation
  const keyboard = await auditKeyboardNavigation(page, { gridSelector: '.ag-root' });

  assertNoViolations(mergeResults(domResult, axe, keyboard));
});

All three sources are merged into one report, so axe findings and grid-specific findings appear together.

What it cannot do

Please read this part before relying on it:

  • Automated checks find only a subset of accessibility problems. You still need manual keyboard testing and screen reader testing (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver).
  • Several rules are heuristics and can produce false positives: visual-only-cell, abbreviated-number and kbd-tab-trap in particular.
  • Passing this audit does not mean WCAG conformance.
  • The test fixtures in the repo are hand-written approximations of AG Grid markup, not captured output from a specific release.

What is next

Planned work includes integration tests against real AG Grid output for each major version, Home/End and Page Up/Down navigation, cell-editing keyboard flow, a visible-focus check, and row selection and group expand/collapse state.

If you try it on your own grid and a rule misfires or misses something, please open an issue with your AG Grid version, the rule id, and the smallest HTML snippet that reproduces it (remove any confidential data first). Pull requests are welcome too.

  • GitHub: Hitesh-Gharate/accessibility
  • Issues and ideas: open an issue

Not affiliated with or endorsed by AG Grid. AG Grid is a trademark of its owner.

title: AI-written styles typecheck. Some still render nothing
description:
Box Kite's MCP server runs your AI assistant's props through the real styling engine mid-task, and names each value that would render nothing. Below: the mistakes it catches, a worked session with every answer pasted from the server, and what it can't know about your project. It documents @box-kite/mcp 2.2.12.

The examples here are screenshots; they run live in the original article.

The problem

Three props an assistant wrote for a settings row, handed to the server:

check_styles { "props": { "jc": "between", "fontSize": 4, "lineHeight": 1.5 } }

Some of these write no CSS, or CSS they almost certainly did not mean.

- ❌ `jc` does not accept "between" — no rule and no class name were written. It takes start, end, flex-start, flex-end, center, left, right, space-between, space-around, space-evenly, stretch, safe center, … (17 in all — call `get_props`).
- ⚠️ `fontSize` → `.fontSize-4{font-size:0.25rem}` — fontSize={4} is 4px text: fontSize's divider is 16, not the spacing scale's 4, so the number is the pixel size. For 16px write fontSize={16}.
- ⚠️ `lineHeight` → `.lineHeight-1\.5{line-height:1.5px}` — lineHeight={1.5} is a 1.5px line: lineHeight is direct pixels, not the unitless multiple CSS also takes. Write the pixels (lineHeight={24} is 24px), lineHeight="font-size" for a multiple of 1, or css={{ lineHeight: 1.5 }} for any other multiple.
…

And here is what those props draw:

The two numbers typecheck, the build passes, and nothing fails loudly. In development the engine logs a [box-kite] warning once the component renders. A production build says nothing.

Why a server and not a docs file

Box Kite's prop names look like the utility classes you already type, so an assistant brings its habits along. Three of them fail:

  • Each prop takes a closed set of values. Anything else writes no rule and no class name, so a typo can't become a broken declaration.
  • Numbers mean different units per prop. p={4} is 1rem (÷4), fontSize={14} is 14px (÷16), b={1} and lineHeight={24} are direct pixels.
  • HTML attributes go in props. A top-level href or data-* typechecks and is then dropped.

The package ships a rules file, but an agent reads it once, at the start of a task. It can ask a server at the moment the question comes up. No document can answer "does this exact value work?" either. The server bundles the engine of its own release, and check_styles runs each prop on a fresh engine of its own.

Install

Node 22 or newer. No key, no network. In Claude Code:

claude mcp add box-kite -- npx -y @box-kite/mcp

Cursor, VS Code, Codex, Zed and any other stdio client:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "box-kite": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@box-kite/mcp"] }
  }
}

On connect, the server also hands the model the library's four core facts (the dividers, no style, the element comes from the component, attributes in props), plus "before believing a value, call check_styles".

A settings panel, start to finish

1. Find the component.

search_docs { "query": "toggle switch" }

- **Switch** (component) — The APG switch: an on/off control drawn as a track and a thumb.
…

2. Read its contract. get_component returns props, parts, keyboard map and ARIA. Two rows change the code:

get_component { "name": "Switch", "include": ["props", "a11y"] }
…
| `label` | `React.ReactNode` | — | The text beside the switch, rendered inside a label that wraps the input. |
| `labelProps` | `BoxProps<'label'>` | — | Styles for the wrapping `<label>`: the row's layout, not the track's own appearance. |
…

So the row needs no Flex and Span of its own. The label names the switch and makes the whole row clickable.

3. The first draft, written from habit:

import Flex from '@box-kite/react/components/flex';
import { H2, Span } from '@box-kite/react/components/semantics';
import Switch from '@box-kite/react/components/switch';

export function NotificationSettings() {
  return (
    <Flex d="column" p={6} rounded="xl" shadow="md" bgColor="white" color="gray-900" borderColor="gray-150">
      <H2 fontSize={5} fontWeight="semibold">
        Notifications
      </H2>
      <Flex jc="between" ai="center" py={3} borderBottom={1} data-setting="email">
        <Span lineHeight={1.5}>Email me about new comments</Span>
        <Switch name="comments" defaultChecked />
      </Flex>
    </Flex>
  );
}

4. Check it, one check_styles call per element. The verdicts, summarized:

Draft Verdict Fix
rounded="xl" ❌ no prop of that name borderRadius={3}
borderColor="gray-150" ❌ not a palette step "gray-200"
fontSize={5} ⚠️ 5px text fontSize={20}
fontWeight="semibold" ❌ takes 100 to 900 fontWeight={600}
jc="between" ❌ not accepted jc="space-between"
borderBottom={1} ❌ no prop; suggests borderColor bb={1}
data-setting="email" ⚠️ HTML attribute, dropped props={{ 'data-setting': 'email' }}
lineHeight={1.5} ⚠️ a 1.5px line lineHeight={20}

One of those answers, as the agent sees it:

check_styles { "props": { "jc": "between", "ai": "center", "py": 3, "borderBottom": 1, "data-setting": "email" } }

Some of these write no CSS, or CSS they almost certainly did not mean.

- ❌ `jc` does not accept "between" — no rule and no class name were written. It takes start, end, flex-start, flex-end, center, left, right, space-between, space-around, space-evenly, stretch, safe center, … (17 in all — call `get_props`).
- ✅ `ai` → `.ai-center{align-items:center}`
- ✅ `py` → `.py-3{padding-block:0.75rem}`
- ❌ `borderBottom` no prop of that name. Try: `borderColor`.
- ⚠️ `data-setting` an HTML attribute, not a style prop. Written at the top level it typechecks and is then dropped — it goes in `props={{ "data-setting": … }}`.
…

TypeScript catches the ❌ rows, one error per element, so it takes a few rounds. It never catches the ⚠️ rows. Two fixes came from elsewhere: search_docs for "rounded corners" returns borderRadius first, but nothing led to bb. Once you know the name, get_props confirms that bb={1} writes border-bottom-width:1px.

5. The second draft. Every call now answers "Every prop writes CSS.":


import Flex from '@box-kite/react/components/flex';
import { H2 } from '@box-kite/react/components/semantics';
import Switch from '@box-kite/react/components/switch';

const row = {
  width: 'fit',
  d: 'row-reverse',
  jc: 'space-between',
  gap: 3,
  py: 3,
  bb: 1,
  borderColor: 'gray-200',
  fontSize: 14,
  lineHeight: 20,
} as const;

export function NotificationSettings() {
  return (
    <Flex d="column" p={6} borderRadius={3} shadow="md" bgColor="white" color="gray-900" b={1} borderColor="gray-200">
      <H2 fontSize={20} fontWeight={600} mb={2}>
        Notifications
      </H2>
      <Switch name="comments" defaultChecked label="Email me about new comments" labelProps={row} props={{ 'data-setting': 'email' }} />
      <Switch name="digest" label="Weekly digest" labelProps={row} props={{ 'data-setting': 'digest' }} />
    </Flex>
  );
}

d: 'row-reverse' puts the text first, because the label renders the input before it.

To skip the typing altogether, get_blocks has a ready settings panel: get_blocks { "name": "settings-form" } answers with npx shadcn@latest add https://www.box-kite.dev/r/settings-form.json.

Field notes from a production app

From a team running the server on a real app, each checked against the source.

Pin the server next to the library. Each release builds @box-kite/mcp from the same commit, at the same version, with that release's engine inlined. npx -y @box-kite/mcp runs whatever version npx resolves, not the one in your lockfile. So the team installed it as a dev dependency at the library's version (npm install -D @box-kite/mcp@2.2.12) and pointed the project's .mcp.json at its bin:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "box-kite": { "command": "npx", "args": ["box-kite-mcp"] }
  }
}

Your own tokens look wrong to it. The app's colours came from Box.extend():

check_styles { "props": { "bgColor": "ui-primary/20", "borderColor": "ui-primary" } }

Some of these write no CSS, or CSS they almost certainly did not mean.

- ❌ `bgColor` does not accept "ui-primary/20" — no rule and no class name were written. It takes currentColor, transparent, green, red, blue, gray, black, white, vi, slate-50, slate-100, slate-200, … (326 in all — call `get_props`).
…

The server can't load your configuration. It reads no config file, environment variable or argument, so read its rejection of your own token as "unknown", not "wrong". What still works:

  • Every other prop in the bag is judged on its own, so those verdicts stand.
  • Your app's engine knows your tokens. With Box.extend({ 'ui-primary': '#3355ff' }, {}, {}), bgColor="ui-primary/20" renders with no warning, and the typo ui-primry/20 gets a [box-kite] … wrote no CSS warning in development. For your own tokens, the console is the check.
  • A design that only recolours the components can use Box.palette(). Its accent-* and base-* tokens are built in, and check_styles accepts them.

get_blocks goes through the shadcn CLI. The server installs nothing. The CLI copies a block's files into your project as code you own. That suits starting a new page, not editing an existing one. It needs a components.json (setup on the registry page), and installed blocks don't update.

The honest limits

  • Values, not layouts. jc="space-between" passes whether or not the element is a flex container.
  • Not your project. Your Box.extend() tokens and props and your Box.components() designs are invisible to it.
  • Keyword search. "on/off toggle" didn't find Switch, and "border bottom" never found bb. Searching by the CSS property name works best.
  • Gaps in coverage. VisuallyHidden and the SVG elements have no get_component entry, and the tool says so.
  • It can't make the agent ask. Ask for check_styles in your prompt or your rules file.

Try it

Built for AI runs check_styles in your browser on the same engine, before you install anything. Then:

claude mcp add box-kite -- npx -y @box-kite/mcp

Originally published on box-kite.dev. Box Kite is open source under MIT — if it is useful to you, a star on GitHub helps other people find it. Install it with npm install @box-kite/react.

title: Building a Federated Copilot: Part 6, Ionic React, Fingerprints and Persistent Sessions
description:
After the browser produced a verified document-backed answer, the next requirement was a phone application that could demonstrate the integration without repeated deployment windows and several logins.

The agreed target was Ionic React on a Pixel 6 Pro running Android 17, delivered directly as an APK. The owner wanted a remembered 30-day enrollment, fingerprint unlock, a new chat on every entry and access to supported documents inside the existing approved SharePoint site.

This article describes both the implemented design and its current verification boundary. The native device-test build passed owner-observed fingerprint and background-clearing checks. The live v5 APK is installed and distributed, and the backend is deployed. Live mobile sign-in is still under investigation: tapping Sign in has not yet been observed to redirect successfully to PF. There is no claim of completed mobile Copilot acceptance.

Step 1: Separate the mobile project from the server

The Ionic application lives under apps/mobile with its own package and Android build. It does not add its UI dependencies to the dependency-light simulation.

apps/mobile/
  src/                 React UI, controller and fixed HTTPS transport
  tests/               Lifecycle, transport and proof tests
  android/             Capacitor application and native plugins
  scripts/             Local Android build helper
src/mobile/            Server-side enrollment and execution components

There are two explicit build modes. The default is a labelled offline device test. The live mode uses the fixed agent API and never returns a local success message when real services fail.

# Run from apps/mobile after installing its pinned dependencies.
npm test
$env:VITE_MOBILE_MODE = 'live'
npm run android:build

The repository helper checks the configured JDK and SDK, builds the web application, synchronizes Capacitor and runs native assembly, unit tests and lint. It signs with a dedicated local demo key outside source control. That key is a distribution credential, not a PF, Graph or agent credential.

Step 2: Make fingerprint unlock cryptographic

A JavaScript flag such as authenticated: true is insufficient evidence for resuming a delegated session. We implemented a small native boundary that creates an authentication-bound P-256 Android Keystore key and signs a challenge through a strong biometric CryptoObject operation.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Ionic app
    participant N as Native biometric plugin
    participant K as Android Keystore
    participant B as Mobile backend
    A->>B: Request nonce bound to enrolled device and request key
    B-->>A: Short-lived one-use challenge
    A->>N: Sign challenge for mobile presence
    N->>K: Initialize authentication-bound signature
    N->>N: Show strong fingerprint prompt
    K-->>N: Signature only after allowed key use
    N-->>A: Signature and public metadata
    A->>B: Complete challenge
    B->>B: Verify key, purpose, nonce, expiry and current authority
    B-->>A: Short-lived foreground session

Android's biometric cryptography guide and Keystore documentation explain the platform primitives. Our enrollment and server authorization protocol is additional application logic.

The native policy requires strong biometric authentication for key use, uses separate aliases and domains for local testing and live mobile presence, and checks reported hardware security level. It does not collect fingerprint images or templates.

The selected app policy has no device-PIN substitute for biometric session unlock. Fresh sign-in is the recovery direction, but the current enrollment path still checks that strong biometrics are available. Do not advertise a complete biometric-unavailable recovery experience until that case is designed and tested.

Step 3: Preserve the hardware-attestation boundary

The phone can report that its key is backed by TEE or StrongBox and can produce a valid signature. Without verified remote attestation, the backend has not independently proved that every remote client enforces the same biometric policy.

We therefore label server evidence as registered-device-key possession with hardware attestation UNVERIFIED. The owner approved this explicit PoC assurance limit. A signature does not justify inventing a stronger assurance claim.

The APK contains no PF confidential-client secret, agent signing key, Graph key, Direct Line secret or Vault bootstrap credential. Its durable local state is limited to device-bound references and the consent preference. The native key stays in Android Keystore.

Step 4: Keep first login in the system browser

We use backend-assisted PF login rather than embedding the provider page in the WebView. The backend owns the confidential client and provider tokens; the phone starts a device-bound transaction.

sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Mobile app
    participant B as Backend
    participant F as PF A
    participant W as System browser
    M->>M: Create device key and native pending claim secret
    M->>B: Device public key and hash of claim secret
    B->>F: PAR with PKCE, state, nonce and private_key_jwt
    B-->>M: Fixed-provider authorization URL
    M->>W: Open approved provider URL
    W->>F: Human sign-in
    F-->>B: Code at fixed backend callback
    B->>F: Redeem code with PKCE and signed client assertion
    B-->>W: One-use HTTPS App Link handoff
    W->>M: Return to verified app
    M->>B: Claim handoff with native transaction secret
    B-->>M: Enrollment challenge requiring device signature

The handoff is short-lived, one-use and bound to the initiating device and claim hash. It is not a provider access token in a deep link. Process loss or missing native custody requires a fresh sign-in.

The return path is an HTTPS Android App Link. The association binds the exact hostname, package ID and APK signing certificate. A successful HTTPS GET of assetlinks.json does not prove Android has verified the association on the installed phone. That is a separate device check documented in Android App Link verification.

Step 5: Separate enrollment, foreground proof and delegation

The 30-day period is an absolute device enrollment ceiling. It does not make a PF access token valid for 30 days and does not move the original PF auth_time forward.

Object Purpose and bound
Device enrollment Original verified human, device public key and absolute 30-day expiry
Resource consent Separate chat/document grants, revocable and bounded by enrollment
Foreground session Up to 15 minutes, replaced on fresh unlock
Request proof At most 60 seconds, one use, exact method/path/body
Mobile authority assertion Profile-specific short-lived issuance under current evidence
PF A and PF B tokens Narrower audience-specific child evidence
Provider access/refresh session Server-held Generic OAuth session, separate from delegated authority

A foreground session ID alone grants no access. The app creates an ephemeral request key and signs a JWT binding session, configured audience, exact route, body hash, validity and unique jti.

The server consumes replay identifiers durably and rejects a proof for access status when it is reused for chat or approval. Extra identity, scope and resource fields are not accepted in the chat body.

Current device, human, actor, organisation, grant and resource checks run again during execution. A successful fingerprint cannot override a revoked grant or suspended agent.

Step 6: Treat resumed interaction as its own evidence type

We did not reuse an expired OIDC login or switch the operation to autonomous mode to bypass recent-login checks.

The mobile authority preserves the original login issuer, subject, client audience and authentication time, and records current registered-device-key presence separately. It requires the current resource grant and an independently signed registered-agent assertion before issuing delegated evidence.

The original object returned by the trusted device authority is held in an instance-private registry. JSON copies cannot be reconstructed into authority. A future cross-process handoff would need authenticated transport and replay protection, not a serialized object accepted on trust.

Real Vault/PF container verification exercised the mobile chat and document chains with their own keys and clients. The current profile uses authority/PF A/PF B maximum lifetimes of 180, 120 and 60 seconds, while enforcing remaining parent validity. This is separate from the 60-minute provider user token used for Microsoft sign-in.

Step 7: Design foreground lifecycle as a state machine 

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Locked
    Locked --> Starting: Sign in
    Starting --> Browser: Fixed-provider launch
    Browser --> Completing: Bound App Link return
    Completing --> Consent: Manual review selected
    Completing --> Chat: Current approval available
    Consent --> Chat: Explicit approval
    Locked --> Completing: Fingerprint resume
    Chat --> Locked: Background or lock
    Starting --> Error: Native or network failure
    Completing --> Error: Verification failure
    Chat --> Error: Authority or service failure
    Error --> Starting: New explicit sign-in

Backgrounding clears the current messages, cancels owned work and discards foreground signing authority. A legitimate system-browser departure preserves only its pending native login transaction.

Generation counters prevent late callbacks, duplicate App Link events and delayed network results from opening a chat after cancellation or crossing into a new session. A failed credential-bearing operation does not automatically replay.

Every successful entry or unlock starts an empty chat. Multiple questions are supported while that foreground session is active. The app and backend do not write a durable transcript or document cache. Microsoft-hosted conversations and traces have their own retention and are not deleted merely because the app clears its screen.

Step 8: Separate default approval from identity

The visible default-on checkbox approves only the configured chat and document capabilities for the registered agent and existing site. It does not approve new sites, scopes or arbitrary model actions.

Turning it off requires manual resource approval. A revoked resource permission cannot be restored by a later automatic check under the same revoked binding. Unknown or unsaved preference state fails closed.

The device enrollment consent and resource delegation IDs remain different records. A phone that proves possession of its key is not automatically entitled to read documents.

Step 9: Refresh provider credentials without creating a replay loop

The dedicated mobile login client requires PAR, S256 PKCE and signed client authentication, with authorization code and rotating refresh grants. Provider credentials remain in CAS-protected Vault records.

Before refresh, the old refresh credential is persisted as spent. An uncertain response requires fresh sign-in. Fresh access tokens are checked for issuer, audience, subject, signature and lifetime before release to the server-side Copilot adapter.

The provider must have enough remaining validity for the foreground chat. The deployment profile requires 960 seconds before opening a 900-second conversation, keeping a margin instead of starting a session with a nearly expired token.

Compatibility of this new private-key-authenticated provider client with the already published Copilot Generic OAuth configuration remains a live gate. Sharing issuer and audience is not proof of that compatibility.

Step 10: Prepare persistent hosting without unlimited authority

The owner requested demos without 45-minute deployment windows or one-question limits. We introduced a separate persistent profile, preserving all spent historical allowances.

The approved standing ledger permits 100 attempted questions and 20 conversations, with additional fixed request ceilings. Counters persist across failures and restarts. This is a bounded operational allowance, not a currency meter or guaranteed enforcement of the existing $50 budget.

The private API binds only to loopback HTTPS. Exact Cloudflare routes expose the mobile API and App Link association; PF A gains only the reviewed PAR route. Workload certificate roles, durable usage, one-day audit retention and dependency supervision are separate from UI unlock.

An owned Windows startup task is prepared to run under the existing account without a stored password or operator Vault credential. It is intentionally not installed until owner phone acceptance succeeds. Docker, unsealed Vault, the host, network, Microsoft entitlements and certificate expiry remain real availability dependencies.

Step 11: Record deployment findings accurately

Actual deployment exposed several mismatches that the local contracts did not catch:

  1. PF rejected the new client because offline_access was absent from its global catalog. We obtained approval for that exact static scope addition and preserved every other setting.
  2. PF serialized scopes in a different order. We verified exact set equality, retained pending history and reconciled the successful write without repeating it.
  3. The new token manager could not publish a key ID already published by the original manager. We retained the approved signing key and disabled duplicate publication in the new manager.
  4. The service manifest omitted an APK certificate field. We completed metadata from the already approved certificate and APK pin while preserving the original packet.

The private runtime became ready, the five mobile clients were enabled and public configuration and association endpoints returned HTTP 200. Those facts still do not establish phone sign-in.

Step 12: Install, distribute and diagnose on the actual phone

The v5 candidate was installed in place using the same signing certificate. ADB inspection should target the owner's known device and must not automate fingerprint or password entry.

adb devices -l
adb -s <owner-device> install -r <verified-apk-path>
adb -s <owner-device> shell pm verify-app-links --re-verify <package-id>
adb -s <owner-device> shell pm get-app-links <package-id>

When the owner moved off-network, we added an exact, time-limited APK download route through the existing public hostname. The server serves one hash-pinned artifact, refuses other paths and query variants, and does not expose a build directory. We downloaded the public artifact and verified its hash before sharing the link.

The current reported failure is that the app stays at its sign-in button. A bounded backend initiation check returned a valid authorization destination at PF A, so the next investigation is on the native client path. We initially suspected the offline page policy, then inspected the built artifact and confirmed live mode already replaced it correctly. That suspicion was withdrawn; no unsupported fix is claimed.

This is why the next acceptance test requires the actual phone: observe the preparing state, native key operations, pending login, browser launch and verified return without logging URLs, handoff secrets or credentials.

Current outcome and production work

At the activation preparation checkpoint, 896 backend production tests, 372 simulation tests, 41 mobile tests and 12 native tests passed. Later isolated tests cover the scope amendment and APK route. These are historical checkpoint counts, not a claim that every subsequent change reran every suite.

The browser PoC has a verified document answer. Mobile core cryptography and lifecycle have local coverage, and the owner verified fingerprint behavior in the device-test build. Live mobile login, refresh, multi-turn document chat, Android association behavior and revoke/resume acceptance still need end-to-end verification.

Production work includes hardware-attestation policy, Microsoft trace protection, stronger workload isolation, rotation, reliable host recovery, billing enforcement, supported document formats and sustained availability testing. The useful result of this series is a set of explicit trust boundaries and measurable integration milestones, including the ones that remain open.

title: More of the Java API, and an Experiment With Unity Games
description:
This post is about code you already have: Java code you want to reuse, and, as an experiment, Unity games.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Much more of the Java class library

Codename One always shipped a subset of the Java API. That kept apps small, but it also meant that a library from Maven Central or a utility class from your server often needed edits before it compiled. That gap is now much smaller. 116 classes and interfaces joined the class library:

Package What arrived
java.util.function The functional interfaces: Function, BiFunction, Supplier, Predicate and the primitive variants
java.util.stream The core of the streams API
java.util Optional, StringJoiner, UUID, Base64, HexFormat, Spliterator and more
java.util.concurrent Executors, Future, Callable and friends
java.time LocalDate, LocalDateTime, Instant, Duration, ZonedDateTime and the rest of the basics
java.text SimpleDateFormat, DecimalFormat, MessageFormat, NumberFormat
java.io BufferedReader, BufferedWriter, PrintWriter, InputStreamReader and other readers and writers

String's regular expression methods now go through one engine on every platform, so split, matches and replaceAll behave the same on iOS, Android and the browser.

The obvious worry is size. I measured it, and the overhead is minor. ParparVM and the obfuscator strip whatever your app doesn't call, so an app that never touches streams doesn't carry them.

What hasn't changed: there's still no reflection and no class loading. That's a deliberate choice, and it's a big part of why Codename One apps are small, start fast and can be translated ahead of time. I talked about this, and about why Java is a better fit for this world than people assume, in my interview with Frank.

Running Unity 2D games: would this be useful?

This one is an experiment, and I'd like your opinion on it.

We wanted to learn what Unity does right for game developers and what parts of that we can offer. The best way to learn was to try running Unity games. So we built it: a Unity 2D project, with its C# scripts, scenes, prefabs, sprites and settings, copied into a Codename One project. The build compiles the C#, translates it to Java bytecode and runs it on every Codename One target, including iOS, Android, the browser and the desktop.

Fruitopia, a tile map platformer.
Asteroids.
Snake.
Sokoban.

Five open source games run with no change to their scripts or assets. No Unity player and no .NET runtime ship with the app. Scripts become ordinary classes, scenes become generated code, and a runtime that implements the UnityEngine API draws the game into a Codename One component. The .NET SDK is only needed on the machine that builds, and no Unity install or license is needed at all.

That component is the interesting part. The game sits on a Codename One form, so everything around it is regular Codename One: a toolbar, a side menu, a store, sign-in, in-app purchases, push, and ads. Java and the game's scripts call each other:

@Override
protected Form createForm(UnityGameView gameView) {
    Form form = new Form(new BorderLayout());
    Toolbar toolbar = new Toolbar();
    form.setToolbar(toolbar);
    form.setTitle("My Game");
    toolbar.addMaterialCommandToRightBar("", FontImage.MATERIAL_LEADERBOARD,
            e -> callInFrame(() -> services.ShowLeaderboard(score().get_Best())));
    form.add(BorderLayout.CENTER, gameView);
    return form;
}

The scope is 2D: sprites, tile maps, 2D physics, animation controllers, particles, the canvas interface and scripts. You can't take any Unity game and run it. Working on this improved the Codename One gaming API too, and those improvements are what Skirmish's arena uses.

So, would this be useful to you? A way to bring a small Unity game into an app that also needs real app features, or to keep a game going on targets you don't want to pay for? Tell me in the comments below. Your answer decides how far we take it. The Unity guide has the details.

A faster XML parser

XMLParser got a round of fixes and a lot faster. The fast path needs one call, because strict parsing follows the XML rules exactly where the classic parser was forgiving of HTML-like input:

XMLParser parser = new XMLParser();
parser.setStrict(true);
parser.setStripNamespacePrefixes(true); // w:p is reported as p
Element root = parser.parse(reader);

On the desktop JIT a benchmark document went from 13.8 ms to 8.3 ms. Interpreted, where it matters most on older devices, it went from 751 ms to 488 ms, and to 358 ms in strict mode. Mappers.fromXml uses it, so XML mapped to objects gets the same speedup.

Run the samples right in the docs

Every sample in the API docs now has a button that runs it, labeled Try It. Press it and the code compiles and runs in your browser, with the in-tree Java compiler and the ParparVM JavaScript translator. After the first load, a snippet takes about a second. Change the code and run it again.

Try It on the Button docs page.

Tomorrow: Native Menus, File Dialogs and 3D Models.

title: I mapped 66 JVM internal components into an interactive 2D/3D explorer (Open Source)
description:
Reading the Java Virtual Machine Specification (JVMS) or static block diagrams makes it difficult to see how the ClassLoader, Runtime Data Areas, JIT Compiler, and Garbage Collector operate together at runtime.

I built JVM Atlas, an interactive 2D and 3D architecture explorer that maps 66 internal components and traces code execution step-by-step from .java source down to native machine execution.

yakshjethva / jvm-inside-out

JVM

JVM Atlas

Explore the machine behind Java programs.

JVM Atlas is an independent, open-source, interactive atlas of the Java Virtual Machine: its runtime architecture, memory management and execution. Beginners start with one question, "What happens when you run a Java program?", and follow a single line of Java from source code to the processor. Experienced developers open the same machine as a technical plate and a 3D model where every part is a real component they can select, inspect, take apart and watch at work.

One machine. One source of truth. Multiple levels of understanding.

It is a static site. There is no backend, database, account, analytics or paid service, and after the first visit it keeps working offline.

  • Primary site: https://jvmatlas.vercel.app (Vercel, deployed by its GitHub integration)
  • Mirror: https://yakshjethva.github.io/jvm-inside-out/ (GitHub Pages, deployed from main)

What is in this release

See docs/LEARNING_EXPERIENCE.md for how the site teaches docs/3D_EXPERIENCE.md for…

View on GitHub

Live Interactive Tool: https://jvmatlas.vercel.app

What's inside:

  1. 66 Mapped Nodes: Full connectivity across ClassLoader subsystems, Heap/Metaspace, PC Registers, C1/C2 JIT compilers, and GC phases.
  2. 3 Depth Tiers: Switch any node between Simple, Developer, and Deep Dive (HotSpot implementation specifics).
  3. Execution Walkthroughs: Guided state-by-state flows showing how bytecode verification, interpreter loops, and JIT tiering actually run.

title: Amazon Connect Customer lets agents pause and resume emails
description:
Amazon Connect Customer lets agents pause emails while waiting for information or approvals, freeing them to handle higher-priority contacts and resume their work later. For example, an agent waiting for a supervisor to approve a refund can pause the email and take an incoming call. Supervisors can monitor paused emails and pause duration in real time, and use flows to automatically resume or transfer emails that remain paused beyond a configured threshold.

Amazon Connect Customer email pause and resume is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London) regions. To learn more and get started, please refer to the help documentation or visit the Amazon Connect Customer website.

title: Designing for Cognitive Accessibility & Neurodiversity
description:
• Make Content Understandable with Plain Language and Structure
  • Design Patterns That Reduce Cognitive Load and Increase Predictability
  • Progressive Disclosure That Respects Working Memory and Accessibility
  • Testing with Neurodiverse Users and Meaningful Success Metrics
  • Practical Application: Checklists, Protocols, and Code Patterns
  • Sources

Cognitive accessibility is product quality: when people with attention, memory, language, or learning differences can’t use your features, you lose customers, increase support volume, and build brittle software. Treating cognitive accessibility as an engineering and content discipline — not a one-off UX tweak — yields measurable reductions in errors and abandonment.

The product symptoms are familiar: high drop-off during multi-step tasks, support tickets for "I can't find X," low comprehension scores on content pages, and failed onboarding metrics on top of accessibility compliance gaps. These are not abstract UX problems — they represent real friction for people with ADHD, dyslexia, dementia, or other cognitive differences, and they map directly to the WCAG objectives around readable, predictable, and navigable content.

Make Content Understandable with Plain Language and Structure

Clear content is the fastest, highest-leverage accessibility win you can ship.

  • Use plain language as your baseline: short sentences, active voice, and one idea per sentence. The federal Plain Writing Act and government content teams codify this because it improves comprehension for broad audiences.
  • Structure for scanning: front-load headings, provide a one-sentence summary at the top, use bulleted steps for actions, and add a short tl;dr or checklist for long pages. WebAIM and other accessibility practitioners recommend these patterns to help readers with limited working memory or attention regulation.
  • Replace jargon with defined terms; expand acronyms on first use. Wherever you must keep technical language, provide a short definition or an optional “learn more” footnote that doesn’t interrupt the main path.

Practical copy example (before → after):

Before (dense, long) After (plain, scannable)
If the asynchronous provisioning process fails due to an improperly configured token, the operation may abort and require re-initiation. If provisioning fails because the token is invalid, the operation will stop. Fix the token and try again.
Complex transaction histories are stored in a paginated view under the Reports tab. See Transaction history → Reports. The list is paginated; use filters to narrow results.

Why this matters: Readable content reduces extraneous cognitive load (the processing your interface forces on people that does not help them reach their goal). Short, scannable content reduces time-to-decision and decreases support calls.

Design Patterns That Reduce Cognitive Load and Increase Predictability

Design choices are cognitive choices. Make them predictable and minimal.

  • Chunk information: group related controls and content so users can rely on short-term memory less. Use clear labels and consistent placement. This reduces the need to hold context in memory.
  • Minimize choices where possible — apply defaults and progressive defaults for advanced options. Hick’s law shows selection time grows with the number of choices; fewer visible options = faster decisions.
  • Make interactions consistent across the product: identical icons, labels, and flows build mental models so users learn once and reuse that model. WCAG explicitly calls out predictability and readable content as success criteria.
  • Avoid disruptive interactions: popovers, unexpected modals, and auto-playing visuals increase extraneous load — prefer inline, contextual feedback instead.

Table: patterns vs cognitive benefit

Pattern Cognitive problem it addresses Implementation note
Chunking (clear headings & shorter lists) Overwhelm / scanning difficulty Headings = navigation anchors; keep 3–5 items per list
Defaults & smart suggestions Decision paralysis Pre-fill or suggest values based on past data
Visible focus + large targets Motor & attention friction 44x44px targets, strong focus outlines, outline-offset for clarity
Inline validation with helpful error copy Memory + recovery Show exactly which field failed and why; don't only show an error code

A contrarian point: displaying every feature on the first screen can feel honest, but it usually weaponizes cognitive load. Instead, design a fast-path for the top 80% of goals and surface advanced controls when they become relevant.

Progressive Disclosure That Respects Working Memory and Accessibility

Progressive disclosure works when it respects discoverability and assistive tech.

  • Principle: show only what users need now; keep the rest discoverable and reachable. The W3C supplemental cognitive guidance recommends design patterns (including progressive disclosure) as a way to make content usable.
  • Use semantic HTML first: the native <details> / <summary> pair provides a keyboard and screen-reader-friendly disclosure pattern with minimal JavaScript. MDN documents the element behavior and keyboard affordances. details has built-in toggle semantics and emits a toggle event you can hook for analytics or lazy loading.

Example: native, accessible disclosure (preferred)

<details>
  <summary>Why your payment failed</summary>
  <p>Common reasons: expired card, insufficient funds, or a blocked merchant. Try these steps:</p>
  <ol>
    <li>Check your card expiry date.</li>
    <li>Contact your bank to confirm the transaction.</li>
  </ol>
</details>

When you need custom accordion behavior (visual design or grouping), prefer a pattern built from semantic controls (button), with explicit aria state and keyboard handling. Minimal accessible accordion pattern:

<!-- Accordion header -->
<button aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="panel-1" id="accordion-1">
  More details
</button>

<!-- Associated region -->
<div id="panel-1" role="region" aria-labelledby="accordion-1" hidden>
  <p>Details shown here.</p>
</div>

// Minimal toggle handler
document.querySelectorAll('button[aria-controls]').forEach(btn => {
  btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
    const region = document.getElementById(btn.getAttribute('aria-controls'));
    const expanded = btn.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true';
    btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(!expanded));
    if (!expanded) region.removeAttribute('hidden'); else region.setAttribute('hidden', '');
  });
});

Key rules for progressive disclosure:

  • Ensure keyboard users can reach and toggle every control (no hover-only reveals). Keyboard-first equals accessibility-first.
  • Make hidden content reachable in the accessibility tree (role="region" + aria-labelledby) and avoid removing content from DOM if it should be discovered by assistive tech.
  • Avoid hiding critical warnings or error states behind a disclosure. If something is required for task success, surface it.

Testing with Neurodiverse Users and Meaningful Success Metrics

Testing is the only reliable way to validate cognitive accessibility assumptions.

Recruitment and representation:

  • Recruit participants who identify across the neurodiversity spectrum (ADHD, autism, dyslexia, intellectual disabilities, age-related cognitive decline). Specialist recruiters (e.g., AbilityNet, Fable) or local advocacy organizations accelerate finding participants and advising on accommodations.
  • Compensate fairly and schedule sessions with flexibility, breaks, and the option for alternative communication formats. AbilityNet documentation covers practical planning and recruitment approaches for inclusive testing.

Study design and protocol:

  1. Define clear, goal-based tasks that match real-world use. Convert goals into scenarios, not abstract test steps.
  2. Use moderated sessions where you need qualitative insight or have accessibility-specific probes. Observe, record, and collect think-aloud notes, but avoid interrupting the user during task attempts.
  3. Combine metrics: task success rate, time-on-task, error rate, and subjective workload (NASA‑TLX). NASA‑TLX provides a validated measure of perceived mental workload across six dimensions and is widely used in HCI studies.

Quantitative and qualitative metrics that matter:

  • Task success (complete / partial / fail) — primary signal for functional accessibility.
  • Time-on-task (median + IQR) — watch for long tails where neurodiverse participants may need more time.
  • Error taxonomies (where they stalled and why).
  • NASA‑TLX or an abbreviated workload measure to quantify perceived cognitive effort.
  • Comprehension checks: 2–3 short questions after a content page to measure retention.
  • Support funnel changes: reduction in "how do I..." tickets after fixes.

Sample size guidance: iterative testing of 4–6 users per round uncovers major issues quickly; for accessibility and edge cases, run multiple rounds with different neurodiverse profiles. Jakob Nielsen’s discount-usability guidance remains useful for iterative discovery, but accessibility testing benefits from slightly broader representation across conditions than a single generic usability cohort.

Practical Application: Checklists, Protocols, and Code Patterns

Shipable, prioritized actions you can run in the next sprint.

Content clarity checklist (low friction)

  • Use a one-line summary at the top of every page. Bold the action word.
  • Keep sentences under 20 words where possible. Flesch-Kincaid grade 7–9 target for general audiences.
  • Headings: H1 for page purpose, H2 for top sections, H3 for step-level subheads. Each heading should be usable as a quick summary.
  • Replace “click here” links with descriptive anchors.

UI / interaction checklist

  • Keyboard: all interactive controls reachable and operable without tabindex hacks. (Remember: summary in <details> is inherently focusable.)
  • Focus visible and high contrast (2:1 visible offset).
  • Reduce simultaneity: avoid auto‑playing media; allow users to pause/stop.
  • Error messaging: show what happened, why, and the next actionable step.

Progressive disclosure patterns (three-tier)

  1. Summary (one line) — for scan & quick decisions (use <summary> or button).
  2. Inline expand — for contextual help and short details (use accessible accordion).
  3. Off-page deep dive — link to full documentation or printable guide when the user wants complete instructions.

Testing protocol (30–60 minute moderated session)

  1. Pre-study: consent, an intake form with accessibility preferences, and baseline context.
  2. Warm-up (5 min): an easy task to orient the participant.
  3. Core tasks (20–30 min): 3–5 goal-directed tasks that reflect realistic scenarios. Collect task success, time, and errors.
  4. Subjective measures: NASA‑TLX (short mode) + Single Ease Question (SEQ) for each task.
  5. Debrief (5–10 min): open-ended feedback, what confused them, and what helped.

Quick engineering fixes to prioritize (48–72 hours)

  • Add meaningful heading summaries and a short page TL;DR.
  • Replace ambiguous icons with labelled buttons.
  • Convert long blocks of text to bulleted steps.
  • Implement simple details/summary where extra explanation is optional.

Code pattern to include in your component library (accordion example shown earlier) — standardize aria-expanded, aria-controls, role="region", and keyboard handling. Add unit tests that assert aria-expanded toggles and that the region becomes visible and focusable.

Important: Put cognitive accessibility checks into your Definition of Done. Automated checks (axe, Lighthouse) catch many issues, but only real user testing with neurodiverse participants reveals the cognitive friction your metrics will miss.

Treat the practices above as instruments, not one-time fixes: measure, iterate, and prioritize by impact on task success and workload scores.

Sources

Cognitive Accessibility at W3C WAI - Definitions, WCAG connections (Readable, Predictable, Navigable), and the COGA task force guidance on design patterns and supplemental guidance.

PlainLanguage.gov - Federal plain language guidance and checklist for writing clear, usable content; practical rules that reduce misunderstanding.

WebAIM — Writing Clearly and Simply - Practical, web-oriented plain-language techniques focused on accessibility and cognitive readability.

MDN Web Docs —

element - Browser behavior, keyboard support, and examples for the native disclosure widget.

AbilityNet — A Step-by-Step Guide to User Testing - Practical guidance for recruiting, running, and reporting inclusive user tests with people with disabilities.

NASA Task Load Index (NASA‑TLX) - Overview of the validated subjective workload instrument used to quantify perceived cognitive workload.

Nielsen Norman Group — Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users - Rationale for small, iterative usability studies and how to run efficient test cycles.

GOV.UK — Writing for GOV.UK (Content Design) - Strong, research-backed advice on front-loading content, scannability, and plain English practices used at scale.

Microsoft Accessibility — Inclusive Design resources - Inclusive design training, toolkits, and research that highlight cognition and mental-health considerations in product design.

title: Play Minecraft in Rust - Open Source Engine
description:
TL;DR: Horizon implements Minecraft Java Edition from scratch in Rust, sitting on top of modern graphics APIs like Vulkan and Wgpu while relying on a custom launcher to prepare game assets from an existing user installation.
Best for: Rust developers and Minecraft enthusiasts wanting native performance and programmatic agent control.
Repository snapshot: ⭐ 6 226 stars · 🍴 854 forks · Rust · MIT
Daily picks: Follow GitHub Open Source on Telegram

What it is

Horizon is an independent implementation of Minecraft Java Edition written from scratch in Rust. It bypasses the Java virtual machine to deliver native performance, advanced rendering features, and a programmatic control interface.

How it works

The engine relies on modern graphics stacks like Vulkan and Wgpu for rendering. It uses a custom launcher to prepare game assets from an existing user installation and employs 281 differential harnesses to check parity against the vanilla game.

Key features

  • Run vanilla world generation, mobs, redstone, and commands without Java
  • Render distant terrain up to 1024 chunks using modern graphics APIs
  • Control the game programmatically or over control interfaces using horizon-ctl
  • Import CurseForge and Modrinth modpacks containing content and data packs
  • Manage and host servers locally or on a VPS without Java dependencies

Getting started

Clone the repository from GitHub, ensure you have a Rust toolchain installed, and use the Horizon launcher to prepare your game assets from an existing legitimate installation.

When not to use it

Do not use this if you expect complete zero-bug compatibility today, as the project is still tracking hundreds of open parity gaps with the original Java release.
